The granting of the post of gatekeeper to Śiva, named Mahākāra, by Nandin and the Vaiśya; the majesty of devotion to Śiva. (Chapter 2: When Śaunaka and others raised questions regarding the conduct of Raṅkara in abandoning his wife to engage in the worship of the Liṅga, Lomaśa, the Sūta, related the account of that engagement in the worship of the Liṅga.

There, in the Dāruvana forest, all the wives of the sages were infatuated upon beholding the beautiful, naked form of Śaṅkara as he wandered about for alms; they followed him out of passion. Seeing their hermitage become empty due to their following him, those sages, being distressed, uttered a curse which caused the linga of Śiva to fall. With that fallen linga, the entire Brahmāṇḍa, including all moving and non-moving beings, remained pervaded by a state of universal trembling. At this, the gods were struck with fear.

The life-breaths of Viṣṇu and Brahmā were [seized] by Surā and the others; at the request of the gods, Viṣṇu went to the peak [of Meru] to investigate this, and Brahmā also went to the sky. On Mount Meru, they saw the cow Surabhī; she gave him a *ketakī* flower. At the request of Brahmā, Surabhī and the *ketakī* both falsely testified, "Brahmā was seen on the peak of the Linga. After the promise of a curse was made, Brahmā turned back and, upon his return to his original position, stood before the gods.

Following the false testimony offered by Surabhī and Ketakī—namely, their boastful and false statement that "I saw the top of the *liṅga*," and Viṣṇu’s subsequent agreement with them—the Lord, having turned toward Viṣṇu, spoke these truthful words: "By me, the end of the *liṅga* was not seen. Upon hearing the false speech of Surabhī and Ketakī, the enraged Blessed One, with his face turned away from Surabhī due to her impurity and Ketakī’s unworthiness of worship, [pronounced a curse].

The bestowal of wealth upon the Brahmins, such as Bhṛgu and others, who were intent on poison because of their impurity regarding Brahman—due to their participation in the use of whips and the like, and their approval of that act—as well as the seeking of refuge with the Liṅga by Brahmā and the others who were delighted by the voice from the sky; thus [it is described].

Oṃ. The praise of Śiva by Brahmā and the gods; the issuing of a command by Śiva—satisfied by the praise offered by Brahmā and the others—to Viṣṇu for the purpose of consuming [the offering]; the hymn of praise to Viṣṇu by Brahmā and the others; the assumption of the form of the *śivaliṅga* by Viṣṇu through his manifestation as the *piṇḍī*; then, the worship of the *śivaliṅga* by Vīrabhadra, acting under the direction of Śiva, together with Brahmā and the other gods; and finally, the installation of *liṅgas* bearing various names in many locations by Śaṃkara, along with numerous deities and others.

In various places, there is the installation of the *vīrabhadra* [liṅga] following the worship of the *liṅga*; the origin of the lineage of preceptors (*guru-paramparā*) beginning with Vīrabhadra and ending with Nandin as the first teacher who praised the greatness of the *liṅga*, and ending with Skanda as the teacher who worshipped the *liṅga*; and thereafter, the continuous succession of the lineage of preceptors who worship the *liṅga*. [It also contains] the majesty of devotion to Śiva, including the narration of the account of how a female moth (*pataṅgī*) attained the status of a daughter of King Kārtavīrya through the merit of cleansing a temple of Śiva.

The dialogue between King Udayana of Kāśī and the daughter of the king named Sandhyā; in connection with the greatness of devotion to Śiva, the account of how a thief who was stealing the bell from the temple of Śiva attained the world of Śiva; a description of how the entire universe consists of devotion to Śiva; and therein, the manner in which men are joined with the *liṅga*.

The state of being a mass [of the elements] having been exhausted; the description of the non-difference between Śiva and Viṣṇu; the description of the worship of the Liṅga made of jewels and other materials by Brahmā and others; the description of how the Daityas such as Prahlāda, Bali, and Bāṇa were devoted to the worship of the divine Liṅga; the effort made by the gods—whose senses were overcome by the unbearable majesty and power of Rāvaṇa—to propitiate Śiva through the recitation of hymns; and in that context, the incidental description by Nandin of the reason for his own monkey-like face resulting from a curse by Rāvaṇa.
"Nandini, you shall meet your death at the hand of someone who has come together with Nandi and possesses a monkey-faced appearance"; thus was the prophecy given to Rāvaṇa.

Then, having gone to Mount Nandiprṣṭha with all the gods, [Nandin] lowered the pedestal of the *liṅga*. The descent of Viṣṇu as Rāma for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa; the gods' seeking of refuge with the Blessed Viṣṇu; the description of the partial incarnations (*aṃśāvatāra*) of all the gods among the monkeys by the command of Viṣṇu; the incarnation of Rāma; the slaying of Rāvaṇa by Rāma; the attainment of union (*sāyujya*) with Śiva by Rāvaṇa; and the greatness of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga—these are the subjects concerning the auspiciousness of the *daṇḍaka* forest.

Due to the humiliation of Bali, there was the downfall of Śakra’s kingdom; defeated by Bali, Śakra went with Brahmā and the gods to the realm of Viṣṇu and made a request to Viṣṇu; at the instruction of Viṣṇu, Śakra and the others went to the sacrifice of Bali.

The honoring of Śakra, who had come for refuge, by Indra in accordance with the words of Nārada; the praise of the method for churning the ocean as requested by Indra, who desired jewels; then the departure of the gods and demons toward Mount Mandara for the purpose of churning the ocean; the bringing of Mount Mandara with great effort through the assistance of Viṣṇu, and the appointment of Vāsuki as the churning rope; the commencement of the churning of the ocean by the gods and demons; and the emergence from the ocean being churned of the [divine] horse Uccaiḥśravas.

Regarding the origin [of the world]: even though Nārada had stated that Viṣṇu should be remembered in times of distress, the gods, disregarding his words and desiring to obtain the nectar for themselves, proceeded with the churning of the ocean; therein is described the burning of the entire Brahmāṇḍa, including its eight enclosures extending as far as Veṅkaṭa, by the fire of the breath of the Prabhava serpent. [...]

The manifestation of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) from Sadāśiva—who is pleased by the prayers of the sages seeking the cause of the universe after their efforts to perceive it through the application of various means such as meditation, mantras, and rituals; therein, incidentally, the narration of the birth of the son named Heramba as desired by Saunaka and others; therein, the account of the birth of Heramba from the Supreme Power; the performance of a hymn of praise to Śrī Śiva joined with Śakti by that wise Gaṇeśa; and [the appearance] of Śiva in the form of a Liṅga, being gratified by the hymn of Heramba.

The consumption of the *kālakūṭa* poison; thereafter, the construction of a linga by all the gods and divine sages; the manifestation of Śiva, who was pleased by that hymn of praise; and the instruction that after the daily consumption of food, one should worship Gaṇeśa at the commencement of any undertaking.

A description of the ritual for the worship of Gaṇerā as proclaimed by Śiva; following Śiva’s disappearance, the churning of the ocean by the gods and others; thereafter, the birth of the Moon; the account of Garabha as told in the *Suhūta* regarding the cause of the Moon’s emergence from the ocean; the production of the jewels, beginning with Kāmadhenu, from the ocean being churned, and the manifestation of Lakṣmī; and the selection of Viṣṇu by Lakṣmī.

Furthermore, during the churning of the ocean for nectar (*amṛta*), both Dhanvantari holding the vessel of ambrosia and the mountain Mandara were brought forth; then, after the Daityas had seized the jar of nectar, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of Mohinī at the request of the gods, deceived the Daityas and gave the nectar to the deities. While Rāhu was seated in the row of the gods, he was pointed out by the Sun and the Moon, and his head was severed. As for the Daityas who had begun to drink the nectar— [The text continues with the subsequent events.]

Description of the manifestation of wrath. ... [The contents of] the sixth chapter of the Vudhalanga-kuṭhaṭhapapṛmadhyāyāḥ: Description of the battle between the foremost gods and the Daityas; in that battle, the covering of his own head with a garland by Rāṅkaraṇa; a description of the Śiva-dharma, such as devotion to Śiva and the wearing of the tripuṇḍra and rudrākṣa beads, arising from that connection; during the conflict between the gods and the Daityas, when the gods were defeated by Kālanemi, their praise of Viṣṇu; and Viṣṇu’s [preparation] for battle against Kālanemi.

Ka, Ā; the disappearance of Viṣṇu after he had slain Kālanemi; then, when Śakra began the slaughter of those who had fallen in fear due to his unjust conduct, Nārada’s intervention to stop it; thereafter, the victory of Indra, preceded by his departure for Amarāvatī accompanied by the celestial army, and the description of his consecration; the flight of the remaining defeated Daityas toward the preceptor Śukra; and the performance of penance by Śukra for the sake of achieving victory for the Daityas.

When Bṛhaspati was insulted and absent, Śakra appointed Viśvarūpa, the son of Viśvakarman, as his domestic priest. Seeing that the Daityas were offering oblations to the gods in the form of Viśvarūpa—who had assumed all forms—Śakra struck him with his thunderbolt, thereby severing his heads. Afflicted by the sin of Brahmin-slaughter (*brahmahatyā*) resulting from that act, Śakra submerged himself in the waters. Thereupon, the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) approached their preceptor and reported the account of the Brahmin-slaughter committed by Śakra. Then...

The consultation regarding the installation of Nahuṣa in Indra’s place at the word of Nārada; Śacī’s departure for the inner apartments out of grief upon hearing that Nahuṣa had been installed in Indra’s place; the approval of all the gods for Nahuṣa’s ascension to the rank of Indra; the consecration of Nahuṣa as Indra; and Nahuṣa’s dispatching of Vāsava (Indra) into the presence of Indrāṇī out of lustful desire for her, and his sending Saṃdeśahara (the messenger) to Indrāṇī with instructions to bring her by means of a vehicle, [and] by Nahuṣa...

The employment of Agastya and other Brahmins to carry his palanquin; then, the granting of a curse by the enraged Agastya that Nahuṣa would become a python; thereafter, after Nahuṣa fell from heaven due to his transformation into a python, Yayāti was established in Indra’s place; and how, through the proclamation of his own merits, he fell downward upon the exhaustion of those merits; and then, the gods all fell into anxiety.

For the purpose of bringing Indra back, Śacī issued commands to Bṛhaspati and others; Bṛhaspati, having been insulted by his own [disciples], pronounced a curse. Out of fear of Śacī’s curse, the terrified Bṛhaspati went to the shore of a lake to bring Indra back. While Indra was being summoned, Hyahtyā, who resided on the shore of that lake, made a request to the gods for her own dwelling place. In response, he cast four parts of her into the earth, trees, water, and women, granting them boons as he did so.

The sinless Indra was brought from Amarāvatī to the city of Nirmāṇarati by the Ṛṣis, and there he was consecrated in the position of Indra. Then, having propitiated Tvaṣṭṛ—who had become enraged at the slaughter of Viśvarūpa—by means of his asceticism, Indra requested a son who would be a source of great terror to the gods. Consequently, by virtue of a boon from Brahmā, he obtained a son named Vṛtra. When that Asura Vṛtra, having grown in power, began to oppress the Ṛṣis, they returned to the presence of the gods. Upon seeing him, the gods were struck with fear and consulted one another.

The composition of the mantra; by the command of Brahmā, the gods went to the hermitage of Dadhīci and requested his bones for the sake of the sacrifice; at the request of the gods for the bone-sacrifice, Dadhīci relinquished his own body through yoga; Surabhī, the wish-fulfilling cow, fashioned a body from the marrow of Dadhīci’s bones using her own tongue; the gods obtained weapons such as the thunderbolt from those bones; and by means of the vessel called *khuvaca*, the wife of Dadhīci bestowed upon the gods the gift of offspring.

The story of Svācā, who, having instructed her son Pippalāda while he was staying near the Aśvattha tree, followed him in death (samādhi) together with her husband; the commencement of the battle between the gods and the asuras; the commencement of the battle with the asura Vṛtra; Indra’s propitiation of Śiva by performing the Śanipradoṣavrata at the command of Bṛhaspati for the sake of slaying the asura Vṛtra; the procedure for the Śanipradoṣavrata; and [the account] of the asura Vṛtra, who in a previous birth was the Gandharva Citraratha.

The description of the attainment of the state of being an Asura through a curse; the procedure for the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the Śanipradoṣavrata; the attainment of valor by Indra through the power of the Śanipradoṣavrata and his subsequent engagement in battle with the gods; the description of the code of combat among the Daityas who fled from the field of battle; the depiction of the tumultuous war between the Devas and Dānavas; the fall of Indra in battle due to a blow dealt by Vṛtra; and thereafter, the [restoration] of Indra, whose consciousness had been lost, by the command of Brahmā.

The performance of austerities in the form of worshipping Śiva for the sake of slaying Vṛtra; considering Vṛtra invincible by Śiva’s own words, Indra’s failure to act and his subsequent making of peace with Vṛtra after a thousand years had passed; his dispatching of an emissary to Vṛtra’s presence to slay him; Vṛtra’s arrogance; the worship of Umākeśvara on the banks of the Narmadā by the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) through the Pradīpa-vrata; and Vṛtra’s loss of splendor due to the decline of his ascetic power resulting from falling asleep at the time of the Pradīpa-pūjā while forgetting the worship of the Liṅga.

The frustration of his desires; then, by means of the *vrata* of the three nights (*tri-rātra*), Indra attained the status of the Lord of the Gods. Satisfied by Brahmā’s prayer, the Blessed One spoke to Brahmā through a voice from the sky, describing how the Daityas had caused obstacles by creating a seat (*pīṭikā*) for Rāhu during the *pradoṣa-vrata*. In connection with that, the procedure for the worship of the goddess Kālikā is described. Then, by the command of Śiva, the gods performed the worship of the quarters (*dig-pūjā*) according to the scriptures. By the power of that, the ocean became calm.

The piercing [of Vṛtra], his exit from the body, and the description of the falling of Vṛtra’s head; the falling of the body between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in Antarvedī, and the falling of the head at Mākhva; the subsequent chapters concerning the regions with the gods; the cutting off of Vṛtra’s head after six months of effort; Indra’s attainment of victory; then, by the command of Śukra, the acquisition of that chariot which was being offered in the sacrifice despite the news of Vṛtra’s slaughter reported by the Daityas; and having mounted that chariot—

The departure of Bala, accompanied by the enemy of the Daityas (Viṣṇu), toward his own abode after achieving victory over the gods; Indra’s grief upon hearing of that arrival; and seeing the gods returning to heaven, Bṛhaspati’s instruction for Indra and all the other gods to assume the forms of birds such as peacocks and others, their departure from heaven, their arrival at Kaśyapa’s hermitage, and the reporting of their own suffering to their mother Aditi; and the granting of a boon to Aditi by Kaśyapa when she was entreated for protection from the gods. On the twelfth day of the month of Śravaṇa, [Aditi]...

The description of Viṣṇu’s worship by Aditi; the manifestation of Viṣṇu through Aditi’s performance of that vow; and the incineration of Bali by the Blessed Lord, who, having been praised by Aditi for the sake of protecting her, commanded his own discus and mace to subdue him when he declared his own incomparability.

The narration of how Bali, having been consecrated upon the throne of the Lord of the Gods (Indra) by Śukra, bestowed the wealth of Indra equally upon the Brāhmaṇas; and in connection with that, the description of how any Indra whatsoever, while seated on the throne of Indra, failed to give gifts, and consequently, upon the exhaustion of his merit, lost his status as Indra; and the account of a certain merchant who, seeing a handful of flowers and other offerings brought for a courtesan fall to the ground through his own negligence, thought, "May this be an offering to Śiva! and so forth.

Through his intellect, he attained certainty and was cleansed of all sins; thereafter, following his death, according to the words of Yama, he reached the station of Indra after three and a half *ghaṭikās*. At that moment, he recounted to the great sages such as Agastya the gift of Airāvata and other [treasures]. After three and a half *ghaṭikās*, the former Indra, remaining in his own abode, rebuked Rātri; subsequently, having rebuked her, he praised the Moon who had been made king by her. Then, the former Indra attained the status of Indra.

The King of Elephants (Airāvata) rebukes the gambler before Yama upon seeing his own wealth, such as elephants and horses, being given away by the gambler; then, Citragupta, commanded by Yama, describes the gambler’s exemption from hell due to the greatness of that gift; hearing this, Indra, filled with joy, returns to heaven; the gambler enters the womb of Suruci, the wife of Virocana—the son of Prahlāda—and Indra, in the guise of a Brahmin, [approaches] Virocana.

The account of Bali returning to beg for his head; the description of how Śakra, having assumed the deceptive guise of a Brahmin, cut off and gave his own head to Virocana; the birth of Baka from Suruci after the death of his father named Virocana; and the sequence of Suruci’s offspring.

The chapters on the subject matter of the *Hiraṇyakaśipu* [section]: thereafter, the departure for the world of the husband; the consecration of Bali’s father, Virocana, upon the royal throne by Bhārgava; then, after the defeat of Indra and the others by Bali, Bali’s establishment in heaven and his issuing of commands to all; and then, Bali’s deliberation on whether to remain in heaven, following the words of Śukra.

The description of [Pṛthu] returning to the holy ford of Guruṅasītīra on the bank of the Namadā river on the surface of the earth along with all the Daityas and Śukra, and performing many sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha; then, during that very sacrifice of Baṭu, the descent of the Blessed One in the form of Baṭu, who was pleased by the vow performed by Aditi; thereafter, following the rites of his initiation (upanayana) and so forth, his journey toward the cow-pen of Bali; and the description of the hospitality shown to the boy Vāmana by Bali, and how the Blessed One, in the form of the boy Vāmana, [acted] according to Bali's earnest request.

The request for three paces of land; when Bali had made his promise to grant him the land, his preceptor Śukra forbade that gift to the boy after first describing Viṣṇu’s true nature. [Seeing Bali’s persistence in granting the land to the boy, Śukra gave the earth to Bali as a ransom. When Bali had given the land according to his resolve, Śukra praised the Lord’s greatness through the illusory boy, [describing how with two steps he pervaded the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings].

Vāmana’s request for three paces of land measured by his third step; then the departure of Bali toward the tip of the mountain [Garuḍa] for that purpose; thereafter, the return of Bali along with Vidyutprabhā to the presence of the Lord Vāmana; then, by her [Vidyutprabhā], the fulfillment of the placement of the three steps in the form of Vāmana upon the three heads of herself, her son, and her own feet; and finally, the command given by the gratified Lord for Bali to go to Sutala at the request of Bali.

The residence at Viṣṇupāda in the presence of Baṅi; herein is the description of the power and majesty of divine devotion, exemplified by the attainment of sovereignty by a gambler in a previous birth.

The description of the battle between the gods and the demon Tāraka; the account of the defeat of the gods and their departure to the presence of Brahmā; the proclamation by a celestial voice regarding the necessity of a son born of Śiva himself for the slaying of the demon Tāraka; the command given to Śiva—though separated from his wife—to make efforts to obtain a consort; and the subsequent journey to the Himālayas by [the gods] to produce a daughter.

The contents of this chapter are as follows: Bharadvāja’s request; the narration of Himavat’s petition to his wife Menā for the birth of a daughter; Menā’s description of the suffering of parents upon the birth of a daughter; then, considering himself a mere instrument for the sake of helping others, Himavat’s awakening; the bearing of the Mother of the World (Jagadambā) within her womb by Menā at the request of Himavat; and the description of the nature of the Mother of the World.

...the arrival of the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) with Pārvatī from the Himavat mountains for the purpose of bestowing her; Śiva’s joy at Gaurī’s devoted service; Gaurī’s performance of service to Śiva; in the meantime, Madana, instigated by Devendra, discharged his arrow at Śaṅkara; the description of how Śaṅkara, pierced by Madana’s arrows, became afflicted by passion upon seeing Pārvatī; and then, through discernment, the examination of the mind’s cause of delusion and [his] self-restraint.

Beholding Madana with his bow strung and desiring to pierce [Śiva], Śiva, under the sway of anger, reduced Madana to ashes with the fire from his third eye. Then, all the gods offered prayers to Śiva for the sake of restoring Madana to life. Thereupon, the day vanished. Seeing Madana burnt, Madana’s wife, Rati, was filled with grief. Girijā sat down in a vow, preceded by a promise to restore Madana to life through the power of her asceticism. Then, at the very place where Madana had been consumed by fire, Rati...

The commencement of the practice of asceticism (tapascaryārambha). In the meantime, Nārada approached Rati and engaged in conversation; Rati’s deception of Nārada; Nārada going to the demon Śambara and issuing orders for the abduction of Rati; Śambara forcibly taking Rati back to his own home and appointing her as the superintendent of the kitchen; then, Pārvatī performing ascetic practices with the desire to attain Śiva; and Viṣṇu [intervening] regarding that asceticism of hers and the foremost of the gods.

The performance of the marriage rites for Diva with the recitation of mantras; the return of Brahmā and the other gods to Śaṅkara, who was established in meditative absorption upon the seat of yoga on the far shore of the ocean; the hymn of praise offered to Mahādeva by Brahmā and the others; the description of the burning of Madana (the God of Love) as he was about to be wedded to Pārvatī by Śaṅkara, who was pleased by the praise of the gods; the instruction given to the gods regarding the renunciation of desire; and then, while Śiva remained in meditative absorption, the dismissal of all the gods by Nandin, including Diva.

The state of absorption (*samādhi*) in the bliss of one's own true nature (*svarūpānanda*); thereafter, due to the power of the penance performed by Girijā, Śiva’s entry into meditative absorption; Śiva’s arrival at the site of Girijā’s penance in the form of a young brahmin student (*baṭu*); the performance of a censure of Śiva by the one in the form of a student for the purpose of testing Girijā’s mind; when Girijā, unable to tolerate that, called out "O friend! and addressed the student, Śiva vanished and manifested his own true form; Śiva’s speech regarding the crossing of the river; and [his request] for marriage according to the path of the bridegroom.

The fulfillment of the request for a boon, followed by the granting of boons to Pārvatī and the departure of the Lord to his own auspicious realm; the departure of the various regions toward the world, and then, after Pārvatī’s penance had reached its consummation, her formal return to her own home with Brahmā and the other gods in great ceremony.

... [the sending of] the Seven Sages by Śiva toward the Himālaya to act as intermediaries for the giving of his daughter Pārvatī; the dialogue between Śiva and the Seven Sages; after the decision regarding the marriage was made by the Sages, [Nārada’s] return to Śiva and the reporting of the decision on the marriage; and Mahādeva’s dispatching of Nārada to invite Viṣṇu and the other gods, followed by the arrival of Viṣṇu and the others at Śiva’s presence and Śiva’s great preparations for the wedding.

After performing the preliminary rites of worship and other ceremonies, the departure of all the hosts of gods together with Śiva toward the city of the King of Mountains for the wedding is described. Therein is the account of Himavān, for the sake of his daughter’s marriage, placing the preceptor of the Gaṅgā at the head and having Viśvakarman construct an unprecedented pavilion; and how, upon hearing from Nārada of the skillful arrangement of the portraits of all the deities within the wedding pavilion built by Viśvakarman, a state of apprehension arose among all the gods, and subsequently, Himavān [invited] Śiva.

The bringing back to his own city; the dwelling of all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, in their various respective abodes; after all the gods had dwelt in their individual celestial realms, the satisfaction derived from seeing the splendor of Manasā as she was led to heaven; thereafter, Pārvatī, having donned her bridal garments and placed a necklace upon her hand for the purpose of choosing the bridegroom, remained there meditating on the Supreme Lord for the sake of the marriage ceremony. For the sake of taking her hand in marriage...

The arrival of Śiva at the wedding pavilion with great ceremony during the auspicious moment prescribed by Garga; the marriage celebration of Śiva and Pārvatī; the ceremonial lustration (*nīrājana*) of Śiva and Pārvatī performed by Lopāmudrā, Arundhatī, and other holy matrons; then, during the formal rite of giving the daughter (*kanyādāna*) by Himavat, who was dressed in white, in the course of an inquiry regarding the desire to proclaim the name and lineage of Śiva, the description of Śiva as the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*) by Nārada. ... Sa.

The giving away of the daughter by Himavat; the account of the emergence of sixty thousand Vidyādharas from the marks made on the Brahmarandhra by the toenails of Pārvatī during the occasion of the domestic fire-sacrifice performed by Śiva and Pārvatī; and then the description of the marriage festival, preceded by the hospitable reception of the bridegroom’s party by Himavat.

Then Viṣṇu, belonging to the groom's party, performed appropriate honors for the various members of the bride's party, such as Sadya, Caravinda, Caṇḍa, and others; thereafter, the commencement of the bridal procession took place. During the bridal procession, Śiva and Pārvatī were seated upon an excellent palanquin. Then all the gods departed for their respective abodes. Following that, Śiva and Pārvatī sported on Mount Gandhamādana. Then, in a secluded spot, Śiva and Pārvatī...

The commencement of the act of sexual union; the sending of the gods, who were overcome with fear and trepidation arising from that exceedingly wonderful coitus, to a secluded spot near him; the arrival of Agni at the time of the sexual union under the pretext of being a messenger, and his consuming Śiva’s semen while approaching Pārvatī; the description of how all the gods became pregnant by means of the semen originating from the mouth of Agni; and then, the seeking of refuge by all the gods with Viṣṇu.

At the instigation of Viṣṇu, that [seed] was swallowed by the gods; then, by the command of Śiva, who was pleased, the seed was vomited out by all the gods. [This is] the description of how the seed vomited by all the gods became a golden lotus. Then Śiva gave the command for Agni to deposit the seed in the womb. Thereafter, by means of the entry of the atoms of that seed into the bodies of the six Kṛttikās—the six star-clusters known as the Pleiades—who had gathered near Agni to offer him hospitality, [the seed was conceived].

While immersed in meditation, Śiva’s semen was released simultaneously into the Gaṅgā upon the summit of Mount Himavat—himself being scorched by those drops out of fear of transgression. At the very moment that semen was emitted, the six-faced boy was born; at the time of that child's birth, the breasts of Pārvatī suddenly began to flow with milk; and at that same instant, Nārada returned to Śiva and related the news of the Kumāra’s birth.

For the sake of seeing that Kumāra, all the gods, together with Śiva and Pārvatī, returned to the presence of the Kumāra; the commencement of the festival for Kumāra’s exaltation took place; and then Śiva and Pārvatī experienced great joy. Thereafter, at the command of Śiva, all the gods set out, placing Kumāra at their head, for the purpose of conquering the demon Tāraka. At that moment, a voice from the sky proclaimed the victory of the gods. In this very interval, the maiden named Senā, the daughter of Mṛtyu, arrived.

The choosing [of Kumāra] by the word of Brahmā; thereafter, the description of Kumāra’s attainment of the office of generalissimo; at that very time, Gaṅgā, Gaurī, and Ṛttikā arrived and requested Skanda to be their son, and he established them as his group of Mothers (mātṛgaṇa); then, Kumāra set out against the Asura Tāraka together with all the gods; and finally, the arraying of the armies of the gods and the Daityas.

In the battle between the gods and the asuras, where even the gods were defeated, Viṣṇu performed the upholding of the earth; then, when Kumāra stood face-to-face with Tārakāsura in the sky for combat, Tārakāsura discharged his own terrible shower of arrows. These are the [described] matters.

The command that the messengers of Śiva must lead those [souls] to the world of Yama; the description of King Śveta’s attainment of union with Śiva; and the introduction of the story of the Kirāta regarding the Śivadharma—[namely]: once, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, the great Śivarātri, while a certain Kirāta named Caṇḍa was wandering in the forest in search of deer and other animals to be killed for food, he stood by night at the foot of a Bilva tree; there, without knowing and without effort, he cut off a leaf of the Bilva tree.

The worship of Śiva situated below the well, the bathing of Śiva with water from a water-pot, fasting through the exertion of meditating on the sound of the bell, and—due to his lack of food—the fasting of his wife as she awaits him; furthermore, on another day, when his wife had brought and placed food upon the bank of the river, these were the subjects of her study.

[In the section] on the defeat of the gods in the battle with Tāraka and others by Kumāra, who had attained full maturity through the grace of Bhavānī; the description of the fierce battle between the Lord of the Gods (Kumāra) and the demon Tārakāsura; the battle of Kumāra; the consolation of Himavat and the others—who had arrived to witness the battle and were distressed by it—by Kumāra; then, the severing of Tāraka’s head by Kumāra; and thereafter, [the state] of Kumāra following the death of Tāraka.

The description of the festival celebrating the victory over the demon Tāraka performed by all the gods, including the single worship of Jayadratha; ... the description of the majesty of Kumārasvāmin; therein, having perceived that even sinners attain purification merely by the sight of Kumāra, Yama—considering his own realm to be devoid of merit—approaches Śiva after placing Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods before him, and having praised Śiva, he reports to him that due to the majesty of the sight of Kumāra, all sinful people are attaining heaven, thereby rendering his own office useless. Then...

Śaṅkara’s imparting of instruction on the nature of pure Dharma for the sake of Yama’s liberation from saṃsāra and the attainment of contrary realization; the description of Yama’s attainment of a purified self through Śaṅkara’s instruction; then, the offering of praise by all the mountains to Kumāra; Kumāra’s granting of the boon of the form of Śiva’s vehicle to the mountains; and the great joy arising from the thought that, when [the deer] had been eaten by a hunter who arrived with an arrow, it had resulted in the gift of food to the Kirāta.

Therefore, [this section contains] the bringing of the celestial chariot by the attendants of Śiva to lead the Kirāta to the world of Śiva due to the power of the Śivarātri vow undertaken despite ignorance; the departure of the Kirāta toward the world of Śiva together with the attendant of Śiva; the description of the origin of the Śivarātri vow; and, in connection with the greatness of the Śivarātri vow, the account of how the son of a widow and a Nāgara born of a Caṇḍāla woman obtained birth in another life from Śiva under the name Vīramadra through the influence of the Śivarātri vow—[all concerning] the Śivarātri vow.

An account of the attainment of perfection by kings such as Bharata and others... "Then once, while Śiva and Pārvatī were seated comfortably in their own palace on Mount Kailāsa, a game of dice was played; when all the wealth had been won by Pārvatī and Śiva had lost everything, he left Kailāsa and departed for the forest of asceticism."

Chapter Nine: Then, after Pārvatī had become distressed by separation following her departure for Śiva’s abode, Nandin assumed the form of a forest fire while she was absorbed in meditation in a secluded place; when he caused a lapse in the worship of the Liṅga of the Lord of the Mountain, Kumāra explained the greatness of worshipping the various types of Liṅgas of the Lord of Mountains. Chapter Ten.

In this context, following the glorification of the greatness of worship during the day, there is the narration of the life of the king named Śveta. While King Śveta—who had been devoted to devotion to Śiva from birth—was absorbed in meditation at the time of his death, Yama and the other guardians of the world, though possessed of the power of destruction, saw Kāla (Time) making an effort to slay him with a sword. Then, for the sake of protecting his own devotee, the Supreme Lord Śiva reduced him to ashes with the fire of his third eye. Subsequently, King Śveta, having arisen from his meditative absorption, [beheld] before him...

[The story of] the crow who was being burned: how he remained standing after becoming a pillar while offering praise to Rudra; how Rudra, wishing to kill him, declared, "This pillar has been burned by me"—thus explaining the cause of the pillar's burning; and finally, how Maheśvara restored the pillar to life at the request of King Śvetaketu.

The praise of the Blessed One by Kālī; thereafter, Kāṭa’s failure to offer alms to King Śveta, who was devoted to the welfare of others; then, having bowed to heaven along with Yama and the other deities and having extolled King Śveta, Kāṭa returned to his own abode and, after describing the greatness of the Śiva-dharma consisting of the application of the *tripuṇḍra*, matted hair, the wearing of the *rudrākṣa* beads, and so forth, departed toward the presence of Śiva; upon merely being seen by Śiva, he was roused from his meditative absorption (*samādhi*) by the Lord.

As soon as Pārvatī was seen, her state of separation during the day became apparent; then Śiva’s request for her hand to the Śabara woman; thereafter, the sage who had been afflicted by the god of love’s arrow requesting his father to bring him to Mount Gandhamādana so that he might obtain her; Śiva’s own request for the maiden from Himālaya; and meanwhile, Nārada arriving there and reporting the matter to Śiva.

Now, regarding the chapters of the Śiva-skānda: Chapter 10 describes how Pārvatī, observing her own words being disregarded by Śiva, desired to depart for another forest out of anger; then, when the gods led by Indra and others placed Girijā at their head and offered prayers, the description follows of the consecration of Śiva upon the divine lion-throne on Mount Gandhamādana after his anger had subsided. Thus, in connection with the majesty of Kedāranātha, there is a description praising all the duties of Śiva (Śivadharma).
Thus ends the first section, the Kedāra-khaṇḍa, within the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the second section, the Kāmarikākhaṇḍa, within the Māheśvarakhaṇḍa.

In the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka, at the commencement of the description of the majesty of the holy sites (*tīrtha*) situated on the shore of the Southern Ocean, there is the account of the majesty of the Pañcāpsaras-tīrtha. Within that, regarding the narrative of Arjuna’s pilgrimage to the holy sites: when Arjuna had set out for the purpose of bathing in the holy sites along the shore of the southern sea, he was prevented from bathing by the ascetics dwelling there due to the threat of crocodiles in those waters. Then, having perceived Arjuna’s righteous intent, the ascetics bestowed upon him the boon of long life.

Then, having arrived at the Saubhadra-tīrtha, Arjuna descended to perform his ablutions; while he was engaged in bathing, he was seized by Rāhu. Upon Arjuna’s rescue of Rāhu by means of his strength, Rāhu assumed the form of a woman. The account of how that woman—having entreated a Brāhmaṇa for sexual pleasure along with her four thousand female companions—was cursed by him and consequently attained the state of being Rāhu is described. Furthermore, according to the words of Nārada, the dwelling of Rāhu in five sacred sites (tīrthas) is described, and thereafter, in the other four.

Having bathed at the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) after performing the ritual extraction of the local *brahma-rāhu*, there follows a description of the deliverance of all the *apsarases*. Then, with the intention of ascertaining the cause of the obstruction of the sacred ford by Aja, Nārada is seized by doubt; the *apsarases* tell him that he should question them regarding this matter, and having spoken thus, they return to their own abode.

The meeting of Aja with Nārada; following the hearing of the account of the Lavaṇa-Kuśa war from the mouth of Nārada, Aja’s inquiry of Nārada out of a desire to know the greatness of sacred fords (tīrtha-māhātmya); then, upon Nārada’s narration of the events in the world of Brahmā, preceded by praise, the narration of the dialogue between Suśravas and Kātyāyana-Sārasvata; therein, the great sage Sārasvata’s exposition of the essence of Dharma to the great sage Kātyāyana; and thereafter, the narration of the greatness of giving (dāna-māhātmya).

Following the hearing of the greatness of giving, there is the account of how Nārada, whose mind was eager for the sake of giving, traveled through various lands for the purpose of obtaining wealth to bestow as gifts; [the narrative continues with] Nārada’s arrival at the hermitage of Śukra on the bank of the Narmadā while wandering the earth; after Nārada had related his own story to Śukra, Śukra described to Nārada the sacred places worthy of giving, specifically providing a description of the majesty of Stambhatīrtha located at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.

Therein: the account of a certain Brahmin named Subhadra residing on the bank of that sacred ford; his offering of the merit of his own Caturthī-vow to that Brahmin who was performing a Śrāddha at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; and Nārada’s contemplation of establishing a residence at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean upon hearing the greatness of Stambhatīrtha situated there, as described by his brother.

Nārada, having understood that for the establishment of a sacred site at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, material wealth was required according to the principle of faith (*śraddhānyāya*), and finding that the means for acquiring such wealth were not yet available, went in person to King Dharmavarman. Having heard the king’s intentions, he explained the six foundations (*ṣaḍadhiṣṭhāna*) as the cause for the attainment of merit. Satisfying the king by explaining the meaning of these verses and so forth, he provided assistance for the accomplishment of the religious gift (*dānadharma*) prescribed for him. ... .

Then, having thoroughly examined [the brahmins] everywhere for the sake of obtaining those brahmins whose external purity was established by the merit of their gifts, Nārada subsequently set out toward Kaṅkāprāma in the guise of a brahmin. Having arrived there, he assumed the form of a leper in order to test the brahmins; and among those brahmins, it was a young boy of only eight years who gave the correct answer to the extremely profound questions posed by Nārada.

Then, after Nārada manifested in his own form at the great holy site (mahātīrtha) of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, he requested [the Lord] to establish [the settlement] by providing means of livelihood for the Brāhmaṇas; this is the description of how he was established there upon the Daṇḍāmrava mountain. Following that, is the description of the arrival at Kaḍāpagrama. At the time when Nārada was washing the feet of the Brāhmaṇas, a guest arrived; out of hospitality toward that guest, Nārada offered eight thousand Brāhmaṇas from among those who had been brought there.

At the time of the Madhuparka offering, when the Brāhmaṇa Hārīta first placed his left foot forward upon the washing stone, Nārada pronounced a curse upon all the Brāhmaṇas, saying, "You shall become fools. The Brāhmaṇas likewise returned a similar curse to Nārada. The reason for placing the left foot forward is described; thereafter follows the account of Nārada’s departure.

The Table of Contents (*anukramaṇikā*): [Chapter on Mahīśvara] Chapters and Subjects. [Chapters and Subjects]. Therein, the recollection of the account of the Brahmin Cirakārin out of remorse; therein, [the story] of Medhātithi Gautama’s son, Cirakārin.

Prākārakarṇa, having learned through his own wind-born knowledge that his father was indifferent toward Indrajit, and by the command of Nāḍījaṅgha, went to kill his wayward mother at his father’s order; however, due to reflection, he desisted from the act. To demonstrate the necessity of this very knowledge, Prākārakarṇa himself, while on Mount Gandhamādana, was instructed by Śakra—who had arrived in the guise of a Brahmin—and consequently felt remorse. [This concerns] the mother who was present for the purpose of killing... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Rāmāyaṇa*, specifically the *Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa*. The translation reflects the narrative of Prākārakarṇa’s intervention regarding his mother’s infidelity and his subsequent encounter with Indra disguised as a Brahmin.)

The bringing of Bhartṛdhanvan, Ākaṇḍeya, Nāḍījaṅgha, and Vakas to the presence of the vulture; by that vulture as well, the journey of Gautama behind Cirakārin as he was going toward the vulture; and upon seeing his father, Cirakārin’s narration of the account of how his own long arms had grown due to the lack of recognition regarding Indra’s command, preceded by the inquiry into the matter, and his making a request to his father after throwing down the branch.

Gautama’s father, Cirakārin—due to his habit of acting slowly—was unaware of the wind from Mount Gandhamādana; having seen the arrival of the food brought by the vulture, he first offered it with great joy to his wife and son before taking it home himself. Then Nārada, having learned of the vulture’s deceptive act of bringing the food, went to the presence of the long-lived Kṛśa, who dwells on Lake Mānasa, and related the story of Indradyumna, Kaṇḍu, Nāḍījaṅgha, and Pāka.

Regarding the eye: there, as the tax (dāpa) paid by the fishermen who had gathered on the shore of the lake would result in a profit for Kaṭa, the author of the curse [Śiva] ordained that all of them, upon seeing King Indradyumna, would immediately dive into the water after making a sign with their hands like a tortoise. Then, the Brāhmaṇas reached the great ocean, and after performing gifts of gold, cows, land, wealth, and so forth, they themselves had the city of Mahīnagara constructed by Viśvakarman.

Description of the Installation... To him, not by that [means], indeed not... Having brought a celestial chariot and a rain of flowers from the gods to the peak of Mount Indradhanu, King Indra, at the request of Nārada who desired to hear in detail the majesty of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, dispatched a messenger to the abode of Brahmā. Upon his arrival, Indra made preparations for the journey; then, with the permission of the gods, he began the detailed description of the majesty of the Mahī and the ocean.

In this regard, the following is the commencement of the narrative concerning the arrival [of the sage]: having declared his lack of desire to go toward Brahmā, he proceeded to pose a question to Kratu out of a desire to know the cause of that very [lack of desire].

After Indradyumna had remained there for a long time in a state of invisibility, Brahmā, after a long period, descended to the earth by means of his yogic power. Following a narration of his own previous birth, and after providing hospitality to Indradyumna and the others, he performed a display of his power in order to make them recognize him once again. Upon returning to the earthly realm, Indradyumna approached the vicinity of the six great mountains and rivers, both small and large.

Having approached Mārkaṇḍeya—who was long-lived among those who were long-lived—Indradumna went into his presence to receive instruction regarding his own speech and the scope of his knowledge. [In this context, there is a fault of inconsistency in Indradumna’s statement of ignorance despite possessing such [knowledge]; thereafter, following the meeting of Indradumna and others with the great sage Lomaśa, even though they were exceedingly long-lived, due to their lack of dispassion (*vairāgya*), they were surpassed by Nāḍījaṃghavaka, who was longer-lived than even they.

In its vicinity is Tannayana; there, in response to Indradyumna’s inquiry regarding the cause of his lack of subjugation by the senses, Lomaśa describes the nature of worldly existence and then recounts his own divine knowledge. Subsequently, Nāḍījaṅghaka, questioned by Indradyumna, describes the cause of his own long life and tells of his own past deeds, including a description of the greatness of worshipping Śivapurī.

Immediately after hearing the words of Somaśarman, [Prakāṇḍaka], out of his singular devotion to Śiva, requested Śivadīkṣā from him. Then, for the sake of attaining knowledge of the wind (vāta-vijñāna), he also requested initiation from Nāḍījaṅgha, who was long-lived. At the request of Lomarāma, [Somaśarman] bestowed Śivadīkṣā upon all of them and sent Prakāṇḍaka and Indrada toward a certain Uḍūka named Śivaliṅgarakṣaṇa; by him, Prakāṇḍaka...

The instruction regarding the performance of *sūja* (the *sūkta*): thereafter, the commencement of the practice of *kriyā-yoga* by Mākaṇḍeya and the others; the narration by Raikva of his own lack of knowledge regarding Indradyumna; the explanation by Indradyumna himself of the cause of his own long life; the arrival of Nārada before those who were performing penance; the hearing of the path from him; the description of the greatness of Viṣṇu as perceived through the company of Nāḍījaṅgha and others; and the desire to know the means for one's own liberation.
The introduction: Nārada [related] to them the great [account] of Saṃvarta residing in Vārāṇasī. (Skanda Purāṇa, Māheśvara Khaṇḍa, Chapter 5)

Chapter 86: The instruction on how to go to Dīnāra; the description of the means for determining the *saṃvarta* [fire] in Vārāṇasī; having gone to Vārāṇasī by way of Nāḍījaṅgha and others, the recognition of the *saṃvarta* through the method taught by Nārada and the subsequent meeting with him; the granting of permission by Saṃvarta—having been liberated from the curse of Nāḍījaṅgha and the others—to depart for the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, along with related matters.

It contains an account of the origin of the Mahī river; a description of the incident involving Naṅgula, which occurred because Yājñavalkya remained at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; and a detailed exposition of the majesty of the Mahīsāgara-saṃgama tīrtha.

From Saṃvarta, [the sage] heard the majesty of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; then follows the description of how even birds such as cranes, water-fowls, vultures, and eagles, having approached the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, attained divinity and liberation through the installation of *liṅgas*. Next is the description of living liberation (*jīvanmukti*) from the mouth of Mārkaṇḍeya, and therein, the description of the majesty of the *Indradarśana* stone *liṅga* installed by Indra.

[The section begins with] the description of the greatness of Mahīsāgarasaṃgama, Śatarudriya, and Ardikhigama; then follows the description of the majesty of Kumāranātha, which commences with an account of the conduct of Māra in connection with that [topic]. Therein is the birth of a son named Vajrāṅga to Diti, who was known as Daśakanyā; then, having gone to heaven at his mother’s command, Vajrāṅga seized Indra by the foot and brought him back to his mother’s presence; thereafter, through the mediation of Brahmā and Kaśyapa, Vajrāṅga secured the release of Vāsava; and finally, by the command of Brahmā, Vajrāṅga engaged in ascetic penance.

[The section on] *pravṛtti* (active engagement): While he was engaged in asceticism, his wife named Varāṅgī, who was solely intent upon serving him, was subjected to various terrifying illusions and mental derision by Śakra. Then, having desisted from his austerities after failing to obtain [his goal] from Brahmā, Varāṅga questioned his wife, named Varāṅgī, regarding the cause of her terror, and she related it to him.

Having witnessed the mockery of his own emaciated state, Vajrāṅga—though already freed from demonic tendencies through the power of his asceticism—performed penance once more out of a desire to do what was pleasing to his beloved and for the sake of attaining the body of Mahendra’s wife. Then, by virtue of that penance, Brahmā granted Vajrāṅga the boon of a son capable of crushing the pride of the gods and brought him back from his ascetic practice. Subsequently, Tārakāsura was born from Vajrāṅga through a woman of the Asuras, and [the narrative continues] with the enmity between Tārakāsura and the gods.

He was a seeker of the kingdom as his prize; then, having gone to a cave in the Pāriyātra mountain range with the desire to conquer the gods, Tārakāsura performed austerities. While he was performing those austerities, the gods were distressed. Brahmā granted him the boon of invincibility against all beings except for a six-day-old child. Consequently, when Tārakāsura had been subdued, his own kingdom came to an end.

After deliberating with his ministers, Tārakāsura prepared his army for mobilization and marched toward heaven for the purpose of conquering all the gods. Thereupon, with the approval of Bṛhaspati, Indra, the lord of the gods, organized the entire celestial host for battle. When the war began, as the armies of Tārakāsura and the gods clashed, a fierce hand-to-hand combat took place between Yama and Prahlāda; therein, the defeat of Yama in that battle is described. [...]

In the battle between Dhanādhipa and Jambha, when Dhanādhipa had slain Jambha, there was a battle between Ujambha and Dhanādhipa, resulting in the defeat of Dhanādhipa. Then, in the battle between Kujambha and Niketa, Niketa was defeated; Varuṇa bound the arms of Ujambha with his noose. Thereafter, when Mahiṣāsura and Nirṛti were intent on devouring the flesh [of the enemy], they were [confronted] by Candra.

The description of how the spreading of cool rays caused extreme distress to all the Daityas; then, observing the cessation of the cold brought about by Kālanemi through the emission of fire from his mouth, Sūrya, under the guise of Śambara, took up an arrow and, by means of the *Indrajāla* illusion, effected a transformation of the forms of both gods and Dānavas; and thereupon, having fallen into a state of delusion, Kālanemi killed only those Daityas whom he perceived as gods.

Then, having heard the words of Nigina, Kālanemi employed his powers of illusion (*māyā*). Thereupon, the awakened Kālanemi released a great shower of stones to ward off all obstacles. Bhāskara, mounting the staff of Mahendra and assuming a terrifying form, scattered the army of the Daityas with the spreading rays of his intense heat. Kālanemi, assuming the form of a dark cloud, produced a torrential downpour; however, by means of a rain of weapons, [Bhāskara] subdued all the gods, including Śakra.

The defeat of Kālanemi: thereafter, having heard the prayers of all the gods, the Blessed Lord Mahāviṣṇu rose from the depths of the Milk Ocean, mounted Garuḍa, and returned to the battlefield; there, after engaging in battle with Kālanemi, he brought about Kālanemi’s defeat. Furthermore, in a battle for the sake of the gods against Viṣṇu, who was intent on destroying the innumerable Daityas, Jambhāsuru met with defeat and fled from the field of battle, turning his back in retreat.

Then, the stabilization of Viṣṇu after he had been made to drink [the poison], through a hymn of praise composed by Indra; the description of the tumultuous battle between Indra and the Asura Jambha, preceded by Indra’s preparation for the sake of slaying the Asura Jambha at the command of Viṣṇu; the killing of the Asura Jambha in that battle; and following the slaughter of the Asura Jambha, the return of all the Daityas—the Kandarīkas who were terrified by the army of the gods—to the presence of the Asura Tāraka; and then, the arrival of Tāraka with all those Daityas at the field of battle.

Having encountered [the enemy] with great prowess, he brought about the total destruction of the army of all the gods; beholding that [destruction], Viṣṇu informed all the gods and, having commanded their protector, himself vanished. Following the victory over Tārakāsura, [the king] ascended with great ceremony the throne upon the royal seat at Stambhapura on the bank of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean (in the city of Khambāyatana); and as Tārakāsura sat enthroned, the Fortune of the Three Worlds approached him.

The entry [of Viṣṇu], preceded by the bringing back of Indra and the other gods in the form of a boar from Tārakāsura by means of Nārāyaṇa, and the granting of fearlessness to Indra and the others from Tārakāsura; thereafter, having incurred fear from him, the departure of Indra and the other gods toward Brahmā at the command of Viṣṇu; and the installation of his own Daityas in the positions of Indra and the other gods by Tārakāsura...

Śaṅkara, having gone before Indra and the other gods, made a representation of his own suffering preceded by praise; Brahmā informed the gods that the Mother of the World would descend into the house of Himavat; then the gods, having offered praise to the Goddess Rātri, made a prayer for the entry of the Great Goddess, the Mother of the World, into the wife named Menā; by the prayer of Brahmā, the Great Goddess entered the eyes of Menā; and from Menā, the Mother of the World [was born].

The manifestation [of Śiva]; the description of the festival at the time of the Mother of the World’s birth; the arrival of Nārada to Himavat at the command of Śakra, and his discourse regarding Pārvatī’s extraordinary beauty; the seating of the two, Himavat and Menā, who were distressed with anxiety, after they had been addressed by the gods, and the subsequent generation of contentment by recounting the boon obtained from Mahādeva; the description of how Pārvatī always kept her hand upraised as a sign of granting fearlessness and protection to all living beings; and [her resolve] for the service of Śiva.

Himavat’s instruction to Pārvatī regarding her marriage; then, Nārada’s arrival from Himavat at the request of Indra, his reporting of the entire account of Śiva’s misfortune, and his command for Śiva to be united with the Goddess through marriage; Śakra’s command to Madana to delude Śaṅkara; Madana’s discharge of his arrow into Śiva’s heart during the festival of Pārvatī’s service; and then, Hara, afflicted by passion upon seeing Madana—

The burning of Madana by the fire of the third eye; then, at the request of Rati, the restoration of Madana to life by Śaṅkara in the form of Anaṅga (the bodiless one). Furthermore, the description of Pārvatī’s undertaking of penance for the sake of attaining Śiva, following the instruction of Nārada who had returned to the Himālaya mountains; the testing of her steadfastness by Śiva, who approached Pārvatī while she was engaged in penance in the guise of a brahmin; and finally, the consolation of Pārvatī by Śiva, who, being well-pleased, revealed his own true form.

Then follows the invitation of all the gods to the great festival of Śiva and Pārvatī; there, Śrī Dakṣa arrives having assumed the form of a goat; there, the Daityas such as Tāraka and others who have assembled are driven away to their respective abodes by the mere utterance of the syllable "Hakāra" by Śiva; then all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, return to the wedding grounds; thereafter, in the presence of all the gods, [Pārvatī...]

The offering of the Vairaṇamāḍa to the feet of Śrī Daṅkara; thereafter, preceded by the approval of Brahmā and the other gods, a description of the festive rites for the marriage of Rukmiṇī and Vaitaya according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.

Following the wedding, Śiva went with Pārvatī to the beautiful and splendid palace on Mount Mandara for dalliance; at that time, after the gods, terrified by the demon Tāraka, offered hymns of praise, Pārvatī entrusted Gaṇapati—who was already present upon her own body—to the gods as their ally, and Gaṇapati proceeded to incessantly wage war against the Daityas for the sake of the gods' welfare. Thereafter, the account of how the Gaṇa named Vīraka was adopted as a son by Pārvatī is described.

Then, when Śiva called Pārvatī by the name "Kātī" in a joking manner during their mutual conversation, she became angry and rebuked Śiva with words that struck at his most sensitive points. Thereupon, as Pārvatī was departing from her residence, she issued a command to the attendant named Vīraka to prevent any other woman from entering Śiva’s presence. Taking Gaṇapati with her, she then [departed] toward Himavat along with her own childhood friend.

The command given by Kṛtadrumāmodinī to another woman, who was going to Śiva’s hermitage, to announce her entry; then, the creation of obstacles by that woman; and in this very interval, the arrival of the Daitya named Andhaka in the form of Pārvatī near Śiva, and his being questioned by Śiva regarding her.
Thus it is said.

Vṛddha-vākya: Having perceived the illusion, Śiva, amidst his own attendants, suddenly assumed a phallic form and killed him through sexual union; then, at that very moment, Vāyu whispered into Pārvatī’s ear near Śiva, uttering the sound "anthasīpra-verāvāra"; hearing this, Pārvatī bestowed a curse upon the Vīraka-gaṇa.

The departure of Śiva in the form of a lion from the root of her breast; the arrival of Brahmā near Pārvatī as she was performing penance; the granting of a boon to the Goddess by Brahmā; thereafter, the emergence of a goddess of golden complexion from the body of Goddess Pārvatī; the naming of her Kārtikeya; then, the restoration of Pārvatī’s former whiteness; and then, Pārvatī’s journey toward the presence of Śiva, where she was sung of by the Vīraka-gaṇa stationed at the gate.

Then follows the entry [of Vīraka] inside and his reporting [of the events]; having heard Vīraka’s words, Pārvatī feels remorse, thinking, "I have given this curse to him in vain"; thereafter, Pārvatī recounts her own story to Vīraka and grants him the boon of obtaining the son of Śilāda, Nandin, as a husband.

The goddess, having approached Śiva, engaged in dalliance with him; thereafter, the commencement of the amorous union between Śiva and Pārvatī took place. Therein, at the request of the gods, Mahādeva urged Agni—who had arrived in the form of a pigeon—to consume his semen. By that command, Agni consumed the seed. Then, seeing her husband desiring the wives of the sages, Svāhā, assuming the forms of the six Kṛttikās—the wives of the six sages—approached Agni from his side through the power of desire.

Having taken the semen according to the sequence of the six spokes, its deposition in the *Ṛarartamba* [fire]; the consolation by a voice from the sky of Agni, who was tormented by grief due to exhaustion from union with the wives of the sages; then, by Agni, the casting of the glance of the goddess upon the son within the sacrificial pit situated in the midst of the reed-thicket atop Mount Śveta; the account of the conduct of the six wives of the six sages; then, Viśvāmitra’s arrival near Kumāra and the offering of praise to Kumāra with one hundred and eight names; and [the account] of Skanda-Kumāra by the great sage Viśvāmitra.

Following the performance of the birth rites (*jātakarma*) and other ceremonies, the rite of naming (*nāmakaraṇa*) was performed; then, after the Lord gazed upon the Kumāra with affection and joy, he bestowed a name upon him. Thereafter, the Kumāra was beheld by Indra and the other gods; then Śiva and Pārvatī, having returned to the Kumāra, felt parental affection for him. Finally, the Kumāra brought joy to all by fulfilling their every desire.

This is the description of the consecration of Kumāra as the commander-in-chief of the army of the gods at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, where the *tārakāstra* (the star-missile) was present. Kumārasvāmin made a vow to slay the demon Tāraka; having gone toward the city of Tārakāsura with all the divine troops, Kumāra fought, and Nārada was dispatched against Tārakāsura. At that moment, the sound of Kumāra’s victorious drum was heard from the mountain of Kṛmijaya, which had been ascended by Gavākṣa and was being shaken by the Kinnaras.

**Hearing** (Chapters, Subjects, Verses): Having heard the hymn of praise to Kumāra being sung by the Kinnaras, Tārakāsura, having resolved upon the slaughter of the Rākṣasas who had approached him, consulted with his ministers; following this, he marched out from his own city for the purpose of battle with the gods after preparing the entire Daitya army. Then followed the commencement of the conflict between the gods and the Daityas. In that terrible battle, [the account of] the defeat of the Daitya host by the army of Tārakāsura at the hands of Lord Kumāra, and then, in the presence of Tārakāsura, of Lord Kumāra...

The positioning for the purpose of battle; the non-compliance of Kumārasvāmin with Viṣṇu’s instruction despite his being a devotee of Śiva; at that juncture, Viṣṇu’s instigation of the gods, beginning with Rudra, against the demon Tāraka; the arising of Kumārasvāmin’s desire to slay the demon Tāraka upon seeing him approaching Śaṅkara; and thereafter, Kumāra’s departure from Mount Meru for the sake of killing Tāraka, having set out toward him with his head.

Having observed that Śakti had departed, he discharged his own Śakti against the powerless Tārakāsura and brought about his slaughter; thereafter, at the request of Kera, he reduced to ashes the Krauñca mountain, which was filled with Bāṇa and other Daityas as well as Vyākha and others, by means of his own Śakti. Following this, there is a description of the joy of victory celebrated by the gods, Gandharvas, and others for Kumārasvāmin.

The description of Kumārasvāmin’s grieving due to the fear of sin arising from the killing of Rudra-bhakta by the slaughter of the demon Tāraka; thereafter, the account of how Kumārasvāmin, having had three divine *liṅgas* fashioned by Viśvakarman at the command of Mahāviṣṇu, installed within them the *liṅgas* of Pratiṣṭheśvara and Chidreśvara; and finally, the installation of the *liṅga* brought by Brahmā under the name Umāriśvara by Kumārasvāmin.

After Kumāra’s crossing over, he hears the procedure for the worship of Śiva from the Roka; Kumāra offers praise to Kumāreśvara-Mahādeva; Kumāreśvara grants a boon to Kumārasvāmin; following a description of the eternal presence of Jagadambā in the vicinity of Kumāreśvara, she grants a boon to Kumārasvāmin; thereafter, Kapardi-Gaṇeśvara grants a boon; and Kumārasvāmin remains stationed at the side of Kumāreśvara.

Description of the Greatness of Kumāreśvara Mahādeva situated at the Confluence of the Mahī and the Ocean. Now, following the prayer of the gods, [the Lord] established a pillar of victory (*jayastambha*) at the confluence of the Mahī and the Ocean; on top of that, he installed a third *liṅga* fashioned by Viśvakarman, which was named after the pillar, and constructed the Kūpa Tīrtha. [This is followed by] the description of the greatness of Stambheśvara. Index of Chapters: Chapter 1: Description of the Confluence of the Mahī and the Ocean. [Subsequent chapters follow... [End of Chapter] [The text continues with further details regarding the sacred sites and their glories.]

The installation of tens of millions of *liṅgas* by deities such as Jadyendra, Radra, and Pāṇmukha, and their majesty; then, the description of the life-story of the Siddha named Mahākāṭha; therein, the glorification of the greatness of Māṇṭi, a resident of Vārāṇasī, and the account of the five *liṅgas* beginning with Siddhāmbikā, Siddhakūpa, and Siddheśvara.

Although the fetus remained in the womb of the great sage’s wife Caṭikārī until the end of the fourth month, due to the occasion of the majesty of Barbarīkā, the account of the life of the maiden Kumārikā—the immortal girl who is the cause of the destruction of the Komaṛika-khaṇḍa—was narrated; and seeing that the fetus had not yet emerged from the womb, Māṇḍitā issued a command for its delivery by means of a surgical incision.

Having observed the fetus's lack of desire to emerge from the womb due to the fear of birth and the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), Māṇṭi offered propitiation to Śiva; [the text then contains] a description of the origin of the world through the union of the *tattvas*, the dimensions of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), and the manner in which the universe is situated within the *mūrdha* (the crown of the head). ...

Then, O Lord, for the sake of comforting that child within the womb, Śiva—having previously established his residence in the sky by swallowing the entire extent of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) through his own manifestation, and having commanded his own powers (vibhūtis) to act—comforted the child with his own manifestations beginning with Dhara. When this consolation had been performed, the birth of the infant occurred from the womb-chamber; and after some time, that child, having swallowed the entire extent of the cosmic egg, descended into the netherworld (pātāla).

A description of the various hells situated below the surface of the earth; a description of the tortures experienced by those who committed specific sins within their respective hells; likewise, a description of the entire Brahmāṇḍa, including its inhabitants such as the gods and the Vasus; similarly, a narration of the supreme majesty of Maheśvara, who possesses the splendor of an infinite number of Brahmāṇḍas; then, a discourse on the measurement of time; and thus, [a description] of the entire creation consisting of the Vedhas and the Prapañca.

Description of the established order; then, in the context of explaining the cause for the birth of a girl with a camel’s face among the nine children of Ratnaśṛṅga—the son-in-law of Araṭa, the son of Ṛṣabha—there is the narration of how she immediately attained a beautiful face through the casting of her own hair into the confluence of the Mahī and Sāgara rivers during a previous birth, following the recollection of that past life's events; and by that girl, the establishment of the Vakra-edā [the crooked-edā].

The description of the granting of boons by Vaka-reśāna to his daughter named Kumārī; the narration of how that region became famous by the name of that division—known as the *Kaumāra-khaṇḍa*—due to the granting of one of the nine divisions of Bharata-khaṇḍa to his daughter Kumārī; the enumeration of the number of cities of the gods located within Bharata-khaṇḍa; and the pillar [of history] recording how that Kumārī, having divided her own portions among her brothers and sons according to their respective numbers, bestowed them upon them.

Having returned to the sacred ford (tīrtha), [the narrative describes] the attainment of the boon from Bhavānī, who was highly pleased by the performance of the Kumāraśadharakumāreśvara rite; through that increase [of merit], the description of the excellent Siddha named Mahākārṇa situated on the bank of the Sarasvatī, as well as the wife of Mahākāla; the description of the excellence of Citralekhā, an Apsaras, attained through the power of her penance; and the description of the majesty of the Liṅga of Vṛṣeśvara.

While Kālabhīti was performing penance beneath a *vilva* tree at Kāśmīrapura, Śaṅkara approached him in human form and, having filled a hollow with the big toe of his foot, created a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) and revealed his own true form. Then, at the request of Kālabhīti, the Lord remained there in the form of a great *liṅga*. Because Kālabhīti was liberated through the grace of the Great Liṅga, and following the prayer for the boon of Mahākāla, the Lord Mahākāla, by his grace, appeared in the form of Nandikeśvara.

Description of the account of the return from the encounter with Pratihāra Satavagra; then, by Mahākāla, the description of the instruction on the nature of Dharma, the four ages (*caturyuga*), the established order, and other religious duties to King Karandhama.

Then follows the removal of the doubts of the devotees of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Revā as requested by Karaṃdhama; an extensive exposition on the various types of karmas and their fruits; a concise description of the procedures for Śiva-pūjā according to the scriptures; a description of the eternal conduct and virtuous practices; and finally, an account of the Mahākālasiddha’s departure for the world of Śiva.

Now follows the description of the account regarding the majesty of Vāsudeva as brought forth by Nārada; in that context, the movement of the Aitareya and other minor [Vedic] branches is described. Furthermore, there is the account of the birth of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, who was born from the womb of a wife named Itarā to a Brāhmaṇa named Māṇḍu—belonging to the Hārotā lineage residing on the bank of the confluence of the Mahī and the Ocean—who, despite being a perfected soul (*siddha*) in a previous life, assumed a state of muteness in this present birth and remained constantly devoted to the silent recitation (*japa*) of the Lord’s mantra within the temple of Hari.
