The granting of boons by the Lord Tārāyaṇa, who was pleased by the exceedingly sweet hymns of praise; the marriage of the Brāhmaṇa Agavalrasapadinitrayan; the description of the gift of a village after the enjoyment of all the pleasures of the earth; ... [the account of the story of the image of Mādhvāditya-Sūrya established by Nārada at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean].

The description of the ritual for the worship of the Sun according to the rules through contact with the *talmasa*; the narration of the eightfold divine methods, such as the ordeal by heated axe (*kṛtapāṣāṇa*), which produce immediate conviction regarding the Lord Āditya; the performance of the *cakrāṅka* (branding with the discus) upon the merchant Nandabhadra by the deity installed at Kapi; and the description of the merchant Nandabhadra’s excellent conduct and pure lifestyle, preceded by a reflection on the worthlessness of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). The True Dharma...

While Nandabhadra, who was devoted to the practice of the *Cāraṇas*, was suffering due to his wife’s son Nāra, a certain Nāstika named Satyavrata, living nearby, offered long-standing instruction with the intent of causing a rift in his understanding; consequently, Nandabhadra—having refuted those opposing doctrines and established the true nature of the Deity—returned to the Bahūdaka hermitage at Bhadraṭarāka to practice the true Dharma.

Having worshipped the Lord residing on Mount Kailāsa with great devotion, Nandabhadra prepared to renounce his own body; however, as he was about to leap from the mountain peak, he was approached by a certain Brahmin son who was suffering from a severe disease. This Brahmin offered instruction in spiritual knowledge (*jñāna*) to Nandabhadra. Then, at the request of Nandabhadra, the Brahmin recounted the narrative of his own life and experiences. Having heard this instruction from the Brahmin, Nandabhadra became deeply gratified, and according to the teacher's advice, he [prepared to give] the preceptor’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*).

The description of the account of the installation of Bālāditya by Gurunandin; the description of the installation of the fourteen great goddesses (Mahārākīs), such as Siddhāvikā, along with their retinues, by Nārada for the purpose of protecting the Vahūdaka Tīrtha; the description of the majesty of all those Mahārākīs; the description of the majesty of Somanātha; therein, the description of the account of the Brahmin named Ayaṭapraṣṭeya of Cauḍaderī; and the description of how those two, intent on going to the Prabhāsa-kṣetra to behold Somanātha, were delayed on the way due to extreme exhaustion.

The greatness of Somanātha as manifested through the grace of the two wandering [sages] on the middle path; the description of the greatness of the Somakuṇḍa bath and the cave of Somanātha at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; the description of the greatness of the pilgrimage to Dāṭakeśvara...

Chapter [X]: Subjects. Page [X]. In the context of describing the majesty of the various holy places (*tīrtha*) situated in Mahīnagara established by Nārada, there is a description of the majesty of Jayāditya. Therein, when Nārada, having gone to the Sūryatāḍaka lake for the purpose of seeing Sūrya-Nārāyaṇa, offered praise to the Brāhmaṇas residing in Mahīnagara established by himself, Sūrya-Nārāyaṇa, desiring to grant a boon to those Brāhmaṇas present there, arrived in the guise of a guest. There, he sought a supreme vessel for the discussion of knowledge.

The narration of the account of how Bhāskara attained extreme satisfaction through the Lord Sūrya by providing very clear answers to the questions regarding the motion of the soul established in the Vaiśākhrīya-siddhānta by Kamaṭha, the son of Harīta, who was eight years of age. Next, the thorough answering of Bhāskara’s question concerning the definition of the ten bodies (*daśa-deha-lakṣaṇa*) by the one named Kamaṭha, through the statement of the definitions of the bodies established by his own branch of scripture; and, in connection with that, the description of the soul’s movement according to the Pāratantrika doctrine.

Then, by means of the narration of the ripening of the karma of the merchant Sarākhagrahaṇa—who was performing various meritorious acts for the sake of his son Kamaṭa—the Lord Bhāskara provided a correct answer; in connection with that, he gave an exposition on the Dharma. Delighted by hearing the correct answer given by the Lord, Bhāskara declared his own name, preceded by the granting of prosperity to his son Praśasti and other prominent citizens residing in that city, such as Hārīta. Then...

Due to the preeminence of the Brahmins, the Lord Bhāskara, known by the name Jayāditya, established his permanent residence in that city of Mahīnagara; the praise of Jayāditya by Kamaṭha through the *Aṣṭaka-stotra*; the granting of a necklace to Kamaṭha by the Lord Bhāskara, as well as the granting of boons to the Brāhmaṇas there; and the description of the great majesty of Jayāditya.

Next, the description of the account regarding the majesty of Koṭitīrtha established by Brahmā at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; the majesty of Īśvara, Bharadvājeśvara, Gautameśvara, and others situated near Koṭitīrtha; and, in the context of describing the Ahalyā-saras, the narration of the account concerning Indra’s flight, his laughter, and so forth.

Then follows the majesty of Rākṣā, preceded by the account of the installation of the image of Madahīsakhāgarasa, the protection of the site established by Nārada, and the arrangement of the branches of the Niṣpurusa; then the majesty of the Nāradīya-sarovara and Nāgeśvara; and further, the description of the majesty of Dvārakottarahārakā.

Chapter 1: Subjects of the First Chapter; Subjects of the Second Chapter; Chapter 3: The Account of the Establishment of the Sage Nārada at the Confluence of the Mahī and the Ocean, and in connection with that, the Encounter between Vābhravya and Arjuna; Chapter 4: The Entrance into the Palace of Kāmakaraṭaṅkā by Ghaṭotkaca; Chapter 5: [The account] of Kāmakaraṭaṅkā with Ghaṭotkaca.

Through Bābhravya, by means of the pretext of installing the image of Nārada made of *arjuna* wood, and preceded by the narration of the dialogue between Ugrasena and Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [the king] was rendered speechless by the Lord via the narration of unprecedented stories while remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Then, for the sake of removing the distress of Ugrasena through the means of war, preceded by the narration of the praise of Nārada, the performance of the hymn of the eight verses to Nārada (*nāradāṣṭaka*) is described; [and finally], having defeated that Kāmakaṭakaṭā and having mounted upon her back.

The narration of the worship of Nārada by Ghaṭotkaca in the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍavas; the description of the majesty of Nārada. ... His arrival; then the marriage of Ghaṭotkaca and Kāmakaṭaṅkaṭā. Then, in the forest of Hiḍimba, Ghaṭotkaca, having heard from the mouth of Vābhravya the majesty of Nārada, went to the sacred field of Rāptakṣetra preceded by a vow and established his kingdom as a Rākṣasa king; [the account] of Ghaṭotkaca in the city of Kāmakaṭaṅkaṭā.

The bending of the eyebrows out of a desire to hear the account of the daughter named Barbarīkā; the narration by Nārada to Arjuna of the greatness of the goat of Gotameśvara situated at Guptakṣetra; and, in the course of that narration, a detailed description of the nature and characteristics of the principles of Yoga. ... ... |

Then follows Ghaṭotkaca’s departure for the city of Dvārakā to see Śrī Kṛṣṇa, taking his son Bāṇa with him; then the description of the greatness of the Lord of Brahma-saras (Brahmeśvara) located at Mahīnagara-kāpyūta; then the account of the liberation of Akrūra—also known as Mokṣeśvara—from the serpent [Kāliya], following the duties of a Kṣatriya, preceded by a brief exposition of the fourfold dharma by Śrī Kṛṣṇa to Bādarāyaṇa, and including the establishment [of the deity] by Nārada.

The bestowing of the name Sudṛḍhada on Kavaṭaprāpta for the purpose of worshipping the Goddess, following instruction; and then, by the instruction of Śrīkṛṣṇa, the greatness of Kedāra Caranīṭakaṇṭha.

Having come to the burnt *ṣaṭī* at the *Ghaprakṣetra* with his compassionate wife, he performed the propitiation of the goddesses; then, by the permission of the well-pleased goddesses, the description of the reason for which that region of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean acquired the name *Ghaprakṣetra* is told. While staying right there out of compassion for the people, during the spring season (*madhūpaka*) in the world of Brahmā, while in the company of the one named Vijaya—a leader of the Āgama—and in the presence of Siddhāmbikā, during the occasion of describing the greatness of the sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrthakṣetra*).

Upon arriving at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, as he set out to accomplish the Great Vidyā, Suhaṭa and others provided assistance to ward off obstacles. While [the rite] was being performed by his own mouth and his own attendants, Dharma—the eldest son of Brahmā—caused its non-publication for him. [Then follows] the description of how, at the outset of the accomplishment of the Great Vidyā, Vijayan Brāhmaṇa performed the worship of Gaṇeśvara.

The granting of the gift; then, following the hearing of those words of the curse, Guha’s arrival there and his recounting of the dream as told by him; then the description of the origin of Gaṅgeśvara Kṣetrapāla; the description of the ritual procedures for the worship of Kṣetrapāla and others; then the departure [of the deity] by chariot; then Dhamaṇa’s seeking forgiveness for his transgression from Guha with hymns of praise; the attainment of the Vaṭayākṣiṇī-vidyā by the Brahmin Vijaya at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean;
and thereafter, the attainment of the Aparājitā-mahāvidyā...

[The narrative begins with] the description of the origin of the place known by the name Stambhatīrtha, which is famous for its form as a *kaṣatra* (a sacred site), preceded by an account of its history. Then, at the end of the first watch of the night, after the killing of the great *jihvārākṣasī* who had arrived to create obstacles, there is the narration of the greatness of the confluence of the Mahī and the Sāgara—also known by the synonym Ghaṭotkara—and the account of Arjuna’s completion of his pilgrimage to the holy sites (*tīrthayātrā*). Following that, [there is the account of] Damana, the son of [Arjuna], and then, at the time of midnight, [the arrival] of one who had come to create obstacles.

The description of Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Bhiṣma; his subduing by Arjuna’s son, Sutasoma; then, at the end of the third watch, the arrival of the one named Duhśalā for the sake of arranging the marriage; then the majesty of Siddhāmbikā, the goddess of Siddheśvara; in connection with that, the meeting of Ghaṭotkaca—the son of Bhīma—known as such, with the Pāṇḍavas during their pilgrimage to the Pāṇḍava-tīrtha; then the consultation regarding the wedding festivities of the Pāṇḍavas with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Then, having heard the account of the woman named Kāmakaṭaṅkaṭā from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Ghaṭotkaca’s marriage to her was arranged following his victory; with the permission of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the others, Ghaṭotkaca set out for Prāgjyotiṣapura. When she was slain by him with great compassion, the fame of his prowess as a slayer of enemies was proclaimed at that very spot. Then, in the fourth watch of the night, [he encountered] one who had arrived to cause obstacles...

[The killing of] the Daitya Paṭāśīna, who was wearing the guise of a Kṣapaṇaka, together with his nine crores of Daitya armies, by Bhīmaputra Sṛhṛdaya after he had followed him into the cave of Pātāla; and furthermore, the gratification of the Nāgaras by that slaying of the Daitya as they heard of it.

The granting of a boon for the sake of happiness; then, having descended to the earth by the path prepared by the daughters of the *nāgas* who worship the jewel-peaks situated in the underworld (*pātāla*), the arrival of Siddhāmbikā before the Brahmin named Vijaya standing in front of her; thereafter, the bestowing of blessings upon Sudṛḍhadayā by the Brahmin Vijaya, who was highly pleased due to his attainment of the perfection of all great vidyās; and then, for the purpose of protecting the Pāṇḍavas in the future battle—

By the permission of the gods and goddesses, Siddhasena performed the naming ceremony for Sudṛḍhadaya, beginning with the reception of the vermilion, sacred ash from the *vijaya-homa*, and other auspicious rites. Now, while Siddhasena remained in the presence of the Goddess Siddhāmbikā, intent on her worship, Bhīma—extremely distressed by the hardships of forest life—stood before the Goddess among the Pāṇḍavas and entered the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Upon this, Siddhasena became exceedingly enraged.

After Bhīma engaged in battle with him, he was worn out by Bhīmasena; then, as Siddhasena was about to seize Bhīmasena and cast him into the ocean, the blessed Lord Rudradeva approached him in the sky and described to Siddhasena that Bhīmasena was his grandfather. Upon hearing those words of Rudra, Siddhasena felt remorse and asked for forgiveness for the offense committed against Bhīmasena, after which Bhīmasena embraced his own grandson. Then...

Siddhasena, despondent due to the fault of his offense against his grandfather, set out toward the ocean intending to give up his life; Bhīmasena also followed after him in order to prevent that. Then, by the goddesses Siddhāmbikā and others, together with Rudra, Siddhasena was consoled and given the name Caṇḍiṭa. Bhīma, accompanied by Caṇḍiṭa, went into the presence of Yudhiṣṭhira and the other Pāṇḍavas and reported the entire account of what had occurred.

The Description of the Greatness of the Excellent Rudra-liṅga Established by Bhīma as Bhīmeśvara; then, having heard the hymn to Siddhāmbikā composed by Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena rebukes Yudhiṣṭhira for his devotion to praising women; subsequently, due to that contemptuous disregard for a woman, Bhīmasena suffers a physical deformity, whereupon Bhīma composes a hymn to Siddhāmbikā, the Mother of the World, to seek forgiveness for his transgression; thereafter, the Mother of the World grants him a boon; then, [the account] of Duryodhana’s...

By means of various manifestations, there is a diversity of names and locations such as Lohāṇāsthaka, Keṭeśvarī, Durgāvatteśvarī, Gayatā, and so forth; therein, after describing the presence [of the deity] in that sacred site (kṣetra), there is the granting of fearlessness to all the Pāṇḍavas, followed by the performance of a pilgrimage after first installing the image of Veerīka for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas in that very place. Om Om Om Kai Kai.

Which chapters and what are their subjects? Now, after thirteen years, when the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas had returned to the field of battle with their armies for the purpose of regaining their respective kingdoms following their forest exile.

When the enumeration of heroes capable of slaying their own kinsmen and armies had reached its conclusion, Ghaṭotkaca’s son, Caṇḍaṭa—having previously made a vow before the Goddess to display his extraordinary prowess by giving away his own body—discharged an arrow that was joined with a mass of clouds of all his own weapons, which were as brilliant as the sun, in order to give away his life; by this discharge of the arrow, he caused the destruction of his entire army. Then, for all of them...

While a great cry of "Well done! was breaking out from Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, preceded by a surge of grief, Kṛṣṇa suddenly severed the head of Ghaṭotkaca’s son with his own discus. Then, as Kṛṣṇa cut off that head, the Siddhas on that battlefield spoke these words concerning the Pāṇḍavas and others who were overwhelmed with sorrow, and regarding Ghaṭotkaca himself.

The arrival of the fourteen goddesses, beginning with Ambikā; their consolation of everyone after recounting the story of the Yakṣa named Suvarcās, who had been born as Caṇḍīḍa through his own past deeds; then, the description by Śrī Kṛṣṇa of how that head was severed; and finally, the immortalization of that head by the Goddess through the sprinkling of nectar.

Then, Śrī Kṛṣṇa granted a boon to Caṇḍīra, who was in the form of a head; then, by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Barbarīka ascended a mountain peak near the battlefield and observed the battle between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas; then, the conclusion of the great Bhārata war.

Immediately thereafter, after Śrī Kṛṣṇa—acting through the mouth of Barbarīka and being a certain Supreme Person whose form is non-different from Hari—had confirmed that the entire army had been destroyed by another Supreme Person, he related the account of how Bhīma’s pride was removed by the respectful handling of the skull-bowl of Baka, who had been standing in the sky. Then, having arrived at the field of battle, Śrī Kṛṣṇa granted a boon to Ghaṭotkaca’s son, Varbarīka. Then...

The Praise of Barbarīka; the Greatness of the Worship of Barbarīka; then the Greatness of Kedreśvara located in Mahīnagara; the Greatness of Atraiśvara; the Greatness of Nīṭakeśvara; the Greatness of Jayāditya; and thus the declaration of the fruits resulting from hearing, reciting, and so forth, concerning the Greatness of the Milk-Ocean at the confluence of the Madī, which is another name for the Guptakṣetra consisting of seven thousand *karas*. Thus ends the second section, the Kaumārikākhaṇḍa, within the Madaśavarakhaṇḍa.

Speak, O Vaṭaka! Herein, in the third section concerning the greatness of Aruṇācala within the Mahiṣmaśvara-khaṇḍa, the subjects are: the conclusion of the previous chapter; the description of the stationary and moving forms of Āruṇācala; and the description of the identity between the stationary and the moving. Thus ends the first part of the greatness of Aruṇācala.

The introduction of the dialogue between Brahmā and Sanaka at the commencement of Sūta’s narration of the *Aruṇācala-māhātmya* in response to the request of the Ṛṣis dwelling in the forest of Nābhi; the description of the commencement of the narration of the majesty of Aruṇācaleśvara by the Blessed Brahmā—preceded by meditation upon the Tejasa-Śivaliṅga—at the request of Sanaka, who had inquired out of a desire to hear the majesty of the Tejasa-Śivaliṅga; and therein, the purification of Viṣṇu and Brahmā.

While the two were fighting against one another, preceded by mutual insults and threats, the Lord appeared between them in the form of a pillar of fire, and through His speech they were diverted from their combat. Then, having gone in the form of a boar to the bottom of that infinite Lord who was a pillar of fire in order to determine its lower limit, Viṣṇu, being unable to find the end of the Infinite One, fell into despair; immediately thereafter, he returned to the original spot. [He likewise went] to determine its upper limit.

After Brahmā, having assumed the form of a swan, became despondent because he was unable to find the end of Ananta—that is, to determine his limit—he learned of Ananta’s true infinity from the words of the Siddhas residing in the upper world. Then, returning to the rear, he stood before the Blessed One and described the situation.

Oṃ Bha. Now follows the hymn of praise to the Blessed One consisting of the Pillar of Fire (Vahni-stambha) by Brahmā and Viṣṇu; then the granting of boons to Brahmā and Viṣṇu by the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) who consists of the Pillar of Fire; the description of His own form by the Supreme Lord as the Pillar of Fire at the request of Brahmā and Viṣṇu; and therein, the description of the deeds of the Lord of Aruṇādri, including how the Goddess, the Mother of the World, once closed Her three eyes during play with Śiva in secret. Of Śaṅkara—

When the three eyes of Pārvatī, which resembled the moon, the sun, and fire, were covered by her knitting her brows, there occurred an untimely dissolution of the entire world. At that time, the Siddhas—whose splendor was augmented by their penance and whose vision was the eye of wisdom born from the shade of the penance-tree—perceived that this was the manifestation of Sāmbasadāśiva. Having heard the hymn of praise offered by the Siddhas with folded hands, and perceiving through his own divine power that the time for the destruction of the world had been exceeded by the measure of ten million days, [he withdrew his wrath].

When it was said, "O Daughter of the Mountain, you have committed this unworthy act," Pārvatī performed a penance to remove the sin born of causing the destruction of the world; once that penance had been completed, the Blessed One instructed her in the teachings of the nine chapters [of the Śiva Purāṇa] and granted her permission to perform further austerities. Then, by the command of Śrī Śaṅkara, Pārvatī went to Kāmatantra on the bank of the river Kampā in Kāñcīpurī for the purpose of performing penance. [...]

Then, at the foot of an *ekāmra* tree situated on the bank of the Kampā river, Pārvatī established a sand *śivaliṅga* and performed austerities while following her own religious duties; thereafter, Śaṃkara [appeared].

In order to test her firm devotion, when the Goddess was completely overwhelmed by the flood of a river in spate, she firmly grasped a *śivaliṅga* made of sand; even as she was being swept away by the current of the flood, she did not abandon the *liṅga* and go elsewhere. Due to Pārvatī’s firm embrace, the *liṅga* made of sand was described as being marked with the seal of the impression of Pārvatī’s nipple. Then, after the Goddess was consoled by a voice from the sky, a boon was granted for the worship of that *liṅga* made of sand.

Having bestowed [the boon], she went toward Aruṇācala and granted permission for the performance of penance according to the instruction of Gautama. Then, the Goddess Pārvatī gave orders to the gods and the ṛṣis who had arrived there at the bank of the Kāverī river for the purpose of seeing her and for service, to worship the earthen Śiva-liṅga. Thereafter, Pārvatī proceeded with all the gods toward the hermitage of the great sage Gautama on Mount Aruṇādri.

Then follows the hospitable reception of Pārvatī by the great sage Gotama; at the request of Pārvatī, the great sage Gautama’s description of the majesty of Aruṇācala; and, in connection with that, a description of the account of the majesty of Bahāpuṣkara. [Next is] a detailed description, preceded by their respective accounts, of the various sacred sites (tīrthas) established at Aruṇācala by the hosts of gods beginning with Śrī Mahāviṣṇu, as well as by the hosts of great sages and royal sages.

Then, when asked by Pārvatī the reason for the presence of the word *upaśānta* at the end of the name of the Liṅga made of cloud-stone (*abhramaya*), the Lord sang this hymn, which describes the different names of Īśvara according to the four ages (*yuga*).

Therein is the description of the incident concerning the Lord Śītaṭaṭārka, who was praised by the gods; then follows the account of the descent of the eight holy sites situated in the eight directions, established by the eight World-Guardians (Lokapālas) at Aruṇācala; and then the description of the unification of all those holy sites by the Lord Maheśvara at the request of Mārkaṇḍeya. Next, having heard the greatness of the holy sites, Pārvatī, being highly pleased, initiates a dialogue with the Great Gautama out of a desire to know the worship of the illustrious Supreme Lord.

Then, with great devotion, Gautama related to Pārvatī his own account beginning with the grace of Śrī Śaṅkara-Naṭeśvara; [this is] the description of the greatness of the worship of Śrī Śaṅkara-Bharatāgamokta-Sarvārthasādhaka-Naṭeśvara.

The description of the various names of Śoṇādri by Śrīṅkara; then, the narration of the greatness of the circumambulation of Śoṇādri; in connection with the greatness of the circumambulation of Śoṇādri, the account of King Dharmaketu; the description of the greatness of offering various services to the Lord; and [the account of] Gautama bringing the Lord and the Goddess named Pārvatī, who is also called Apītakacchā, to his own presence for her initiation into asceticism.

The narration of the future events beginning with the [Bhagavān’s] return, and the instigation of the goddess Pārvatī; then, the description of how Pārvatī, having performed her penance and being encouraged by Gautama, settled for some time within the Naimiṣa forest at Gautama’s hermitage and engaged in ascetic practice according to the prescribed rules; and finally, the arrival of all the gods, headed by Indra, who were terrified of Mahiṣāsura, before the Goddess as she was performing penance there. In the *Indrādipadaprada* [chapter]:

Having perceived the dejection of the gods upon seeing their own terror caused by the demon Mahiṣāsura, the Goddess made a vow for the sake of slaying Mahiṣāsura and brought comfort to the gods. When the gods had departed after receiving consolation from the Goddess, she established four Caṇḍeśvaras on the mountains in the four directions surrounding her own self for the purpose of providing protection. Furthermore, she issued a command for her four personal attendants to go to Aruṇādri very quickly. Thus it is.

Having established the arrangement, Pārvatī performed penance in the vicinity of Gautama’s hermitage; then, due to the power of Pārvatī’s penance, the description of universal tranquility in that hermitage follows; then, once upon a time, [the story] of Mahiṣāsura as a deer...

The meaning is as follows: first, the sporting on the slopes of Mount Oṇā; then, Mahiṣāsura, obstructed by the young students at the abode of the Goddess, approached her in the guise of a guest and, after offering praise, announced his intention to choose her as his bride; subsequently, the Goddess declared her resolve to Mahiṣāsura for the purpose of battle; and finally, seeing Mahiṣāsura ready for combat, that Jagadambā, who had assumed the form of a maiden, displayed her terrifying aspect.

Her manifestation in physical form; the summoning of his own army by the demon Mahiṣāsura; the Goddess’s display of various of her own weapons against the enemies; the Goddess’s command to the monkey-faced Bṛhaspati (the preceptor of the gods), who was fleeing in fear upon seeing her true form, to return and prevent [the enemy] from approaching; and hearing the Goddess’s instruction as told by Bṛhaspati, the exceedingly enraged Mahiṣāsura fought with the Goddess on the Aruṇācala mountain and was destroyed along with the entire Daitya army.

Beholding the army of the Daityas arrived, the Goddess, by means of her own splendor, caused the hosts of various beings—the Ṭāṭakās, Māṭhakās, Yoginīs, and others—to assume their forms; this is the description of the fierce battle between the army of the Daityas and the army of the Goddess. In that battle, the commencement of the fight with Mahiṣāsura is described; the subjects of the Goddess’s victory include the slaying of the demon Mahiṣa by the Goddess in their duel. Then follows the hymn of praise offered to Durgā, the slayer of Mahiṣa, by Indra and the other gods. Now...

The description of the Goddess’s hand resting upon the head of the bird [Garuḍa] while she stood upon the chest of the demon Mahiṣāsura; then, the Goddess, the Mother of the World, perceiving that the slaying of the devotee of Śiva had occurred by her own hand, makes a formal resolve for a pilgrimage to sacred sites and announces it before Gautama; thereafter, Gautama, after first pacifying the Goddess, recounts the slaying of Mahiṣāsura and describes the means for the removal of the fault of the cow, which consists of bathing at the sacred site on the peak of Aruṇācala.

Then, having fashioned Khaḍgatīrtha with his own sword while chanting the *Atharva-kaḍavā* hymns, he performed an immersion there for the duration of the month of Kārtika. On the bank of Khaḍgatīrtha, he installed the Liṅga situated upon the head of the demon Mahiṣāsura, which had fallen from his own hand. Subsequently, in the month of Kārtika under the constellation Kṛttikā, Aruṇādra manifested himself. Then, the Lord Aruṇādrīśvara, appearing in the form of light and then in the form of the Golden Person (*Hiraṇmayapuruṣa*) who has entered within that light, granted a boon to Jagadambā.

Then, the performance of circumambulation by the Mother of the World (Jagadambā) around the Lord of Aruṇādri; thereafter, the description of the meeting of the Mother of the World with the gracious Lord Śoṇādrīśvara, who is Śaṅkara; then, the application of musk-paste upon Pārvatī’s body by Śiva out of a desire to sport with her after having first granted boons to Pārvatī; the account of the origin of the musk and the narration of the life-story of the Daitya named Puṭaka; and [the story] of the tortoise that arose from the hand of the Goddess.

The narrative; the prayer addressed to Śiva by Pārvatī for the increase of the majesty of Aruṇācala, prompted by her attachment to it; the granting of a boon to Pārvatī by Śiva; and the description of the great majesty and power of Aruṇādriśvara—this concludes the first half of the third section, the *Aruṇācalamāhātmya*, within the *Māheśvarakhaṇḍa*.
Now, in the third section of the Māheśvarakhaṇḍa, the latter part of the Aruṇācala-māhātmya.

(—) In the dialogue between Sūta and Loma-harpaṇa, the commencement of the conversation between Mārkaṇḍeya and Nandīśvara; therein, the description of the introduction to the majesty of the sacred site (*sthānamāhātmya*) in the form of Mārkaṇḍeya’s prayer to Nandikeśvara, accompanied by various eminent sages, with the desire to hear the divine mysteries previously spoken [by him]. Herein, the subjects of the chapters (*adhyāya*) are as follows: [list of chapter titles/subjects].

This is the section that inspires a great desire in the assembly of the great sages (*maharṣigaṇa*) to hear [the teaching]. Now, for the purpose of ascertaining the extent of the limit of his splendor, Brahmā, assuming the form of a swan, ascended upwards. Then, after Nandikeśvara had praised Mārkaṇḍeya together with his disciples, he departed from the Draviḍa country situated in the southern direction toward the world of Śiva; there, at a very great distance from the mountain peak where Brahmā was present, he arrived.

...the detailed description of the great majesty and *māhātmya* of the sacred site of the glorious Aruṇācala-dhara; ...—[the meeting of the sages]. Then, by means of Nandikeśvara, for the sake of strengthening devotion to Śiva through the occasion of describing the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* dispositions of persons—the Lord, having been entreated by the *ketakī* flower, returned to the abode of Brahmā and [described] the ripening of various karmas... [end of fragment].

[The text describes] the offering of a *liṅga* to Viṣṇu with the juice of *ketakī* leaves; the swearing of an oath by means of false testimony; the selection of various penances for the removal of sins such as *sakaḍamaṅā*; and, in connection with this, the description of the various duties to be performed at Śrī Ghuṇācala. Then, having determined that it was untrue, Viṣṇu bathed to remove the blood-stain and for the sake of withdrawing his own splendor from Brahmā; and [finally], the performance of a hymn of praise to the Blessed One, whose nature is the form of Mayaṅiga.

... Now, on Mount Śoṇādri, Maheśvara—out of compassion for Brahmā and to accept his worship—revealed the specific rituals of worship preceded by the greatness of particular offerings, as well as the rites for fulfilling desired goals (*kāmya-dharma*), based on the distinctions of time such as the days of the week starting with Sunday, the lunar dates (*tithi*) starting from the first day (*pratipadā*), the asterisms (*nakṣatra*) starting with Aśvinī, the zodiac signs (*rāśi*) starting with Aries (*meṣa*), the divisions of the day (*ahnaḥ-pūrvāhṇa*, *madhyāhna*, *sāyāhna*), and the solstices (*ayana*) and months. Furthermore, he established the sequence whereby the *ketaka* flower petal serves as the means for his own worship. [Ha, , & and the bestowal of the curse of form. Then the hymn of praise by Brahmā and Viṣṇu. Then begins the detailed narration of the greatness of the life of the illustrious Śrī Aruṇācala Śaṅkara; therein, the offering of a hymn of praise by Brahmā and Viṣṇu to Śrī Śaṅkara; then, through the medium of the praises of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the manifestation of Brahmā and Viṣṇu from the right and left limbs of the Lord Śaṅkara, respectively, due to the qualities of *rajas* and *sattva*.]

Having first granted boons to Indra and Viṣṇu, [the Lord] again issued commands resembling the rending of his own authority; then, at the hip, he performed the joining of the bones. Thereafter, by the command of the Blessed One, Brahmā was assigned the role of sustainer (*sthitikārya*) and Mahāviṣṇu the role of creator (*sṛṣṭikārya*), and they were made to carry out those orders accordingly. Following that, under the direction of the Blessed One, Brahmā and Viṣṇu went to the Śarogācha lake; due to their subordination to authority and their forgetfulness of the Blessed One—their own source—they were deprived of their respective qualities and bodies.

[The narrative] concerning the attainment of the cows, the account of the boon, the digging of the earth, and the arrival at the abode of the Lord of Aruṇācala, preceded by the city of Aruṇa... (Ka) ...Then follows the description of the pastimes of Śiva and Pārvatī; and in the description of the events of the performed penance, there is the depiction of a great dispute between Virañci and Acyuta regarding their own superiority born of delusion, based on the pride of their respective offices.

The description of the account of the four-faced Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa [seeking] Śiva, and of the six-faced Kārttikeya. Now, as Brahmā and Viṣṇu were disputing with mutual jealousy, there appeared before them from that very place a Liṅga composed of radiant splendor, O Śaṅkara. Then, having emerged from the ear of Pārvatī who was enraged by a lover’s quarrel, the Lord manifested His own form; the description of this account of His appearance. Thereafter, [the account of] Brahmā and Viṣṇu [searching] for the upper and lower limits of that Liṅga.

The return to the hermitage of Gautama with her friends for the purpose of performing penance; then, following the instruction of Gautama, making a firm resolve to purify herself, she performed the ritual bathing at the end of the month; thereafter, in the vicinity of that hermitage, she performed penance in the form of daily worship of Aruṇācaleśvara preceded by the observance of extremely rigorous vows; and then, for the sake of cutting through the path to the lower regions of that mass of splendor, [she beheld] Viṣṇu assuming the form of a boar.
