At the command of Indrayamna, resident of the city of Ardatī, who was intent on a pilgrimage, his brother-in-law Viyāpati—his domestic priest—set out for the supreme field of Puṣpa, surrounded by Rohiṇī, Kuṇḍakalpa, Varaka, and others; on the way, there was a meeting with Śavaradaśca, as well as a conversation between Viyāpati and Dābara.

Having fasted for two days and nights, Vidyāpati saw the royal body and resolved that he would not take food without first performing the worship of the Blessed One. Knowing his determination, as Śabara was reflecting on it, he set out for the forest with Vidyāpati and proceeded to the Rohiṇī mountain. There, they beheld the Blessed One, and Vidyāpati offered hymns of praise to Him. Afterwards, the account of Vidyāpati’s preparation to depart for his own country is described; while Vidyāpati was still intent on going to his own land— [The text provided ends abruptly.]

And at an improper time, a fierce wind scattered sand from the eyes of all the gods; because their vision was thus impaired, they were deprived of the sight of the Blessed One. This is followed by a description of their praise of the Blessed One upon obtaining the opportunity to behold him. Then follows a description of the Blessed One’s own words stating that henceforth no one at all would be able to see him. After that, Vidyāpati returns to Avanti at the close of day; there, amidst the honors such as rising from his seat offered by the king, Vidyāpati [places something] around the king's neck.

The description of the superimposition of the pride of Nirmāṇapañcama; the performance of praise to the Blessed One by Vidyāpati and Indrayudha; and the description of the power of the holy sites (tīrthas) such as Puruṣottamakṣetra, Rodhasī, and Aṅkaṇī as recounted by Vidyāpati. ... , ...

The description of the state of Indradyumna, who, having reached the supreme goal through his devotion to the Lord residing within the banyan tree at Badarikāśrama and having visited many sacred sites, was distressed by a fierce wind in the evening; meanwhile, Nārada’s arrival near him, Indradyumna’s hospitable reception of Nārada, and Nārada’s narration to Indradyumna of the greatness of the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa].

"Oṃ! Having heard the words of Nārada—who said, 'Knowing that this one is eager for the sight of the Blessed Lord, I shall lead you there'—and having observed the faces of all the citizens which were filled with longing equal to that of the King himself, he took leave of his parents and, together with Nārada, set out from the city with a fourfold army accompanied by drums, kettledrums, and other instruments, in order to behold Nīlamādhava. On the way, he beheld the goddess named Caṇḍikā, who stood at the border of the Utkala country."

Description; description of the welcome offered by Indradyumna to King Oḍhra. Following their mutual conversation, Nārada—who had departed after King Oḍhra’s visit to Indradyumna—relates to Indradyumna the account of a temple of Śiva situated on a mountain peak along the way. Therein is described how Śaṅkara, while sporting with Gaurī, established the Avimukta-kṣetra near Vārāṇasī, and how King Kārīra obtained a boon from Śiva.

During the war between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Karṇa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa dispatched Sudarśana against the city of Karṇa; desiring to fight, Karṇa set fire to the city of Aṅga. Enraged by this, Śiva discharged the Pāśupata weapon at Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Having conquered the Pāśupata, when the city was consumed by fire, the terrified Śaṅkara offered hymns of praise to Viṣṇu. Pleased by the hymn, Viṣṇu commanded him, "Establish a sacred field named Puruṣottama on the shore of the ocean known as Mannāra. At Viṣṇu’s command, Śiva did so.

It is not that the establishment of the field [of Puruṣottama] was from a man; thus, by means of a heart purified by faith, he performed a hymn of praise to Puruṣottama, who is like the Veda. Then, having gone to the Ambika-field named Ekānaṅga and having worshipped Him, he performed a hymn of praise to Koṭidigīśa. By him, being pleased, the lineage of the Vāsudeva of Indradyumna was described, as well as the final dissolution into Śiva. Then, together with Nārada, Indradyumna went to the supreme abode of the Lord (Kapatin).

Having paid obeisance to the deities beginning with Viśveśvara and mounting his chariot along with Nārada, Śiva assumed the guise of a pigeon and performed worship of the Lord; by His grace, he established the shrine of Kapoteśvara. Then, seeing the earth oppressed by the Daityas residing in Pātāla, Śrī Kṛṣṇa took up the discus and performed worship of the Lord; through the grace of Tryambaka, having conquered the Asuras, he established the sacred field of Viśvarūpa.

The departure of King Daśaratha, together with his priest Vasiṣṭha and Nārada, toward the Niṣadha forest; on the way, having seen inauspicious omens such as the throbbing of the left arm, the king, deeply distressed, spoke to Nārada; [the contents include] the description of the events beginning with his return to his own city after learning of the [death of Rāma].

That Indra-dyumna went to the presence of the Blessed One in the forest of Naimiṣa; thereafter, by the instruction of Nārada, he was consoled with the promise: "Having gone to the sacred field of Puruṣottama together with you, even though the Blessed One has vanished, I shall certainly cause you to behold His form as a horse and make you eat of the Blessed One's food."...

Then, having departed from Nīrakaṇḍa to behold the Lord standing upon the water above the sacrificial rice-offering (indryanna) along with the Brahmins and Nārada, [Indradyumna] beheld the vision of Narasiṃha atop the peak of Mount Nīka; he received the grace of the Blessed One, and then, together with Nārada, he reached the sacred site of the Blessed Puruṣottama. Thereafter, he performed the praise of the Blessed One along with everyone. Pleased by the hymn of praise, the Blessed One, through an unembodied voice, [commanded] Indradyumna to perform the horse sacrifice (vājimedha).

The command "Do it," and the description of the commencement of the horse sacrifice performed by Indradyumna at the command of the Blessed Lord. (Page [number]): By the permission of Nārada, Indradyumna’s departure to the east for the purpose of installing the Narasiṃha deity; the conversation of the son of the divine architect (Viśvakarman), who, having approached the sandalwood tree, said to Indradyumna, "I shall fashion for your sake the one named Narasiṃha"; then, by the command of Indradyumna, the construction of the temple by the divine architect; and thereafter, by the hand of Nārada...

The installation of the image of Narasiṃha; a description of the hymn of praise offered by Indradyumna to the installed image of Narasiṃha; a description of the greatness of Carasiṃha. ... [Indradyumna], having praised and addressed the gods including Indra for the purpose of performing a sacrifice, conducted a great festival of the Vājimedha horse-sacrifice with the assistance of the deities. By the power of that sacrifice, Indradyumna’s splendor increased day by day, until he became arrogant and gave alms to the Lord lying on the serpent Śeṣa; [the account] regarding Nārada concerning this matter.

Nārada then gave a detailed explanation of the excellent dream he had related. Subsequently, having seen a certain tree that had suddenly appeared on the shore of the ocean near the vicinity of Viśveśvara, the king was filled with wonder; his guards then reported the account of seeing the tree to him. Following this, the sacrifice was completed with a ritual bath. Nārada then described the majesty of that tree, stating that it had been fashioned from the hairs of the Lord, and [described] its installation upon the chest.

Then, at a certain time, while Indradyumna was standing there to perform worship, he saw the form of Viṣṇu and spoke thus to Nārada: "Who indeed will fashion such a form? He thought upon this, for that king had never before seen the true form of the Lord. Having said, "I shall fashion that form," he vanished right there on that altar covered with cloth, along with his wife Rukmiṇī, who was in the form of a woman.

The king, enlightened by Nārada, performed a hymn of praise to Viṣṇu; Nārada, moreover, offered a prose eulogy to Sthāṇu, who assumes the form of the Blessed One; others as well, such as Atri and Kaśyapa, described the Blessed One; and Indrayuj worshipped the Blessed One along with his retinue using numerous mantras and sūktas. Thereafter, the king bestowed ten million cows upon the Brahmins there; then, Candrasuśreṇi began the construction of a temple for the Blessed One.

The arrival of the gods there by the command of Brahmā for the purpose of performing the consecration of the temple established by Indradyumna; and [the account of] Nārada’s desire to go to his own world, Brahmaloka, in order to invite Brahmā at the time of the consecration—after first instructing King Indradyumna in the worship of the Lord as known through the Vedas—following his hearing from a certain Brāhmaṇa reciter of the Ṛgveda a description of the greatness of the wooden person (dāruvapurmahātmya) regarding how the eating of the Lord cannot occur without the means prescribed in the Śruti and other scriptures.

The manifestation [of the desire]: even the King’s manifestation of his wish to invite Brahmā toward the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) through Nārada. Then, the departure of Indra together with Nārada toward the world of Brahmā by means of a celestial chariot (*puṣparatha-vimāna*); on the way, Nārada’s inquiry regarding the cause of the King’s sorrow to the monarch whose mind was agitated by anxieties concerning his kingdom; and having heard the cause of the King’s anxiety, Nārada’s providing of consolation to the King.

The removal of [Indradyumna’s] anxiety follows; then, after Indradyumna and Nārada have traversed all the worlds and reached the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), there is a description of the hospitality received from the gatekeepers and others. When Brahmā asks Indradyumna the purpose of his arrival, Indradyumna replies: "O Lord, please come to the temple that I am constructing so that you may be installed as the presiding deity."

Having dispatched Brahmā to the future Kakudmin, [Viṣṇu], together with the goddess Lakṣmī and the treasure of the lotus (Padmanidhi), arrived there and performed the marriage ceremony for the Lord’s portion by bestowing [him] upon Indradyumna.

After Mūta had related the account of Bahukākhasya, the Lord, together with the gods, issued a command for him to descend to the earth; he granted him consolation regarding his own arrival during the rite of installation (*pratiṣṭhā-karma*). Then, by the Lord's command, King Indradyumna returned to the earth along with the gods, Padmanidhi, and the sages.

Having taken that [image], he performed a hymn of praise to the Blessed One with the *Puruṣasūkta*. Thereafter, a voice from the sky commanded the Blessed One: "Establish the image through the medium of Padmanidhi."

The collection of materials for the construction of the chariot as recorded by Nārada; the fashioning of the golden chariot by Padmanidhi at the command of Śrī Indrayudha; the construction of the three chariots by Viśvakarman at the command of Nārada; the installation of that chariot by the hand of Nārada; a description of the procedure and method for the installation of the chariot in that context; and the description of the installation of the Lord’s form within the chariot after fashioning the figure of Garuḍa upon the chariot’s banner with mantras and performing a prayer to Garuḍa.

The description of the defects such as being "fallen" (apāta) regarding which part of the chariot was used by whom to perform the propitiation of the five Bhagavatsarās, and the description of the manner of establishing the deities of the directions after the chariot had been prepared; the description of the true nature of the Bhagavat; and the granting of boons to the worlds by the Bhagavat.

[The narrative describes] how King Gāla, together with his army, arrived there; how Indra-dyumna, the lord of the Gaṅgā, was struck with wonder upon seeing the abundance of horses brought by Indra; how he then related the entire account of his journey to the battle against Indra after having become a cloud in the sky; and how, following the conversation between the Gaṅgā and Indra-dyumna, the king of the Gaṅgā recognized Indra-dyumna as a person of pure and holy character.

Having first established [the deity] upon the throne of the *svarāñji*, Indra accepted his command. Then, a description of the arrival from the world of Brahmā to the world of Indra by Brahmā, Indra, and others, who had come to behold the divine temple constructed by Indra; thereafter, Indra’s prayer to the god Brahmā out of satisfaction at his arrival; the acceptance of the gift of chariots, palaces, and other items by the god Brahmā, followed by the composition of a hymn of praise to the Blessed One; and then, the chariot of Subhadrā.

Chapter [X]: Indra’s performance of worship for the Blessed One installed in the temple; the arrival of King Svarṇa and others; the description of the praise of Brahmā, Varuṇa, and Sumadrā after having gone there; the composition of a hymn by Babhadra; and the narration of the fruit of worshipping the three chariots.

Then, the sudden appearance of the terrifying Narasiṃha in a fearsome form was described, along with the depiction of the gods, including Indra, being struck with terror. At the word of Nārada, Brahmā recounted the manifestation of Narasiṃha; Brahmā then offered a hymn of praise to Narasiṃha. During the installation of the deities, those respective deities became visible through the mantras recited at that time and remained established in their own places. Even the Vedas and other scriptures arrived there in personified forms. Then, by the grace of Lord Viṣṇu, [Indra attained his sovereignty].

The imparting of the mantra-instruction; then the performance of pacification rites for Lakṣmī and Nṛhari; a description of the greatness of worshipping the wooden deity; the propitiation of Indra’s charioteer Mātali with the twelve-syllable mantra of Varabhadra, of Nārāyaṇa with the Puruṣasūkta, and of the Goddess with the Devīsūkta; then the composition of a hymn by the wood-cutter Badma-deva for the purpose of breaking Indra’s chariot; [the verse] "dāra pacha pṛṇa."

The chapters and their subjects: a description of the procedure for the great festival of Mahādevī, including the worship of Madhānadeva, the offering of food, and the distribution of gifts; a description of the procession after preparing the chariot and installing the image of the Lord, including the consecration of its boundaries and other rites; a description of the attainment of great fortune through the chanting of the names of Viṣṇu while seated upon the chariot; a description of the fruits of the vow of Mahādevī, including the worship of Puruṣottama, Balabhadra, and Sumadrā; and the fruit of beholding the wooden body on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha.

The greatness of the illumination of the lamp of the assembly of the virtuous; a description of the greatness of the lake-tīrtha which is an ancillary of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha); the greatness of Jindutīrtha; a description of the fruit of the ancestral rites (pitṛ-karma) performed at Mahāvedi; and a description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other acts at the tīrthas of Indradayāmnasa, Siṃhakṣetra, Vanajāgaraṇa, Vītha, Hṛṣīkeśa, and others.

The description of the chariot guards and the covering; therein, the praise of Puruṣottama, Balabhadra, and Subhadrā, and the description of the manner of their worship. (And) the description of the ritual for the festival of the lying down [of the deity] and the vow; from the full moon of Āṣāḍha until the full moon of Kārttika, during the meritorious period of the four months (*cāturmāsya*), the Lord granted a boon to Indradyumna in his wooden body; and from his own mouth, through his wooden form, he described the majesty of the sacred site (*sthānamādātmya*) according to the specific conjunctions of months, lunar days, and so forth.

A description of the fruits of recitation, charity, and other rites; a description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and so forth during the eighth month; and, preceded by a description of the greatness of the locations of Mārkaṇḍeya, Avaṭapa, Vāruṇa, Nyagrodha, Nārāyaṇa, Sīradhvaja, Syandana, Trayastha, Rudradeha, Viṣṇubala, Madra, Subhadra, and others, as well as Svargadvāra, Catur-svastika, Koṇaka, Sidhurāja, and various other sites for deities and yakṣas, a statement of the results of the performance of various rites such as hymns of praise and worship.

Then follows the description of the greatness of bathing at the Anaradrayunasa lake, including an account of attaining great fruit through the recitation of the Nṛsiṃha mantra; the greatness of beholding Puruṣottama as He resides there; the greatness of bathing at Puruṣottama during the month of Āṣāḍha; a description of the city; the washing away of various kinds of sins through bathing at the holy ford (tīrtha) during the Cāturmāsya; the fruits of bathing at the holy ford and beholding Puruṣottama and other deities; a discourse on the consideration of what items are acceptable or unacceptable during the Cāturmāsya; a description of the rules to be observed during the Cāturmāsya; and the fruit of hearing the greatness of the vows arising from this Cāturmāsya.

...a description of the sequence of observances during the meritorious period marking the commencement of the southern transit at the time of the Karka-saṃkrānti; the fruit of worshipping Puruṣottama during the southern transit; the enumeration of the names of the deities stationed in the ten directions of Puruṣottama and the description of the fruits of worshipping them accordingly; the offering of a hundred cows by Indradyumna; the worship and hymn of praise offered by King Śvetaketu to Puruṣottama and Narasiṃha; and the granting of boons to the king by the Blessed One.

The granting of boons to Śvatarāja and the disappearance of the Blessed One; the description of the fruit of consuming the remnants of the Blessed One’s meal; the description of the ritual manual for the hymn to Puruṣottama, the best of trees; the description of the fruit of seeing all desired results through the vision of Puruṣottama; the description of the fruit and greatness of seeing Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the description of the vow of the five Jyeṣṭhas; and the description of the fruit and greatness of the Puruṣottama tree born on the day of Mahājyaiṣṭhī, [accomplished] by lighting five lamps.

The description of the greatness [of the text] beginning with the injunction that the worship of Nṛsiṃha must be performed; the statement of the fruits of fasting on the full moon and new moon days, such as the drinking of the water from Kṛṣṇa’s bath and the wearing of the *nimāla*; the determination of the nature of the Kali age; the description of how fruits are obtained through meditation on the Lord in the Kali age; the description of the Lord’s nature of compassion, kindness, and so forth; the arrival of a certain twice-born man at the sacred field of Puruṣottama; and [the account of] the twice-born man, who was possessed by a spirit, regarding [the food] as the remains of the Lord’s meal—[the Lord] Bhagavān...

The narration of how the food offered by Janī was not eaten and how that led to suffering for his body; furthermore, O Blessed One, the description of other things, such as the fruit of worshipping a certain auspicious *druma* (tree) by the twice-born... (Ma)
The account of how a certain twice-born man attained a state equal to the gods by eating what was offered to him, and how he reached the Lord after abandoning his sacrificial offerings.

Liḥ Kaktiḥ: What is the essence? Having made a prayer, the narration of the immediate attainment [of the goal] through the grace of the Man-Lion (Narasimha) that arose; the narration of the origin of the Sugandhinirmala tree at the time of the battle with the demon Damanaka; and the description of the ritual for worshipping the gods, preceded by the worship of the Lord’s devotees—this is the second section, the Puruṣottama (Jagannātha) Kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.
(-) dhai ||

The contents of the chapters are as follows: first, the description of the fruits resulting from the consumption of food blessed by the lion-like [deity]; second, the narration of the attainment of the fruits of all pilgrimages through the performance of the festival of the gift-giving (dāyana), the observance of vows, and the circumambulation of the southern-facing cave; third, the description of the period for the Lord’s reclining and His turning over; fourth, the description of the ritual for the great festival of awakening known as Kausudī; and fifth, within that same section, the description of the materials required for the worship of the Blessed One.

The description of the fruit of worship; the statement that by this very worship, the practitioner attains the fruit of the consecration (abhiṣeka) on the path proclaimed by the Trika; the description of the festival of the covering (*prāvaraṇotsava*) on the sixth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, and the description of the rules and procedures for the vow of the festival of the covering; the description of the rules for the day of the vow and the festival of the *puṣya* bath; the narration of the ritual worship, the materials, and other details of the vow and festival of the *puṣya* bath; and the description of the fruit of bathing in the sacred waters and beholding the Lord at the time of the northern transit (*udagayana*), preceded by the rite of the entry into Capricorn (*makarasaṃkramaṇa*).

The description of the piercing of the sprouting pulse-beans (*dālyarohaṇāvedha*) in the month of Phālguna; the prescription for the *Sāṃvatsaravrata* on the full moon day of Phālguna; the description of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the image of Viṣṇu; the description of the *Jyeṣṭhapañcaka-vrata*; (the description of the spring festival of *Damanabhañjikā-yātrā*; the description of the *Akṣayamokṣa-yātrā*; the description of hymns (*stotra*) to the Blessed One during that pilgrimage—including the description of the Blessed One’s wooden body as it stands upon the *Nīṭaḍā* river, and its *drāṇaka* [wound] marks).

—Following the consecration of the temple, what did Indradyumna do? This [section] contains the description of the Lord’s true nature as performed by Indradyumna, the granting of a boon by the Lord, and the conclusion of the *Puruṣottama-māhātmya*. [This concludes] the chapters and topics of the hearing of the fruit of the *Māhātmya*. Now, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, the third [section]: the *Badarikāśrama-māhātmya*.
(-) || [End of section] ||

In the context of the dialogue between Sūta and Lomaśa, regarding the question "By what means may liberation be attained?", begins the dialogue with Śivaskanda. Therein, following the description of many holy places such as the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Yamunā, and Narmadā, there is the description of the greatness of Ayodhyā; then the description of the greatness of the sacred field of Ayodhyā, the description of the ritual for bathing at the Gomatī Tīrtha, the fruit of the pilgrimage to Pañcakrośī Tīrtha, and the fruit of bathing at Viśrānti Tīrtha.

The greatness of the gift of a cow at Rāmatīrtha; the description of the greatness of bathing in the Mākaṇḍaya lake preceded by the narration of its fruit; the greatness of the knowledge regarding the Indradyumna lake; the description of how all fruits are obtained through the recitation of the name of Badarī; the description of the origin and greatness of the sacred field (kṣetra) named Badarī; and the narration of the incident in which the head of Brahmā was severed by Śiva when he caused the daughter [of Dakṣa] to reunite [with her husband], ending with the holding of that skull-fragment in his hand.

Having accepted [the gift], Śiva went to all the holy fords (*tīrtha*) for the sake of removing the fault of the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*); thereafter, he went to Badarikāśrama, the hermitage of the Lord of Girijā. By going to Badarikāśrama, Śiva was freed from the sin of killing a Brahmin. Then follows a description of the Daśāśvamedha Tīrtha; by the word of Vyāsa, [Śiva] proceeded toward Badarikāśrama. There is a description of the hymn of praise (*stuti*) offered to the Blessed One, a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Abhitīrtha, and a description of the majesty of Nāradaśilā and Mārkaṇḍeyaśikhā.

The description of the majesty of the Śainateya stone; the majesty of the Vārādī stone; the offering of praise to the Blessed One there by Devadyūta and others; the majesty of the Nārasida hill-peak and the description of the Blessed One’s southern face; the sight of the Blessed One bestowing knowledge upon Vidyanāga; the gods, headed by Rahasa, offering praise to the Blessed One at the Ocean of Milk; the manifestation of the Blessed One; and the Blessed One’s disappearance after declaring, "I have withdrawn myself for fear that the pride of the sages might increase."

The establishment of the Blessed Lord by Śiva; the attainment of the fruit of gifting the entire universe (*brahmāṇḍa-dāna*) through the utterance of the name "Badarī" and the sight of Badarī; the description of the greatness of giving gifts such as feeding Brāhmaṇas at the Badarī grove; the description of the origin and history of Pitrītīrtha, Kapālamocanatīrtha, and other holy sites; the performance of penance there by Brahmā; the propitiation of the Blessed Lord who was pleased upon seeing Brahmā; and the manifestation of the Vaiṣṇava Saṅkīrtana by the grace of the Blessed Lord.

—The *Gurukalpa* of Śatakaṇṭha. Chapters and Subjects. Chapters and Subjects. 1. The qualification for the creation and manifestation of Brahman; the attainment of the qualification for knowledge of the meaning of all the Vedas by Brahman; the bath at Sarasvatī, the characteristics of the superior, middling, and inferior types [of persons], and praise of the husband (Bhartṛ). 2. The fruit of bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*); the characteristics of human beings; the attainment of the qualification for composing the *Saṃhitās* such as the Purāṇas by Vyāsa through the power of the bath at the confluence (*saṅghāta*).

The greatness of Kāmyatīrtha; the protection of the fourfold bath; the greatness of Vasudhārātīrtha; a description of the great Samyavarṇana; the determination of daily duties beginning from dawn; therein, the rules for the evacuation of urine and feces, the cleansing of the teeth, and so forth; the greatness of the five Tīrthas such as Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Gayā, Naimiṣa, and Kurukṣetra; the ritual for the construction of monasteries (maṭha) at the five Tīrthas; the performance of bathing and other rites; the definition of sacrificial food (haviṣya), forbidden food, and the like; and the determination of the directions for facing while eating.

Oṃ. [This section contains] the departure of those [sages] for the hermitage of Badarikā in order to remove the aforementioned [faults]; the description of the origin of Somakuṇḍa and the determination of its measurement; the greatness [of that place], along with the proper procedure for visiting the four-cornered Varītīrtha together with its attendants; the determination of what should and should not be done during Kārttika, as well as the giving of gifts on that occasion; and the departure of Indra and the other gods toward Virāṭa after leaving Mera, due to their satisfaction with the Lord’s dwelling in Viśākhā at that time.

The greatness of offering lamps in the temple of Viṣṇu, including the narrative of Kṛtsadrijaka; in connection with the greatness of rekindling another’s lamp—the establishment of a *māru* (lamp-stand) there by Viśākhā for the sake of the happiness of Indra and other gods; the performance of hymns of praise to the Lord; the narration of the ancient history of Indumatī; the greatness of the offering of lamps through their form and other qualities; the narrative of the crow and the cat; the dwelling of the gods in that very place by the command of the Lord; and the establishment of the *rokapāra* (boundary-mark) at Badarikāśrama. Badarikāśrama.

In that very section, through the dialogue between Candraśama and Sunanda, there is a description of the performance of the Kārttika vow; the majesty of the lamp; how all fruits are obtained through giving, including the attainment of the status of Indra and the fulfillment of a husband’s desires; the description of the Daṇḍapuṣkariṇī Tīrtha; the procedure for offering lamps in the sky; the account of liberation from the state of a Piśāca by offering a lamp in the sky; and the offering of lamps on the five days [of the lunar fortnight]. Thus ends the third chapter, the Badarikāśrama-māhātmya, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

[Chapter on] Charity, the locations for preparing lamps, the anecdote of Hari-karṇa regarding the offering of lamps, and the *kapūra-dīpa*; now begins the fourth [chapter], the Greatness of the Month of Kārtika, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

—The six gifts complete; the auspicious invocation; Raunaka’s inquiry to Sūta regarding the majesty of the month of Kārtika; and in response to that question, the narration of the greatness of Kurukṣetra, in the course of which Harimedha, Sumedhas, and the Brahmin Citradāsa [are introduced].

And there is the *Sutākti*; in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, preceded by an introduction, the inquiry regarding the *Kārttika-vrata* [is presented]; the determination of the time for the *Ekāṅga-gopāla* and other vows; the performance of the *Vatsadvādaśī-vrata*; the observation of omens in the five lamps (*pañcadīpa*); and the resolution concerning the performance of the *Ekāṅga-gopāla* and other vows through the *Vatsadvādaśī-vrata*.

Ha Ma: A description of the accounts concerning the body, wealth, grain, and happiness; the procedure for Yama-trayodaśī; the story of Hemanaka; Brahmā’s instruction to Nārada regarding the duties of the Kārttika vow; therein, the laughter of Medhas, who was distressed by the song of his preceptor while engaged in service; the procedure for Naraka-caturdaśī; the procedure for Dīpāvali; therein, the meaning of the word *kaumudī*; the history and religious duties of Pārvatī, Raṅga, Trikaṇṭha, and Sumati; and [discourse] on the occasion of the gift of food.

The narrative of Syaketu and the twice-born; the performance of *śrāddha* and other rites; the evening worship of Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, and Mahāsarasvatī; the festival of the awakening of Lakṣmī (Lakṣmīprabodhotsava); the history of the Brahmin Sumati in connection with the gift of cows (*godāna*); the narration of the history of Puṣkara in connection with the remembrance of names (*nāmasmaraṇa*); the section on the lamp festival (*dīpotsava*) and the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*); and the observation of auspicious and inauspicious omens during the game of *vaccirājyavāra*.

And [the text contains] the narration of the history of the dull-witted Brāhmaṇa in connection with the greatness of reciting the *Gītā*; the expulsion of all the *Trādayas* outside at midnight in connection with the giving of gifts by the learned; the description of the *Sukharātri-vrata*; the narration of the *Raṇokā-kathā*; the description of the acceptance of messengers; the determination of the acceptance of the *Baṅgirājya*; the ascertainment of the lunar day for the acceptance; and the description of the performance of the vow preceded by the investigation of the time for its commencement and conclusion, including the application of cow-dung on the courtyard and other details.
The worship of Tipu, the worship of Govardhana, the viewing of the combats and sports of buffaloes and bulls at Barīvadā, and the Māgha-pāḍī festival.

The determination of the time for digging, the procedure for bathing, the procedure for bathing at wells, holy watering places (*tīrtha*), and other locations which bestow progressively greater merit; the ritual for the worship of Varuṇa at night; the description of the sport of the cows; the observation of the *yaṣṭi* omen... [the determination of the time for digging, the determination of the fruit of bathing at the Tuṅgabhadrā and Kāverī, the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Pañcanadī-tīrtha, the procedure for the Yamadvitīyā vow, etc.]

The chapters and their subjects: the greatness of the *dhātrī* tree; therein, the ritual procedure for the worship of the *dhātrī*; the narrative of the origin of the *dhātrī* tree; the description of the deities residing within the *dhātrī*; the greatness of the *dhātrī*'s shade; therein, the ancient history (*itihāsa*) of Vaikya; the liberation of a mouse through hearing this story; the greatness of eating under the *dhātrī*'s shade; the description of the removal of defects by eating under the *dhātrī*'s shade; the wearing of *dhātrī* fruit; the offering of a garland of lamps under the *dhātrī*'s shade; [the greatness of] the *dhātrī*'s shade—...

The fruit of eating the *dhātrī* (myrobalan) with one's husband; the greatness of the *dhātrī*; the fruit of bathing with *āmalka* (myrobalan), as well as [the fruit of] *vañya* and *kaṭa*; the fruit of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍadāna*) in the shade of the *dhātrī*; the description of specific parts of the body for wearing *dhātrī* fruits; the fruit of worshipping Brahmā in the shade of the *dhātrī*; the lunar days (*tithi*) for the worship of the *dhātrī*; the rule for eating in the forest; the greatness of touching the *dhātrī*; and the greatness of the *dhātrī* tree within the home. ... ;

In this dialogue between Satyabhāmā and [Kṛṣṇa], there is a description of how, through the merit of the Kārttika vow performed in her previous birth, Satyabhāmā attained the status of being Kṛṣṇa’s wife; and when asked by Satyabhāmā why the month of Kārttika is the most excellent among all months, Kṛṣṇa explains its preeminence to her by recounting the slaying of the demon Raṅka.

The majesty of the sacred site of Prayāga; how Tulasī arose and how Irigriyā was born; the narration of the origin of Jaḍandhaya when Śiva, struck by Indra’s thunderbolt, was scorched by the fire of his wrath; then the description of Jaladhara’s conquest of the quarters and his attainment of victory; the description of the cause of Bṛhaspati’s loss of his life-force; and the manifestation of Viṣṇu, who appeared before the gods defeated in battle and engaged them in combat upon being praised by them.

In the assembly of Jaṭādhara, by the instruction of Nārada, Khīralana seized Pārvatī; this caused Rāhu to fall [in shame]. Thereupon, from the middle of the eyebrows of Śiva, who was enraged by that, there arose the description of the emergence of the Kīṭimukha Gaṇas. Then follows the description of Rudra’s defeat by the gods in the battle between the Devas and Asuras, the falling of Vīrabhadra, and subsequently, the battle between Jaṭādhara and Divyabhadra.

The contents of the chapter are as follows: 10. Viṣṇu, reflecting that the killing of Jaladhara would result from the violation of Vṛndā’s chastity, bestowed a *māyā* (illusion) upon her; then follows the description of the events occurring between those two, Vṛndā and Viṣṇu; when Vṛndā performed the renunciation of her body (*dehavisarjana*), Viṣṇu’s trampling upon her ashes; then, having killed Jalandhara in battle, by the command of Śiva—who remained bowed down in prostration—the gods [prepared] to strike Viṣṇu.

The hymn of praise by the Rādiśṣaktis; then, the goddesses, being pleased, bestow the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) upon the gods for the purpose of awakening Viṣṇu. *Haḥ* [and other syllables]. From the merit-bestowing gift made by Dharmadanta during the month of Kārtika, there is the liberation from birth as a *rākṣasī* for Kaṭadahā, who was the daughter of Tulasī, the wife of the wood-cutter.

In the month of Kārttika, during a dispute over the distribution of alms, there is the narration of the great gift; the embrace of Kaṅka’s neck by her as she ascended the celestial chariot brought by the messengers of Viṣṇu; and the granting of a boon to Dharmadatta by the messenger of Viṣṇu, who declared: "In another birth, you shall become a king renowned by the name Daśaratha in the Solar dynasty, and the Lord Viṣṇu himself shall descend as your son."

Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ. [The narration of the greatness of devotion to Viṣṇu; and, in connection with that, the telling of the history of the twice-born Viṣṇudāsa, king of Aṭarāja. The twice-born named Viṣṇudāsa’s pursuit of a Caṇḍāla who had stolen his coarse food, for the purpose of giving him alms out of faith; then, seeing the Caṇḍāla fallen and unconscious, the compassionate Viṣṇudāsa’s honoring of that Caṇḍāla; and thereafter, by the Lord assuming the form of a Caṇḍāla, [the testing] of Viṣṇudāsa—]

The act of bestowing grace; the arrival of a celestial chariot from heaven for the Brahmin Viṣṇudāsa by the Lord’s favor; while Viṣṇudāsa was departing after ascending that [chariot], his entry into the city of the Cola king; thereafter, the manifestation of the Lord’s true form to him; the dialogue between the Cola monarch and the Brahmin Viṣṇudāsa; and the attainment of the supreme state of Viṣṇu by Jaya and Vijaya through bathing in the Gaṇḍakī river.

...a description of how the son of Dhaneśvara attained birth through the merit accumulated during his wanderings; a description of the attainment of merit and demerit by those who have not given [gifts]; the narrative of the Patitavrata; the rules for the Māsopavāsa vow; the procedure for the Kūṣmāṇḍanavamī; the narration of the marriage rites of Tuṭasī; the rules for the Bhīṣmapañcaka vow; the majesty of Śravaṇadvādaśī; the rules for Dvādaśī; and the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the Kārtika vow.

Chapter 1: The Greatness of Para-Vikuṇṭha-Catardaśī; Chapter 2: The Greatness of the Śrīpura Festival. [Forbidden items: Cow’s milk, black gram (*rājamāṣa*), drinking or eating from a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*), twice-baked bread (*dvidakhāna*), eggplant (*vṛntāka*), the greatness of the three final lotus-pools on the festival day, the description of the fruits of the rules for hearing the Purāṇas. [Additional forbidden items: Radish (*mūlaka*), *tekhama*, defiled food, citron (*jambīra*), and sexual intercourse during the day.

Now, in connection with the eternal greatness of the month of Kārttika, the rules that must be observed and those that must not be transgressed by those undertaking the Kārttika vow are first set forth. || 1 ||

In this regard, the rules for what must be performed are as follows: constant remembrance of the Name; the worship of Rādhā and Dāmodara; the recollection of the names of Viṣṇu, Hari, and Śiva; mastery over the senses; restraint of the mind; compassion toward all living beings; meditation upon the Lord; worship of the Lord; truthful speech; eating sacrificial food (haviṣya); the vow of eating only at night (naktavrata); the vow of the completion of concentration (dhāraṇāpāraṇāvrata); the vow of silence (maunavrata); the vow of celibacy (brahmacaryavrata); association with the virtuous; the worship of the *dhātrī* tree; and the worship of Viṣṇu in the shade of the *dhātrī* tree.

Listening to discourses on the eternal; the gift of land; service to one's mother and father; service to one's guru; constant worship of the deity; singing in the temple of the deity; the offering of a perpetual lamp at a place called *deva*; the offering of a lamp at a crossroads; the offering of a lamp to a Brāhmaṇa; the offering of a lamp at a cow-trough; the worship of *turusī*; the worship of the *aśvattha* tree; the worship of deities, Brāhmaṇas, and cows; performing circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇā*) of the deity; performing circumambulation of a hundred thousand *turusī* plants; circumambulating the *aśvattha* tree; and feeding Brāhmaṇas.

The giving of food; the giving of cows, bulls, buffaloes, and elephants; the giving of gold, minerals, and gems; and the feeding of the destitute—one should certainly observe these observances during the month of Kārttika. Now, the prohibitions to be avoided: desire for another’s property; performing actions for others; slandering others; dwelling with others; eating the food of others; stale food; yellowish food; association with sinners; intimacy with other men; sexual intercourse with the wives of others; deceit toward others; intolerance of others' excellence; proclaiming the faults of others; and contemplating what is undesirable for others.

Proclaiming what is false; approaching those who should not be approached; eating food that should not be eaten; that which is not declared by the Śāstra; articles of worldly enjoyment (āmiṣa); false Śāstras; lack of faith in the Śāstra; doubt; speaking falsehood; association with the wicked; evil speech; meat; the milk of a cow whose calf has died; food seen by a woman in her menses; water drawn by a low-born person; the fruitlessness of bathing after eating molasses-mixed food; the fruitlessness of bathing after eating *dakha* or *daka*; indulgence in passion;
selling liquids—these one should avoid during the Kālika month. What must be done during the Kālika month is now to be determined.
Thus ends the fourth [chapter], the Greatness of the Kārtika Vow, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the fifth section, the Māgha-māhātmya, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

In the context of the dialogue between Sūta and Nakasavāda, the Blessed One describes to Brahmadeva the attainment of all desires and the mastery of the chariot by one who hears the greatness of Mārgaśīrṣa; he then describes the morning bath performed by the cowherd women at the confluence of the Mārga river, followed by the description of the greatness of wearing the *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* after bathing—preceded by the knowledge of the various rules for the morning bath, its merit, the appearance of Kṛṣṇa before the cowherd women due to that merit, and the performance of the entire ritual procedure including the application of unguents and ointments.

The procedure for wearing the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with clay from the banks of the river flowing from Dvāravatī; the description of the procedure for wearing the *gopīcandana* and the *sudarśana*; the fruit of wearing the marks of the Lord’s incarnations upon one's own body; the statement regarding the attainment of the fruit of merit for one whose body is marked by the weapons of the Lord; the description of the eligibility for all rites for one whose body is consecrated with the eight-syllabled name of the Lord; and [the rules] for wearing the discus-marked *mudrā* and the wearing of the lotus-marked fourfold rosary.

Description of the *phaḍa* mark; the greatness of wearing the *dhātrī* fruit; the greatness of wearing *tulasī* wood; description of the methods for installing, meditating upon, and worshipping the image of the Lord; description of the ritual sequence for the worship of the *rākhā* [protective thread] and so forth, including the mantras; and the description of the fruits resulting from the worship of the *rākhā*.

The description of the greatness of the *vaṭa* tree; the worship of the form of the Blessed One (*bhagavat-mūrti-pūjana*); the narration of the offering of sandalwood paste by Tuṅgasīkra; the greatness of the twelve-night vigil (*dvādaśī-jāgara-māhātmya*); the description of the greatness of *jāti* flowers and fruits offered for the sake of the Blessed One; the description of flowers dear to the Blessed One; the greatness of the *jāti* flower as the most excellent among all flowers; and the fruit of placing a garland adorned with a hundred *jāti* flowers upon the neck of Viṣṇu.

The description of greatness; the description of the greatness of the *tulasī* plant; the attainment of the merit of giving all things by the gift of a *tulasī* leaf; the description of the fruit of worshipping the Lord with *tulasī*; the greatness of the fruit of offering incense and lamps; the greatness of a lamp provided with a thousand wicks; and the explanation of the rules for the ritual procedures regarding the vessels for the sacred thread, food offerings, and so forth.

The narration of the greatness of the power of the Lord situated to the north of Vaidyanātha; the description of the fruits of circumambulation and other rites; the fruit of reciting the thousand names of Viṣṇu; the explanation of the cause for the Lord’s acquisition of the name Dāmodara; the greatness of partaking in the holy waters and sacred offerings; the conclusion of the ritual of worship, its formal completion (*udyāpana*), and the description of its fruits; the story of King Vīrabāhu; the greatness of the Ekādaśī beginning with the *Sedrinapūrva*; and the performance of a great sacrifice by Bharadvāja for King Vīrabāhu. By Bharadvāja...

In the narration of the account of Vīrabāhu’s previous birth: first, the description of how he attained the status of a king in this life due to the merit arising from his respectful reception of a Śūdra in a former birth; then, the description of how Vīrabāhu, having been questioned by Devaśarmā regarding the cause of his own attainment of Śūdra-hood in a previous life, was told the story of how even a twice-born man who had attained the status of a Brahmin became a Śūdra due to the fault of accepting the twelfth day [of the lunar fortnight] when conjoined with the tenth day, followed by the explanation of the prohibition against observing the twelfth day when it is joined with the tenth.

The description of the procedure for the concluding ceremony (*udyāpana*) of the Ekādaśī vow by King Bharatarāja, including the account of how he attained a noble mind even while in the womb due to his virtuous deeds such as hospitality toward Brahmins in a previous birth, and the narration of the unbroken Ekādaśī vow.

A description of the sequence of rites such as giving gifts during the vigil; a description of the qualifications [of the officiant]; on the twelfth day, a narration of the greatness of the Matsyotsava (the Fish Festival), followed by an exposition of the rules for bathing, giving, worship, and other rituals; the prescription for the recitation of mantras during the Matsyotsava; the statement of the mantra for praying to the river at the time of bathing; the description of the offering of fruits, flowers, and water to the Blessed One; a description of the greatness of the gift of an image in the form of a fish; and a description of the manner of honoring the Lord on the way back.

The greatness of the gift of cows, land, gold, clothing, beds, ornaments, and food; the greatness of the gift of fruits and flowers at the time of worshiping the Blessed One; the greatness of providing Brahmins with excellent requisites such as sandals and other items during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; and the greatness of the fast on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) and the hearing of the *Śravaṇa* chapter from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*. These are the chapters concerning the self-nature of the fasts and the greatness of the worship of the Blessed One. Mārgaśīrṣa... [text fragment].

The majesty of remembering the names of the Blessed One (1); meditation on the Blessed One and its majesty; the description of the section concerning the instruction of hymns to the Blessed One; the characteristics of the guru and the disciple; the description of the majesty of the Bhāgavata; the hearing of the fruit of the Bhāgavata; the description of the fruit of reading the Bhāgavata text preceded by worship; and the description of the majesty of Mathurā—thus ends the fifth [chapter], the majesty of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the sixth [section], the Māhātmya of the Bhāgavata, within the Vebhṇava-khaṇḍa.

In the context of the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka, there is a description of how, after consecrating Vajra as the successor to the thrones of Mathurā and Hastināpura, Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍavas departed for their own abode; following the conversation between Vajra and Parīkṣit, Śāṇḍilya Ṛṣi arrived; Śāṇḍilya explained the meaning of the word "traja" and described the sporting of Kṛṣṇa with the three girls; and by performing the cow-sacrifice and establishing his rule over Mathurā and other regions, he attained the vision of Uddhava. (Having spoken thus, Śāṇḍilya...)

His return to his own hermitage; the arrival there of King Parīkṣit from the region of Mathurā; the establishment by King Vajra and King Parīkṣit of the sites where Govinda and the gopīs had played; the establishment of many *bhāmas* (sacred mounds) all around Jāthurā; the installation of a *śivaliṅga* at Kuṇḍa-kūpa and other places in Mathurā as a means of purification; the description of the forest of Dvārakā created by Kṛṣṇa’s wives due to their separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa; and the description of the battle between the Lord and the demon Dāva near Mount Govardhana.

The description of Uddhava’s departure to see Parīkṣit and others; then the dialogue between Uddhava and Parīkṣit, in which Uddhava describes the majesty of the Blessed One; the description of Kṛṣṇa’s childhood sports and pastimes; the description that by reading the Bhāgavata one attains the fruit of all desires; the description that where the Bhāgavata is, there is the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the description of the attainment of liberation through hearing the Bhāgavata; and [the account of] that which was performed by the glorious Blessed One.

The description of the instruction on the maintenance, origination, and dissolution of the world as the effects of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva, who consist of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; and the purification of the soul through the grasping of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, which destroys the accumulation of the quality of tamas.

Ka, Ke, Ka-Kha: Kākaḥ (The Crow). Chapters and Subjects: The power of a serpent gained through hearing the greatness of the month of Vaiśākha; the narration of that very serpent’s account of its previous birth; the dialogue between Śaṅkha and the hunter (vyādha), including the narration of how the hunter attained the state of a Vālmīki in another birth; ... [the description of the greatness of the lunar days occurring on Sundays]; the definition of the duties of the Kaṭi [month]; ... [the greatness of Akṣayya-tṛtīyā].

(The greatness of the goddess Uddharadākṣī; the story of the deity and the brahmin residing in the land of Kāmarūpa; the description of the greatness of the thirteenth, fourteenth, and full-moon days of the month of Vaiśākha; and the description of the fruit of hearing the Vaiśākha-māhātmya. Thus ends the seventh [chapter] on the greatness of the month of Vaiśākha within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.)
Now begins the eighth [section], the Greatness of Ayodhyā, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

The *Sūta-kratu*, followed by the hymn of praise (*stavana*) offered by Vyāsa and others; the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Ayodhyā, adorned with various trees and creepers, in the context of the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka; the arrival of the sage Agastya at Ayodhyā; the description of Agastya’s overwhelming joy upon perceiving the power of Ayodhyā; the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word "Ayodhyā" through the description of Ayodhyā as existing in the form of the three qualities (*tri-guṇa-tattva-svarūpa*); and [the account] preceded by the dialogue between Agastya and Vyāsa regarding Ayodhyā, concerning the deeds performed by Viṣṇu.

The description of the means of recognition; Viṣṇudāman’s composition of a hymn of praise to the Blessed One; Viṣṇuśarman’s arrival at the Blessed One; the granting of a boon by the Blessed One to Viṣṇuśarman; the bringing of a torrent of water by the Blessed One with his own discus at that very spot; the description of the renown of that sacred ford under the name Cakratīrtha; the installation of the form of Viṣṇuhari preceded by the name of Viṣṇu; and the description of the greatness of Viṣṇuhari.

The arrival of Brahmā in Ayodhyā; his performance of processions and other rites, as well as the conduct of a sacrifice; the establishment of the *brahmakuṇḍa* in his own name; the description of the greatness of the *brahmakuṇḍa* by the god Brahmā; the description of the greatness of the *pāpamocanatīrtha*, which effects liberation from sins through the power of the *ṇemo* located on the bank of the Sarayū; the description of the greatness of the *sahasradhārā* by Agastya; and the narration of the greatness of the *svargadvāra-tīrtha* by Agastya. **Chapter Summaries:** 1. The arrival of Brahmā in Ayodhyā, his performance of processions and other rites, and the conduct of a sacrifice; the establishment of the *brahmakuṇḍa* in his own name, and the description of the greatness of the *brahmakuṇḍa* by the god Brahmā. 2. The description of the greatness of the *pāpamocana-tīrtha*, which effects liberation from sins through the power of the *ṇemo* situated on the bank of the Sarayū. 3. The description of the greatness of the *sahasradhārā* by Agastya. 4. The narration of the greatness of the *svargadvāra-tīrtha* by Agastya.

The majesty of the *Suktidrāra* pilgrimage site; the description of the procedure for the concluding rite (*udāpana*) of the *Candraharitra* vow; the description of the majesty of the concluding rite of the *Candrasahasrakalpa* vow; (the majesty of Dharmahari); therein, the arrival of the Blessed One upon seeing the bowing performed by King Dharma; the offering of praise to the Blessed One by Dharma; the granting of boons to King Dharma by the Blessed One; and [the account of] the king named Raghu, who, having performed a world-conquest (*digvijaya*), at the command of the Sun, performed the sacrifice known as *Sarvasvadakṣiṇā*.

After the completion of the sacrifice, the arrival of the sage Kautsa; the manifestation of the sage Kautsa’s desire to depart for another place due to his lack of wealth upon seeing the provisions brought for his own worship; Raghu’s departure with the intent to conquer Kubera in order to obtain divine wealth to bestow upon Kautsa; the raining down of wealth by Kubera out of fear of Raghu; and the description of Raghu’s gift of that wealth along with the Veda to Kautsa. By Kautsa—

Thereafter, at the request of the distressed Brahmā, Śaṅkara commanded him to perform a sacrifice on Mount Gandhamādana in the Southern Ocean for the purpose of dispelling the false accusation of guilt. By the Lord’s command, Brahmā performed a sacrifice on Mount Gandhamādana with the intent of propitiating Śiva; there, manifesting once more, Śaṅkara [bestowed grace] upon Brahmā.

The granting of boons following the bestowal of the excellent *vara-bhadra*, which consists of the worshipful status for all rites; the granting of boons at the holy site named Brahmakuṇḍa; the majesty of Brahmakuṇḍa; then the description of the majesty of Hanumānchaṇḍa; in connection with that, the narration of the life of the king named Dharmasakha; the account of the scorpion sting of Ukha-candra, the son of King Dharmasakha; and then, by the word of his own minister, King Dharmasakha, who was desiring to have many sons, [prepared] the materials for a sacrifice.

Having performed the rites together with all his attendants and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), he set out toward the Hanumān-muṇḍa peak on Mount Gandhamādana situated on the shore of the western ocean. Having bathed there and performed the *putrīyeṣṭi* sacrifice, he reached Hatocadaṣṭa; after bestowing villages, agrahāras, and other gifts upon the Brahmins, he performed an ablution with Bhāyoraṭa and returned to his own city. There, by the power of Hanumān-muṇḍa, among the hundred wives of that Dharmasakha—

The attainment of a hundred sons by Bhavyā; then, at the time of his end, King Danuma approaching the Hanumat-kuṇḍa and performing penance with his friend the king; thereafter, his attainment of the realm of Vaiṅuṇṭha; the performance of the funeral rites for his father by his son Sucandra; a description of the brotherly affection of all the sons, including Sucandra, and their enjoyment of royal pleasures; the majesty of the Hanumat-kuṇḍa; then, a description of the majesty of the Agasti-tīrtha; and, in connection with that majesty—

The account of the deeds of Kakṣīvat, the son of Dīrghatamas. Therein is described how Kakṣīvat, having completed his study of the sixty-four branches of knowledge at the house of his teacher named Udaṅka, caused his teacher to swear an oath so that he might return home; thereafter, the teacher’s daughter spoke of a means for his marriage. By the command of the teacher, Kakṣīvat went to the Agastya-tīrtha, and mounting a brilliant, four-tusked lordly elephant that had emerged from that sacred bathing place, he proceeded along the road by means of a signal with his finger to one named Svanaya.

The king’s journey toward his city with him; then, at the request of King Svanaya, Kakṣīvat sent word to his father through the priest named Sudarśana to invite him for the purpose of giving his daughter in marriage, and having done so, brought him back to his own city with due honor; then Kakṣīvat offered salutations to his father Dīrghatamas and reported the circumstances of his own study of the sciences; and then, at that holy site of Agastya, by King Svanaya—

The honoring of the sage Dīrghatamas. In the meantime, at that very spot, the great seer Udaṅka arrived at the Agasti-tīrtha with his assembly of disciples. There occurred a meeting between Udaṅka and Dīrghatamas; King Svanaya approached for the sake of Droṇa and announced his own purpose. Then, with the consent of Udaṅka, King Svanaya agreed to give his daughter to Kakṣīvat. Subsequently, King Svanaya had the maiden brought from the city of Madhurā by his attendants and [performed] the marriage ceremony according to the prescribed rites.

The giving of a maiden in marriage to Kakṣīvat; thereafter, the granting of gold, cows, female slaves, villages, and other riches, as well as the bestowal of the Arāśarata gift; then, King Dīdhitimakhu’s departure with his son and daughter-in-law from the sage’s hermitage to return to his own abode situated in Vedāraṇya; King Svanaya’s journey toward his own city after bathing at Agastitīrtha along with the women of the inner apartments; the majesty of Agastitīrtha; and finally, the description of the majesty of the holy site known as Rāmakuṇḍa.

In connection with that, there is a description of the sage Sutīkṣṇa, the disciple of Agastya; the performance of austerities by Sutīkṣṇa at the holy site of Rāmacandra-saras; the offering of praise to Śrī Rāmacandra by Sutīkṣṇa while performing those penances; and, in the context of describing the perfection of Sutīkṣṇa’s eightfold austerities as he performed them, a description of the majesty of Rāma-kaṇḍa. || 20 ||

In the *Kāyī-yiti-rākā*, there is a description of the majesty of the venerable Śiva-liṅga installed by Rāma on the banks of the Rāmakuṇḍa; in connection with that, an account of how Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was freed from the fault of speaking untruth. Therein, during the Bhārata war, in order to defeat Droṇa, Kṛṣṇa caused a false report to spread that Aśvatthāman had been killed in battle by Bhīma’s wife. Having heard that report—and having heard it likewise from Yudhiṣṭhira himself—Droṇa believed it to be true and, through his yogic power...

The act of sacrificing one's own body; the acquisition of sin by Yudhiṣṭhira—who had always spoken the truth—due to uttering a falsehood at that moment; and, after the conclusion of the war, during the time of his royal consecration, the proclamation by a celestial voice that he was unfit for the coronation due to the sin born of speaking untruth under a pretext; the feeling of remorse by Yudhiṣṭhira; and at that occasion, the address directed toward Yudhiṣṭhira by the great sage Vyāsa who had arrived there.

At Rāmatīrtha, situated on the shore of the Southern Ocean, the performance of the *śrāddha* rites was undertaken. Then, Yudhiṣṭhira, having installed his younger brother Sahadeva upon the throne, set out toward Rāmasetu along with his preceptor Dhaumya and his own brothers Bhīma and the others; reaching Rāmatīrtha by means of a boat according to the prescribed ritual, he performed his ablutions there following the path instructed by the family priest. By the power of that bathing, giving of gifts, *śrāddha*, month-long fasting, and other observances at Rāmatīrtha, [he attained] the voice of *namaḥ*.

The description of Yudhiṣṭhira’s fitness for ascending the throne following his purification from the sin born of speaking untruth; then, the majesty of the Rāmakuṇḍa tīrtha; next, the description of the majesty of the Lakṣmaṇatīrtha; and in connection with that, the account of Balabhadra’s liberation from the sin of brahmin-slaughter. Therein, Balabhadra—unwilling to witness the slaughter of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas—goes to a great assembly of ascetics in the forest under the pretext of a pilgrimage to the sacred sites; and there, by Balabhadra...

While Sūta was seated upon the Brahmāsana to narrate the Purāṇas, he unintentionally struck a sage with the tip of a blade of grass raised by his own hand; consequently, he incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin. Then, at the word of the sages, desiring to perform an expiation for the sake of the world’s welfare, he made a request to the sages. The sages instructed him to perform an expiation in the form of a pilgrimage to sacred sites after slaying a Rākṣasa named Bāṣkala, who was oppressing the earth. Thereupon, Balabhadra slew the Rākṣasa named Bāṣkala.

Then, for the duration of a year, there is the description of performing a pilgrimage to all the sacred bathing sites (*tīrthas*) situated on the surface of the earth; and even after that pilgrimage to the *tīrthas* has been completed, the description of liberation from the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) by merely bathing at the Rakṣmaṇatīrtha located on Mount Gandhamādana in the southern ocean and by beholding the *liṅga* of Rakṣbhaṇeśvara, provided one has attained detachment from the objects of the senses through the practice of meditation.

The greatness of the Rāmaṇa-tīrtha: when Śuka asked Vyāsa for a means to purify his mind, Vyāsa narrated the ancient history of Śrī Śukra and Varuṇa, followed by a description of the majesty of Jaṭā-tīrtha located at Rāmasetu. Then, having heard Vyāsa’s instruction, Śuka went to Jaṭā-tīrtha; the description of the purification of the mind through mere bathing there is given, as is the greatness of Jaṭā-tīrtha.

Then follows the description of the greatness of Lakṣmītīrtha; in that context, an account of Yudhiṣṭhira’s history is told. While Yudhiṣṭhira was staying on Mount Indrabhaṭṭa, he posed a question to Śrī Kṛṣṇa regarding the dharma that bestows great sovereignty. In response, Śrī Kṛṣṇa related to Yudhiṣṭhira the majesty of Lakṣmītīrtha at the site of Gandhamādana, preceded by numerous ancient histories. Thereupon, Yudhiṣṭhira went to Lakṣmītīrtha and performed ritual bathing for a full month according to the prescribed rules.

Having established [the kingdom] and returned to his own city, he then, by virtue of the unsurpassed wealth and sovereignty attained through that very state, undertook with great effort and the assistance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa the performance of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

The majesty of Lakṣmī-tīrtha; then the description of the majesty of Abhritīrtha, along with an account of the purification of Sītā in connection with that. There, having slain Rāvaṇa at Laṅkā, Rāmacandra, together with Indra and the other gods, returned via the path of the bridge to Gandhamādana. Standing on the bank of Lakṣmī-tīrtha, he summoned the fire for the sake of purifying Jānakī. Then, Agni arrived there and, in the presence of Rāma, declared Sītā’s purity. Following the words of Agni, by Rāmacandra—

The acceptance of Jānakī; the establishment of the place where Anala emerged as being famous by the name Abhitīrtha; and, in the context of the majesty of Abhitīrtha, the narration of the life of a preeminent merchant named Paśuman, who, among his six sons, was the sixth son named Duṣpaṇya—a man of extreme wickedness who committed the murder of a city gardener—and who, upon the king observing the blood of that victim on his sword-blade, was banished from the country; thereafter, even though he had fled to the forest...

When Tenograśravas, the son of a sage, was drowned and killed after being cast into the matted locks (*jaṭā*), Satyubhraśravas, the sage, seeing this, pronounced a curse upon him, saying, "Because you have caused [your son] to be immersed in the matted locks, he shall become a crocodile. Then, during a great deluge in the Vaṣaukaṭha region, Duṣpaṇya caused the corpse of a dead elephant to enter the midst of the matted locks; that elephant's body was then carried away by a massive torrent of water into the ocean. Following this, there is a description of the greatness (*māhātmya*) of Jaṭātīrtha, and in connection with that, a description of the life story of Dukācārya.

In that regard, when the objects of sense belonging to Bhavyā—namely *ka*, *ka*, *ka*, *ka*—are entered by Śaḍuka, there occurs the death of Duṣpaṇya who resides within them. Immediately thereafter, he attains the state of a Piśāca. Then, having returned to the vicinity of Agastya’s hermitage in the form of a Piśāca, he makes a fervent plea to the great sages for his own liberation. Subsequently, for the sake of his release, the great sage Agastya directs him toward the sacred bathing place known as Suvīkṣṇa.

The performance of the bath according to the command; the liberation of the *piśāca* from his state as a *piśāca* through the sight of Sutejas when he had performed his bath at the Abhitīrtha; his ascent upon a divine celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and his departure for the divine realm after bowing to the great sages; the majesty of the Abhratīrtha; then, the description of the majesty of Cakratīrtha; in connection with that, the narration of the worship of the Sudarśana [mantra] performed by a *brāhmaṇa* named Ahivudhnya; and the liberation of that *brāhmaṇa* by the Sudarśana discus.

The destruction of the Rākṣasas who caused obstacles to penance; the renown of the sacred ford as Cakratīrtha due to the presence of the discus of the Lord of Satyasandha; at the command of Brahmā, the performance of a sacrifice to Maheśvara by all the gods who were terrified of the Rākṣasas in the vicinity of Cakratīrtha; the narration of the account of how the hand of the god Savitṛ was restored with a golden palm merely by bathing in Cakratīrtha upon the word of the sage Aṣṭāvakra, after his hand had been severed by the mere touch of the sacrificial ladle (*prāśitra-pātra*) during that sacrifice;
and the majesty of Cakratīrtha. ... ||

32. Now follows the description of the greatness of Śivatīrtha, and in that context, the narration of the account of Kāṅbharava. When a dispute arose between Gaṅgā and Viṣṇu regarding their mutual superiority, and although the superiority of Śiva was described by means of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), Gaṅgā and Viṣṇu, due to their persistent obstinacy, did not acknowledge Śiva’s preeminence; thereupon, Śiva manifested his own true form. Upon seeing Maheśvara, Jahnu nevertheless treated him with contempt.

The conversation between Gava and Utkīrṇa; then, Maheśvara’s dispatching of the personage named Kārbherava to Brahmā; the severing of the fifth head of Brahmā by Kārbherava during the battle with Brahmā; thereafter, the propitiation of Brahmā by the Blessed Maheśvara; the offering of praise to the Blessed Śaṅkara by the god Brahmā; the granting of fearlessness to Brahmā by Śaṅkara; and then, by the command of Śiva, [the subduing] of Kālabhairava.

For the purification of the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), one should sever one's own head and hold it in the hand, and wander for a year while performing pilgrimages to all sacred sites (*tīrtha*). By bathing in the Śiva-tīrtha located at Gandhamādana on the shore of the Southern Ocean, the sin of killing a Brahmin is removed. It is there that Kālabhairava established the *kapāṭa* (the skull/door-panel); thus, that Śiva-tīrtha is designated as the *Kapāṭa-tīrtha*. [The following is] the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Diva-tīrtha: [here begin] the chapters (*adhyāyas*) and their respective subjects (*viṣayas*). Now...

Description of the Greatness of Śaṅkha-tīrtha: The renown of this sacred ford as Śaṅkha-tīrtha arises from its being established by the sage Śaṅkha after he had performed austerities there. In connection with the greatness of that tīrtha, the narrative of the person named Vatsanābha is related; while that twice-born man named Vatsanābha was performing austerities and remained motionless upon an anthill there, Indra, seeking to obstruct his penance, caused a calamity by raining down a great shower of mud, at which point the Blessed Lord Dharmadeva [intervened] with a great bull...

Having assumed the form of a bull and stood upon Vāmīka, he caught the torrents of rain on his own back and protected the sage. Then, having withdrawn from his meditative absorption (*samādhi*), Vasunābha—determined that his mind had become agitated again because he had failed to offer worship to his protector Dharmanātha who was nearby in the form of a buffalo—made an effort to cast himself down from Mount Arvudagiri in order to give up his life and atone for the fault of his transgression. At that time, by the god Dharma...

Having abandoned the form of a buffalo and appeared in his own true form, [the Lord] prevented the Brahmin Varasānu from committing suicide; he then performed the purification of the sin of ingratitude for him and, for the sake of his mental purification, caused him to bathe at the holy site (tīrtha) known as Śaṅkha situated on the shore of the southern ocean. Through this instruction in Dharma, it is described how the Brahmin Varasānu attained liberation into Brahman preceded by mental purification immediately after the mere act of bathing at Śaṅkha-tīrtha, thereby removing the sin of ingratitude—the majesty of Śaṅkha-tīrtha.

Now follows the description of the triad of sacred fords known as Yamunā, Gaṅgā, and Gayā; in connection with that, the account of King Jānaśruti is narrated. Therein is described the birth of one who was lame from birth—also known by the name Sayugvā—who, while performing austerities for many years on Mount Gandhamādana situated in the western ocean, was afflicted by a disease. Then, desiring to bathe in the triad of sacred fords called Yamunā, Gaṅgā, and Gayā, he invoked the three fords through meditation preceded by the recitation of mantras; at the mere utterance [of the first], Yamunā...

The presence of the triad of Gaṅgā, Gayā, and Prayāga in that vicinity; the perpetual proximity of that triad of sacred fords there by the word of the great seers (maharṣis); and on one occasion at that time, during the middle of the night, while Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was standing at the window of his palace, the arrival of the great seers in the form of swans near him for the sake of rest—among those sages, by one great seer in the form of a swan, [Jānaśruti] was awakened from sleep by the sound of their speech regarding sacrifice.

Having offered praise to the great seers, they departed together with their own followers toward the world of Brahmā; then, after those great seers had gone, Jānaśruti sought refuge with the great seer Raikva, who was accompanied by his wife, in order to obtain the knowledge of the Self. 21.

Then, by the command of King Reka, Viṣaya and Sayugvana performed ablutions at the three holy fords (tīrthas) of Yamunā, Gaṅgā, and Gayā; following that purification of the mind, the attainment of the state of Brahman by King Janaśruta through the instruction on the knowledge of Reka is described.

Now begins the description of the majesty of Koṭitīrtha; in connection with that, the narrative of the life of Śrī Rāmacandra. Therein is described the account of how, after the slaying of Rāvaṇa, Śrī Rāma, in order to dispel the sin arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin, installed the divine Liṅga named Rāmanātha on Mount Gandhamādana in the southern ocean, and for the purpose of bathing it, remembered the Gaṅgā and pierced the earth with the tip of his bow to bring her down from the netherworld (rasātala). Following that, [the description] of that sacred ford (tīrtha).

The renown of Koṭitīrtha as a sacred ford; an account of the greatness of Koṭitīrtha; and a description of the life of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Therein, after Vasudeva’s marriage, as he was setting out for his own city by chariot, Kaṃsa—having heard from his spies that Devakī would give birth to a son destined to kill him—prepared to seize her. Vasudeva, however, pacified him with gentle words and a promise to deliver the child, and thus prevented the slaughter. Then...

After the transfer of the embryo from Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva—who was pregnant with her sixth child—to Rohiṇī by means of Yogamāyā, the birth of the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa occurred. Vasudeva offered hymns of praise to the Blessed One; then, by the command of the Blessed One, Vasudeva took Śrī Kṛṣṇa to Gokula and brought back the daughter of Yaśodā to Mathurā. Subsequently, while Kaṃsa was about to crush her against a stone slab out of fear of his enemy, that primordial Māyā emerged from her hand and ascended to the sky.

The departure in the form of the Bhavya and Abhavya; the Goddess’s prediction to Kaṃsa that his death would come from someone "wherever he may be"; the attainment of worship at various sites after the killing of Nibhaṇḍin; the description of the water-sports of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rāma while staying in Gokula; then, having gone to Mathurā and slain Kaṃsa, the performance of the royal consecration of Ugrasena; and then, on one occasion, regarding Nārada and others who had arrived to see him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa [acted] for the sake of expiating the fault caused by the killing of his maternal uncle.

The commencement of the expiation; then, by the words of Nārada and others, Rāmaseta arrived and, merely by bathing at Koṭitīrtha, [was freed from] the fault arising from the killing of his maternal uncle—these are not the subjects of the Madhyamā [Purāṇa]. Next, the description of the greatness of Sādhyākhṛta-tīrtha; in connection with that, the narration of the history of King Purūravas; therein, the union of King Purūravas with the Apsaras Urvaśī; then, after some time, due to the failure of his promise regarding the appointed time.

Following the narration of the reunion with her son, preceded by the account of his birth at Kurukṣetra during the separation from the excessively sorrowful Kuntī, there was a joyful reception; then, after one night had passed, the king’s meeting once again with Padmāvatī at the lotus-lake in Kurukṣetra; the handing over to the king by Urvaśī of her own son, Āyuṣmān, born through her union with him; and subsequently, during the course of a single night, the implantation of the seed of Pañcacūḍa within that same womb of Urvaśī.

Then, following that indication, Purūravas made a request to the Gandharvas for the sake of obtaining Urvaśī without interruption; at their request, the Gandharvas, being satisfied, gave the fire-vessel (*agnisthālī*) to Purūravas and instructed him on how to perform the sacrifice. Due to his dissatisfaction with having obtained only half of her, Chyavana threw the fire-vessel right into the middle of the forest and departed for his own city. From the place where the fire-vessel was deposited, the *śamī* and *aśvattha* trees grew; then, from that *aśvattha* tree...

Having kindled the fire by churning the fire-drill (*araṇi*) twenty-four finger-breadths long, and having performed many sacrificial rites (*yajña*), Urvaśī attained the world of the Gandharvas and sported with King Purūravas. Then, once, while they were looking at each other with smiles before Śakra during the commencement of a sacrifice, the preceptor of the gods, Tumburu, pronounced a curse upon them, saying that their separation would come to pass. Thereafter, Purūravas made a request to Indra.

Desiring to employ the means prescribed by him, she descended to the earth and reached the Sādhyāmṛta tīrtha located at Gandhamādana on the shore of the southern ocean; merely by bathing there, she was released from the curse and returned to the world of Urvaśī, where she enjoyed dalliance with Urvaśī. This is the description of the majesty of the Sādhyāmṛta tīrtha, followed by the description of the majesty of the Sāvitrī tīrtha.

The narration of the extraordinary life of the Brahmin named Sucarita, prompted by his attachment to worldly existence; therein, the Brahmin Sucarita, afflicted by old age and devoid of all desire, having come to Mount Gandhamādana in the Daṇḍaka forest with the longing for knowledge of all sacred sites (*tīrtha*), took up the initiation of Śiva and performed penance; when Śaṅkara appeared before him due to that penance, the Brahmin Sucarita offered a hymn of praise to the illustrious Śiva; and the illustrious Śiva, in order to fulfill the wish of Sucarita, [appeared] in the presence of Sucarita’s friend... all [of this].

Having invoked all the sacred fords (*tīrthas*) together in one place and performed the ritual union of all the fords, the sage Sucarita was commanded to bathe; thus, by the sage Sucarita, at the head of Śibi, [the rite was performed]. Now, in connection with the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, follows the narration of the life of Aśvatthāman. Therein, in the chapters concerning Aśvatthāman, the topics are: the performance of a bath in the Tīrtha; through the performance of the bath in that Tīrtha, the Brahmin named Sucarita attained freedom from old age and the recovery of youth, beauty, and other qualities; and the majesty of the Tīrtha known as Sarvatīrtha.

Oṃ. (Now begins the description of the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha; the description of the power of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha to destroy various kinds of sins; in connection with the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha, the description of how Śrī Rāmacandra, at the request of Vibhīṣaṇa, drew a line with the tip of his own bow so that other worlds would not enter the Saṅkaṭa [narrow passage], thereby describing the breaking of his own bridge; the description of the presence of all the deities at Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha; and [the description of the rites] in Dhanuṣkoṭi during the months of Māgha and others...)

The description of the greatness of bathing at the Ṣkoṭi-tīrtha: Having made a vow to slay all the brave warriors stationed in the camp, he approached the gate of the camp at nightfall with Kṛtavarman and Śatānīka; having propitiated Mahādeva and received from him a victorious sword, he first gave it to his father’s slayer, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and thereafter slaughtered the entire army—including Draupadī’s sons and others—stationed within the camp, starting from the entrance of the camp.
