The slaughter of the army leaders who had brought the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), along with their armor-makers, charioteers, and preceptors; then the flight of Aśvatthāman and the others from the camp to various different regions; then, after Aśvatthāman had entered among the great sages on the banks of the Narmadā and was declared fallen (*patita*) by the Brahmins, he emerged from there and undertook a pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*) at Aśvatthāman’s command; then, having heard of Vyāsa residing at Badarikāśrama, he went to him for refuge; and then, through the instruction of Vyāsa, Aśvatthāman—

For the sake of pacifying the fault of his own death, [the sage] reached Rāmasetu and performed service to Lord Rāmanātha Śiva at Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha preceded by ritual ablutions; thereafter, having risen from his bath, he offered praise to Śiva. Then, the Great Lord, being pleased, granted him a boon at Aśvatthāna. [The text continues with] the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha, and then, in the course of describing the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha once more, [the account of] Dharmarāja, the son of King Nandana, who was born in the lineage of Soma.

Description of Conduct: In that regard, after Nanda had departed for the forest to perform austerities, Dharmagupta was consecrated as king. Once, having entered the forest for the sake of hunting, he mounted a bull out of fear of lions and other wild beasts during the night. There, a certain wicked sage, desiring to protect his own life from being taken by some hunter, approached the king who was situated in the tree. Following this, there ensued a mutual conversation.

Having inspired confidence, he established a system of alternating sleep and wakefulness for the king and the tiger by dividing the night into two watches. Then, while the king was asleep and the tiger was awake, although the tiger addressed the king with words of humble devotion, the king—out of a desire to protect the dharma of trust—did not abandon him, but instead spoke to the tiger regarding the consequences of treachery and malice. Thereafter, when the king had awakened and it was that same lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the tiger [attacked] the king.

When he said, "I shall sprinkle [the ground] with my garments," the king and the sage both fell from their high position. At that moment, that sage, having mounted his footstool with his feet resting upon his own nails, spoke out of passion, stating that he had assumed the form of a sage through meditation. He then pronounced a curse upon the lord of the earth, saying, "Become insane! Having thus bestowed the curse, he related the ancient account of how he himself had attained the state of a horse by the power of a curse previously uttered against him.

Just as the lion immediately ascended a celestial chariot (*vimāna*)—having previously attained his true form and appearance through the hearing of the *Dhyānakāṣṭha* sage—and departed for the realm of the Yakṣas; and how the sage Dhyānakāṣṭha, having assumed the form of a bear by his own will, traveled at his pleasure into the interior of the forest; and how, after the sage Dhyānakāṣṭha had brought about the onset of madness upon Dharmagupta, he returned to his own city; and thereafter, [the story] of that Dharmagupta who was utterly mad.

The bringing of Dharmagupta into the presence of his father, King Nanda—who resided on the banks of the river Nairamada—by his ministers; then, thereupon, King Nanda’s making a request to the great sage Jaimini for the sake of curing the fault of his son’s excessive pride; thereafter, by the command of the great sage Jaimini, King Nanda took his son Dharmagupta and went to the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha located at Rāmasetu, where he performed a ritual bath; and [the result] from merely bathing at the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha.

The subduing of the pride of Dharmaga; then the penance of Nanda and his subsequent departure for the penance grove; the performance of the coronation of Rāmanātha by Dharmarāja preceded by the distribution of vast wealth, followed by his return to his own city with his ministers; the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha; and further, in connection with the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, a description of how the Brahmin named Parāvasu was liberated from the great sin of Brahmin-slaughter, including the account of the sacrificial session (*satra*) of that universal emperor (*cakravartin*).

While Rebha and the son of Mahadhi were traveling on their way to the sacrifice of Parāvasu, Parāvasu returned to his own hermitage at the conclusion of the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) of that sacrificial rite. At that time, as he was walking along the path at night clad in a deerskin, he killed his own father—who had been sleeping—with a sharp sword. Then, Parāvasu approached him and beheld that it was indeed his own father whom he had slain.

Having endured great sorrow for his father and having completed the funeral rites, Āvatsāra gathered at the sacrificial session (*sattra*) and reported to his younger brother Parāvasu the circumstances of his father’s killing. Then, having instructed his younger brother to perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the sin of patricide, Āvatsāra himself performed the sacrificial work at the session of King Vahyashva. Thereafter, in order to remove the guilt of Brahman-slaughter, Āvatsāra remained at the sacrificial session for twelve years, performing penance according to the prescribed rites.

When they had arrived, his elder brother Parāvasu falsely attributed the sin of Brahman-slaughter to his younger brother Ārvāvasu and, through King Bahulāśva, had Ārvāvasu expelled from the sacrificial hall (*satrasadana*). Thereupon, the innocent Ārvāvasu, having no other recourse, departed from the sacrifice and went to the forest to perform penance. Satisfied by that penance, the Ādityas and other gods granted Ārvāvasu a boon consisting of the restoration of his father to life.

[The brothers] requested a boon from their father consisting of relief from the sin of Brahmin-slaughter; then, having adopted the means prescribed by the god, Arvāvasu—the younger brother—took Parāvasu, the elder brother, to the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha located on the southern bank [of the ocean] for the removal of the sin of Brahmin-slaughter from Parāvasu, and performed a ritual bath there. By the power of that bath, the sin of Brahmin-slaughter against Parāvasu’s ancestors was removed. Then, when Arvāvasu and Parāvasu had returned to their own home, their father— *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a Sanskrit narrative (likely from the *Dhanuṣkoṭimāhātmya* or similar Puranic text). The translation reflects the available portion.*

The restoration of life for Raibhya at Kāñcī; the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha, which destroys all defects such as the murder of a Brahmin; then, in connection with the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi, the narration of the account of the dialogue between a bird and a monkey; therein, during the mutual conversation between a certain bird and a monkey who remembered their former births, each relates the history of his own previous existence; while the bird and the monkey were thus conversing with one another, in their presence—

The arrival of the sage Sindhudvīpa; then, having been questioned by those two, Śveta and Vānara, regarding their own means of livelihood, the great sage Sindhudvīpa first gave instruction on the excavation of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, followed by his narration of the account concerning the rescue of the Brāhmaṇa named Sumati, who was drinking liquor with Kirātīs. In that context, [the story of] the son of a wealthy Brāhmaṇa named Sumati, who resided in Mahārāṣṭra and had set out for theft in order to acquire wealth because he was seized by passion for a Kirātī woman.

Due to the killing of a certain Brahmin, the sin of *brahmahatyā* (the murder of a Brahmin) arose. Then, because of that terrible and most grievous *brahmahatyā*, Sumati, being afflicted, wandered over the entire earth and returned to his own village; he sought refuge near his father. His father forbade the protection of him who was thus struck down by *brahmahatyā*. When Sumati was beaten by that *brahmahatyā* in the presence of his father and others, all of them, including his father, wept in sorrow. Now...

At that very moment, Yajñadeva, having arrived there with his wife Duvasā, offered prayers for the removal of the faults of his son; thereafter, Duvasā instructed him to bathe at the Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha of Śrī Rāma for the removal of the sin of killing a Brahmin. In connection with the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha, the account of how the sin of violating the guru’s wife was removed for the Brahmin named Dutinīta is narrated. Then, [Yajñadeva spoke] to Duvasā...

The description of the conduct of the twice-born named Durvinīta, who was difficult to discipline, told by Śranna to Yajñadeva out of a desire to know about the wicked behavior of the ill-behaved; therein, after his father—the son of Dhanāha, whose name was Īṣmavāha, a ruler of the Pāṇḍyas—had passed away, Durvinīta performed the funeral rites for his father and, due to famine, came with his widowed mother to reside in this land. While he was living there for a long time, that Durvinīta of dull intellect...

When his own daughter, afflicted by the arrows of Kāma, cried out, "Do not come to me," he forcibly dragged her, a widow, for sexual intercourse. Then, after the emission of semen, the ill-behaved man felt intense remorse and approached the great sages for the purpose of performing penance to purify his body. Although all the sages rebuked him for that great sin and expelled him, the most compassionate great sage Vyāsa [acted] toward him...

In order to turn him away from the sin of approaching his preceptor’s wife, Vyāsa gave instruction regarding Dhanuṣkoṭi. Having heard the instruction from Vyāsa, Durvinīta, together with his mother, bathed at the holy site of Dhanuṣkoṭi according to the prescribed rite; then, having performed the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*) at the end of a month-long fast, he returned to Vyāsa and made a request for further instructions on what must be done next. Thereupon, Vyāsa gave the necessary instruction to Durvinīta concerning all that was to be done. Then, [the account] of Durvinīta...

Having performed the marriage ceremony according to the rules prescribed by Vyāsa and followed the duties of a householder, the practice of dharma is described as leading to liberation in the end. Thus, having heard the greatness of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha as told by Durvāsas, the Brahmin Yajñadeva took his son, who was afflicted by the sin of killing a cow, went to the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, and performed a bath there; by the power of that, [the sin] then vanished into the sky.

Furthermore, in connection with the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, there is the account of the Brahmin named Durācāra; the removal of the multitude of grave sins, such as the slaughter of a Brāhmaṇa, of the son of the twice-born Yajñadeva, who was named Sumati, through the power of the sacred syllables (*viṣayāḥ vāṇyā*); and having thus heard the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha as spoken by Sindhudvīpa, the two—Khagaṅga and Vānara—went to the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha and performed their ablutions. By the power of that, the description of how Khagaṅga and Vānara attained liberation is given. This is the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi.

There, a twice-born man named Durācāra, who lived on the banks of the Gautamī, was seized by a Vetāla due to his association with great sinners, which had completely destroyed his Brahminhood; having been carried from the region of the Gautamī to the Dhanuṣkoṭi holy site and immersed in the waters of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, Durācāra was instantly liberated from the Vetāla through that mere bath in the sacred water. Then, having gone to Śrī Dattātreya, he offered a prayer out of a desire to know his own history, and [Dattātreya] spoke to him.

The narration of the greatness of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha, preceded by the account of the Vetāḍa beginning from his capture and ending with his liberation; in that connection, the description of how the Vetāḍa attained the state of a Vetāḍa in a previous birth due to his failure to perform the *pitṛśrāddha* on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada; and as a further consequence, the description of the fruits of performing *śrāddha* on each lunar day during the Mahālaya period, including the case of Hariścandra and others who attained [liberation] through the power of performing the Mahālaya *śrāddha*.

A description of how the royal sages (rājarṣis) and other great ṛṣis, after first crossing over all suffering, attained the fruits of all supernatural powers (siddhis), such as sarvāṇimā; the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha from Śrī Dattātreya; and the fruits of the greatness of the Mahālaya-pakṣīya śrāddha and others. Then, having heard these things, the Brahmin named Durācāra—who had abandoned his evil conduct—returned to his own home by the path taught by Dattātreya, and through the performance of his own duties, a description of his attainment of liberation. Finally, the glorification of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, which effects the cessation of one's own sins.

Then follows the account of the Milk-Pond of Sudakṣiṇa (Masthakṣīrakuṇḍa); a description of it, and in connection with that, a description of the life of King Sudakṣiṇa. While a sacrifice was being performed there by Sudakṣiṇa, Mahāviṣṇu appeared at that sacrifice; he was propitiated by Sudakṣiṇa through hymns of praise. Then, in order to fulfill the desires cherished in the mind of Sudakṣiṇa, Lord Viṣṇu had a vast pond excavated in the hermitage of Sudakṣiṇa by Viśvakarmā, and having commanded Surabhī to fill it with milk, [Surabhī]—

When that pit was filled with broken milk, the Blessed One gave it to Mudgala for the purpose of performing the morning and evening fire-sacrifices (*homa*). Having named it the "Milk Ocean" (*kṣīrasara*) and granted a boon to Mudgala, he brought the narrative to its conclusion. In this chapter, the subject matter concerns how Vibhāvasu and Supratīka, due to a mutual curse, became an elephant and a tortoise, and how they were eventually released from their state of being food for one another.

Chapter Four: The attainment of liberation by Mudara, the son of Para, through the performance of his own duties beginning with fire-offerings (*homa*) and other rites; the narration of the account concerning the removal of the sin born of deceit committed by Kaṭā, the wife of Kaśyapa and sister of Chalakārī, in connection with the majesty of *kṣīrakhaṇḍa*; and the description of the majesty of *kṣīrakhaṇḍa*.

Once, between the two co-wives Vinatā and Kadrū, a wager was made regarding the color of the horse Uccaiḥśravas’s tail: that if Vinatā declared it black, she would become a slave to Kadrū; but if Kadrū declared it white, she would likewise become a slave. When Vinatā had spoken thus, and Kadrū had indeed declared the horse’s tail to be white, Kadrū commanded her own sons, the Nāgas, to cover Uccaiḥśravas’s tail with their own bodies so as to make it appear black. When the Nāgas refused to comply with her command, Kadrū cursed the Nāgas. Then, by the Nāga named Karkoṭaka—

O charioteer, the covering of the tail of the Sun-horse with her own body by Vinatā; then, having seen that Sun-horse with his black tail, Vinatā—who was defeated and consequently distressed—made a wager with Kadrū, and together with her son Garuḍa, carried Kadrū along with the sons of Kadrū, the Nāgas; then, Garuḍa, having learned from his mother the cause of her slavery, [flew] toward her... the snakes.

From his mother’s presence, for the sake of liberation from slavery and for the purpose of fetching nectar, he went to his mother’s side and ate the śavara; then his mother gave the command to Garuḍa to eat the śavaras stationed in the middle of the ocean; and Garuḍa, having devoured the śavaras, [presented] the Brahmin who had come amidst them along with his wife.

The account of how [the elephant and tortoise] were made to vomit from their mouths by means of a Kirāti woman; then, after Garuḍa had devoured the Rābarā birds, his arrival before his father Kaśyapa out of exhaustion and his request for food in order to cease the slaughter of Śūdras; Kaśyapa’s command to Garuḍa, treating him as his son; thereafter, Garuḍa seizing those two—the elephant and the tortoise—with his talons and climbing the tree named Rodiṇa on the bank of the river called Viṭaṃbā in order to remain there while consuming them.

As soon as he had climbed up, while the great sages—who were being carried on that branch—were distressed by the fear of falling when the branch broke, Garuḍa lifted that branch high into the air and placed it upon a certain mountain peak in the middle of the ocean; there, amidst the intervals [of the journey], he feasted upon elephants and tortoises. Then, when Garuḍa desired to place the nectar (sudhā) in his own world (Svargaloka), Indra caused calamitous portents to appear in Svargaloka, and consequently, the nectar remained in the other world (Pātāla). (Skanda Purāṇa, Māheśvara Khaṇḍa, Chapter 2).

The unjust matters... the account of the occurrence of the curse given by the Vālakhilyas to Indra for his act of obstructing the rain; then Garuḍa’s return to his own abode; the description of Garuḍa’s battle with the gods; in that battle, Viṣṇu’s proclamation of Garuḍa as his own vehicle under the pretext of granting a boon; then the granting of a boon to him by Śakra; and Garuḍa’s bringing of the nectar (sudhā), placing it upon the grass near the snakes, and [his own]—

The liberation from his mother’s servitude; then, while the Nāgas were returning after having bathed, Śakra carried off the jar of nectar (*sudhā*). When the Nāgas arrived and, suspecting it was nectar, began cutting it with their claws, the Nāgas’ tongues were split, resulting in the revelation of their "double-tongued" nature. Then, having addressed his own mother, Garuḍa inflicted a curse upon Kadrū—the deceitful one—in the form of perpetual service to him. Thereafter, Kaśyapa rebuked Kadrū; then [the story of] the virtuous woman...

At the request of Vinatā, Satyavatī, Kadrū, having pacified the fault arising from the curse, commanded [Garuda] to go for the sake of the *sarpa* sacrifice to the milk-lake situated within the village of Phulla on the shore of the Southern Ocean; by bathing in that milk-lake, the fault born of the curse was pacified, and the majesty of the milk-lake is described.

|| Śa || ... Next, the description of the majesty of Kapitīrtha: there, after the slaughter of Rāvaṇa and the other Rākṣasas, all the monkeys constructed a holy ford (*tīrtha*) and performed ablutions; the granting of boons to Kapitīrtha by Śrī Rāmacandra is recounted. Kapitīrtha.

In connection with the greatness [of the place], there is the narration of the life of Viśvāmitra; therein, while Viśvāmitra was performing penance to attain the status of a Brahmin, Ramā arrived to create an obstacle to his austerities and obtained the fulfillment of her desire from Viśvāmitra. Then, when a Rākṣasī approached for the purpose of harassing the sage Śatānanda, he hurled a stone to drive her away. That stone struck and killed the Rākṣasī and fell into Kapitīrtha; by the power of that holy ford, she was purified once again.

The attainment [of status] from Rambhā; the attainment of the state of Dhṛtācī by that celestial nymph (rāśasyā) after being released from her curse; the majesty of Kapitīrtha. ... [Folio missing]. Now, the description of the majesty of the two holy sites of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī; in connection with that, the slaying of Brahmā by Śiva out of passion toward his own daughter; the restoration of Brahmā to life by Śiva through the prayers of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī; the offering of praise to Śiva by Brahmā; and [the events] by the command of Śiva...

The presence of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī at Mandhātṛvana on Mount Mandara, preceded by the description of their two bathing pools (kuṇḍa); the majesty of the two Gāyatrī-Sarasvatī kuṇḍas. ... Chapter 10: Contents. Now, in connection with the majesty of the Gāyatrī-Sarasvatī kuṇḍa, the narration of the account of the Brahmin named Kāryapa; therein, [the account] of the Brahmin Kāryapa who was traveling for the purpose of warding off the arrows born from the portion of the future [incarnation] of the sage Raibhya’s son, Capya, who had taken the form of Parikṣit.

Having taken money from Takṣaka on his way back, he was pursued by the king’s life-force (*jīvitāra*), which caused him to bring along many people; then, the sage Śākalya, having learned the cause of the king’s death, acted for the sake of removing that fault.

By the instruction of Śākalya, having gone to the two *kuṇḍas* of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī situated on the chest of the Southern Ocean, [Śākalya] attained the instrument of knowledge (*jñānakaraṇa*). At that time, Kāśyapa offered a hymn of praise to Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī who had appeared there; they granted him boons, and by their grace, the Brahmin Kāśyapa was described as one whose sins were cleansed. [This is] the majesty of the two *kuṇḍas* of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī.

Then follows the description of the greatness of the Aṇemocana-tīrtha, Apeca-pāṇḍava-tīrtha, Devatīrtha, Suprīva-tīrtha, Nakhu-tīrtha, Gavāśva-tīrtha, Aṅgada-tīrtha, Gaja-gavaya-śarabhaṅga-tīrtha, Udumbara-nimitta-tīrtha, Vibhīṣaṇa-tīrtha, and the fourfold tīrtha established by the ministers of Vibhīṣaṇa, preceded by the description of their majesty; followed by the description of the greatness of the Sarayū river and the great god Rāmanātha situated on Mount Gandhamādana; then the description of the greatness of the Rāmanātha-liṅga installed by Śrī Rāmacandra. Therein—

A detailed description of the praise and greatness of the worship and other rites performed with devotion at the great shrine of Śrī Rāmeśvara; a description of the life of Śrī Rāmacandra in connection with the supreme excellence of the Śrī Rāmeśvara Liṅga; and therein, how Śrī Rāmacandra, having built a bridge across the ocean, slew Rāvaṇa in battle at Laṅkā, recovered Sītā, and [resided] on Mount Gandhamādana on the shore of the southern sea.

The arrival at Prayāga; then the sages, headed by Agastya, coming there to offer their salutations to Śrī Rāma; then, for the sake of removing the sin of Brahman-slaughter caused by the demon Rāvaṇa, the sages, following the instruction of Śrī Rāma, resolve to install a Liṅga of the illustrious Maheśvara; the command given to Hanumān to go to Kailāsa to fetch the Śiva-liṅga; and upon Hanumān’s return from Kailāsa after bringing the Śiva-liṅga, his seeing a Bilva fruit on the way.

Out of deference to the sages and out of fear of missing the auspicious hour, Śrī Rāma performed the installation and worship of a Śiva-liṅga made from the thatched hut belonging to Jānakī. Thereupon, Śrī Sadāśiva, who was stationed within the Liṅga, emerged from the center of the Liṅga and bestowed a boon upon Śrī Rāmacandra. Śrī Rāmacandra, having established Nandikeśvara before the Lord Śrī Rāmeśvara, performed the consecration of the Lord with his own bow-tip for the sake of the Liṅga’s installation. The Liṅga was thus established.

Then, after the auspicious installation of the Śiva-liṅga made of sand had been performed by Śrī Rāma, Hanumān brought a Śiva-liṅga from Mount Kailāsa. Seeing the Śiva-liṅga installed by Rāma even before his own arrival, Hanumān became filled with anger; the description of how he then began to cry out in lamentation follows. Then, Śrī Raghunātha consoled Hanumān. Subsequently, at the command of Rāma, Hanumān installed the Hanumadīśvara [liṅga]. Thus, there is a description of the eleven Śiva-liṅgas, beginning with Rāmeśvara. Now, [the account continues]:

When Hanumān, having undertaken a rash act to uproot the sand-idol (liṅga) that Rāma had established as a sign of Sītā’s discovery, found his efforts to be fruitless, he fell down while uttering the name of Māruti. Thereafter, Śrī Sītā and Rāmacandra made efforts for the sake of Māruti’s recovery; Māruti offered hymns of praise to Śrī Rāma and Jānakī; and Śrī Rāmacandra, having bestowed divine boons upon Māruti, [established] the Gaṅgā and Yamunā at the spot where Māruti had fallen.

The granting of permission for bathing at the holy site (tīrtha) in the form of Hanumatkuṇḍa, which embodies the three rivers of the Sarasvatī; the installation of the Liṅga brought by Hanumān near Rāmanātha; and, in the context of describing the cause of the manifestation of Śrī Rāmacandra’s laughter, the account of the birth of Rāvaṇa and others from the sage Viśravas upon the Kekeyī named Sumālī, a daughter of the Rākṣasas; and likewise, [the account] of Rāmacandra’s [confrontation] with Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa.

Upon the commission of the great sin of Brahmin-slaughter resulting from the killing of that [demon], Rāmacandra established the Rāmeśvara Liṅga at Setubandha to avert it; having constructed a bathing place known as Brahmahatyādhimocana (the Liberation from Brahmin-slaughter), he led the sin of Brahmin-slaughter into a nearby cave and, after it had subsided, installed Bhairava upon it. To the south of the great Liṅga Rāmanātha resides Girijā, along with her entire retinue and the guardian deities of the directions, all of whom were installed by Rāmacandra for the purpose of worshiping and serving the Rāmeśvara Liṅga.

The granting of agrahāras and other means of subsistence to Brāhmaṇas; King Śaṅkara wandering in the forest for hunting and the killing of a certain Śākalya Muni while he was wearing a tiger skin, as well as the killing of his wife who was likewise dressed in a tiger skin; the killing of his own parents [described in] the first chapter; the causing of grief by Rāmacandra to Hanumān when the latter was lying on the ground; then, after Hanumān had returned from the earth—(now, in connection with the majesty of Rāmanātha).

The description of the life of Śaṅkara Rāja, the sovereign of the Pāṇḍya country; then, at one time, the description of the manifestation of Setumādhava; and in connection with that, the description of the life of the king named Puṇyanidhi. Therein are the following topics: [the king] seeing [the deity], the weeping of Vajra; having heard his weeping, the arrival of the sage Śaṅkara near him.

Thereupon, Dayārāma returned to the vicinity of Bāulaka; having beheld King Dhanurdhara, his weeping parents, and the boy Bāulaka, he offered consolation by imparting the instruction of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) to Bāulaka. Following the command of the sages, that son of the sage performed the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) for his parents, and at the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara, located at Rāmeśvara, he performed the rites of *śrāddha* and other ceremonies accompanied by the enshrinement of his parents' bones.

Description of the appearance of that [fire] by its radiance; then, the Brāhmaṇas issued a command to King Śaṅkara, filled with indignation, for the purpose of entering the fire in order to expiate the sin of Brahman-slaughter. Thereupon, at the command of the Brāhmaṇas, King Śaṅkara instructed his minister to consecrate his own son upon his kingdom; when the king had made the effort to enter that kindled fire, a voice from the sky, preceded by a prohibition against King Śaṅkara’s falling into the fire, [spoke].

To expiate for the sins of killing a female donkey and killing a Brahmin, Śaṅkarabhūpa was commanded by Lord Rāmanātha to perform service; then, when the Brahmins likewise gave their approval, he served the Śrī Rāmeśvara Liṅga for one year with great devotion. By the power of that praise, the weight of the combined sins of killing a woman and killing a Brahmin—which had issued from the mouth of King Śaṅkarabhūpa—was destroyed by the command of Śiva. Then, the Lord Śrī Rāmanātha appeared before the terrified Śaṅkara.

The granting of boons; the description of King Śaṅkara attaining union with Śiva through the grace of Śrī Rāmanātha. ... Then, the performance of a hymn of praise to the Blessed Lord Rāmeśvara by Śrī Rāmacandra, Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, Hanumān, and all the monkeys, as well as by all the sages, gods, and others; thereafter, the description of the granting of boons to Śrī Rāmacandra and the others by the pleased Śrī Rāmeśvara; and [the account of] once digging at Rāmadhanuṣkoṭi in the holy place of Puṇyanivāsa in the city of Madhurā.

Regarding the gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa* and others: when [Puṇyanidhi] was about to set out for his own city, he was protected by a maiden who had assumed a female form. That maiden spoke her intention daily to King Puṇyanidhi, saying, "I shall become your daughter and dwell in your house without fear. Thereupon, Puṇyanidhi brought that deceitful maiden back to his own home and raised her like a son in the presence of his wife, named Vindhyāvasinī, after performing the rites of a son. Then, of her—

The search for Lakṣmī; Viṣṇu’s arrival there disguised as a Brahmin; the forcible seizing by the hand of Lakṣmī, who had assumed the form of a maiden while gathering flowers in that garden; then, hearing the weeping of the maidens, Puṇyanidhi led that Viṣṇu in the guise of a Brahmin through his own gatekeeper to the temple of Śrī Rāmanātha and bound him with fetters; thereafter, in a dream at night, Puṇyanidhi [saw] that Brahmin in the form of the Lord Viṣṇu.

And the manifestation of his own daughter in the form of Lakṣmī; then, having taken his daughter at dawn and gone to the one named Rāmanātha, seeing that brahmin who possessed the form of the Lord as he had been seen in his dream, recognizing him as Viṣṇu, and offering praise followed by a request for forgiveness for his transgressions; and the offering of praise to that Lakṣmī who was in the form of his own daughter; and by virtue of that prayer, the granting of boons to that devotee by the gracious Lord accompanied by Lakṣmī at Puṇyaniketa. Of that devotee...

For the sake of the uninterrupted praise of King Puṇyanidhi, the Blessed One, known as Setumādhava, caused himself to remain there by binding his own form with fetters; King Puṇyanidhi performed service to the Blessed One Setumādhava; at the end of King Puṇyanidhi’s life, he attained liberation; and the majesty of Setumādhava is described. (Now follows the description of the sequence of the procedure for the pilgrimage to Setu: having made a resolve in one’s own home preceded by bathing...)

First, a detailed description of the procedure for the pilgrimage preceded by the observance of constant and regular vows; then, a description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, following a specific account of the Setubandha; a narration of the story of the granting of boons by Śrī Rāmacandra at the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha; and, in the context of giving gifts, a praise of the worthy recipient as presented in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa regarding the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha at Rāma’s Setu.

The first section of the Brahmakhaṇḍa begins with the Setumādāra (the origin of the bridge), including the description of the performance of auspicious rites such as bathing and the offering of arghya, followed by the exposition of virtuous deeds such as worship, vows, and observances; the greatness of reciting and hearing the Setumāhātmya and the greatness of its gift-giving; and finally, the conclusion and completion of the Setumāhātmya. Thus ends the first [section] of the Brahmakhaṇḍa, beginning with the Setumādāra.
Chapters and Subjects, Paṭalas; Chapters and Subjects: Now begins the second section, the Dharmāraṇyakhaṇḍa, within the Bālakhaṇḍa.

The wandering of Saṅga; the gathering of Śaunaka and other great ṛṣis at the Naimiṣa forest to honor Sūta with due ceremony out of a desire to hear stories concerning the Dharma-raṇya; then, the commencement by the great ṛṣi Sūta to recount the majesty of Dharma-raṇya; therein, the journey of Yama-dharma-deva to the assembly of Brahmā; and there, in that assembly of Brahmā, [the account of] Yama-dharma hearing the divine narrative of Dharma-raṇya being recited by the great ṛṣi Vyāsa.

The Lord’s journey toward his own city; Nārada’s arrival there before Yama, the King of Dharma; and, upon being questioned by Nārada regarding the cause of his joy, Yama, the King of Dharma, recounting to Nārada the story of the *Dharmāraṇya* as he had heard it directly from Brahmā in the world of Brahmā; and Nārada’s return to the earth to meet Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, after having heard [the account] from Yama, the King of Dharma, by means of Nārada.

To Dharmarāja, who was desirous of hearing the *Camariṇya-kathā*, [Nārada] said: "Go and bathe in the Gaṅgā during the month of Māgha; before long, the great sage Vyāsa will arrive, and from his mouth you shall hear the *Camariṇya-kathā*. Having spoken thus, Nārada vanished. Then, the arrival of the venerable great sage Vyāsa before Dharmarāja occurred. Thereafter, Yudhiṣṭhira, having seated Vyāsa upon the throne and honored him, inquired after his health. Then, by Vyāsa, to Yudhiṣṭhira...

The commencement of the discourse on the *Dharma-āraṇyaka*; a description of the various holy places, forests, and other sites of merit; Yudhiṣṭhira’s inquiry to Vyāsa Mahārṣi out of a desire to know its greatness; Vyāsa’s undertaking of the narration of the *Dharma-āraṇyaka* story; therein, the description of Dharmadeva’s performance of penance after going into the middle of the forest with the intent to behold the true nature of the Blessed Lord and meditating upon Mahādeva; and the splendor of the mountain peak produced by that austerity.

Having gone to Kailāsa along with Paśupati, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and other deities, they offered praise to Śrī Mahādeva. Then, at the word of Rudra, Dharma realized the absence of fear among all the gods and returned to their respective abodes. Indra, however, became suspicious for no reason; with the permission of Bṛhaspati, he sent the Apsaras named Urvaśī to Dharma to disrupt his penance. At her command, she approached Dharma and, accompanied by singing and dancing, [attempted to seduce him].

Next, the description of the majesty of the forest-dwelling (*dhamāraṇya*), which is a place of supreme bliss and a synonym for *nirvāṇa*. Therein, the subjects of that forest-dwelling include the king of Dharma’s cultivation of a mind free from worldly distractions; an incidental description of the Apsaras Vardhanī, followed by a recounting of the faults inherent in the nature of women; then, the encounter between the King of Dharma and the Apsaras Vardhanī; the granting of a boon to the Apsaras Vardhanī by the King of Dharma; and subsequently, Vardhanī’s report to Śakra regarding her resolve toward the Dharma.

Having descended from Śakra’s abode, he went to his own place; then, after the departure of the Apsarases, Dharmadeva performed intense penance through the practice of the *pañcāgni* (five-fire) austerity. When the gods and others became distressed in mind by that severe penance, they went to Kailāsa and offered praise to Śiva. Then, together with the gods, they returned to the forest where Dharmadeva was performing penance. Dharmadeva offered praise to the Blessed One, and Śaṅkara, pleased by that hymn of praise—

In the context of granting boons, following the establishment of the fame of the Dharma Forest (*Dharmāraṇya*) within the Tapovana of Yama, which extends for two *yojanas*, there is the granting of a boon to the god Yamadharma; then follows the installation of the presiding deity of the Dharma Forest. Therein, first, by Yamadharma, the self-manifested image of the Lord Viśveśvara was established under the name Dharmeśvara, and the Dharmavāpī tank was constructed. Furthermore, the identity between Dharmavāpī and Dharmeśvara is described, along with the associated legends.

Description of the majesty of the eighteen *khaṇḍas* of Yama-dharma; then, by King Yama-dharma himself, preceded by a description of the splendor of Dharmāraṇya, the granting of boons and the preeminence of the sacred ground established by him; then, the description of the majesty of the eighteen thousand Brahmins created by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa in the forests of Dharma; and in connection with that, preceded by a description of the good conduct of the various stages of life (*āśrama*), a description of the daily obligatory duties common to all, beginning with morning recollection (*prātaḥ-smaraṇa*).

...a description of the conduct and duties pertaining to the householder, the chariot, the stone, the fire, and the guest; therein, the excellence of honoring guests; then, a description of the eight types of marriage; a description of the duties such as the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) to be performed by the householder; then, a description of the actions to be avoided by the householder; and a description of the benefits of serving the elderly, giving gifts, and so forth. ...

Contents: A description of the greatness of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and other rites at the Dharmavāpī pond located in Ghamoraṇya; then, in response to the inquiry of Śaunaka and others, a description by Sūta of the conduct of a fallen woman and the duties of a devoted wife (*pativratā*); as an incidental discussion on the duties of a devoted wife, a demonstration of the evil consequences for women of immoral conduct; a description of the rules and duties for widows; and a description of the greatness of the *śrāddha* ceremony, preceded by a detailed account of the merit of giving gifts such as sesame seeds and cows at the Dharmavāpī pond. Then, in the form of a dialogue between Indra and Skanda—

The section concerning the destruction of Dharma-raṇya: there, Śiva, having heard from the mouth of Skanda that the gods beginning with Indra had arrived, suddenly rose from his seat and, desiring to depart, was about to mount his bull; however, Skanda, wishing to know the reason for Śiva’s haste to go, made an inquiry. Then, Śiva, addressing Skanda, preceded by a description of the conduct of Khaṣṭṛthā and others, narrated a Puranic story, in which [the account of] Marīci, the son of Brahmā, [is told].

Following the description of the entry of the primordial Great Lord (Mahāviṣṇu), there is an account of the greatness of Dharmāraṇya, which was established by Yama—the son of Sūrya—and Rājanirbhita. Then, with a desire to go to Vaikuṇṭha in order to bring Śrī Mahāviṣṇu to Dharmāraṇya, Skanda and the other gods, including Brahmā and the rest, set out for Vaikuṇṭha along with Śiva. Having arrived there, Brahmā and the others offered praise to Viṣṇu; by virtue of the praise from Brahmā and the others, Viṣṇu arose, and then Viṣṇu [addressed] the gods, beginning with Brahmā...

When the reason for his arrival was asked, Dharma, after first reporting the state of Dharmāraṇya, requested Viṣṇu to go there. Then, Viṣṇu, having said "So be it," mounted Garuḍa and arrived at Dharmāraṇya along with Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the other gods. Yama, the King of Dharma, offered worship and performed hymns of praise to all the gods. Then, Viṣṇu made a request to Yama, the King of Dharma, for a boon. Thereafter—

When Yamadharma made a request to establish great hermitages within his own Dharmāraṇya, Viṣṇu and the other gods brought from various regions Brahmins endowed with virtuous conduct, accompanied by their disciples and retinues; having settled them in that Dharmāraṇya, they established well-provided hermitages for those sages.

Then, among the Ārāḍyaṇas residing there in the Dhamāraṇya forest together with their sons, grandsons, and others, there follows a detailed description beginning with the lineages, ancestral clans (*gotra*), and *pravara* of the four hundred and twenty chief great sages (*maharṣi*), as well as a description of the character of the Bāhyaṇas born of those respective lineages; and then, in connection with the majesty of the Dhamāraṇya, a narration of the account of the Yakṣa named Jasbhaka.

There, at the request of all the brahmins who were terrified by the yakṣa Jumbhaka, all the gods established the venerable Vṛpraśruti-yoginīs—each appearing in the form of the deity of a specific lineage (gotra) and ancestral rite (pravara)—within that Dhamāraṇya forest for the protection of those brahmins. Consequently, the brahmins protected by the yoginīs attained well-being. Then, once, when Rudra and the other gods had arrived there in the Dhamāraṇya forest, Viṣṇu approached Brahmā in order to perform service and worship for the lords of the gods. "Na... [the text continues].

The objects of the senses are the nourishment for passion; thereafter, by Brahmā, for the sake of destroying the lineage of the twice-born, when the recollection of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) was made in the Ghamāraṇya forest, Kāmadhenu arrived in the presence of Brahmā in that forest. Then, by Brahmā, through the granting of boons to the merchants from Kāmadhenu, the offering of a sacrifice was announced. Thereafter, when the earth was moistened by the stream of her own milk by Kāmadhenu, there arose from that [milk] sixty thousand sons of merchants wearing topknots and sacred threads. Then—

By Brahmā, who was instructed by all the gods, a system for the *gotra*, *pravara*, and other lineages of those Brāhmaṇas and their attendants was established, corresponding to each Brāhmaṇa and his followers, according to the specific speech of each of those merchants; immediately thereafter, all the gods offered praise to the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*); then, at the request of those cow-protecting merchants, Rudra brought the Gandharva maidens from Viśvāvasu and the Gandharvas, and with them—

The taking of wives by the Gobhuja [Brahmins] together; thereafter, the procedure for their marriage and domestic life; the description of how those thirty-six thousand Gobhuja merchants, along with their sons, grandsons, and countless lineages, resided in Dharmāraṇya and performed service and attendance upon the Brahmins; and then, at one time during the Tretā Yuga, when the Rākṣasa named Rauhineya came to Dharmāraṇya and was causing havoc, [the land was protected] by the lineage goddesses (gotradevīs) such as Oṃmātā and others against that Rākṣasa.

The account of the battle; at that opportune moment, Viṣṇu arrived and, being impelled, slew the Rākṣasa Khōṭajihva with his own discus; thereafter, out of fear of the Rākṣasa, the Brāhmaṇas and others residing in the Dhamāraṇya forest fled from Paṭhā, and by the command of Viṣṇu, they were invited by the gods and re-established in Dhamāraṇya; [the description] of the city established for the welfare of the Brāhmaṇas after the Blessed One had come from Satyaloka, slain the Rākṣasa, and settled them there.

The description of the fame of the name Satyamandira; then, following the account of the establishment of [the deity] Tyāndri, a description of the splendor of the city of Satyapura, preceded by a description of the abodes of all the deities beginning with Gaṇeśa and the Sun throughout all its parts; therein, in connection with the installation of Gaṇeśa, the narration of the events concerning the birth of Gaṇeśa from Pārvatī; and the offering of prayers by the inhabitants of Dharmāraṇya for protection, preceded by the praise of that Lord Gaṇeśa.

The leader of the Gaṇas having accepted the request of the gods made by the inhabitants of Dharmāraṇya, all the people there discussed matters concerning marriages and other auspicious rites. Then, in Dharmāraṇya, to the west of Śambhu, follows the detailed narrative of the birth of the two Nāsatyas (the Aśvins) from the sage Chyavana through the grace of the Sun-god. There, after Saṃjñā—the wife of the Sun—had established Chāyā near the Sun because she could not endure the Sun’s brilliance, she departed to perform penance. By Chāyā...

Due to the imbalance caused by his excessive affection for his son, Yama struck him with his foot; consequently, the sage cursed Yama. Then, having heard the account of his mother’s death as reported by Yama, Sūrya perceived through meditation that his wife Saṃjñā was performing penance in the form of a mare. Assuming the form of a horse, he went near her. Thereupon, after inserting his phallus into the mare's nostril and engaging in sexual union, the two sons Yama and Yamunā were born. [The text describes] him who had assumed the form of a horse...

The origin of the two *tapaḥkuṇḍas* on the ground where the eastern and western hooves of the Sun struck; a description of the greatness of that *Tapaḥravikuṇḍa*; then, the installation of the Sun there by Brahmā and the other gods under the name Bakulāditya, as well as the installation of Saṃjñā and the twin Aśvins; a description of the greatness of the *Bakulākhya-ravikuṇḍa*; the reason for the fame of the name Bakulākhya; and then, the performance of penance by Viṣṇu in the Dharmāraṇya forest after having subdued the horse-headed Hayagrīva, accompanied by Śiva and Skanda.

The narration of the events: when the other gods had begun their deliberations on the surface of the earth regarding the invocation of Viṣṇu, Rudra and the others set out for Veṅkaṭa. At that time, the Blessed One was performing penance through the yoga of meditative absorption with his bow in hand in a secluded place. Then, in order to awaken him, Vyāsa employed the stratagem described by Bṛhaspati; he enticed a female termite to bite the string of the bow held in the Blessed One’s hand by promising her a share in the sacrifice.

The gods issued a command; then, as soon as it was consumed by Daśagrīva while he was bearing the burden, Viṣṇu severed his head with a stroke of his discus. When that head was severed and remained stubborn despite repeated cleansing, Brahmā and the other gods spoke these words.

The command for the purpose of rejoining the head of Viṣṇu; then the promise by Viśvakarman to the gods regarding the granting of a share in the sacrifice; thereafter, when the horse of the chariot drawn by the *suyas* had reached the middle of the sky at midday and was brought by the gods, Viśvakarman joined the head of the horse to the trunk of Viṣṇu; then the gods performed hymns of praise to Viṣṇu with the horse-head as the foremost; then, by Hayagrīva, who was pleased by that hymn of praise—

Brahmā caused the gods to be born from the Valā-savatī; then Rākā granted a boon. Thereafter, Brahmā and the other gods performed the sacrificial rite (*yajña-karma*). During that sacrificial rite, they bestowed upon the Vabhrīs and Viśvakarman the sacrificial portions (*yajña-bhāga*) that had been previously promised to them. Having completed the sacrificial rite, Brahmā and the others departed for their own respective worlds.

Then, in the context of explaining the cause of Viṣṇu’s transformation into a horse-headed being, there is a description of the incident involving the falling of Viṣṇu’s head in the assembly of Brahmā due to a dispute with Brahmā; then, Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of a horse, established the Devasaras Tīrtha in Dharmāraṇya and performed penance, while Brahmā also stood before him and performed penance; thereafter, the restoration of Viṣṇu’s horse-head to its former state and natural color through the power of that Tīrtha is described; and then—

The description of how that fifth mouth of Brahmā—which, with its speech, had uttered a curse upon Viṣṇu—became like a crow's beak; the narrative of how that fifth mouth of Brahmā was cut off by Hara at Dharmāraṇya; the account of Brahmā’s establishment of Mokṣeśvara preceded by the creation of the Mokṣatīrtha; the description of the restoration of his barrenness and the attainment of a virtuous son through the power of bathing at the Devasaras Tīrtha; and the majesty of Mokṣeśvara.

Description of the Power of the Devakhāta Lake. Now follows the description of the establishment of the Śrīmātā and other gocara goddesses in various distinct locations within Dharmāraṇya for the purpose of destroying the fear of Rākṣasas and other evils for the people residing there, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. This includes a description of the nature, names, and other attributes of those goddesses who manifest in the forms of their respective sites, followed by a description of their specific modes of worship. Therein, the majesty of the goddesses beginning with Śrīmātā and ending with Ānandā on the eastern direction is described.

Now, following the description of the majesty of the goddesses beginning with Śāṃtānī situated in the southern direction, [this is] the majesty of the venerable goddess Mātā. In the context of describing the majesty of the venerable goddess Mātā, there is a description of the account of the goddess Mātangī’s appearance and other events for the sake of slaying the demon named Gīṭaka, who had carried off the wife of a twice-born man living in Dharmāraṇya after disputing with him. Therein is the description of the battle between Mātangī and the demon Kaṇauṭaka; in that battle, Kaṇauṭaka, having bewildered Mātangī through his illusory power—

Having returned to Śrīmātā Devī, he made a request for her hand in marriage; then, Śrīmātā Devī, having spoken with Śyāmalā, sent the Karṇāṭaka Daitya to Śyāmalā Devī on the pretext that her own marriage was difficult to accomplish. Thereafter, following the account of the Karṇāṭaka Daitya’s defeat in battle by Śyāmalā Devī, and then the description of the circumstances of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s rebirth through the power of the greatness of Śivā, [Kṛṣṇa] performed the slaying [of the demon] for Pārvatī; thereafter, [the story continues] with Saṃtuñjā and others.

A section concerning the Śrīmātā, Mātaṅgī, and Śyāmalā Devīs, including: a chapter addressed to the goddess Śrīmātā by those desiring to know the specific ritual of worship (*viśeṣopacāra*) and the preceding rules for worship; the description of the procedure for worship as taught by the goddess Śrīmātā to them; a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the goddesses Śrīmātā, Mātaṅgī, and Śyāmalā; and, in the context of describing the majesty of Indrasaras and the majesty of Puṣkara, an account of the performance of penance by Śatānanda at the site of Śatahṛdayā; and the majesty of Indraratīya-tīrtha.

In the vicinity of that very place, there is the description of the greatness of Jayantīśvara as told to Jayanta; the description by Śiva of the seed-syllables (*bīja-varṇa*) of the *Mātaṅga* mantra; how the Goddess attained a wicked state of mind through the recitation of such a mantra; then, Śiva’s sudden fall upon going toward Dharmāraṇya; the birth of the Kūṭagaṇas from the sweat of his limbs; and when those Gaṇas stood upon the peak of Mount Kūṭa and performed the mastery of the Kūṭa-mantra, they declared themselves to be Śiva himself due to their success.

Having heard of Pārvatī’s state of being afflicted by a stone, she then performed penance at the command of Śiva and gratified Śiva; the description of that place of penance becoming famous by the name Dharā-kṣetra, and the glorification of the majesty of that Dharā-kṣetra. Then follows a detailed description of the deities Bhaṭṭārakā, Viṅkur, and others situated in Dharmāraṇya, as well as the lineage-origin deities of the Brahmins residing in Dharmāraṇya, such as Vaṭeka and others.

Now, in Dharmāraṇya, there were yoginīs established by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, whose numbers extended to the ends of the quarters, beginning with the East. Then, once, having been defeated in battle by the Dānavas, the Devas fled toward the north. Thereupon, by the command of Brahmā, they returned to Dharmāraṇya and commenced a sacrificial session (*satra*) lasting for a thousand years. In that sacrifice, the Brahmins were won over by being provided with various kinds of cooked foods as offerings. Thus, in Dharmāraṇya...

The description of the departure for heaven after the destruction of those who had attained excellence through the power of giving; then, at one time, an asura named Hāsuraka arrived at Dharmāraṇya and caused extreme harassment to the Brahmins and merchants residing there; terrified by him, the Brahmins and merchants fled in all directions, wandering aimlessly and seeking refuge here and there.

The establishment of a residence in the village of Imbhu-prāma, not far from Dhamoraṇya; and by those merchants, the establishment of a residence for the venerable Śrī Rāmacandra beginning from his childhood, along with the narration of the causes for their naming—namely, his marriage, forest exile, battle with the rākṣasas, the slaying of Rāvaṇa, the recovery of Sītā, his return to Ayodhyā, and his coronation as king—and for that very reason, [the account] of the merchants residing there.

A description of the division among the kinsmen; likewise, a detailed account of the life of Ekapaiṭha. Then, following the abandonment of Dharma-vaṇya by the Asura Khodā, there is a description of Rāma’s departure for his own abode after informing Vasiṣṭha that his own holy place is the most excellent of tīrthas. [Therein is] the offering of a gift out of a desire to know the majesty [of the place]. Oṃ. 01101641.

Then, having heard from the mouth of Vyāsa that Dharmāraṇya was free from fear in this manner, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, went to Dharmāraṇya. Thereafter, Rāma, for the sake of removing the fault incurred by the slaughter of the Brāhmaṇa-Rākṣasa he himself had committed, approached Vasiṣṭha at the most excellent of all holy places (tīrthas). Having gone there and bathed in the tīrtha, and having performed the rites of *iṣṭāpūrta* and so forth, he returned to rule his kingdom while residing at Dharmāraṇya. Then, the great sage Vasiṣṭha, after first describing the greatness of the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and various other tīrthas...

The description of the greatness [of Dharmāraṇya], preceded by a description of its being the most excellent of all holy places (tīrthas) and its supreme status; then, having heard the majesty of the Dharmāraṇya field as recounted by Vasiṣṭha, the account of the arrival of Sarasvatī from Satyaloka into Dharmāraṇya; and in connection with that narrative, the visit of the sages led by Mārkaṇḍeya, and the establishment of the three holy sites in Dharmāraṇya by Śrī Rāmacandra along with his retinue, including the city of Māṇḍalika.

The description of the consultation; therein, the account of Mārkaṇḍeya himself bringing the Sarasvatī from Satyaloka; then, at the word of Vasiṣṭha, the poet [Vyāsa] abandons the palanquin along with the merchants and the people, and the description of the fruits of bestowing knowledge, performing *śrāddha*, and other rites upon the Sarasvatī; then, having personally performed the ritual of pilgrimage according to the scriptures on foot together with all his soldiers and retinue, the description of the majesty of the Dvārakā-kṣetra situated in the Dharmāraṇya forest.

[Having installed the Liṅgas known as Śrīrāmeśvara, Kāmeśvara, and Varāha, and having performed the rites with a composed mind: Now follows the description of the greatness of the Govatsaliṅga situated in Dharmāraṇya, which was worshipped by the cowherd boy who had been wandering in that forest; the description of the Caṇḍāla residing at Govardhana; and the account of how Śrī Rāma, having arrived here himself while the Gaṅgā was present near the Govatsaliṅga, declared his intention to relate his own history.

Then, having approached the cremation ground by means of messengers, he related the words of that woman; thereafter, Śrī Rāma himself went to the vicinity of that woman—the one called Sarasvatī on the Lohayaṣṭikā mountain—and when asked the reason for her weeping, she spoke to him. [The text then proceeds with] the description of the fruits of knowledge, charity, faith, and so forth. Thus ends the section concerning her.

Then, after the goddess Śrīmātā had previously [manifested] as Śrī Rāmaparāṃsā, there occurred the manifestation of her own form in the Dharmāraṇya forest created by the demon Loha. There, on the bank of the Sarasvatī, the demon Loha performed penance to please Śiva; meanwhile, in that Dharmāraṇya, [the goddess] established the conduct of all people, beginning with Urmimān and others, through her constant wandering. While he was thus performing penance, she struck him with her fist to obstruct his ascetic power; thereafter, the gods [intervened].

The offering of prayers to Śrī Rāma by all beings with the intent for victory; hearing the words of Śrīmātā, Śrī Rāma’s engagement in battle against the demon Dhundhu—who had fallen face-down—and his placing of Śaṅkara upon that demon’s chest, Brahmā upon his neck, and Viṣṇu at his feet; furthermore, the description of his taking a vow before the Mother of the World to establish the city of Satyamandira as it was previously, and his remaining there.

Then, at the word of Brahmā, the Asura [Dharmarāja] placed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara within his own body and dispatched his own messengers; through them, he summoned all the Brahmins residing here and there, and being satisfied by their hymns of praise, prayers, and presence, he remained in that Dharmāraṇya in a state of prostration. Then, having brought them with great honor as before, he performed worship and hospitality for them, and gave them wealth, garments, and ornaments, while Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva [remained] within the Asura.

And the description of the granting of boons: "O people, may you protect me—ka, ka, pa, ṅa, ta, ta, ṇa, ma, va, ka, ka, na, ti, oṃ, pra, śti, ba, hu, vi, dha, dā, na, pra, dā, na, e, śa, ṣku, ti, na, pā, na, na, rā, ya, da, ri, sa, ki, ni, ka, na, pa, yā, ā, dā, ya, ra, śa, ka, ka. Then, Śrī Rāma, having made arrangements for the restoration of the dilapidated Dharmāraṇya region and for its future prosperity before those Brāhmaṇas residing in that sacred field, made a formal request for the bestowal of gifts accompanied by a sacrifice; thereafter, by them...

Having gone everywhere and consulted together, [the gods] described their own duty as being intent on turning away from receiving gifts from Śrī Rāma, and recounted how they were commanded by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. Then, Śrī Rāma remembered all the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu; by the mere act of remembering them, all the gods, starting with Brahmā, arrived. Śrī Rāma then honored all those gods with worship and other marks of respect. Thereafter, by all the gods...

Having heard of Śrī Rāmacandra’s desire to restore the dilapidated Dhamāraṇya-kṣetra, they offered him praise; then, having obtained the permission of those gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others—Śrī Rāmacandra began the restoration of the sacred site of Dhamāraṇya-kṣetra, and having constructed various large branches, intermediate branches, and Brahma-branches, he filled all of them with an abundance of diverse wealth, grain, gold, jewels, and other materials.

The bestowal of one hundred and forty-four women upon the Brahmins; the issuance of commands to the thirty-six thousand cowherd merchants to perform service for the Brahmins, preceded by the granting of white chowries, swords, and other gifts; the issuance of orders at the time of marriages and other occasions to bear royal insignia such as the chowrie, and for the worship of the goddess Gurāṅkukhdevī; and [the granting] of chowries, swords, and so forth to the merchants of Ṭīkamaṇḍaleśvara, including those of the Sapādaṣaṭkṣa group.

Having performed service to the twice-born and carried out their commands, he then established the shrines of his own ancestors and lords; having first installed deities such as the river goddess Śrīmātā, Culyasvāmin, and Harigaṇādhyakṣa, he constructed fortifications, ramparts, moats, religious tanks, and other structures beneficial to the city. Having inscribed an unbroken edict upon a copper plate and bestowed it upon learned Brāhmaṇas, he [granted] that Dharma-Araṇyakṣetra to the Brāhmaṇas, merchants, and others residing therein.

The protection provided by Māruti, who was none other than [Hanumān], and his carrying out of orders; likewise, having performed the *jīrṇoddhāra* (restoration of the ruins), Śrī Rāma worshipped and prostrated before the venerable Mother, and then accepted the gift of land from the gods and the twice-born. A description of the settlement follows: the Brāhmaṇas performed service day after day according to the copper-plate charter (*tāmrapaṭa-śāsana*) granted by Śrī Rāmacandra; thereafter, Śrī Rāmacandra sent word to the Brāhmaṇas and merchants there that they should always proceed toward Bhārata.

Now, the description of the return to the city of Ayodhyā after Śrī Rāmacandra had received the command of the Brāhmaṇas—preceded by the granting of a promise of safety stating, "He shall always perform for you whatever task you desire"—which was inscribed in the middle of the copper-plate charter granted to the Brāhmaṇas; and then, the account of how Śrī Rāma, on one occasion during a conversation in Ayodhyā, heard from the mouth of Śrī Vasiṣṭha the story of the sage Araṇyakṣetra.

Having heard of Prayāga, Niveṇī, Tīrtha, Siddhakaṣatra, Kāśī, Gaṅgādhama, Araṇya, Vaṇau, Harikṣetra, and other such places, he went with his attendants to Dharmāraṇya in order to perform a pilgrimage there again. Staying in Moherakapura, he completed the sacrificial rites together with Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, and other great ṛṣis such as Ūrṇavābha. Upon concluding the sacrifice, he performed the ritual ablution. There, at the end of the sacrifice, having been requested by Sītā, he established the city named Sītāpura in front of Moherakapura for the sake of the learned.

The entrustment [of the land] to the Brāhmaṇas; then, having gone toward Dhamaukha, the narration of the account of Śrī Rāmacandra’s gift of fifty-five *rāmas* (units of land) beginning from Sītāpura and ending at Satyamandira—preceded by the performance of the great gift (*mahādāna*) of sixteen types (*ṣoḍaśa*) to the Brāhmaṇas according to the words of Sītā and the command of his preceptor; and for the sake of serving the eighteen thousand great sages (*maharṣi*) of the Vātsyāyana lineage residing in those fifty-five *rāmas*, [the gift of] sixty-four thousand courtesans and their fourfold retinues.

The granting of gifts to the Brāhmaṇas; then, at the request of the Brāhmaṇas, Rāma’s command that the *veśyās* and Śūdras perform service for those Brāhmaṇas; thereafter, the return of Śrī Rāmacandra to his own city; thus, the description of the account of Śrī Rāmacandra’s restoration of dilapidated holy sites (*tīrtha-sthāna*) within the Dharmāraṇya region; and finally, the description of the well-being of Dharmāraṇya due to the power of the protection established by Hanumān, as told by Brahmā to Nārada.

In the *Yudhiṣṭhiravijaya*, Yudhiṣṭhira inquires of Vyāsa whether the Dharma-forest has ever been destroyed; thereupon, the great sage Vyāsa recounts the events of the previous Kali Yuga, including the account of King Śālivāhana Āma, the sovereign of Kānyakubja. Having heard from his own preceptor the power of Kaṅka, that king Āma, with a mind agitated by the influence of Kaṅka, sought to uproot the Vaiṣṇava dharma.

King Āmabhūpa, having embraced Buddhism, then begot a daughter named Ratnagaṅgā upon his wife Āmā; the description of how that girl named Ratnagaṅgā became devoted to the Jaina religion after being deluded by the Kṣapaṇakas; the giving of Ratnagaṅgā in marriage to King Kambhoja, the lord of Brahmāvarta; and at her wedding, the granting of the city of Moherakālī, situated in Dharmāraṇya, to her husband by King Āmabhūpa. Then, by the king...

Having arrived at Dhamāraṇya, he made the city of Modiraka his own capital; there, he caused the Jaina religion to spread throughout his entire kingdom. At that time, all castes attained devotion to the Jaina faith. When the *randharāsana* (seated on a hole) and *patrāṇa* (leaf-eating) ascetics were driven out by Bhārīrāmacandra, those same Brahmins, having been led away, went to King Sāvabhauma in the Kānyakubja region and reported to him the matter concerning the *kṣātra* and *patra* given by Rāma.

The report of the news regarding his own conduct, brought about by his own disposition; the sending of an order by King Āma through him to his own son-in-law, Rāma, to confiscate the royal edict; and how, despite the command of his father-in-law, Kumārapāla—under the pretext of a pilgrimage to Mount Arbuda—disregarded the edict of Rāma and, having prepared to seize the livelihoods from the Brāhmaṇas, spoke to them, saying: "Let proof be given by the summoning of Māruti through the doctrine of Nāstika."

Then, in order to bring back Māruti who was staying at Sedabandha, all those Brāhmaṇas gathered together at that place of dharma; having formed themselves into groups and established a consensus with the leaders of the twice-born, they made a firm resolution to go toward Rāmeśvara as a collective body to fetch Māruti, and they took a written agreement. Then, for the purpose of preventing the eighteen thousand Brāhmaṇas who were about to set out for the site of Rāmeśvara, [they addressed] all the rulers...

When King Kumārapāla issued a command, thirty-six thousand Jaina lay-devotees (śrāvakas), including merchants and Brahmins, took a vow of silence out of fear of the king’s curse and to avoid violating their religious duties. Subsequently, the king dispatched certain Śūdras from among those residing in the place called Āḍā—who were devoted to the Jaina Dharma—to restrain the Brahmins; and by the king’s order, several of those Śūdras, whose hearts were hardened by the intense impressions of the Jaina faith, [acted accordingly].

Having approached those three Brahmins, he engaged them in conversation using reasoned arguments for the purpose of turning them away from their hostile intent. Upon hearing the words of those Śūdras based on reasoned argument, fifteen hundred among the eighteen thousand Brahmins—having first offered their respectful salutations and disregarding the command of Rāmabhadrācārya—departed toward the sacred site of Rāmeśvara, thereby turning back from their hostility. As for the remaining three thousand twice-born ones...

With firm resolve, they set out toward the sacred site of Śrī Rāmeśvara for the sake of sporting with Māra; however, becoming exhausted by the great fatigue of the journey along the way, they were moved by the inspiration of Śrī Rāma to approach Hanumān. Desiring to see the Lord, they requested him to act as their guide, yet Hanumān explained that a vision of Rāma was impossible for them due to their sinful nature. Then, the Brahmins offered hymns of praise to Hanumān, who was known as Vālisuta (the son of Vāli). Satisfied by their eulogy, Hanumān provided those Brahmins with various kinds of assistance.

Then Hanumān, having examined them and revealed his own form to them, brought those Ādyaṇas back to Rāmeśvara at Setubandha; after causing them to perform the vision of the Great Lord Rāmeśvara and other rites, he expressed his own sense of blessedness through that vision and offered his prostrations.

He gave fruit to the beggars for them to eat; then, as a token of recognition for those brahmins, he gave each of them two small pouches filled with hair from his own armpits, and instructed them to present these in turn to the king.

And for the sake of reviving the dog once more, he issued an order to throw it at the king’s gate; then, taking those two earthen pots, the highly delighted and joyful Brāhmaṇas stayed for three nights near Śrīmāruti on the banks of the Śrīrāma [Tīrtha], performing the Brahma-yajña and other rites. Then, on the night of the third day, Hayumanta placed those twice-born ones upon a bed spread over ten yojanas and made a request for rest. When those Brāhmaṇas had fallen asleep, Māravidā [saw] his father’s body rising up.

The transport of that stone to Dhamoraṇya; then, when they had arrived at Dhamoraṇya along with Viśākhā Śikhā, those Brahmins, accompanied by their sons and grandsons, returned to her presence through the power of their ascetic energy. After a festival of meeting and conversation with all three thousand Brahmins and their families, they returned to their respective homes with great ceremony. Then, on the following morning...

Having thus spent five days in fasting, immediately thereafter, on the sixth day, he went to the royal assembly hall and delivered his message from Mārutideva to the king. Upon hearing the message from Mārutideva as related by that Brahmin, while King Kumārapāla was preparing for battle against him, [the messenger] threw a single hair-pouch from among the hair-pouches located in the left armpit of that hero Mārutideva toward the palace gate; by the mere act of throwing it, at that very moment, his—

The burning of the entire wealth of King Kumārapāla—including his sons, elephants, horses, and so forth; the description of the extreme suffering of the Jaina mendicants (*nagnakṣapaṇakas*) due to the king’s intense wrath; then, the sudden departure of those brahmins from the presence of King Kumārapāla; and finally, their presentation of a small pouch of hair from the right side of Bhīmaratha’s beard to the *chṛṣālu* (the executioner) at the royal gate, as soon as it was cast down, [the king’s]— [Note: The source text appears to be fragmentary. The final sentence is incomplete.]

There was the attainment of all peace, preceded by the restoration to life of all the cows, sons, elephants, horses, and buffaloes that had perished. Then, having gained conviction through the power of Śrī Rāma and Hanumān, that king issued new land-grant charters (*vṛtti-śāsana-patra*) for those Brahmins, similar to those of former times, and carried out the expulsion of heretics such as Jains, Buddhists, and others who were outside the Vedic fold from his own kingdom. Furthermore, he restored the merchants of the thirty-six thousand [guilds] who were endowed with virtuous conduct, as well as the cowherds and traders, to their former status.

An investigation into the purpose of serving Brahmins; then, a description of the authority granted by the King to three thousand Brahmins residing at Setubandha via a document concerning their livelihood; an examination of the lack of entitlement to *bhūmivṛtti* (land-grant sustenance) for those Brahmins numbering fifteen thousand who had accompanied him to Setubandha as attendants fulfilling his own vow; and [the account] of the three thousand Brahmins named Jayīvidya, who were making their vow true, within the city of Meheraka.

The establishment of a residence; the settlement outside the village of Meherakamra of all those known as Cāturvidyas—numbering fifteen thousand Brāhmaṇas who were breaking their own vows—in a place for their comfortable dwelling; the description of the performance of the worship of family deities by these [Brāhmaṇas] belonging to the Moṇḍhabeśaja Śaiva Cāturvidya community on every thirteenth day of the month of Pauṣa; and the performance of honors and worship for them by the merchants known as Gobhijas.

Then, after Taitaba and the other non-gods had individually assigned the distinct modes of livelihood for those Brāhmaṇas dwelling in the Dharma-araṇya, they returned to their own abodes. Subsequently, there is a description of the settlement of fifteen thousand Brāhmaṇas—both those learned in the four Vedas (*cāturvidya*) and those ignorant of them—in the five groups of villages (*pañcapañcaka-grāma*). This includes the names of the fifteen *gotras* of the *cāturvidyas*, the enumeration of the names of the twenty-five villages beginning with Sītāpura, and so forth. Now...

A detailed description of the lineage, origins, and nature of the Cāturvidya Brāhmaṇas residing in the fifty-five villages on the left side, beginning with Sītāpura; then, a description of the seventeen villages, such as Rīṭakhā, belonging to the Traividyas who arrived from the vicinity of Hanumān; a description of how a conflict arose for some time between the twenty-four Cāturvidyas and the Traividyas; and finally, a description of the distinctions among certain castes based on the influence of their respective traditional conduct. Then...

When the Kṛta Yuga had arrived, among certain warriors residing there, due to the influence of the eightfold conduct and the practice of independent conduct, there is a description of the emission of the syllable *khaṃ* and so forth; now, [regarding] the ancients...

Then, at one time, there was the arrival of the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others—at Dharmāraṇya. Due to fear of the Cedis, those residing there abandoned Sītāpura and went to dwell on the banks of the Sakhāvatī river. Upon their return, the description follows of their joyful settlement in that dwelling place, their subsistence through the practice of tending cattle and gathering milk products, and how, among the widows and maidens of those four classes of Brahmins, children were begotten by the Gopas who maintained the livelihood of cowherds.

The description of the fame of the Kātībhagokhaka-ghenu-janāsna Kumāras; then, regarding the three thousand Brāhmaṇas who had come from the presence of Hanumān and held the office of village officials (*grāmadvātyadhikārin*), among them were certain individuals who were extremely foolish, deaf, one-eyed, lame, mute, and so forth. Due to their inability to obtain brides for marriage within their own caste, they entered into matrimonial alliances with Cātuvidya girls; thus, there arose those Brāhmaṇas known as the Bhiśrasabhūtas.

The description of the three banners and their respective divisions; then, following the aforementioned manner, after the emergence of the division among kinsmen in Moheraka-pura, the description of the drafting of a formal agreement (vyavasthāpatra) by common consent of the Brāhmaṇas and others in the Kali age—due to fear of sinful conduct—to establish the worship of the Mother, the lineages (gotra), the ancestral sages (pravara), the branches (śākhā), and so forth, according to the traditional religious practices, family customs, and local usages inherited through succession; and the enumeration of the lineages, ancestral sages, and sub-branches of all the Moḍha Brāhmaṇas.

Thus concludes the second [chapter], the "Māhātmya of Dharmāraṇya," within the Brāhma-khaṇḍa, which describes the greatness and the fruits of hearing the glory of Dharmāraṇya—preceded by an account of how merchants and Śūdras dwelling in Dharmāraṇya attained the state of being devoted to the twice-born and the gods.
Now begins the third section of the outer portion, the subsequent section of the exterior.

Now, in the Naimiṣa forest, there is the narration by the great sage Sūta to the great sages headed by Śaunaka, concerning the greatness of Śrī Śaṅkara and the means of attaining Him; therein, the great sage Sūta first describes to the great sages headed by Śaunaka the greatness of the five-syllabled mantra of Śrī Śaṅkara, the rules for its acquisition from a qualified preceptor, and, as an incidental account, the narrative of King Daśāha, the lord of Mathurā, who, having married the daughter of King Karīra of Kārīravaṇa...

Then, driven by a sudden impulse and a desire to sport with her, the king forcibly drew her toward him; as soon as he touched her body, it became exceedingly hot like a mass of glowing coals. At that very moment, she rose up in terror, and when asked the cause of her burning limbs, she described to the king the power of the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva which she had been practicing. Thereupon, the king, out of curiosity, made an effort to receive the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva from his daughter-in-law.

Then, having heard those words, when the king had received the instruction on the Śrīśiva-mudrā from the preceptor Garga on the banks of the Kāverī at a most meritorious spot, the sins of that king—numbering as many as a hundred crores—emerged from the apertures of his body in the form of crows and were reduced to ashes. Thereafter, by the command of Guru Dvibhārīva, the sandal-paste for the purified body of that King Dākṣāyaṇa was prepared.

The governance of the kingdom preceded by the enjoyment of pleasures together with his own wife who had returned to her home; the majesty of the six-syllabled mantra of Śiva; then, a description of the majesty of the Great Śivarātri on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha; therein, the majesty of fasting, the worship of the Śivaliṅga, and the offering of *viśvapattras*; in connection with that, a description of the accounts of the kings named Ikṣvāku, Vedāja, and Amitasa; and there, when King Amitasa went out hunting and killed a certain Rākṣasa.

The Rākṣasa’s younger brother, assuming the guise of a courtier, approached the king in a humble manner to wait for an opportunity to search for his elder brother; the king then appointed him as the superintendent of his own kitchen. Subsequently, when the king once invited his family preceptor Vasiṣṭha for a meal, the Rākṣasa, wearing that deceptive disguise, placed human flesh in the preceptor’s food vessel; that impure food—

Having observed this, the great seer Vasiṣṭha, filled with anger, granted the king a boon that he would assume the form of a Rākṣasa for a period of twelve years. Then, hearing of that [boon], the king, provoked by resentment, took water in his hand to pronounce a counter-curse upon his own guru, Vasiṣṭha. Thereupon, Queen Madayantī, having made a plea to the king who was intent on casting a curse upon his guru, caused him to desist. Subsequently, as the king had already taken water in his hand to cast the curse upon the guru...

He threw his own feet [into the fire], and because of that act of burning his feet to a mottled black-and-white state (*kalmāṣatā*), the king became famous by the name Kalmāṣapāda. Then, after attaining the state of a *rākṣasa* and wandering in the forest, King Kalmāṣapāda was about to devour a certain young hermit (*muni-dāraka*). There, the wife of that hermit, who was accompanying him, pronounced this curse upon the king who had attained *rākṣasa*-hood: "When you have sexual intercourse with a woman, you shall become human again."

Having bestowed [the kingdom], there was the performance of the *agnīdhra* ritual; then, after the period of the curse had passed, having cast off the curse and regained his own true nature, he returned to his own home. Thereupon, Madayantī, the wife of the king, having heard the curse upon the wives of the brahmins, prevented her husband—who was entreating her for sexual union out of fear of his own childlessness—from doing so. Then, when the king, having despaired of enjoying the kingdom, had departed for the forest, the sage Vasiṣṭha [performed a ritual] in that royal consort Madayantī for the sake of establishing the Solar dynasty (*sūryavaṃśa*).

The procreation of sons; then, the pursuit of King Kalmāṣapāda—who had gone into the forest—by the hideous Brahmahatyā (the personified sin of Brahmin-slaughter); the king’s flight from Bhīṣmāyodhyā toward the great sage Gautama after being afflicted by Brahmahatyā; then, the instruction given by the great sage Gautama to the king for the removal of the fault of Brahmahatyā, regarding the vision of the Śiva-liṅga at Gokarṇakṣetra and the journey there; and, in connection with that, a description of the majesty of Gokarṇeśvara. Now...
