In this section, following the description of the great majesty of Gokarṇeśvara, Gautama describes his conversation with the messengers of Śiva who had arrived there to lead a certain prosperous Caṇḍālī woman to the world of Śiva; therein, Gautama [speaks] to the messengers of Śiva regarding that Caṇḍālī woman and her journey to the world of Śiva.

When the messengers of Śiva were questioned regarding the cause of her being led back, they related the account of that outcaste woman's previous birth. In that former life, she was the widow of a Brāhmaṇa who, through the power of a boon from Kāma, attained the status of a superior caste; however, having become infatuated with a Śūdra, she unintentionally killed a calf at night with her hand. Upon seeing it in the light and realizing it was a cow's offspring, she cried out "Śiva, Śiva! in repentance. Then, she met her death by means of a wooden post.

A description of the transformation of Devadudhi into the state of an Aṇḍālī after she attained it; and the account of her journey through the forest toward the Gokarṇa region in order to beg for alms such as food from this Aṇḍālī.

The description of how Śiva, through the power of the recitation of His auspicious names performed by the Kṣatriya, remembered her and, having drawn out her life-breath which was held by Śiva, enlivened her with divine luster and led her toward the realm of Śiva; then, in connection with that, when the King asked Gautama about the nature of the realm of Śiva, Gautama’s description of the nature of the realm of Śiva to the King—who was a devotee of Śiva and another name for whom was Kaṣipāda—and the subsequent account. And so forth. And then... [text ends]... And then.

A description of the greatness of the worship of Śrī Śiva; in that context, the account of the king named Vimardana residing in the country of Kirāta and a description of the greatness of devotion to Śiva; in that connection, the account of King Candrasena of Ujjayinī, followed by a description of how he attained the world of Śiva after being purified from the heat of sins such as the slaughter of a Brahmin.

The description: although that king was constantly devoted to the lowest [vices], he remained devoted to Śiva-bhakti. Then, once in private, his wife Kusumatī questioned the king—desiring to know the reason for his exclusive devotion to Śiva despite being utterly intent on wicked conduct—and thereupon King Vimardana described the events of his own previous birth. In a previous life, in the city of Pāpa, while a great worship was being performed in the temple of Śrī Śiva during the Mahāśivarātri by a dog...

The circumambulation of the temple of Śrī Śiva by Bhravate while she was pregnant; the description of how, when certain people there attempted to kill that dog with sticks and stones, he attained birth as a king through the power of the presence of Śrī Śiva; the description of his conduct in the womb of a dog, including his desire for food and his habit of devouring everything out of fear and hunger; and thereafter, the King’s narration of that noble lady’s previous life-story, wherein [he recounts] her former birth.

The narration of how a pigeon, having taken a lump of meat and ascended to the peak of a mountain, met her death when struck down by a vulture with a sharp beak seeking to seize that lump of meat; and how, due to the power of dying in the presence of the venerable Śaṅkara, she attained the status of a queen. Then, at the request of the king, the narration of the future history of both the king and the queen throughout seven births, followed by the description of how they will attain the state of Śiva through the worship of Lord Śiva on Mount Mahendra by the power of such devotion. Om Om.

Oṃ Ca Oṃ Ni Kai. There, having observed the king Candrasena’s devotion to Śiva, a Śiva-gaṇa named Maṇibhaṭṭāraka created a rift [between him and his enemies] and bestowed the Cintāmaṇi jewel upon that king. Wearing that Cintāmaṇi around his neck, King Candrasena ruled his kingdom. Unable to endure the power of that lord of the earth, other kings, seeking to seize that Cintāmaṇi jewel, mobilized for war and laid siege to the city of Avantī.

Having returned and besieged the city of Avantī from all sides, on that occasion King Candrasena sought refuge in the venerable Maheśvara Mahākāla and performed a great worship of him. At that time, Queen Riddhimaṇḍitā, having arrived at the temple of Śrī Ambikā, followed the instruction of Gautama and went with the king to the sacred field of Gokarṇa.

The sixth chapter concerns the power of beholding and worshipping the Great Lord Śrī Gokarṇeśvara. Once, having witnessed a festival of worship performed for the Lord by a certain young cowherd girl accompanied by her own son, the king set out toward his own city. While he was departing, his five-year-old son installed a stone Śiva-liṅga in a secluded, desolate spot near the temple of Śrī Giriśa, and taking the flowers as they had been gathered, [he began to worship it].

Having prepared the offerings of perfumes and other requisites for the worship of Śiva with an undistracted mind, she was then approached by that cowherd girl, who in her anger destroyed the Śiva-pūjā she had performed with her own hands. Upon seeing the destruction of the worship of Śambhu, the boy fell into a swoon due to the excessive grief and lamentation caused by it. Then, after some time, having regained consciousness, that boy beheld right there at that spot a divine, golden temple of Śiva made of jewels.

If it be asked what the sign was: then, by that pleased Bālkha, there was a request for forgiveness before Śrī Śaṅkara for the offense committed by his mother in interrupting the worship of Śiva; then, at the arrival of evening and night, having seen the entire camp of the cowherd community turned into divine gold by the grace of Śrī Śiva, he approached his own mother who was sleeping nearby in a divine form, awakened her, and told her that the entire camp had become golden; then, by that cowherd woman—

Having seen that wonder, he approached the king and reported the entire account to him. Then the king, accompanied by his ministers and others, went to that encampment and embraced the five-year-old cowherd boy Gopāla, who was made of gold and jewels. Thus, with great joy, as that night passed away, at dawn, all those stationed nearby heard the words of the spies.

Having heard this account of the conduct of the cowherd’s son, the king of the enemy kingdom was struck with wonder; abandoning his state of enmity toward the king and establishing supreme friendship, he entered that city. Having received the honors bestowed by the king and having visited Śrī Mahākāla, they went to Gopadivira. There, with joyful hearts, they beheld the celestial temple that had appeared through the grace of the cowherd’s son, and after making offerings of garments, gold, jewels, and other gifts to that son of the cowherd, they departed.

At that very moment, while the cowherds were standing there with their faces turned toward him, the venerable Umā appeared there in the form of a woman; having received the worship and honors of all the kings, she pointed out that cowherd boy in the midst of them all and spoke to all the monarchs.

Having extolled the greatness of the evening twilight (*divasāniproṣa*), he bestowed the name Śrīkara upon that cowherd boy Gopāṅkura, instructed him in the conduct of Śiva, and departed. This concludes the description of how King Candrasena and the cowherd boy Gopāṅkura, named Śrīkara, attained the world of Śiva through the power of their worship of Śiva.

And then follows the description of the greatness of the Pradoṣa-pūjā; in connection with that, the account of the king named Satyaratha residing in the region of Vidarbha; therein, the death of King Satyaratha in battle along with the Śālvas; thereafter, his pregnant wife, having departed from the city with great effort, went to an inaccessible forest; there, at the foot of a certain tree, her son was born; at that time, as she was overcome by extreme thirst, near her—

Then, while the king was wandering in that region, death occurred due to the exhaustion caused by the burden of his old age. At that moment, hearing the sound of the crying of the newborn Takṣaka prince, a certain Brahmin woman named Vidhavā, who had a one-year-old boy, was wandering there; seeing that helpless infant with its umbilical cord uncut, her heart was overcome with compassion, and she, desiring to take him home to nourish him, approached those who were disguised as physicians.

Having gained confidence from the words of Śaṅkara, the female elephant brought that child back to her own home. Then, while residing in the city of Ekacakrā, that Brahmin woman named Umā, out of affection for the boy, provided him with food and nourishment along with her own son. Later, when that Brahmin lady had gone somewhere to visit the deity named Deva together with those two boys, [the boy remained] at that place called Deva.

While the great sage Śāṇḍilya remained there, he recounted the wondrous nature of destiny by describing those two boys and the prince among them; upon hearing his words, when that Brahmin woman questioned him further out of a desire to know the lineage and other details of the boy she had brought, the venerable Śāṇḍilya related in detail the account of that boy’s birth and deeds throughout all his lives, beginning with his previous birth as the Pāṇḍya king.

Due to the fault of interrupting the worship of Śiva during Pradoṣa, there is death at the hands of an enemy in a future birth; for that [other] son as well, due to the fault of neglecting the worship of Śiva during Pradoṣa, there is the attainment of poverty in a future birth; and for his mother, due to the fault of having killed her own wife through deceit in a previous birth, there is death from dysentery (praseka) in a future birth—such is the ripening of karma.

Having recounted the greatness of both of those youths, there follows the instruction for the worship of Śiva during the Pradoṣa hour. Then, at the request of that Brāhmaṇa woman named Mā, by the venerable Mahārṣi Śāṇḍilya, in the context of the Pradoṣa observance, there is a detailed description of the performance of the worship of Śrī Śiva and other rites according to the scriptures and their constituent parts. Subsequently, among those two—the Brāhmaṇa youth and the prince—the Mahārṣi Śāṇḍilya bestowed the name Śucivrata upon the Brāhmaṇa youth and Dharma-rāja upon the prince.

Having performed the naming ceremony for the two of them, he gave the instruction on the Śiva-mantra for the purpose of conducting their daily worship; then, having bowed to and taken leave of the sage Śāṇḍilya along with those two boys, that Brahmin woman departed. Subsequently, at the command of their mother, those two sons of the king of Brahmins remained at home during the evening hours, performing the worship of Śiva. Then, once while the son of the Brahmin was wandering on the riverbank, he discovered a treasure consisting of a golden vessel. This was reported by him to his mother.

The two youths divided the wealth equally and gave the order for its distribution; then the prince, out of his own innate disposition and the fortune he had acquired, gave satisfaction to the Brahmin youth with his own portion of the wealth. Later, while wandering in the forest, the two youths—the Brahmin prince and the king’s son—beheld the Gandharva maidens playing there. Although the Brahmin youth was forbidden by him, the prince nevertheless approached those Gandharva maidens.

Approaching him, the Gandharva princess named Dravidī, known as Aṇḍumatī, arrived alone near that handsome-limbed youth, the prince. As both were tormented by the arrows of Love upon seeing one another, they conversed; then the Gandharva princess, having bestowed her own pearl necklace upon the prince—who was as if a vessel for dharma—made this vow: "Tomorrow, I shall perform my marriage with you."

He went with his own friends into the presence of his father; then, having gone to his own home together with the prince Dharmagupta, who was a young Brahmin named Ujjvalatā, he reported to his mother, Viprabhā, the events occurring in the forest. Then, when the time for the next day had arrived, that prince named Dharmagupta went into that forest together with the son of the Brahmin; and when the two of them had met there, they were honored by the Gandharva Chandraketu.

Having bestowed his own daughter upon Dharmagraprāya, the king of Kasama, after performing the rites of taking her hand in marriage and providing her with a magnificent dowry—including various jewels, elephants, horses, chariots, armor, weapons, garments, and female slaves—and having himself departed for the Gandharva realm by means of a celestial chariot, he lived there together with that Gandharva maiden, Umāvatī, in wedlock with that king named Dharmagraprāya.

Having been given dowry by her father-in-law, she arrived at Vidarbhanagara, the capital of her own paternal kingdom, together with the army of the Śūrasenas and Gandharvas; there, after performing the royal consecration (*rājyābhiṣeka*) and ascending to the throne of her father’s ancestral kingdom, she bestowed honors upon that young Brahmin as her maternal uncle and honors upon him as her brother; and thus, together with that Gandharva daughter, her own wife, [she lived] with that prince named Dharmapra[khya].

A description of the exercise of sovereignty with great happiness through the power of the Pradoṣa vow and the supreme grace of Śrī Śaṅkara in the city of Vidūrba; and a description of the majesty of the Pradoṣa vow and the worship of Śiva.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Somapradoṣa vow; in connection with that, the narrative of Sīmantinī, the daughter of the king of Citravama in Āryāvarta. There, having approached her father, Sīmantinī heard from two Brāhmaṇas skilled in physiognomy—each separately predicting her future great fortune and future widowhood—her fear of attaining widowhood led her to seek refuge with Maitreyī, the wife of the great sage Yājñavalkya.

Taking refuge for the purpose of hearing the means to attain fortune, wealth, and beauty; then, on that Monday, the narration of the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva and Gaurī by her; then, the commencement of the complete Monday vow (*somavāravratārambha*) by that princess Sīmantinī according to the path instructed by Maitreyī; the marriage of Sīmantinī with Citrāṅgada, the son of Indrasena; and then, at one time, as Citrāṅgada was residing in the city named Śvethura, [his intention] to cross the Yamunā river.

The sudden sinking of the boat in mid-stream as it had set sail; the death of all those who had boarded that boat; the learning of Prince Citrāṅgada’s death by the sinking of the vessel and the resulting grief of Citravat and the others; likewise, Sīmantinī’s failure to obtain a husband despite her efforts; and even when she had obtained one, Sīmantinī’s performance of the Monday-vow (somavāra-vrata) until the end of her life, despite having encountered such adversity; and then, [the events] in the sacrificial hall... below, below.

While Citrāṅgada was sinking, Sīmantinī, with her arms embracing his chest, led him toward the king of serpents in the underworld; Takṣaka then [acted] toward that Citrāṅgada... having heard the account of that [incident], she herself approached Sīmantinī and said, "We have honored your husband, and we have performed inquiries regarding the deity you worship," by Citrāṅgada.

He related the story of his devotion to Lord Śaṅkara, whose body he worshipped. Hearing those words, the delighted Takṣaka bestowed great honors upon Citrāṅgada. Then, hearing Citrāṅgada’s request to return to his own home, Takṣaka nourished him with the food of the nectar-yielding *kalpavṛkṣa* trees growing there, gave him much wealth, and likewise provided a Rākṣasa and a serpent for his assistance, as well as a horse that could travel at will and move unhindered.

Having bestowed the horses upon him and bound him with various blessings, he gave the command for Citrāṅgada to depart for his own abode. Then Citrāṅgada, having bowed to the King of Takṣakas, took the horse, mounted it, and having received wealth, set out from there toward the netherworld (Pātāla) accompanied by those two—the Rākṣasa and the serpent—who had been granted as his helpers. Emerging from the waters of the Yamunā, he mounted the steed on its bank and proceeded toward Vidarbha. At that very moment, [he was joined] by his own female companions...

Upon arriving at the Yamunā to bathe together with Sīmantinī, he witnessed her cremation; then, from the mouth of a friend, he was told, "He will return very soon; compose your mind and do not grieve. Having thus consoled Citrāṅgada, [the messenger] departed for the city of his father, who could travel at will like the Siddhas and gods.

Regarding the departure: there, having heard that his father Indrasena had been deprived of his royal status by his non-heirs, Citrāṅgada sent a message through the Nāga youth to the heirs, urging them to relinquish the throne; upon hearing Citrāṅgada’s message as told by the Nāga youth, all the non-heirs restored the royal status to Indrasena, informed him of the news of his son's arrival, and offered propitiatory prayers, asking for forgiveness for their own offenses.

Then Citravarmā went to his own palace and paid homage to his parents; having received a letter from his parents, he was filled with extreme joy. Thereupon, King Indrasena dispatched a messenger to Citravarmā to inform him of the auspicious news of his son’s safe arrival from Pātālakhāta. Upon hearing the news of his son-in-law’s arrival through the mouth of the messenger, King Citravarmā experienced an outpouring of great joy and auspiciousness. Then the king [prepared] for his daughter Sīmantinī... [sahara].
She then reported the matter to Citrāṅgada; thereafter, Citravarmā summoned Citrāṅgada and, having again performed the elaborate rites of the Svayaṃvara, bestowed his daughter Avyā upon him.

In the context of narrating the power of the vow of observing Monday (Soma-vāra) on the part of a woman (sīmantinī), there is the account of Sumedhas and Sāmava, including the great effort made by the woman to bestow the two [sons] who were not born from a womb; then, after Śatrughna had brought objects such as ornaments from the netherworld (pātāla) and satisfied the outcaste woman, he took her with him, returned to his own city, and enjoyed the pleasures of sovereignty with great joy; thus [is described] the worship of Śiva and Gaurī on Monday.

A description of how Ratnaprabhā and Śitrāṅgada attained their desired happiness; a narration of the story of the two sons of the Brāhmaṇa named Mitra-sārasvata; therein, after Sumedhas and Sāmavat, the two Brāhmaṇa youths, had completed their study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (aṅgas) and philosophical systems (vicāra), they went to the presence of the Lord of Vidarbha at their father’s command to acquire wealth for the sake of their own marriage; then, having observed those two sons of the twice-born as they were making their request, the Lord of Vidarbha—

Regarding the task: when [Nala] said, "The two of you should disguise one of you in female attire and become a Brahmin wife; having received hospitality from the queen, come to me. Then I shall give much wealth to both of you," those two Brahmin youths, considering the king's command to be inviolable, disguised themselves as a Brahmin couple and set out for the city of Niṣadha in the guise of an umbrella-bearer and a servant. And then...

On Monday, between those two, the man was worshipped by Sīmantinī with the thought that he was Mahādeva, and the woman with the thought that he was Pārvatī. Immediately after she had worshipped the Brahmin’s son named Sāmavat—who was dressed as her female companion—with the thought that he was Pārvatī, he truly attained womanhood. Then, having taken the jewels, the sword, the ornaments, and other items given by Sīmantinī, as the two young Brahmins were departing, Sāmavat attained womanhood.

The arising of a transformation of passion; then, once Sāmavatī had been born, Sumedha’s making of a request to her for the sake of amorous dalliance; then, after Sumedha had observed his friend’s wife—who was devoted to him—in private both in her physical form and her disposition, and having somehow consoled her as she entreated him with words of love through discerning speech, he took Sāmavatī and brought her to his own home, where he reported the entire account to his father and the others; then, by those two parents who were overwhelmed with grief...

Taking his two sons with him, he went toward the abode of Chyavana and related to him how he had obtained the sword from you through your grace. Then, at the instruction of that sage Bhāradvāja—who was intent on the welfare of the twice-born boy and devoted to the practice of asceticism—the king, together with those two princes, went to the hermitage of Ambikā and performed the worship of the venerable Jamadagnyāmbā. Thus it is told.

The gracious Mother of the World appeared and, declaring that she could not allow the state of her devotee’s suffering to remain otherwise, she commanded Sumedhas to take Sāṃvatī as his wife for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. She then granted a boon, stating that he would have a son of superior virtues compared to his father, the Sārasvata Brāhmaṇa’s previous son. Thereafter, by that Sārasvata Brāhmaṇa, his own daughter named Sāṃvatī was given to that Sumedhas according to the rites of marriage.

The description of the performance of the gift-giving ceremony; the description of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures by the two of them following the wedding rites, including the *Samedha* and *Sāmavatī* rituals; and thus, the description of the devotion and intimacy of the Sīmantinī. ... |

Because that Brahmin named Mandara was entirely devoted to attachment to sensual objects, he made it his constant habit to reside in the house of a prostitute named Piñjalā. Now, while that twice-born man was dwelling in her abode, a righteous-souled divine yogi named Ṛṣabha arrived there. Then, by means of performing complete service for that yogi Ṛṣabha—beginning with the washing of his feet and ending with the massaging of them—those two, the Brahmin Mandara and the prostitute Piñgalā, [honored him].

The production of extreme contentment lasting for a day and a night; then, on the second day, the departure of that Kramayogin who had arrived in connection with the pilgrimage; thereafter, after some time, following the death of the dull-witted Brahmin, the birth of [the child] in the wife of King Javāhu, the lord of Daśārṇa; there, first of all, while she was still in the state of pregnancy, her death occurred due to the administration of poison by her co-wives, yet by the turn of fate she did not die even though it was given, though the effects of the poison—

Hādtyanta was a resident of Īśāvāsa; when Bāraka, born of that Ṛṣabha’s wife, was afflicted by a burning sensation arising from poison, there was no great transgression on the part of the father. Observing that both mother and son were tormented by a terrible and fierce fever, the king, although he had administered medicine through compassionate means, seeing their lack of improvement, concluded by his own intellect that "surely these two have come from hell," and thus had them abandoned in a secluded forest by means of his charioteer and his chariot. Then, by that disciple Bāraka—

While wandering in the forest, that queen, by the turn of fate, entered the city of Caidya by way of a merchant's path far away while blind; then follows the account of her being taken as a slave, and on the occasion of describing the excellent Śiva, the narrative of the events concerning the mountain named Mandara located in the region of Avanti; there, having recognized that woman of noble lineage through the table of contents (*anukramaṇikā*), she was led into the presence of her own master, the merchant Padmākara; thereafter, by Padmākara... [the account] of that queen.

Having offered consolation and established him in his own home with due honor, while that merchant’s wife was living there, at one point, by the power of fate, her husband died from a disease such as a wound. Then, that queen-consort prepared the funeral requisites; and by the turn of fate, on that very same day, the aforementioned Śivayogin, who had been like a father to her, arrived at the house of that very merchant during the course of a pilgrimage.

Then the yogi Aṣeśaśiva, having accepted the worship and hospitality offered by the Vaiśya, went into the presence of that queen who was grieving over the death of her son; after instructing her in the supreme realization of the Truth and commanding her to practice devotion to Śiva, he went to the side of her deceased son and restored his life with ashes consecrated by the mantra of Śiva. Then, when the boy’s life had been revived, [he brought about the joy] of the queen and her kinsmen.

Furthermore, when supreme bliss was attained, the yogi Ṛṣabhaśiva touched both the mother and son with consecrated ashes; by the mere touch of those ashes, both the mother and son attained divine bodies. Then, the yogi Ṛṣabhaśiva gave the boy the name Bhadrāyu, described the future destiny of both of them, and for the purpose of imparting the Śiraḥ-vidyā, he sent them to live for some days in the house of Padākaravaḍaya.

The departure for another place on a pilgrimage; then, by the power of worshipping and honoring the Śiva-yogi named Śivabhaktasiṃha, who was possessed by Piṅgalā, a description of her birth in a future life as Sīmantinī, the wife of King Citrāṅgada; and then, the growth of Bhadrāyo in childhood alongside Sunaya, the son of that Padyākara, accompanied by friendship.

And their playing together and so forth; then, for those two—the prince Vaśaja and the royal prince Bhadrāyu—the performance of the initiatory rites such as the *upanayana* by means of a Brahmin, followed by their attainment of proficiency in the study of the Vedas; then, when Bhadrāyu reached his sixteenth year, the arrival of the aforementioned master of the Ṣaḍbhaya-yoga near him; and the paying of homage by Bhadrāyu’s mother along with her own son to that master of the Ṣaḍbhaya-yoga, for the purpose of instructing Bhadrāyu in the true path.

And [there was] the performance of service for others; then, by the yogi Ṛṣabha, the imparting of instruction on the Dharma appropriate to the hermitage of Śrī Sātātapa to Prince Bhadrāyus; then, for the sake of liberating Śrī Śivaseṇa from his own distress, the imparting of instruction to Prince Yuñjāna; and having given to him the *raṅkha* known as *Sveśataruvi-nārāka*, which brings victory, along with the Śiva-mantra, the sacred ash (*bhasman*) for smearing his limbs, and two thousand horses and elephants.

Having taken up a sword that brings victory by its mere sight, having performed the ritual instructions for the rite, and having bestowed auspicious blessings upon them, he received worship and hospitality from the two of them and departed for his desired destination. Then, the King of Magadha, an enemy of the King of Daśārṇa named Vajrabāhu, arrived with a great army to wage war; subsequently, having fought a battle with the King of Magadha, the lord of Daśārṇa, and having conquered him in that conflict—his...

Having destroyed the entire army and brought the kingdom of Daśārṇa under his control, he bound the king in his chariot and set out for his own country. Meanwhile, Prince Bhadrāyu, who was living in the city of Vaiśyana, heard from the mouths of people the news regarding his father’s kingdom. Accompanied by his friend Sunaya, the son of a merchant from Padyākara, he mounted a horse and traveled with great speed. Upon reaching Daśārṇa, which had been devastated by the forces of his father's enemy, the king known as Magadheśvara, he beheld it from there.

Overcome with fury, he swiftly crushed the enemy army; blowing the victory-conch bestowed by Śiva and raising his sword of victory, he bewildered all the hosts of demons with his illusory power (*māyā*). Having slain many enemies and released his father—who was bound to the chariot—from his bonds, he liberated the wives of his own father and the lords, as well as the wives and daughters of the city-dwellers, along with their cattle and wealth. Then, having comforted his father and all the others, he returned to his own city.

The dispatch; then, having entered the enemy army and seized their wealth consisting of women, elephants, horses, chariots, male and female servants, and other riches, he defeated the Lord of Magadha, bound him along with his ministers and attendants, and returned to his own city. Then, Bhadrāyu, clearly announcing his own name and lineage, first stated in general that he was the son of a Kṣatriya, and thereafter performed the salutation at the feet of his father. Immediately after his arrival before his father, by that one named Sunaya—
Having arrived at Vedaya-pura together with Bhadrāyu, the son of Vadya, he dwelt there. Then, after some time had passed, while Bhadrāyu was practicing devotion to Śiva, [the following occurred].

Then, after the illustrious Śivayogin Varṣabha had bestowed upon him the instruction for the hymn of armor (*kavaca-stotra*) known as the *Sarvarakṣākara-bhīśiva*, Bhadrā related to her own mother, that noble lady named Padyākarā, the account of his own battle and other events. Then, on the second day, regarding Citrāṅgada—the son of Candraṅgada—who was also known by the name Candrāgada, there occurred the arrival of that aforementioned Śivayogin named Ṣaḍbhuja; and [he performed] the bestowal of a maiden upon the prince Bhadrāyuṣ.

First, the Lord performed the preliminary instructions and the formal invitation; then, at the word of the yogi Ṛṣabha, King Citrāṅgada summoned Bhadrāyus and, having bestowed his own daughter named Kauravī upon him, commenced the preparations for the marriage rites. Next, having dispatched a messenger to Vajrabāhu, he extended an invitation according to proper custom for the sake of his son’s wedding. Subsequently, Vajrabāhu arrived there at the capital city of the Lord of Niṣadha along with his retinue.

Upon his arrival, Vajravāhu received a salutation from his son Bhadrāyu; however, because Vajravāhu did not recognize him due to his altered appearance, he tested Bhadrāyu by causing him to fall. When the Lord of Niṣadha had thus explained the circumstances to Vajravāhu—stating that this boy named Bhadrāyu was indeed his own son whom he had abandoned in the forest along with his mother—the King, having heard the account of Vajravāhu’s deed of abandoning both son and wife, [acted accordingly].

Having attained ultimate bliss through the arrival of her own son who had severed Bharata’s distress, she then accepted the honor and hospitality offered by King Citrāṅgada; taking her daughter-in-law Bhadrā along with her son Bhadrāyuḥ, she departed together with Vajravāhana and his retinue of kinsmen.

With great joy, he returned to Khapura; thereafter, Bhadrāyu, having previously performed the duties of crown prince by his father’s command, assumed the sovereignty over the entire circle of the earth following his father’s departure to heaven. After his accession to the throne, Bhadrāyu entered into an alliance with the minister named Hemaratha, the ruler of Magadha who had been imprisoned by Prīti, and secured his release from bondage. Then, Bhadrāyu ruled the kingdom together with his wife Kīrtimālinī, enjoying every pleasure. Thus...

A description of the power resulting from the worship and hospitable reception of Śiva-yogins performed in a previous birth. Now, once Bhadrāyu had attained the throne of sovereignty, he went one day to the forest with his wife and wandered there at his pleasure. At that very time, while a tiger was pursuing and harassing a certain Brahmin couple in that forest, they made a loud cry to the king for protection in order to save themselves. At that moment, the tiger arrived...

The abduction of the brahmin’s wife; then, while she was being carried away by Bhadrāyu toward the regions of Raśakṣpara, the distress of all the sages at the loss; and when the brahmin’s wife had been seized by the tiger, the brahmin’s performance of a curse against the king.

Then King Bhadrāyu made various kinds of supplications for the sake of consoling that brahmin whose wife had been carried off by a tiger. Thereupon, the brahmin made a request to the king to go to the royal village for the sake of quelling his own desire for sensual enjoyment. Then Bhadrāyu, having given his own wife to that brahmin, kindled the sacrificial fires, meditated upon Śiva, and prepared himself to leap into the fire. At that very moment, for the purpose of testing his devotion, [the Lord appeared] wearing the form of a brahmin.

The manifestation of Śrī Śaṅkara in his own true form; the offering of praise by Bhadrāyu to that Śrī Śaṅkara; the granting of boons by the Lord Śrī Śaṅkara, pleased by that praise, to Bhadrāyu along with his wife; the description of Bhadrāyu’s attainment of the enjoyment of happiness through the grace of Śiva; and finally, after entrusting the kingdom to his sons, Bhadrāyu’s attainment of union with Śiva, as well as the account of Bhadrāyuścaṇḍāyu’s son, Vicāṅgada, together with his own wife.

The description of [the sage] attaining the state of Śambhu together with Sīmantinī; then, the description of the majesty of devotion to Śiva; next, the description of the majesty of sacred ash (*bhasma*). In connection with that, the account of the life of the Śiva-yogin named Vāmadeva is told. Once, while that Śiva-yogin Vāmadeva was wandering in the Krauñca forest, a Brahmarākṣasa approached to devour him and squeezed him firmly with his two arms; yet, by the mere touch of his body, he was instantly liberated.

The attainment of the state of a *brahmarākṣasa*; then, by that *brahmarākṣasa* whose mind was filled with despondency upon remembering his own previously committed evil deeds, the description of his past life, the performance of wicked actions, the ripening thereof, the torments of Yama, and the attainment of the state of a *brahmarākṣasa* was related to the yogi Vāmadeva Śiva; and then, regarding Vāmadeva, [he said]: "By the mere sight of your body, the memory of my previous thousands of births has arisen in me, and my mind remains perfectly serene; therefore, such is [the power of your presence]."

When asked by the yogi Vāmadeva, "How was this power obtained?", [the sage] described the efficacy of the ashes by stating, "This is the power of the ashes contained within my own body. In connection with that, he related the account of how a certain Brahmin of evil conduct from the Draviḍa country—whose feet were struck by a dog—attained the world of Śiva merely by the touch of those ashes. Such is the story told by Vāmadeva.

The contents of the Barāhmaka section: the contents of the Dhṛ-ra-abhyāya; the contents of the Pa-pu-e-dāḥ. Having heard the majesty of the sacred ash (bhasma-māhātmya), the Brahmarākṣasa makes a request to Vāmadeva to hear the majesty of the sacred ash once again in detail...

Then, as Vāmadeva begins to describe the majesty of the sacred ash in full detail, a divine celestial chariot (divya-vimāna) arrives at Mount Mandara; having ascended that chariot, the husband and wife, Śabara and his consort, go to the world of Śiva (Śivaloka) and attain the state of being identical in form to Śiva (śiva-sārūpya-mukti). Thus ends the description of the majesty of faith.

This is the description of the greatness of the conduct of Māmadā, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals; in connection with that, the description of the conduct of the daughter of the Vidyādhara king residing in the Ānata region, named Śāradā; therein, the description of the arrival of Indra and the other gods to the place where she resides; there, during the great festival, the offering of praise preceded by worship to the Blessed Maheśvara seated upon his lion-throne together with the gods; and thereafter, [his] being well-pleased.

In this chapter, the great sage Sanatkumāra provides an exposition on the subject of the Tripuṇḍra, as taught by Lord Rudra, in response to the inquiry of Ruru. Having heard that discourse, the Blessed Lord Śrī Rudradeva describes in detail the greatness of wearing the Tripuṇḍra with sacred ash. Furthermore, in the context of explaining the majesty of the ash, he recounts the narrative of the Śabara hunter.

In that place, once while Prince Siṃhaketu of Pāñcākhdeḍīya was wandering in the forest for the sake of hunting, a certain Śabara follower who had gone along for assistance saw, upon a certain stone pedestal in the woods, a divine *liṅga* with its pedestal broken. Taking it, he went into the presence of the prince and began to inquire about the procedure for the worship of the *śivaliṅga*. Thereupon, the prince, in jest toward him, [said] constantly...

He performed the service of providing funeral ashes for the worship of Śiva and gave instructions on the ritual procedure for Śiva-pūjā. Then, that Śavara, having taken those ashes to his own home, would daily fetch funeral ashes according to the path described by the prince and perform the worship of the venerable Raṅka with offerings preceded by a spirit of devotion. Once, however—

While that Śabara was distressed with anxiety regarding the lack of funeral ashes for the purpose of worshipping Śiva, his wife, the Śabarī, consoled her husband, set fire to her own house, and entered it herself to burn her own body within the flames. Then, right there beside the corpse of her deceased husband, that Śabara performed the complete ritual worship of Lord Śiva using the funeral ashes produced by the burning of his wife’s body; and at the conclusion of the worship—

When Śabarī, his own wife, was summoned daily for the purpose of worshipping the Lord of Śrīkṣetra, at that very time, Śabarī continued to come and stay as she had done every day before; the state of that house also remained as it was previously. Then, while he was conversing with her in astonishment and fear, the Brahmin died from a stroke of lightning. Having thus attained widowhood, Śāradā returned to her father’s house, and after some time, she remained there in her father’s home.

Having gone to the sage named Nagnajit who had arrived there, Śāradvatī paid homage to that blind son of Nidhruva; when she had offered her salutations, the sage bestowed upon her the auspicious blessing: "May you be possessed of good fortune and may you have sons. Then, having learned the circumstances of her situation, the sage Nidhruva gave her detailed instructions on the ritual procedure for the worship of Umā in order for her to attain good fortune. Thereupon, by that Śāradvatī—

The undertaking of the Dhumāmaheśvara vow by the sage; then, for the sake of destroying the misfortune and suffering of her father, mother, and others, as well as that of Śāradā, the making of a request to the great sage Naidhruva to remain right there until the completion of all the constituent parts of her vow; then, by virtue of that request, the great sage Naidhruva remaining in that very place, Mēḍhra, until the completion of all the constituent parts of the vow performed by Śāradā; and the performance of the Dhumāmaheśvara vow [by her]. Then...

At the end of that year-long vow, he performed the concluding rite (*udyāpana*). On the night of the completion day, that sage Naidhruva, together with Śāradā, propitiated Śrī Jagadambā through recitation, meditation, and austerity. At that moment, by the power of their devotion, Śrī Jagadambā manifested before them; and at that very instant, by the grace of Śrī Jagadambā, that blind sage Naidhruva regained his sight, remaining together with Śāradā.

When the hymn of praise to Jagadambā was completed, the world-mother, being highly pleased by the request of King Naigama, granted a boon to Śāradā—preceded by a description of her previous birth—stating: "She shall experience the bliss of union with her husband in a dream. Having bestowed this boon upon Śāradā, she issued a command to Kṛtānta (the God of Death) regarding the execution of the task: "When you cause the son born from your own womb to appear directly to the man who has experienced pleasure in a dream, then give him [the fruit] to him. Thereafter...

With that very clear and pure intellect, she [spoke] to her own guru... Then Śāradā, having remained for one year in the presence of that noble guru Naidhruva Mahārṣi, performed worship and hospitality according to the rules. Thereafter, having privately related to the parents of Naidhruva Muni the account of the granting of Jamadagni’s daughter and so forth, and having taken leave of them all, she departed for another land of her own accord. Then, [the story] of Śāradā’s Śrī...

By the grace of Jagadambā, she bore a child because she had enjoyed sexual union with her own husband in a dream; thereafter, hearing that Śāradā was pregnant though she was a widow, all the people gathered together in one place to cast aspersions upon her reputation and performed incantations against her. While such malicious deliberations were being carried out, a voice from the sky declared that Śāradā was faultless. Upon hearing this, all the people became exceedingly delighted.

Then, having learned the true account from Śāradā with joy in a secluded place, Khījanaiṇa offered praise to her and departed for his own home. Subsequently, there occurred the birth of a son in the lineage of Śāradā; when the initiation (*upanayana*) was performed for that son of Śāradā named Rāradeya by his preceptor, it is described how, immediately after the initiation, he attained complete mastery over the four Vedas along with all their limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*) within only four years. Now...

Once, during a great festival of Śiva at the sacred site of Rukarṇeśvara Mahādeva, when a pilgrimage to Prayāga was taking place, Śāradā also set out with her son along with all the inhabitants of that village. There, she saw her husband—a Brahmin from a previous birth who had constantly given her pleasure in dreams—and he too saw her, who had daily bestowed such delight upon him in his dreams.

Then, having witnessed the dream of Śāradā and the direct vision of her son who had emerged from her own body, his mind was overcome with wonder at that bestowal; he approached her and questioned Śāradā out of a desire to know her account. Thereupon, Śāradā related the entire account of what had occurred to him. Then, having taken the boy given by her and Śāradā herself with the permission of her parents, that Brahmin departed for his own home.

Then, in the course of time, after that Brahmin’s death, Śāradā followed her husband into the funeral fire along with her attendants; thereafter, the couple departed for the celestial realm. Thus ends the description of the power of the Umā-Maheśvara vow, comprising two chapters (Paṭala 5, Śukla) concerning both Bhadrasena and Suvasu, the son of the royal minister named Sudhama, and the prince named Tāraka. Sa...

Now follows the description of the greatness of rudrākṣas. In this context, as an incidental account of the merit of wearing rudrākṣas, there is the issuing of a command by the Lord of the Kāmarūpa region for the diligent protection of the Liṅga. Regarding the subjects: from the time of their childhood, the two sons of the minister lived with the king in a state of supreme friendship; both of them, having always renounced ornaments made of divine gems, were seen to possess an extreme devotion to wearing rudrākṣas. Then, the King, overcome with great wonder, [invited] Bhadrasena to his own palace.

Having honored the returned sage Parāśara with the prescribed rites of worship, the two [princes] began to inquire about the reason for his desire to wear those two rudrākṣa beads. Thereupon, that great sage Parāśara described to the prince and the son of the minister the account of their previous births; therein, it was told how they had lived in the house of a certain woman named Mahānandā, who resided in the village of Nandi, possessed great fortune, and was ever devoted to the worship of Sadāśiva.

Kukkuṭa and Makaṭa, who had attained mastery in the art of dancing performed daily upon that sacrificial altar (vedī) while wearing ornaments of rudrākṣa beads, ashes, and peacock feathers, would dance every day on that altar at the time of the sacrifice before Śiva. Then, one day, a certain eminent Śiva-yogin observing the Śiva-vow arrived at her abode; having seen his divine jeweled bracelet, the courtesan, desiring it, [offered herself] to that yogin for the sake of her status as a prostitute.

Even though she had made a vow for up to three days, saying, "Having accepted you as my husband, I shall serve you according to the law of a wife who shares in religious duties," the physician—who was devoted to the vows of Śiva—having heard her words, replied, "So be it. He gave her his own daily object of worship, a *liṅga* made of jewels, and said to her, "If this jewel *liṅga* of mine should be destroyed, my life would perish. Thus he spoke to her, Mahānandā, his wife.

Honoring Śeḍaya’s command, he took the linga from its end and, placing it upon the pillar of the Nāśca pavilion, entered his own house. That night, while she was sleeping comfortably with the Vaiśya on the same path, a fire suddenly broke out at dawn and consumed her dwelling—the pavilion known as Savana. At that very moment, having awakened, she hurried there with the rope called Śaṅkha.

The two—the dog and the monkey—were swiftly released from their bonds; once freed, the dog and the monkey were driven far away from the site of the pavilion out of fear of the serpent. When the entire pavilion was consumed by fire, the pillar standing within it and the silver liṅga placed upon it were reduced to fragments by the burning. Witnessing the destruction of that liṅga, the physician became certain of his own death.

Having given orders for the construction of that funeral pyre, Mahānandā was informed; then, by means of that same messenger, the firm binding of the pyre was carried out outside the city, and the construction of the pyre was completed. Then, when that pyre had been prepared, that devotee of Śiva entered it with his wife. Seeing him enter the pyre, Mahānandā, the messenger, became deeply distressed and made a vow to remain fasting for three nights.

Placing the eternal Dharma before her and having bestowed all her own possessions upon the devotees of Śiva, she circumambulated him three times, remembered Him, and made preparations to enter that fire in order to follow her husband in death. At that moment, the Lord Śaṅkara himself appeared there and, having restrained her, told her how He had come in the form of Vacaidaya for the purpose of testing her devotion, and then [departed] along with all her family members. Thus ends the account of Mahānandā.

Upon leading Vekṣayā toward the world of Śiva, and after those two—the cock and the monkey—who had escaped their bonds at the time of the house fire while fleeing far away with her remaining attendants, had died by being crushed under their respective feet, the monkey attained the status of a prince and the cock the status of a minister’s son; thus, through Parāhara, the account of the previous births of the prince and the minister’s son was related once the shadow [of the truth] had been cast.

The sage Parāśara’s prophetic declaration that the death of that prince named Sudharmavya would occur on the seventh day from today; having heard this, his consolation of King Bhadrasena—who was not yet grieved—through words of awakening; and then, at the king's request, the sage Parāśara’s instruction for the performance of the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya as a means to ward off the death of that prince named Sudharma.

While that prince was being consecrated every day by Brahmins endowed with self-restraint, austerity, and virtuous conduct, on the seventh day, he suddenly fell unconscious as if dead, yet was immediately restored to consciousness. At that time, while the prince was in a state of swoon, there occurred the arrival of the messengers of Death and Śiva, followed by an account of how the messengers of Śiva defeated Death; thereafter, all the sages, including Parāśara and others, offered blessings to the prince.

Having granted the king the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the king then honored all the Brahmins with gifts of food and other offerings. Then, King Bhadrasena performed acts of hospitality toward the sage Parāśara regarding the future destiny of that prince, by providing him with meals and other honors. Subsequently, while King Bhadrasena’s son was seated comfortably upon a high seat together with the great sage Parāśara and other eminent seers, the great yogi [approached] him.

The arrival of the great sage Śrī Nārada; then, by King Bhadrasena—who performed the worship and honor due to the Truth—Nārada related to the king how Vīrabhadra, sent by Śaṅkara upon Yama’s arrival there to take away the king’s son, had executed the punishment of Yama; and after describing how Yama offered salutations and praise to Vīrabhadra, the account of Vīrabhadra’s release of Yama and other events was narrated.

"By the power of the consecration preceded by the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya, the fear of death for your son has been averted; he shall attain a lifespan of ten thousand years, along with all happiness and prosperity,"—having thus bestowed this blessing, Nārada departed. The other great sages likewise bestowed blessings upon the king and his son, and then returned to their respective hermitages. Such is the description of the power of the Rudrādhyāya.

Now, following the procedure for reading and hearing the meritorious Puranic narratives that expound the greatness of devotion to Śiva, and describing the fruits thereof, there is the narration of the sin and punishment of the base Brāhmaṇa named Vidura, who was devoted to the profession of a paramour; and in connection with the description of the greatness of listening to the Purāṇas, there is the narration of the story of Jārakarna and his wife. In that account, on a certain day, although the base Brāhmaṇa named Vidura—who was constantly attached to a courtesan and lived as a paramour—was already engaged with his mistress, he [encountered] her together with the paramour.

"Having struck your own wife, who is devoted to pleasure and has a paramour, with an arrow, take wealth from those [paramours] and give it to me for the sake of the sacrificial altar—that is, for the purpose of bestowing wealth—so that I may enjoy myself with a courtesan while you enjoy yourself with a paramour. Having spoken thus, on the following day, both of those base individuals engaged in their respective debased conduct. In this manner, after some time had passed and following the death of that most wretched of men, Viduṣā, whose youth was somewhat advanced...

Once, on a particular festival day, she went with her own sons and kinsmen for a pilgrimage to the Gokarṇa shrine. Having gone there, while a certain Purāṇa was being recited by a reciter of the Purāṇas, Vidula heard from the mouth of that reciter, during the time of listening to the Purāṇa, the account of Yama’s torments: "The servants of Yama cast those women who are attached to paramours into a red-hot iron cauldron. Upon hearing this, she [was constantly... performed [penance].

With her heart tormented by the memory of the evil deed committed with her own lover, Bidūkhī went in secret to that Paurāṇika Brāhmaṇa; desiring to know the means for the pacification of the consequences of her own wicked act, she began to address him [with the following words]. Then he said: "Ma-ya-na-ka-jā-mā-tā-va-ṭa-ka-ti-nva-skambha-ta-na-na-śa-vaya-ka-ka-na-ja."
And from those [beings] and Yama... [the chapters of the Skanda Purāṇa, Paushkarika-khaṇḍa, Adhyāya 33].

By the mere hearing of the Purāṇa from the Paurāṇika, she remembered her own terrible sin of infidelity, and thus [the sage] became long-lived. Now begins the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, in the great Purāṇa known as the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. 4.

To Ridulā, who was terrified of the torments of hell, he gave instruction on how to cultivate devotion to Śiva by first offering consolation, followed by the chanting of the mantra consisting of the names of Śiva, and finally by listening to the Purāṇic narratives that establish the path of devotion to Śiva. Then, from that very same virtuous reciter of the Purāṇas known as Bindu, she heard the Purāṇic stories that increase devotion to Śiva. [End of] the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa.
(-) || [End of section] ||

Through the power of hearing that Bindu-khā, when the afflictions of *rajas* and *tamas* were gradually pacified in her heart, there occurred the performance of auspicious rites; then followed Vyāsa’s commencement of the narrative of the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*, the arrival of Nārada, and the manifestation of Lord Śaṅkara. Thereafter, daily, having understood the path taught by her guru, she performed the ritual bathing of the holy Śaṅkara with devotion, recited the *Oṃkāra*, and beheld the Vindhya mountain range before her; in this context, [the description of] the Vindhya mountain.

The description of Mount Meru; the words of the sage Nārada stating that Meru seemed to slight him, followed by the description of the obstruction of the path of the sun due to the piercing [of the mountain]; on one side, the description of the instability of the sky due to the fierce heat of the sun’s rays because of its lack of connection with the stars, and on the other, the praise of Brahmā by the gods; the description of the virtuous conduct of the men who have come to Satyaloka in order to demonstrate the absence of fear there, followed by the pacification of the gods performed by Brahmā. Brahmā’s...

In order to dispel the fear of the gods and to prevent the destruction of the world, she was eager to go to the presence of the sage Agastya at Śrīkhetrakārī; she described the battle against the ocean of the gods' fear. By the power of her devotion to Śiva, she completely severed the entire bond of karma and, at the end, departed for the heavenly realm. Having gone there to the presence of Śrī Pārvatī, the Mother of the World, she was honored by Pārvatī. Then, having heard from Pārvatī’s own mouth the account of her previous birth as a jackal...

For the sake of his liberation from that birth as a *piśāca*, she made a request to the Gandharva named Tumburu, who was residing in the body of King Vidhyadhari, to have him recite the *Purāṇas* to her husband. When Tumburu, having been thus requested, went to Vidhyadhari’s abode and recited the story of Śrī Gaurīpati to that *piśāca*, he was liberated from the state of being a *piśāca*. [This concludes] a brief description of Kāśī.

The description of the husband’s ascent in a radiant celestial chariot (vimāna) from his birth as a Piśāca and his journey toward the world of Śiva; the performance of the primary pilgrimage at Maṇikarṇikā in the holy field of Kāśī by the Lord of the Gods (Śiva), following the bath at Maṇikarṇikā; thereafter, the description of how liberation and Kaivalya were attained by that couple through the singing of the praises of the glorious Lord (Śrīmadeśvara); the departure of the glorious Śiva; and the granting of the form of the sage Agastya to the gods who were worshipping him in his hermitage.

Following the description of the Vaimava [Vaiṣṇava] narrative concerning the merits of the Varāhottarakhaṇḍa, which establishes the excellence of that very Varāhottarakhaṇḍa, there is, in connection with the hymn to the sage Agastya composed by Bṛhaspati, a description of the means for the destruction of sins; in connection with this, there is an exposition of the conduct of a devoted wife (pativratā). Then, there is the account of the gods praying to Śiva to prevent the growth of the Vindhya mountain which was obstructing the path of the sun. Thus ends the third section, the Varāhottarakhaṇḍa, within the Brāhma-khaṇḍa.

The consolation of the gods by Agastya according to their words; the departure of the gods to the heavenly realm; and having accepted the request of the gods, the sage Agastya’s journey with his wife from Kāśī to the mountain Kṣīra-dri outside [the city] in order to cause the Vindhya peak to recede; and the deities such as Viśvanātha and Kālabhairava to the sage who was distressed by separation from Kāśī—this concludes the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. 2.

The Sage’s reproachful lamentation preceded by his realization of the truth; Agastya’s refusal to accept the Vindhya mountain’s diminution until his return; and the Sage’s command to the mountain, “Until my return, remain other than high.”

The narration of the sage Kaddha; the arrival of the Sun-god; the granting of boons to Agastya by the sage Agastya; and the departure of Agastya [to the north]. [This includes] the honoring of altruism, the praise of the holy sites such as Śrīśreṣṭha and Ṛkṣavān, and the statement that Kāśī is the best among them. Furthermore, there is the inquiry regarding the greatness of Kāśī, the description of the majesty of sacred fords (tīrtha), and the explanation—within the context of describing the power of those sacred fords—that all sacred fords lead one to the holy field of Kāśī.

And the illumination of the sixfold *kāraka* (grammatical relations). [The narrative begins with] the Brahmin named Śivaśarman, a resident of the city of Mathurā, who, seeing old age come upon his own body, was overcome by anxiety; his departure from home for the purpose of a pilgrimage to the seven cities; his arrival at Prayāga after completing the pilgrimage to Ayodhyā; a description of the greatness (*māhātmya*) of Prayāga as an incidental topic; the Brahmin’s account of his pilgrimage to Kāśī; his journey to Mahākālavana; and, through that association, a description of the majesty of Mahākāla.

The narration of the pilgrimage to the holy site (tīrtha) of Māyāpurī; the death of the twice-born (dvija) in Māyāpurī; and the twice-born’s ascent to the celestial realm (nabhovartman), having mounted a golden aerial chariot (svarṇavimāna) attended by a group of Vaiṣṇavas named Puṇyaśīla and Suśīla. Furthermore, regarding how the twice-born Śivarāma—who died in the city of liberation called Māyā—did not attain release, there is the account of Lopāmudrā’s fall from her status as a chaste wife (satī). Finally, the commencement of the dialogue between Śivarāma and the Viṣṇu-gaṇas in order to demonstrate that direct union (sāyujya) with the Divine does not exist in the six cities beginning with Māyā.

The description of the world of Yama by the Brahmin Śivaśarman, who had arrived there after his virtuous conduct was extolled by the inhabitants of the world—including the twice-born, the radiant ones, the essence-beings, cuckoos, serpents, Guhyakas, and Gandharvas; the arrival of Dharmarāja and the honoring and worship of the Brahmin Śivaśarman upon his arrival at the realm of Yama; and, having heard the gentle words of Dharmarāja of the serene form, the Brahmin’s inquiry as to how this could be, followed by a brief description of the world of Yama in connection with the examination of Yama’s appearance and attributes.

A description of the world of the Apsarases, a description of the world of the Sun, an exposition on the greatness of the Gāyatrī mantra in connection with the description of the worship of the Sun, and an exposition on the ritual for the offering of half [the food].

Description of the excellent city of Sadasakhākṣa; description of the city of Vītihotra known as Arciṣmatī; in the context of narrating the origin of Kaśānu, the account of the sage named Viśvānara residing in the city of Jyotiṣmatī; according to the instructions of Ucciṣmatī, the account of the sage going to the sacred field of Kāśī and performing penance near the Śivaliṅga of Vīreśvara; the composition of the Mahālakṣmī-stotra in the thirteenth month; and [the conclusion of] the Mahā-Śiva[-purāṇa].

4. The vision of Śiva at Phaligrama; the narration of the *Abhiṅāṣāṭaka* hymn; the sage’s departure for his own home, satisfied by the splendor of Śiva’s mountain; in due time, the conception of an embryo in Śuciṣmatī by Viśvānara; the birth of a son at an auspicious moment; the determination of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the birth ceremony (*jātakarma*); the description of the palmistry (*sāmudrika*) according to the words of Nārada; and the causing of grief to the parents upon hearing that the boy named Viśvānara was born under the *gaṇḍānta* [astrological division]; and the [departure] of the sage’s son to ward off misfortune.

The establishment of a sacrificial post (*chiṅka*) in Kāśī and the performance of the *anughṛṣṭhāna* rite; the words spoken by Kulika Yudha, who had arrived to offer the third *saṃvara*, to the young sage (*munikumāra*): "I shall not choose you as my bride"; hearing these words and observing Indra’s attempt to cast down a thunderbolt, the young sage’s attainment of the state of a *mṛcchīva*; the manifestation of Śiva-Rudra at that very spot; and the description of how the monkey Divavara attained the status of a world-guardian (*dikpati*) and other honors.

The description of the city of Taikṛta; the rescue of a caravan of merchants by Viśvanātha, who was wandering in the Vindhya forest, as they were about to depart for the city of Piṅgākṣa, and his subsequent attainment of the status of a protector of the world; the description of the city of Vāruṇa; the abduction of Śuciṣmat, the son of the progenitor Kardama, from the lake while he was sporting in the water by Śuṅmāra; and the arrival of the celestial host before the sage, who remained deeply absorbed in worship even upon hearing that his son had been swept away in the lake.

The bringing of the young son of Suśīśumāra; the performance of penance by the sage Kumāra Śuciṣmat after Kādaya established the Śivaraṭiga; and the attainment of the world of Aruṇa from Śivapraghāsa.

The description of the city of Avantī, belonging to Pavana, the protector of the world; the performance of penance by the pure-souled Kaḍayapaya-putra after installing the image of Śrī Kārīkeśvara; the description of his attainment of the state of Śiva-hood; and the description of the city of Alakāvatī, the abode of the Guhyaka lords. In the city of Kāmpilya, there was a son of a Brāhmaṇa named Yajñadatta who, though a treasury of virtues (guṇanidhi), was addicted to vice and became a drunkard known as A-guṇanidhi; [the account] of his secret misconduct over a long period of time as observed by his mother.

The father’s expulsion of Suta from his own home for his misconduct; then, the description of how he, having offered lamps at Śiva’s temple and performed many fasts, was seized on the night of Śivarātri while stealing food from a place called Śiva, and subsequently attained the status of being the son of the King of Kaliṅga; and there, through his offerings of lamps at the shrines of Śiva, his attainment of the state of being the son of Viśravas in another kalpa, followed by the description of his acquisition of friendship with Śiva and the power to create and destroy through his performance of unbearable austerities.

Chapters and Subjects: Chapters and Subjects: Description of the city of Īśāna, which was pleased by Radara-makata; description of the greatness of the mountain established by the host of Rudras, beginning with Jajaikapāda; description of the asceticism of Dhruva while staying in Madhuvana on the banks of the Yamunā; description of the various obstacles to his penance sent by Indra; description of the world of the Moon; the establishment of a *liṅga* by Soma, who was born from the mind of Brahmā, after he had settled in Vārāṇasī; and the direct vision of the Supreme Lord by Dhruva.

Furthermore, there is the narration of the liberation of Dhruva through the grace of Śiva. [The text describes] the description of the descent of the Blessed Lord brought about by Dhruva: "I shall grant you the foundational station of the celestial sphere (*jyotiścakra*); nevertheless, go with me to Kāśī, which is shared as a single husband among twenty-seven maidens beginning with Rohiṇī. Having performed the worship of the Liṅga there, fulfill your duty. Having thus instructed Dhruva and established his wife with him, [he attained his goal] by performing penance in Vārāṇasī according to the essence of Śiva’s boon.

Having approached Soma as her husband, the illustrious Kārīṣugandhī set out on her journey; having attained the fulfillment of her purpose through the installation of the *dhruva* star, there follows a brief description of the world of the constellations she had achieved, and the departure of Soma, son of Atri, to the house of his preceptor’s wife. [Then] the abduction [of Rohiṇī], the account of the battle between Rudra and Candra, and the cessation of the conflict at the word of Brahmā, by which Candra was granted the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) by Bṛhaspati.

Discourses; the birth of Budha in the lineage of Dvija-prasaṃsana; the propitiation of Śiva performed by Budha; the granting of boons by Śiva to Budha; dialogues with Brahmā concerning those who have assembled; [the section on] *oṃ śara ṣka*; and the description of the nature of dogs. ... (In the battle, the commanders of the Dānavas and the soldiers of Andhaka, who had been slain by the gods, were restored to life once more by Bhārgava Śukra through the power of the Saṃjīvanī mantra.)

The restoration of life: through the prayer of the gods, Śiva, by means of Nandikeśvara, summoned Śukra and placed him within his own mouth; the description of the battle between Andhaka and his army along with the *bhramas*; the departure from the city of Māyāpuri of the twice-born Śukra, who had died, and his attainment of various enjoyments for a year in the world of Viṣṇu at the command of Brahmā; his exit from there; and the granting of boons such as lordship over the world to Śukra due to his performance of penance in Vārāṇasī and his grace by Śiva.

Having attained kingship through the grace of the Lord of the Universe, he reached Kāśī; there follows the description of its greatness... for him, whose joy was born from hearing of that [city], [the Lord] caused [him] to build a temple in Kāśī. Furthermore, by the grace of Śiva, having constructed a temple to Śiva there, [the king] fell upon the ground before the venerable Śiva, his limbs smeared with drops of sweat. Then, while he was performing penance at the Śivaliṅga established there, known as Ṛddhikeśvara, by the grace of Śiva—

The description of how Śiva, having arrived for the purpose of testing him, bestowed upon him the sovereignty over the world and other boons; the account of how Aṅgiras performed penance in Vārāṇasī for the sake of Śiva’s grace, and how Viṣṇu was appointed by him as his minister with the promise that he would become the king's trusted friend; the attainment of the status of Lord of the World and divine Garuda through the granting of boons by Śiva; and the description of the establishment of the Śiva-Śakti-dvijā (the twice-born of Śiva’s power) as proclaimed by the Gaṇas, born from Mātaṇḍa.

The narration of the birth of Śanaiścara in Chāyā; his performance of penance at Vārāṇasī and attainment of the status of a World-Guardian (Lokapāla); the account of how he, together with his wife, circumambulated the venerable mountain [Śrīparvata] and descended to the Kamāradaśa [region]; and the description of his acquisition of the state of Agastya. ... ; Śaiva.

The *Chṛtaskandastotra*; the discourse addressed to Skanda by the great sage regarding the majesty of the *Kādī* [mantra]; the description of the worlds obtained by the sons of Brahmā’s mind-born sons, such as Marīci and others, as designated by Skanda; and the description of the location of the Arundhatī constellation, the vision thereof, and the efficacy of residing in Kādī. (Bha.)

...the description of the unliberated Śatruntapa; the description of Viṣṇu’s penance on the bank of the Cakroṣṇī; and the account of the birth of Śrava, who was residing on his father’s lap but was insulted by his stepmother, as he went to the forest for the purpose of penance at the bidding of his mother; and the exposition of the ritual procedure for the Maṇikaṇikā [pilgrimage]. 6. |||

[The account of] the Bhairavas, the meeting with the sages there, and the instruction of the twelve-syllable mantra to them; and upon the disappearance of the sages, the description of the taking up of the Gaṅgā, and the recitation of the Daśaharā-stotra—[including] the description of how great and minor sins are pacified through the knowledge of the Gaṅgā at Kāśī due to its status as the abode of Śiva; and the killing in the forest by a tiger of a certain Vṛṣīpati, a Brahmin in name only from the region of Vāhīka, whose name was Kaṭhiga, [and how] his flesh along with the bones was taken up.

The vulture’s battle with another vulture; the great merit arising from the contact with the waters of the Gaṅgā when that vulture fell onto the thigh of King Devavrata (Bhīṣma); the amazement of all upon seeing the attainment of happiness even by that Vāhīka, who was being dragged through hells such as Raurava and Kumbhīpāka due to his digging for various kinds of sins; finally, the departure of the Vāhīka to the heavenly realm after ascending a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), and the narration of the majesty of the Gaṅgā for those who are incapable [of performing great deeds] but desire to attain fruits equal to those of knowledge.

The *Mahāghaughanivāraka-Śrīgagā-sahasranāmastotra* (The Thousand-Name Hymn to the Illustrious Gaṅgā, Dispeller of the Great Flood of Sins); the narration of the superior majesty of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) at the confluence of the Gaṅgā brought by King Bhaṃīratha; the description of the location of the northern and southern banks (*tīra*); the appointment of Kiknora to prevent those who enter the inner sanctum of Deharī-Vināyaka without the command of Śiva; the narration of the history of the merchant Dhanañjaya; and the etymological derivation of the name Vārāṇasī.

The severing of Brahmā’s head by Śiva; the birth of Kālarāja from that severed head of Brahmā; the departure of Kālarāja to the earth in the form of a skull-bearer (*kāpālika*) after cutting off Brahmā’s head which caused day and night; the arrival of the sin of Brahmin-slaughter (*brahmahatyā*), which followed him as he went there in the guise of a *Ṣaṣṭhalamā* woman; and the description of Kālabhairava’s dwelling at the Kapālamocana Tīrtha for the sake of purifying all sins.

The narration of the birth of the son named Harikeśa to the yakṣa named Pṛṇabhadra and his wife named Chanakakuṇḍalā, following their worship of Śiva; the departure of Harikeśa from home out of fear of beating his father—who had been devoted to Śiva since childhood—when he did not attend to him; the description of the Ānandakānana forest as assigned by Śiva to Pārvatī; and the account of how Maheśvara, pleased by Harikeśa’s penance in Ānandakānana, granted him the boon of being Daṇḍapāṇi, along with the *Daṇḍapāṇyaṣṭaka*.

Chapter [Ca]: Description of the origin of the holy site named Jñānavāpī, followed by a description of its greatness; the abduction of Hari-svāmikanyā, a resident of Kārī, while she was worshipping Jñānavāpī, by a Vidyādhara infatuated with her beauty; the description of the battle between that Vidyādhara and a Rākṣasa; and the death of both the Rākṣasa and the Vidyādhara in the conflict due to their mutual rivalry, leading Hari-svāmikanyā to feel resentment toward the Vidyādhara.

The account of the renunciation of their bodies; the two of them, having reached the king’s body, the marriage taking place immediately after beholding the portrait there; the journey of Mālyaketu and Kalāvatī to Kāñcī; the performance of the Kārīrī sacrifice there, and the account of both of them departing for the realm of Śiva by means of a celestial chariot following the instruction of Śiva near the Jñānavāpī; the description of the majesty of the Jñānavāpī; and, in connection with the description of the virtuous conduct of the Brāhmaṇa Kādībhāṣaka, the exposition of the duties to be performed daily.

“Description of good conduct and the association with virtuous people; the definition of the duties of celibacy for the twice-born. [Omission]—Without a woman of auspicious marks, there is no fulfillment of the householder stage of life; therefore, the description of the characteristics of women. Description of the eight types of marriage, and a detailed account of the auspicious conduct that enables the twice-born and others to reach Kāśī. ...; (In the context of narrating the story of King Divodāsa, the account of the origin of the Avimukteśvara Liṅga at Avimukta).”

— A description of the prohibited conduct of Brahmins and others regarding the journey to the sacred field of Kāśī; a delineation of the prescribed conduct for those in the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*); an extensive exposition of the duties of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and ascetics (*yati*), including the teaching on Yoga; a narration of the means for attaining liberation for one whose death is imminent, interspersed with the majesty of the sacred fields of Kāśī and Śoma; and an account of how, while Divodāsa was ruling the kingdom of the earth from Kāśī, all the gods, beginning with Viśvaśvara, abandoned their celestial abodes.

The journey to Mount Mandara; a description of the happiness of the subjects during the reign of King Divodāsa; Agni’s departure to heaven after abandoning his own domain; the description of the king’s grief at the separation from Kāśī upon seeing Viśvanātha and Bhavānī stationed on the peak of Mount Mandara as he spoke of his own power; and the description of Śiva sending a host of Yoginīs to cause King Divodāsa to abandon the sacred field of Kāśī.
55. By the command of Śiva, the sixty-four Yoginīs enter the city of Kāśī for the purpose of obstructing King Divodāsa; the description of their names follows.

And here is the account of the arrival of Śiva, as directed by Śivā, for the purpose of expelling Kādyā from Divodāsa’s city; the description of how he divided himself and took up residence specifically within Kādyā, while Divodāsa, having exerted various efforts to find a vulnerability, remained intent on his search; the description of the location of Roṭārka; and the narration of the procedure and the greatness of that pilgrimage site.

The description of the Uttarāka-kuṇḍa; the performance of penance by a Brahmin girl residing there near Uttarāka after the death of her parents; the granting of the boon of being Gaurī’s own companion to her; and the description of the majesty of the Uttarāka-kuṇḍa. ...

4. An account of how Kṛṣṇa was afflicted with the disease of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) due to the insult offered by Nārada to Sāmba, the son of Kṛṣṇa; the cessation of that disease through his performance of penance after digging a pit (*kuṇḍa*) in Kāśī named after himself; the narration of the greatness of that *kuṇḍa* along with the great majesty of Sabāditya; and, in the context of the Pāṇḍavas’ forest exile, their journey to Kāśī, where Draupadī propitiated Lord Śiva, who granted her a boon, and the attainment of a son by her through the grace of the Lord propitiated by Draupadī.

The description of the location, the narration of the taking up of the Sun by Maya, and the description of Uccaiḥśravas; the account of the dispute between Kaṭu and Vinatā, wherein Vinatā was defeated and subjected to servitude by Kaṭu through deceit; the description of Garuḍa’s fetching of the nectar (*sudhā*) to remove his mother’s suffering; the performance of penance by Vinatā and Garuḍa after installing the Linga of Śiva at Kāyāvarohaṇa; and the narration of the greatness of the station of Khoklāditya following the granting of boons to them.
Thus ends the first half of the glorious *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*.
Now follows the second half extracted from the Kāśīkhaṇḍa.

A description of the majesty of Aruṇāditya; an account of the cause of Vinatā’s servitude; a narration of the majesty of Vṛddhāditya worshipped by Vṛddhahārīta; the performance of penance by Sūrya after installing a Śiva-liṅga at Kāyāvarohaṇa at the command of Viṣṇu; a description of the majesty of that deity following its acquisition of the name Kedārāditya; and the enumeration of the various Ādityas residing in Vimāna, Gaṅgā, and other locations.

[The account of] how the place came to be named Daśāśvamedha because ten horse-sacrifices were performed there by the four-faced Brahmā, who had been dispatched by Śiva to excavate the Niṣka at the city of Divodāsa; and a description of the greatness of that sacred site (tīrtha).

Furthermore, [the account of] the departure of Śaṅkukaṇa and others on an expedition to Kāśī by the command of Śiva, in order to ascertain the situation of the Yoginīs and Bhānuvidhis—who had established the lingas of Śiva right there in Kāśī and remained in that very place—and to expel Divodāsa; and [the description] of the journey to Kāśī...

In the context of describing the destruction of Arochi by the multitude of Kapardis who were exceedingly devoted to Śambhu, there is the narration of the history of the twice-born man named Vārmīki; the description of the liberation of the Piśāca created by him; and the proclamation of the greatness of the pilgrimage to the holy site of Pidhyācamocana.

An exposition on the majesty of the Śiva-liṅga installed by the Gaṇas headed by Piṅgala; and how, having observed that those Gaṇas and others who had been sent by Śiva to investigate the state of Kāñcī did not return, [Śiva], by his own command, caused the entrance of the Gaṇa-host into the city through a breach in the wall.

[The description of Gaṇeśa assuming the guise of an astrologer and traveling to Kāśī; his deluding many people residing in the city through his own *māyā*; and the description of his conversation with Raṇekva and other royal ladies in the king’s inner apartments; and, upon meeting King Divodāsa, Gaṇeśa’s prediction of the future—including the arrival of the Brahmin and the instruction on the practice of *brahmacarya*—preceded by the king’s inquiry.]

Now follows a description, in connection with the hymn to Gaṇeśa composed by Śiva, of the name Duṇḍirāja given to Gaṇeśa, and the mention of the locations of Gaṇeśas such as Agastya and Hariścandra. Then, while Śiva remained absorbed in thought after the hymn had been recited, he directed Viṣṇu to effect the expulsion of King Divodāsa from Kāśī; this includes a description of the various locations of Viṣṇu in Kāśī, as well as those of Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, and Garuḍa.

A description of the manner in which the parivrājikā Ariṣṭā established the Buddha-dharma; how she made the subjects averse to that dharma and, following the word of Gaṇeśa, instructed King Divodāsa on the installation of Viṣṇu in the form of a twice-born; and the description of King Divodāsa’s ascent to heaven after worshipping the divine sign and traveling to Kaiṭabhapura.
