[And] the account of how a maiden was born from the seed of the sage Nṛmaṇas, who was pure and whose mind was tranquil, through his union with the Apsaras Śuci. Of her—

The performance of penance by the maiden named Dhūtapāpā at her father’s command; the account of how she attained a state of extraordinary purity through the granting of a boon by Lord Śiva. The description of how Dharma and Kāma, upon seeing her, fell into a mutual passion and were subsequently reduced to ashes due to their union. The narration of the confluence of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, and Kaphiṇā with the Dhūtapāpā as the Pañcanada-tīrtha (the sacred site of the five rivers). The glorification of its majesty, and therein the description of the hymn of praise offered to Viṣṇu by Agni, Soma, and Vasiṣṭha. In that place...

A description of the location of Vidumādhava; a description of the majesty of Bindumādhava; a brief account of Vaiṣṇava sites such as Ādikeśava and Tāpyakeśava; a delineation of the various places and their respective deities as specified by Vidumādhava; and a description of how the sage Viduma obtained the vision of the Sudarśana-cakra from Viṣṇu after entering Kaiṭāsapura according to Viṣṇu’s instructions, while Viṣṇu and the other gods were in the presence of Hara at Mandara.

The journey for the purpose of bringing Śiva; the description of the Kapiratīrtha; and the account of the manifestation of the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) at Kapiratīrtha. The description of the penance performed by Jigīṣavya; the account of how Śiva arrived there; and the narration of the majesty of Uyeṭheśa. Upon arriving at Mandrācala to behold Śiva along with his attendants and Ambā, the vision of the twice-born who had come from various holy places; and the description of the supreme excellence of the sacred field established by Śiva.

The narration of the greatness of various Śiva-liṅgas, such as Parādareśvara, Māṇḍavyeśvara, Jābāḷeśvara, Kandukeśvara, and others; the determination of the locations of the Śiva-liṅgas situated in Kārīketa, beginning with Śeleśvara; the narration of the greatness of the Raleśvara-liṅga as described by Śiva to Gaurī; and the account of a certain Naṭakī who, through her devotion to Śiva, performed a vigil near Raleśvara by singing songs and other acts, and by the grace of Śiva, obtained after death the status of being the daughter of Vasubhūti, the king of the Gandharvas.

Then, the destruction of Gajāsura—the son of Mardīṣāsu—who was invulnerable due to a boon from Brahmā, by means of a divine arrow; the narration of the origin of Kṛttivāseśvara; the account of the majesty of Kṛttivāseśvara; the description of how sixty-eight crores of Jaimadas, residing in various places, arrived together at Kāśī; and [the account of] Oṃkeka.

The description of the installation of nine crores of Caṇḍas, accompanied by their retinues such as Vetālas and others, in various locations for the purpose of slaying the demon Kārīra; the dispatching of Bhagavatī Kālarātri by the Lord to his presence in order to subdue that Daitya, who was invincible to men and had seized the sovereignty of the three worlds; the arrival of the demon Durga near Bhagavatī at the command of Kālarātri with his entire army; and [the sight of] that army of Durga, exhausted from battle, upon being observed.

The description of the emergence of Śakti from the body of the Goddess; the narration of the battle between the goddess Durgā and the asura Durga, including the identification of the names of the powers (śaktis) born from the body of the goddess; the account of the battle between the Daityas and the goddess; the description of the hymn of praise offered by the gods to the goddess Durgā, who were satisfied by the slaying of the Daitya Durga; and the exposition on the fruits of worshipping Durgā and Bhairava.

The counting of the fourteen syllables beginning with *ka* as described by Śiva to Pārvatī; the narration of the origin of Oṃkāreśa in connection with the description of the praise of the syllable *ka* performed by Brahmā; the exposition of the greatness of the Linga of Oṃkāreśa; and the account of the sage named Garga on the banks of the Revā—himself a Kṣatriya who had become detached after studying the sciences under Bharadvāja and Suvadana during the Padma-kalpa—along with the description of the greatness of Oṃkāra as taught by the sage Garga, which serves as the sole means for warding off the sins accumulated over many births.

And [therein is] the description of the division [of the sacred sites], as well as the determination of their majesty. [Therein is] the narration of the greatness of the Śiva-liṅga named Tryekṣaṇa, which follows the account of the Pāyavata forest situated in the temple of the three-eyed palace constructed of jewels and rubies. [Furthermore,] in the context of describing the majesty of Kedāra, there is the narration of the history of the Ujjainīritha-taḍāga, and the determination of the greatness of the Śiva-liṅga named Dharmeśvara, established by King Dharmasādhu. ...

In this [work], there is a detailed description of the *Manoratha-tṛtīyā-vrata*, known as the *Viśvabhujā*, dedicated to the deities Gaurī and Vināyaka; it is witnessed by the Dharma, austerity, and the young parrots, and is intended for those seeking liberation from the cycle of rebirth, beginning from the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra and ending on the third day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika. *Note: The provided source text contains numerous transcription errors and illegible characters (e.g., "kīraśiñayūnāṃ", "śivabarākeḍagdāti", "viṣyāḥ", "puṣkomajāṃ"). The translation above reconstructs the most probable intended Sanskrit terminology based on the context of Hindu ritual literature.*

Upon hearing the words of the Preceptor of the Gods, Indra, tormented by the fear of the sin of killing his teacher, performed penance at Kāśī in the presence of the Lord of Dharma (Yama), who spoke with a northern voice; then follows the account of the attainment of heaven by Indra after the expiation for the slaughter of a Brahmin, and in connection with the majesty of Vīreśvara, the description of the lineage of King Mitrajit; and how King Mitrajit, a great devotee of Viṣṇu, having slain the demon Kaṅkāṭa with a trident, [rescued] the daughter of a Vidyādhara named Gandhinī, who had been seized by the demon Kaṅkāṭa.

Having married her according to the Gāndharva rite, he returned with her to Kāśī. Regarding the desired Tṛtīyā-vrata, Queen Bhāratī and King Prabhāsa, following the instructions of Cṛpaprabhā, performed the Tṛtīyā-vrata dedicated to the deity Gaurī as prescribed by the queen on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. By performing this vow, the queen obtained a son who possessed the luster of the moon. Since he was born under the Mūla asterism, his mother placed him before the goddess Vikaṭādevī and, with the permission of Riddhidevī, sent him to stay near the Māheśvarī temple. His mother—

The manifestation of the Śivaliṅga through Bāṣkula, who had been sent to perform penance near the goddess Pañcamudrā in Ānandakānana; the attainment of the name Vīreśvara for this very Liṅga and the narration of its majesty; how the Lord Vīreśvara granted various boons to him and described the sequence of the holy sites situated at the confluence of the Asi and Gaṅgā, which were established by King Bhṛṅgiriṭi’s son, Vīreśvara, beginning with Rīmadādi and Keśava and ending with the Bhagiratha-tīrtha.

Having established the divine direction in the forest of Bhānandakānana and performed extensive austerities, Duvasi, due to the absence of fruit, cursed Kāḍī; [this section contains] the description of the manifestation of Śiva’s Liṅga and others. Because Duvasi’s desire was fulfilled, that Śivariṅga received the name Kāmeśvara, along with a narration of its majesty. Following the description of the name Viśvakarmeśvara for the divine Liṅga fashioned by Viśvakarman at Kāśī, there is a description of its majesty, preceded by the account of the origin of Dakṣeśvara.

The description of the commencement of the sacrifice by Dakṣa Prajāpati, the enemy of Śiva, due to some attachment to others, without Śiva and Umā; then, having heard the account of the sacrifice from Nārada, Satī’s departure toward Dakṣa’s sacrifice while disregarding the words of Śiva; there, having heard the censure of Śiva from her father’s mouth, she cast off her body in extreme anger; for the welfare [of all], the destruction of Dakṣa’s head by Vīrabhadra, a hero among Śiva’s attendants, following the deception of the sacrifice; and again, by Vīrabhadra...

The auspicious liberation of Dakṣa through the attainment of the form of a ram-faced [god] as known by Śiva; the establishment of a linga of Śiva in Kāśī and the performance of penance by Dakṣa; the narrative of the origin of Dakṣeśvara; the installation of a linga of Pārvatīśa by Pārvatī and the description of its majesty; and the description of the majesty of Gaṅgeśa installed by Bharga (Śiva) on Mount Viśvanātha.

The granting of a boon by Brahmā in the form of equality with himself; the installation of a Śiva-liṅga in Kāśī by Revā after she had performed penance there; the description of the greatness of that place following the account of the boon granted by Nabhodeśvara to Revā; the description of the greatness of the Satīśvara-liṅga installed in Kāśī by Satī as she was about to ascend to heaven; and the description of the greatness of the Śiva-liṅgas known as Amūrteśvara, Karuṇeśvara, and Jyotīrūpeśvara.

In Kāśī as well, having heard in the forest of Vṛkṣavāṭa that "Hāri is to be served" and "Hāra is to be served," [Vyāsa] describes the paralysis of his tongue caused by Śiva and others. Then, at the instruction of Viṣṇu, Vyāsa desists from the paralysis brought about by the touch of Viṣṇu’s throat and performs a hymn of praise to Śiva. ... [This section contains] the account of Vyāsa’s release from the curse, the description of the true nature of Icchārāma and the other [deities], and the narration of the episode of Vyāsa’s expulsion from Kāñcī. ...

The description of all the sacred fords (tīrthas) situated within the field that removes all sins; a detailed account of the great festival of the arrival of Śrī Viśveśvara at Muktimaṇḍapa in Kāśī; the description of the sequence of the final liberation (viśālā) granted by Śrī Kṛṣṇa to the gods beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu regarding the supreme deity of the Kāśī field named Śrī Viśveśvara; the description of the pilgrimage to the various sacred fords; and the description of the merits of hearing and reciting the Kāśī-khaṇḍa—this is the latter portion of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa.
Thus ends the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. || 2 ||
[The syllables] *vi sa ka ni jā ki ka ra ka ca kaḥ i ṭha ta*—[this is] the description of the fruits for men who wear the *vidhivarman* on their bodies.
In the *Bhagavat-Śrī-Kāṇḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, the first part, the Avantya-khaṇḍa.

Ra [Ta. - Oṃ - In the context of the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Vyāsa, the description of the greatness of giving in the Mahākālavana forest, at the feet of Śiva and Gaurī].
Now, in the section on Avanti, first is the majesty of the Avantikṣetra.

The description of the birth of Kalakaṇṭheśvara; the description of the origin of Dānaṅguṇḍa; the description of the greatness of the gift of Kalahanārāyaṇakuṇḍa; the description of the origin and greatness of Apsarastīrtha. First, the hymn to the illustrious Lord Mahākāla by the most auspicious Vyāsa; the greatness of the Mahākāla forest; the description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at that holy site; the description of the greatness of the Apsarakhaṇḍa.
The arrival of Śaunaka near Sanatkumāra; the commencement of the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Vyāsa; therein—

The description of the battle between Śiva and Sanatkumāra at Madākālavana; the account of the defeat of the Rākṣasa named Hāṭaka, who had assumed the guise of a buffalo, by Śiva; the establishment of a Liṅga there by Śiva after defeating the Rākṣasa; the description of the manifestation of Khaṣṭaśuti at the beginning of the Mahiṣakuṇḍa Kalpa; and the account of the origin of the lords Nahuṣa, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, as well as the destruction of the Daityas by the gods.

The praise of Nandikeśvara; the account of his being called *Kapālī* because of the cutting off of his fifth skull and his carrying of that skull-fragment; the description of the majesty of Kauśikīdhara by the gods; the installation of the Śiva-liṅga; the arrival of the knowers of the Vedas, the lords of the earth, the Vasus, and the Vairamas.

Taking a garland of *pārijāta* flowers, [Indra] approached the lord of the Vidyādharas, the enemy of Vāsava (Indra). There, at the command of Brahmā, Menakā was sent by Śiva to serve him; she adorned herself with the earrings and crest-jewel taken from the head of the one who had performed that service. By the order of Brahmā, Śiva dispatched Menakā to the hermitage of Viṣṇu. Seeing Menakā adorned with that garland, Viṣṇu went to Śiva’s abode to destroy the dance-performance. Viṣṇu then gave his discus to Śiva.

The granting of the *khāpa* (sleep-inducing spell) by the Vidyādhara; the arrival of the Vidyādhara lord in Avantī at the command of Śakra; the battle between the two; the combat between the man born from the sweat of Brahmā and the man born from the mouth of Viṣṇu; the departure of the Vidyādhara lord to his own abode through the grace of that holy site (*tīrtha*); the description of the majesty of the Vidyādhara-tīrtha; and the description of the prescription of penance for Brahmā, who incurred the fault of creating Rākṣasas for the purpose of destroying [the world].
Oṃ. [The description of the majesty of Maṇimadrapura; the description of the Rītaka-tīrtha; the account of Sanatukumāra; the description of the Khagadārama-āmalakī-vana.]

The departure of Dharma, Nara, and Nārāyaṇa toward the hermitage of Badarī; their performance of austerities for the sake of the welfare of the world; the majesty of that forest situated on the shore of the great ocean in the midst of the four seas; and there, Śaṅkara, pleased upon seeing King Sumanas, bestowing boons upon Pādapādika and the others.

Nara and Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by their wife Sacīcandrānanā and the son of Dālbhya, Aruṇi, reached the peak of Mount Puṣpāgra. There, at the word of Śiva, they took up residence; and upon Śiva’s command, Brahmā and the other gods arrived there.

The narration [of the events]: at the word of Dāruka, Sudurjaya’s departure for Gandhamādana to worship Śiva; his undertaking of austerities on that mountain for a thousand years until the very end of his penance due to the absence of Śiva; at the conclusion of his penance, his journey to Vāmī by the word of Śiva; the sight of the four oceans in their mortal state through the circumambulation of the four oceans; the gods’ performance of praise to Śiva; Śiva’s granting of boons to the gods; and the destruction of the enemies by the word of Śiva.

The granting of boons to the king by the four Apsarases; the establishment of a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) at that very spot; the establishment of the Four Oceans (*catuḥsamudra*); a description of the greatness of the *kapālamokṣaṇa-tīrtha*; the origin of the Śaṅkara-vāpī-tīrtha; the worship of the Sun by Divākara and a description of the majesty of Kaṅkārāditya; a description of the power and greatness of Nīḍagandhavī; and a statement regarding the fruits of merit.

In the context of the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Āḍhyā, it is described how ten *aśvamedha* sacrifices were accomplished; furthermore, in the description of the origin of Ekānaṃśā Devī, there is the narration of Brahmā’s counsel regarding the destruction of Tāraka, the glorification of the sacred site (tīrtha) of Ekānaṃśā Devī, and the slaying of the two Daityas, Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, at that location during the time of the divine sports of Śiva and Pārvatī. Also described is the establishment of a Liṅga by Śaṅkara under the name Harasiddhi after he had assumed the form of Pārvatī.

In that regard, there is a description of the greatness of the Śivamedhatīya [tirtha] through the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and so forth, including bathing and giving; a description by Manu and others of its purification through bathing; the establishment of it by Brahmā when he was afflicted by a curse and rendered speechless; the arrival of the two [sages]; the naming of those two by Pārvatī; a description of the greatness of Vaṭayakṣiṇī resulting from the attainment of their desires; a description of the greatness of Agastyeśvara; and a description of the greatness of Anādikalyeśvara.

A description of the majesty of Śrārati-tīrtha; a description of the majesty of Mahāmāyā; a description of the majesty of Sakharmadārīthaiyārāma. In the description of the majesty [of that place], after the slaying of Rāvaṇa, the journey of Rāma and the others to Ayodhyā; having gone there, by the command of Vibhīṣaṇa, the installation of the Liṅga on the bank of the lake and the performance of the knowledge-rite by Halumat; [by his command] the description of the majesty of the installation of that very Liṅga in that same place; and the description of the majesty of Kapāṭeśvara at Svaṇajāṭa.

[The description of the final consecration of the kingdom by Danu-makhi; the arrival in Avantī after taking [the linga]; the description of the greatness of the Śivotkaṭa-tīrtha upon seeing the movement of the friend’s linga; the description of the greatness of Yaneśvara; the description of the greatness of Rudrasakha-śoma; the description of the great pilgrimage of Mahākālī as Khaṃka went to the sky to beg for the linga from Lumbā; and the description of the greatness of the pilgrimage.]

The description of Prince Aniruddha, born to the Brahmin named Saṃmati and his wife Kairikī, regarding his abandonment of practice; the description of his repeated encounters with the eight [types of] women; how, because he was unable to satisfy them due to the exhaustion of his vital breaths, he employed a means to bring about their death; how, at their word, he went to the forest and, out of a sense of sharing in their sin, questioned his own retinue; and how his father and others, remaining at home, refused to accept the fruit of that sin.

Śrutavatī, having felt remorse for her transgression, sought refuge in the great sage and offered prayers; thereafter, through the practice of the mantra bestowed by the great sage, the description of her liberation from sin follows. Then, because she was born from a clump of grass (*vālmīka*), the sages gave her the name Vālmīki. Having gone to Kuśasthalī, that Vālmīki propitiated Śiva and established a city after his own name. This concludes the description of the origin of Vālmīki.

The description of the beauty and greatness of Kāḍabana; the description of the majesty of the deities such as Piṅgala who reside on all sides of Kāḍabana; the description of the great glory of Kṛpāsara; the greatness of the pilgrimage to Pañcaśānī; the greatness of Akrūreśvara; the description of the greatness of Brahmakuṇḍa; and the description of the greatness of the Mandākinī Tīrtha.

The description of the place called Aṅkapāda; the narration of the birth of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa; the departure of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who were intent on giving the teacher’s fee to Sāndīpani; their journey to the Yamaloka after killing the demon Śaṅkha residing in the ocean; their defeat of Yama there and their taking back the son of Sāndīpani; and the description of the pilgrimage beginning from Mūlasthāna up to the shrine of Aṅkapāda in Avantī.

The majesty of Candra-ditya-bhāsa; the majesty of Karabheśvara; the majesty of Gajeśvara; the description of the majesties of Kusumeśvara and Jayeśvara; the description of the majesty of Śivadvāra; the description of the majesty of Mākṣaṇḍayeśvara; the majesty of Bahyeśvara; and the majesty of Bhṛṅgīkuṇḍa.

The majesty of Yajñavāṣī; the description of the majesty of the holy sites (tīrthas) such as Pañcūpatīrudrapura, Rūpakuṇḍa, Kedāra, Chaṇḍakarīkuṇḍa, and Ājagaṃpacakra; the description of the majesty of Semavatīśi, Someśvaraṅgi, and others; Chapter 1: [Contents]; Chapter 2: [Contents]; Chapter 3: The description of the majesty of Anaraka-tīrtha, and in connection with that, the description of hell and the description of the torments of hell and so forth.

The greatness of the Anaraka-tīrtha and the offering of lamps; herein, the description of the arrangement of the worship-leaf (pūjā-patra) and the placement of the vessel; the description of the greatness of the Vīryata-kuśasthalī through the offering of lamps; the attainment of prosperity and growth in the months beginning with Caitra; and the description of the greatness of the city named Avanti.

Description of the Greatness of Kedāreśvara Tīrtha: Jaṭātīrtha, Gaṅgātīrtha, Indratīrtha, Cedareśvara, Kuṇḍeśvara, Gopītīrtha, and Vajreśvara. At Ujjayinī, the Asura Tripura performed penance after addressing Brahmā; Brahmā granted him a boon. Description of the greatness of Paṭātīrtha, Nadeśvara, and Rāmeśvara. Therein, Rāma led his father Daśaratha and Indra and the other gods, who were oppressed by the Asura Tripura, before Śiva; Śiva granted them freedom from fear.

The section on the performance of *śrāddha* rites; the worship of the goddess Yogeśvarī at Saubhāgyatīrtha, Gharṛtatīrtha, Raṅkhāvata, Sudhodaka, and Sudheśvara; the worship of Cāmuṇḍā in Avantī by Indra and others by the command of Kīdibāja; and a description of the great majesty of Upasthaviravināyaka, Kāmodaka, and others at the city of Panatopattana, following the words of Cāmuṇḍā.

The section on the causes of defeat; therein, the establishment of Kedāraka by Arjuna at the word of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, due to the arrogance of the Dānava Vṛṣaparvan; the paralyzing of the sun by Arjuna at the word of Kṛṣṇa—these are well-known narratives—and the description of the majesty of Ujjayinī. Va.

The granting of boons by Sūrya to him; the offering of praise by Jañjana; and likewise, by the command of Suyajña, the churning of the ocean for the sake of producing the jewel of men (Narasimha), and the installation of the Sun on Mount Udaya for the purpose of receiving the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*) for two days and nights—this is the description of the majesty of Narāditya. Furthermore, when the gods and demons were dividing the nectar, Bhagavān assumed the form of Mohinī and, while the division was being made, [the account of] the gods and sages beholding [him].

The performance of a hymn of praise by Suyajña, the description of the majesty of Keśavāditya, and the severing of Rāhu’s head while he remained there in disguise; therein [is contained] the removal of the affliction caused by Rāhu and Ketu.

The description of the birth of Skanda; therein, the casting of the seed by Raukara (Skanda); the prayer for the seed by Agni; the arrival at the holy ford (tīrtha); the description of the greatness of Rāhutīrtha; the description of the greatness of Ratnakuṇḍa; the casting of the seed into the Gaṅgā; the account of how that seed entered the wombs of the six Kṛttikās who had come there after bathing; the birth of Skanda; and the description of the majesty of Raktibhadra-tīrtha.

And the description of the splendor of the city of Kumudvatī; the description of the majesty of the nature of Kumudvatī; the description of the majesty of Agastyeśvara... the description of the Mahākālavana forest; within the description of the Nandana forest, the description of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu); the account of the city named Amarāvatī; the description of the sacred fords (tīrthas), preceded by the citation of the names of various liṅgas situated in each Kalpa; and the description of the time of the battle with the demon Andhaka. ... ||
Dhara.
The description of the majesty of Naradīp Tīrtha established by Śiva; the description of the majesty of the city named Viśālā. —... (Ra)

—A description of the majesty of Oṃkāreśvara; the majesty of Abhayeśvara and Ākhaṅga; and a description of the rules regarding the duration of time, beginning from the undertaking of the Aṅgārakīcaturthī vow up until the end of eighty-four kalpas.

The description of Śiva, the bearer of the skull, going to Vaikuṇṭha for the purpose of begging; the description of the Andhaka Asura, unable to endure the humiliation inflicted by the Goddess Caṇḍī, performing a hymn of praise to Śiva; when Śiva struck him there with his trident, the emergence of the entire host of weapons from Viṣṇu’s finger; and the establishment of Cāmuṇḍā and the other Mothers at that very spot by that flowing stream.

Description of the ritual for worshipping Mātṛkā; narration of how Andhaka, having transformed into the form of a river, became famous by the name Śiprā; description of the battle between Bāṇa and Kṛṣṇa, including the account of his attainment of the status of a Gaṇa; description of the mutual sending of messengers during the battle between Śiva and Viṣṇu; the defeat of Raivata in the conflict between the devotees of Śiva (Śaiva) and the devotees of Viṣṇu (Vaiṣṇava); description of that place becoming famous by the name Varanīti; and [other] topics.

Description of the Greatness of Jvaraghnī Tīrtha: In the context of describing Pāpanāśinī Tīrtha, King Daman, a practitioner of unrighteousness, goes into the forest for the purpose of hunting; having tethered his horse there at the foot of a banyan tree, he leaves the king behind at that very spot; then a serpent falls upon the king's head, and while the king is tormented by the serpent, the messengers of Yama arrive there.

Then, at the time of King Yama’s torment, the flesh of the body of one who had gone to the realm of Yama fell into the Śiprā, smeared by crows; by that merit, he went to the world of Śiva. In the assembly of Yama and his attendants, the majesty of the Śiprā was described. Bhikṣādiva went to the world of the Nāgas; because of the absence of alms-food there, the serpents, being terrified, praised Vasuki while consuming the *sakṛt* (cow-dung) situated in the twenty-one pits located there. Then all the serpents went to the Śiprā.

The performance of the hymn of praise to Śiva; the establishment of the Amṛtakuṇḍa there by Him who was pleased by that [hymn]; the description of the majesty of Bhāratī; the gods, oppressed by Hiraṇyākṣa, going to the celestial realm and relating the entire account to Brahmā; Brahmā’s narration to the gods of the cause of the curse upon Jaya and Vijaya; the description of the birth and deeds of Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu; the description of the descent as a Boar for the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa; [and] from the body of the Boar...

Description of the origin of the Riprā; description of the beauty of the Riprā river; description of the majesty of the Riprā; description of the majesty of the tīrtha named Sundara in Mahākālavana; therein, the narration of the story of Devaladdhija.

Description of the majesty of the Nīkhagaṅgā; the performance of penance by Agastya on the Vindhya mountains for the purpose of uplifting the land submerged in the waters of the Revā; the departure of Vindhyavāsinī, who was pleased by that penance, to Ujjayinī; description of the majesty of the temple of Vindhyavāsinī; description of the majesty of the Māndhātṛkṣetra-sarasvatī; and, within the description of the Kṣātā-saṅgama-tīrtha, the account of the birth of Yama and Yamunā following the dispute between Sūrya and Anasūyā.

The Greatness of the Kṣātāsaṅgama Tīrtha (Chapter 1). The Description of the Greatness of the Pitṛmocana Tīrtha (Chapter 2). The Greatness of the Gayā Tīrtha (Chapter 3). In that [chapter], regarding the praise of the Gayā Tīrtha: the departure of the gods, who were oppressed by the Rākṣasa Tuṇḍa, to the abode of Brahmā; the journey of Brahmā and the others to the world of Viṣṇu and the performance of a hymn of praise to Viṣṇu; and, with the permission of Viṣṇu, the departure of them all to the Gayā Tīrtha. The Gayā Tīrtha.

The description of the greatness of the Gayā-kṣetra, including the *Sāmānyavidhāna-pūta-vraka-śrāddha-krama-māhātmya*; the description of the greatness of the river Phalgu situated in the field of Gayā; the greatness of the fruit of bathing and giving gifts at the various holy sites (tīrthas) such as Ādi-gayā, Buddhagayā, Svapnupada-gayā, Kāṣṭhagadādharavedikā, Aśvayavara-pratimukti-karīri, and Ācchoda; therein, within the dialogue between the sage Pañcacūḍā and Nārada, the description of the greatness of the Pañcamī-vrata by Nārada; and the description of the greatness of Puruṣottama, occurring in the context of the dialogue between Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.

The description of the observance of the *malimluca* month; the exposition of the rules for vows and other rites during the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*); the greatness of giving gifts during the *māṅgalya* month; the greatness of residing in Mahākālavana and other places during the intercalary month; the greatness of the sequence of worship of Puruṣottama; the greatness of the Jaṭeśvara-Maheśvara Tīrtha; the greatness of the Bhāgīrathī Tīrtha; the greatness of the Kāverī river; the description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other acts during the intercalary month; the greatness of Gomatīkuṇḍa; and the greatness of Kāṣṭhā.

A description of the attainment of the fruits of merit from bathing and other rites at Gomatīkuṇḍa; a description of Kantheśvara, Laghugartā-saṅgama, Vīreśvara, and Vāmanatīrtha, as well as Māhalya; therein, Bali’s distress upon going to the world of the gods and his reporting of his own situation; the narration by Brahmā of the means for the propitiation of Viṣṇu; and in that context, within the course of a dialogue between Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods, the enumeration of the thousand names of Viṣṇu.

[Chapter *ka*: The narration of the hearing of the fruits of the *Saha-khanāma* [rite]; the description of the greatness and the account of the establishment of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) beginning with the incarnation as Vāmana; the description of the holy sites of Kāverī and Airāvati at Vīreśvara; and therein, the recitation of the eight verses of Bharavi. [Chapter *kha*: In the context of the holy site of Nāgākhyaya, the narrative of Janamejaya the believer; the description of the greatness preceded by the sight of the nine sacrificial pits (*navakuṇḍa*); and the greatness of the Ramāsaras holy site. . . sa.
Following the description of the account of his birth as a householder, [in] the Avanti-khaṇḍa, first is the greatness of the sacred field of Avanti.

Now begins the eighty-fourth chapter, the introduction to the greatness of the *Gaṅgā*, starting with the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara; therein is the description of the greatness of the Pradhānaprannāsyeśvara [liṅga], followed by an account of ancient history in connection with that. In that context, for the sake of the Daityas attaining happiness, Kaṃbhayoni killed the demons; subsequently, fearing the sin of slaughter out of remorse, he performed the propitiation of Īśvara, and by Śiva’s command, established a *Śivaliṅga* in his own name. Then follows the description of the greatness of that Agastyeśvara-liṅga. Now...

A description of the greatness of the Guheśvara Liṅga: there, Maṅkaṇaka performed penance as a parrot; at a certain time, having attained a miracle by swallowing a ladleful of vegetable broth, he caused all beings to bow down. Seeing the dancing that arose among all mobile and immobile beings, the gods departed for the heavenly world. By divine grace, the pride of that Maṅkaṇaka was removed. By the command of Śiva, the installation of the liṅga at Mahākālavana was performed, and the attainment of liberation by Maṅkaṇaka is described.

Description of the majesty of Gudeśvara; then, the description of the majesty of Duṇḍha-Cara; therein, the journey of the attendant named Duṇḍha to the assembly of Indra; there, the granting of a boon by Indra to Duṇḍha, who was moved by passion upon seeing Rambhā being tormented; thereafter, his human birth; and then, in the Avanti-khaṇḍa, the second majesty of the eighty-four Liṅgas situated in Avanti.
(-) || [End of section] ||

Chapters and Subjects: Description of the greatness of Kaḍaṭumba; description of the penance of the ten great gods and others; description of the greatness of Devaprabhāga-tīrtha; the greatness of Ānandabhairava-tīrtha; in the description of Akhaṇḍeśvara-tīrtha, the account of how even the great sinner Jahmadatta attained the world of the blessed upon dying there; and, in the context of the dialogue between Nārada and Brahmā, the description of the greatness of Akhaṇḍasara-tīrtha.

The majesty of the Karkarāja-tīrtha; the description of the Vidhūmrārcis-tīrtha; the description of the Cāturmāsya-vrata; the majesty of the Bindusaras and Ramyasaras tīrthas; the sequential enumeration of names following a calculation of the number of tīrthas; a statement regarding the sequence of the pilgrimage (tīrthayātrā) beginning with the Devayātrā; the description of the majesty of the Avarantī-kṣetra according to the sacred scriptures (śruti); and the conclusion of the treatise.

Bha: The sixth chapter: [The account of] how Jada Kapi, having propitiated Lord Śiva at Mahākālavana, established a Liṅga in his own name; and the description of the greatness of the Duṇḍeśvara Tīrtha.

Now follows the description of the majesty of Ḍamarukeśvara: therein, the defeat in battle of the descendants of Raghu along with Indra and the other gods by the Daitya Vajra, the son of Ruru; the departure to the world of Brahmā of those [gods]; the description of the battle between Vajra and the maiden Sakantakā, who emerged from the body of Brahmā; the description of the humiliation of Vajra after his purpose had been frustrated; the performance of worship to Īśvara by Śruti and others; the description of the battle between Īśvara and Vajra; and the destruction of Vajra by means of the ḍamaru drum wielded by Īśvara.

Then follows the establishment of the shrine of Ḍamarukeśvara there, and the description of the greatness of Umāruka. Next, the description of the greatness of Ānādikalpeśvara; then, the description of the greatness of Svarṇajaḍeśvara. Therein is the account of how Śaṅkara, while sporting with Pārvatī, was burned by the fire of his own virility and subsequently cast himself into the Gaṅgā to quell that fire; and thereafter, the appearance of the first son named Kāñcana from that fire.

The trembling of the mountain; having seen that, the offering of Kāñcana’s son to Śaṅkara by Vahni; Kāñcana’s departure for the Mahākāravana forest by the command of Śaṅkara; Kāñcana performing penance and the attainment of the status of a Gaṇa through the words of Īśvara; and the description of the greatness of Svarṇajākhaścaraṅiga.

[Now begins] the description of the greatness of Triviṣṭapeśvara-Ṛṣiga; therein, the words of Nārada regarding the establishment of the station of Triviṣṭapeśvara-Ṛṣiga in Mahākālavana; the description of the greatness of Triviṣṭapeśvara-Ṛṣiga; then the description of the greatness of Kapāleśvara-Ṛṣiga; therein, during the Great Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha) in Mahākālavana, Śaṅkara’s arrival while holding a skull in his hand; the Brahmins’ showing of contempt upon seeing the appearance of Śaṅkara’s head; and thereafter, by Śiva, there in the sacrificial pavilion—

Having placed the door-panel [in its position], he departed; then, having cast the door-panel from the vicinity of the Nīlakaṇṭha maṇḍapa, he gave a gift of more than a thousand cows. Seeing that miracle, the Nīlakaṇṭhas performed a hymn of praise. He established a *liṅga* under the name Kapāṭeśvara. By the greatness of the *liṅga* at Kapāṭeśvara, there is described the destruction of great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and the avoidance of hell. Thus ends the section.

a. Oṃ. Dha. Da Ṣka Kā Jana -----na----- ---: Ja Ka Aiḥ Bha Kke Va Ka Dda Ka Nā Jo Ma Ka Ka Ka Vada Ka Kaka Ka Vdkaḥ. The objects of the senses. Now follows the description of the Svargadvāra-liṅga-maṣṭha-samyavarṇana (the detailed description of the Svargadvāra-liṅga). Therein is the description of the battle between the divine hosts led by Vīrabhadra and others, on the one hand, and Viṣṇu and the other gods, on the other, following Śiva’s command after he had been insulted by Dakṣa during the sacrifice; therein [is described] the defeat of Viṣṇu and the other gods, and the [triumph of the] Rudra-host.

The construction of the Svargadvāra (Gate of Heaven); the gods, having observed the absence of their own residence in heaven, going to the Mahākālavana forest for the worship of Śiva by the command of Viṣṇu; the installation there of the Liṅga named Svargadvāra; the description of the majesty of the Svargadvāra-khaṇḍa; then the description of the majesty of Karkoṭakeśvara-khaṇḍa; therein, the performance of penance by the Nāga Karkoṭaka in the Mahākālavana forest for the sake of destroying the sin committed against his mother; and [the granting of boons] to him by Śiva, who was pleased by that penance.

The granting of boons; the installation of the *digambara* [ascetic] by his own name; the description of the greatness of Karkoṭakeśvara; then the detailed description of the *liṅga* of Siddheśvara; therein, the departure for the great forest of Mahākāla after hearing a divine voice while performing penance in the Devadāruvana forest for the sake of attaining perfection (*siddhi*); having performed penance there, the attainment of perfection and the installation of the *liṅga*; the description of the greatness of Siddheśvara; then the description of the greatness of the excellent *liṅga* Chokapāṭara; therein—

From the presence of Hiraṇyakaśipu, he, having developed supreme devotion through the glances of the world-guardians (*lokapāla*), went to the Mahākālavana forest to perform penance by the command of Viṣṇu. By the power of his penance, having destroyed the Daityas, he returned to his own abode. He established the quarters in the Mahākālavana forest under the name Lokapāleśvara. This is the description of the majesty of the deity Lokapāleśvara; now follows the description of the majesty of Kāmeśvara. There, Brahmā, for the sake of fulfilling the desire of Śiva, created Kāma and [established] his twelve locations.

The dispatching of Kāma to inflame desire by means of a divine arrow; the reduction of Kāma to ashes by the Lord for obstructing his own asceticism; Rati’s making her home there upon learning that he had been slain by the Lord; thereafter, Kāma’s departure to the Mahākālavana forest after being rendered bodiless (anaṅga) by the command of Śiva; his performing penance there and the installation of a Liṅga; and the description of the majesty of Kāmeśvarī...

Now begins the description of the great and beautiful holy site of Ṅuṭambakeśvara. There, when the Kālakūṭa poison had emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk, Śaṅkara, unable to endure the burning heat arising from it, gave that Kālakūṭa to the Śiprā. Having received it, the Śiprā went to the Mahākāvana forest; and by the Śiprā, on the bank of the Ganges near Kāmeśvara, [the following chapters were established]. Chapter 50. Section 3. Dha.

Then follows the description of the greatness of the Kaṭhkaṭeda Vara Liṅga: therein, during the occasion of the dispute between Umā and Maheśvara, when the three worlds were shaken, the depositing of that Kālakūṭa poison; the description of the imminent death of the Brahmins who had arrived at the presence of the Lord of the Eye due to the ingestion of the Kālakūṭa poison; the restoration of the Brahmins to life by Śiva after he arrived there; the naming of the Liṅga by Śiva as Kuṭumbakeśvara; and the description of the greatness of the Kuṭumbakeśvara Liṅga.

Now follows the description of the greatness of Indreśvara Liṅga. Therein is the account of how Indra, due to the loss of his merit, fell from heaven; and how, out of remorse, he established undecaying fame by taking the advice of Mārkaṇḍeya, going to Mahākālavana at the command of Himavat, and performing the worship of the Śivaliṅga. Having secured undecaying renown there, he installed a Liṅga in his own name. This is the description of the greatness of Indreśvara Liṅga. Now follows the description of the greatness of Īśāneśvara Liṅga, wherein—

By the command of Śiva, Tuhuṇḍa, the son of Muṇḍa, conquered the gods; having gone to the Mahākākha forest, he performed the worship of Śiva. With the Lord pleased, He bestowed upon that Liṅga the name Īśāneśvara. The gods composed a hymn of praise for Īśāneśvara, and the majesty of Īśāneśvara is described.

Next, the description of the greatness of the Apsarasesvara Liṅga: there, having seen Rambhā dancing before Indra while she was being watched by the gods, Śakra, out of anger, pronounced a curse upon her. To counteract the effects of that curse, at the word of Nārada, she installed a Liṅga in Mahākālavana under her own name; by propitiating Śiva through daily worship, she obtained a boon from him and returned to her own world. This is the description of the greatness of the Apsarasesvara Liṅga.

Because the sound "kalakaṭa" arose there from a broken pot, the manifestation of the *liṅga* occurred; thus, that *liṅga* was given the name Kalakaṇṭheśvara. [This is] the description of the identity of the Karkaṭeśvara *liṅga*. Next is the description of the identity of the Nāgacaṇḍeśvara *liṅga*. Regarding that *liṅga* installed by Nāgacaṇḍa, Lord Dadau arrived. When the fault of excessive attachment (*nirmālyasraṅghana*) arose during the worship of that *liṅga*, [the Lord acted] for that Nāgacaṇḍeśvara *liṅga*.
Ṭha | A. (va ca thai ika kadra na- ||

[The text fragment] *ta ṅka, a ka, dhna na | ka-* [indicates the following: Now follows the description of the greatness of Pratihāreśvara Liṅga. While Umā and Maheśvara were sporting there, Nandin, the gatekeeper, remained standing at the door; being unaware, he allowed Agni to enter the inner apartments. Enraged by this, Śiva pronounced a curse upon Nandin. Thereupon, Nandin went to the Mahākālavana forest and installed a divine image under the name Pratihāreśvara. By his grace...

The departure of Nandin once again toward the world of Śiva; the description of the greatness of the excellent *liṅga* at Bhrṛtihāra; then the description of the greatness of the *liṅga* at Kukkuṭeśvara. Therein, due to his constant consumption of cocks in a previous birth, King Kaurika experienced the delusion of being a cock every night by virtue of a curse pronounced by Tāmracūḍa. For the sake of destroying that curse, he worshipped the *liṅga* named Pakṣiyonivimocana in the Mahākāṭa forest, whereby his attainment of the state of a cock was brought to an end.

The installation of the Kukkuṭeśvara Liṅga; a description of the majesty of the Kukkuṭeśvara Liṅga; then, a description of the majesty of the Kakaṇḍeśvara [Liṅga]. In that context, while King Dharmamūrti was desirous of knowing the cause for the attainment of sovereignty, he questioned Vasiṣṭha, who, in the course of their conversation, replied: "In your previous birth, due to a sinful act you committed, you attained the state of being a crow."

The narration of the account: how a certain Rāyasena, having seized a female crab, threw it into the Śivāmraka; thereafter, at the time of death, by the power of Śivadāsa, he attained sovereignty in this very world. Then follows the description of the greatness of the Karkaṭīśvara Liṅga, and subsequently the description of the greatness of the Meṣanāda Liṅga, wherein King Madāndha performed sacrifices out of wickedness and other such motives.

Due to the lack of rain caused by the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the gods departed for the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). Then, by the command of Brahmā, the gods went to the Mahākālavana forest. There, they offered praise to the Liṅga installed by the gods themselves. By worshipping that Liṅga, the cessation of the drought was described. Consequently, that Liṅga established by the clouds was given the name Meghanādeśvara. Next follows the narration of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Meghanādeśvara Liṅga; then the narration of the majesty of the Mahālaya Cakra Liṅga; and then Suktīśa.

The description of the greatness of Raliga: there, while a Brahmin named Mukti was meditating upon Nārāyaṇa at Jayoddeśvara near Mahākāra, a certain hunter suddenly arrived at his cottage. Upon seeing the Brahmin and the holy site, the hunter’s wickedness departed and he attained a state of auspiciousness. The hunter remained there, performing penance while focusing on the objects of the six paths (*ṣaḍbhanyā-viṣaya*). Through the recitation of the eight-syllable mantra (*aṣṭākṣara-mantra*), he attained liberation at that very place.

The description of the liberation of a certain tiger who had attained [the state of a beast] through hearing that mantra; the tiger’s narration of his own story from a previous birth along with the explanation of the cause of his suffering; the departure of both the tiger and the liberated Brāhmaṇa to the place called Bhṛgukaccha; the installation of a *liṅga* there; the description of the majesty of Yuktīśvara; then, the description of the majesty of Someśvara; and therein, the account of how, upon seeing the moon’s lack of affection for any other [wives] besides Rohiṇī, Dakṣa, out of anger, gave [him]—

The departure of Soma to Satyaloka for the sake of removing his curse; his journey with Brahmā to Vaikuṇṭha and the offering of praise to Viṣṇu; by the command of Viṣṇu, Soma’s departure to Mahākāvana and the installation of the Liṅga there; the description of the cessation of Soma’s disease of consumption (yakṣmaroga); the description of the greatness of Someśvara-liṅga. Then follows the description of the greatness of Anarakeśvara, wherein, preceded by a description of the sequence of torments in hell, it is told how Nimi went to the abode of Yama due to even a slight sin despite his great store of merit.

Furthermore, through the sight of Anarakeśvara, when all sins have been destroyed, there is the ascent of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and departure for the world of Indra; the consolation offered by Nimi to those beings suffering from the pain of experiencing the torments of Yama; a description of the greatness of the pilgrimage to Anarakeśvara; then, a description of the greatness of Jaṭeśvara; therein, a description of the greatness of Jaṭeśvara preceded by the narration of the story of King Vīradhanvan; and a description of the establishment of the directions and other matters concerning Jaṭeśvara. Now...

Description of the greatness of Rāmeśvara-Nigama: there, having ruled the earth twenty-one times as a Kṣatriya, Rāma, for the sake of removing the sin of Brāhmaṇa-slaughter, visited various holy places (tīrthas) until his impurity was gone; then, following the instruction of Nārada, he went to the presence of Jaṭeśvara in the great forest of Jāmadagnya-Rāma; having performed penance there, he attained the destruction of his sin and established a Liṅga in his own name; description of the greatness of Rāmeśvara-Nigama; now, Cyavaneśvara.

Description of the greatness of the pilgrimage site (ṅigama-māhātmya-varṇana); therein, the sage named Cyavana, having chosen the daughter of King Śyāti, performed penance in the Mahākāśa forest and established a Liṅga in his own name; description of the greatness of the Cyavaneda-vakhaṭaṇa; [this concludes] the section on those with desires (sakāma). || 0 ||

The objects [of the senses]; then, the description of the greatness of Khaṇḍavara; therein, the departure of Bhadrādavarāja, the son of Bhrīyavrata, for Mahākālavana at the word of Kubhayoni; there, the installation of a linga by Khaṇḍitavrata for the sake of purification; and the description of the arrival of Khaṇḍaśavaraṅiga. Bhi.

Now begins the description of the majesty of the *pattaneśvara-liṅga*. Then follows the description of the majesty of the *ānandeśvara-liṅga*: therein, a certain son of Anamitra named Ānanda, having gone to the great forest of Kāṭavana for a particular reason, established a *liṅga* in his own name; [this is] the description of the majesty of the *ānandeśvara-liṅga*. Now follows the description of the majesty of the *kaṃthaḍeśvara-liṅga*: therein, a Brahmin named Pāṇḍava, having performed penance on account of a rag (*kanthā*), established a *liṅga* named after that rag (*kanthā*).

The description of the greatness of Caradigama at Kanthaḍa; the description of the greatness of Śvarakaṅga; there, due to the falling of his own banner, Brahmā became enraged at Kuradhvaja, the son of Brahmā, and by striking his matted locks against the ground, the demon Vṛtra was born; thereafter, the battle between Vṛtra and Indra, the defeat of Indra, and the departure of Śakra to Mahākālavana at the command of Bṛhaspati in order to slay Vṛtra; and having slain the demon through the power of penance, [his arrival] there for the sake of removing the sin of that slaughter.

The description of the greatness of Liṅga-sthāpana; then the description of the greatness of Darśacara-māhātmya; then the description of the greatness of Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara, including the narrative of the birth of Mārkaṇḍeya and the installation of a Liṅga by Mārkaṇḍeya under his own name in Mahākālavana, followed by the description of the greatness of the Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara Liṅga. — Then follows the description of the greatness of Śiveśvara Liṅga.

Therein is the narration of the story of Ripukshaya; then the description of the supreme greatness of Śiveśvara; then the description of the greatness of the holy site of Kusumeśvara, including the account of how it received the name Kusumeśvara due to its association with those engaged in floral sports; then the description of the greatness of the holy site of Kusumeśvara; and then the description of the greatness of the holy site of Ākarūra, wherein Śaṅkara, having established the deity Mahākāla at that great forest in order to destroy his own cruel disposition, performed worship of him; by that, his cruelty...

The cessation of worldly existence; the renown of that mountain by the name Akrūreśvara; the description of the majesty of Akrūreśvara-Ṛṣi; then the description of the majesty of Kuṇḍeśvara; therein, while Śiva and Pārvatī were seated upon a bull, due to some cause, [Śiva] suddenly vanished from sight; then the internal cause for Pārvatī’s longing for Śiva; the chapters on the subject matter; the bestowing of a curse upon Kagaṇa; and thereupon, by Kuṇḍa, for the sake of removing that curse, [the journey] to Mahākālavana under the name of Sakhā.

The installation [of the deity], and a description of the greatness of the Liṅga at Kuṇḍeśvara. Next, a description of the greatness of the Liṅga at Chaspeśvara: therein, due to the slaughter of a Sāmaga Brahmin, King Chaṃparāja was cursed by that sage; following the instruction of Nārada, he went to Mahākālavana. There, for the sake of curing his leprosy, he installed the Liṅga in the direction [of the curse]. A description of the greatness of the Liṅga of Saikateśvara, and another Liṅga named Khamyeśvara. Herein is the description of the greatness of the Liṅga of Raṅgeśvara. Therein—

The greatness of the *liṅga* established by Bhagīratha on the bank of the R̥pā at the place called Gaṅgeśvara, where the Gaṅgā descends from the matted locks of Śiva onto the earth; and a description of the greatness of the procedure for worshipping Gaṅgādāvara and other rites.

Then follows the description of the greatness of Aṅgārakeśvara; the account of the birth of Aṅgāraka’s son from the body of Śibi; and the description of the greatness of Aṅgārakeśvara. Next is the description of the greatness of Uttareśvara: therein, the departure of Indra and the other gods toward the north at the command of Śiva after being afflicted by the planet Rāhu; the installation of the Śiva-liṅga performed by Uttara-megha; and the description of the greatness of Uttareśvara.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Trilocaneśvara-liṅga. Next, the description of the greatness of the Vīreśvara-liṅga. Next, the description of the greatness of the Nṛpureśvara-liṅga. Next, the description of the greatness of the Abhayeśvara-liṅga. Next, the description of the greatness of the Prathakeśvara-liṅga. Next, the description of the greatness of the Sthāvareśvara-liṅga. Next, the description of the greatness of the Śūleśvara-liṅga; therein, [the story] of the destruction of the demon Aghakānura by Śiva.

Having established the *Śūlanāma-liṅga*, there is a description of the greatness (*māhātmya*) of Śeśvari-ga. (Then follows) the description of the greatness of the *Athokāreśvara-liṅga*; therein is the description of the greatness of the *Athokāreśvara-liṅga* established by the word of Śiva at the request of Śivavrka. (Next is) the description of the greatness of the *Viśveśvara-liṅga*; therein, King Vidūratha, having taken twelve births due to the fault produced by the killing of a Brahmin, [attains] the state of a Caṇḍāla in the thirteenth [birth].

Having reached the presence of Śiva and received various instructions, there is a description of his subsequent birth as a king; remembering [his past] in his previous life, he established a *liṅga* in the great Kaṭavana forest, followed by a description of the majesty of the Viśveśvara-liṅga (and then a description of the majesty of the Kaṇṭeśvara-liṅga, wherein a certain king, defeated by his enemies, [sought refuge with] Vasiṣṭha).

The journey to the hermitage; at his command, the king went to Mahākāraṇya and performed worship after establishing the *Ṛgveda*; through that, he attained a kingdom free of thorns, and thus that *Śaṅkha* became famous by the name Kaṇṭeśvara; then follows the description of the greatness (*māhātmya*) of the pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*) of Kaṇṭeśvara; next, the description of the greatness of the pilgrimage site of Siṃheśvara; there, while Maurya was performing austerities for the sake of attaining Śiva, Brahmā arrived; and at the word of Brahmā, from the mouth of the goddess Karandhā—

The birth and nourishment of the lion, the description of the two breasts of the Goddess flowing with milk, the departure of the lion for the Mahākālavana forest by the command of Pārvatī, the account of his attainment of the status of Śiva’s vehicle, the establishment of a Liṅga by that lion under his own name—the Siṃheśvara Liṅga—and then the description of the majesty of the Revanteśvara Liṅga; there, having installed a deity, Revata, the son of Sūrya, departed for Kāśī, and by the word of Śiva, having arrived at Mahākālavana, [he established a shrine] there under his own name.

The appearance of Daśana; the destruction of Nārada’s ignorance through the grace of Sāvitrī; Sāvitrī’s narration of her own life-story when questioned out of wonder by him; the attainment of steadfastness by Nārada in proceeding to Prayāga at the word of Sāvitrī; the description by Priyavrata of the greatness of the pilgrimage to the Lord of Martanda; the installation of the Linga by Matanga, the son of the Brahmin Sugati, together with Nārada at that place; and their journey to Prayāga in Avantī, where, having arrived, they installed the Linga and performed its worship.

Description of the greatness of Prayāgeśvara-Ṛṅgi... Description of the greatness of Siddheśvara-Ṇiṅga; therein, the instruction given by the great sages Jaigīṣavya and Kapila to King Aśvaśiras; the king’s taking refuge in wonder at the true nature of the Lord as revealed through the illusory power (*māyā*) displayed by those two; his journey to the Mahākāṭa forest at their command and the worship of the *liṅga* after attaining perfection (*siddhi*); and the description of the greatness of Siddheśvara-liṅga.

The worship [of the Liṅga], and the description of the greatness of the Matageśvara Liṅga. Now follows the description of the greatness of the Saubhāgyeśvara Liṅga: there, a queen named Samatī, the wife of King Aśvavāhana, being extremely distressed due to separation from her husband, performed the worship of the Lord of the Mountain (Himavat) according to the instructions for the purpose of attaining her husband; by the success of that [worship], her husband returned, and she attained good fortune—thus is the description of the greatness of the Saubhāgyeśvara Liṅga.

Now follows the description of the majesty of Rūpeśvara. In that regard: King Padma’s journey to the hermitage of Kaṇva; there, being infatuated by lust, he gave his daughter to the sage Kaṇva and committed adultery with her; Kaṇva, perceiving this with his eye of knowledge, inflicted upon them both the punishment of having their thighs severed; thereafter, at Kaṇva’s command, they went to the Mahākālavana forest; there, through the worship of the *liṅga*, the description of how they regained their original forms; and finally, the description of the greatness of the Rūpeśvara *liṅga*.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Dhanuḥsāhasreśvara shrine: therein, the abduction of King Vidūratha’s daughter by the demon Kumbha; thereafter, his battle with the two sons of Vidūratha; and upon learning of the defeat and captivity of his two sons, King Vidūratha, with the permission of the sages, goes to the Mahākāla forest for the sake of their victory and performs the worship of the quarters; through the power of that worship, his—Dhanuḥsāhasra—[bow becomes ready].

The attainment of the bow by Tuṣita; the defeat of the Daitya by that prowess in archery; the description of how that king, together with his sons, daughters, and others, attained liberation at the end after first attaining heaven; the description of the greatness of the Lord of Dhanuḥsāhasra and of worshiping Him; the description of the greatness of the Lord of Paḍupati; then the description of the greatness of the Lord of Braddhavarka; therein, the departure of the Daitya Pukhoma along with his army to Śīrāścha to conquer Viṣṇu.

Then follows the account of Brahmā’s departure for the Mahākālavana forest for the purpose of conquering the Daityas; there, the description of his penance and how Śiva, being pleased, brought about the defeat of the Daityas; the establishment of a Liṅga by Brahmā under his own name and the description of the majesty of that Brahmahṛdaya Liṅga. Next is the description of the majesty of Jvālēśvara, where King Jalpa, having established his five sons in the kingdom, departed for the forest, and subsequently [the account of] mutual discord among his kinsmen.

Having learned that his five sons were dead, King Jaṣpa, distressed by their separation, went to the Mahyaka forest at the command of Vasiṣṭha. There, he established a *liṅga* in his own name; this is the description of the greatness of the Jaṣpedavara-liṅga. Now follows the description of the greatness of Kedāreśvara. There, the gods, including Brahmā, went to Kailāsa while afflicted by the cold. Having meditated upon Śiva, they proceeded toward Kedāreśvara in that direction. By the power of that merit, the affliction of the cold was averted; this is the description of the greatness of the Kedāreśvara-liṅga.

Then follows the description of the greatness of the Piśāceśvara Liṅga: the description of the wickedness and extreme cruelty of the deity named Soma; therein, the narration of the dialogue between the Piśāca and the Brāhmaṇa Rākaṭāyana; the departure for the Madākāṭa forest by means of liberation from the state of being a Piśāca through the words of Śākayāyana; there, having worshipped the goat, the Lord of the Earth grants liberation to that Piśāca; the description of the greatness of the Piśāceśvara Liṅga; and then the description of the greatness of the Saṅgameśvara Liṅga.

Therein is the narration of the story of the previous births of Pannī, Subāhu, and Vacanā; then follows the description of the attainment of liberation by Saṅgameśvara at the conclusion of his reign; the glorification of the greatness of the Saṅgameśvara Liṅga; and then the description of the greatness of the Eraṭaga Tīrtha, which is difficult to behold.

The departure of King Duḥṣanta to the forest for hunting; there, having given his daughter to the sage named Kaṇva, he performed a sacrifice together with her. [Then follows] the chapter on the deer, the lion, and the Śarabha. Next, the description of the majesty of the Paśupatīśvara Liṅga; therein, the installation of that [Liṅga] by King Paḍuphaṭha. By worshipping Śiva in Mahākālavana, he attained kingship, and after enjoying all pleasures, he reached liberation at the end.

The description of the eighth day of the lunar fortnight dedicated to Urdhvaśaṅkara; then, the description of the greatness of visiting Prayāgeśvara: therein, the liberation from human birth attained by Śatānanda through his vow, the journey to Prayāgeśvara at the word of Nārada, the removal of sins through the worship of Śiva, and the description of the greatness of visiting Prayāgeśvara.

Now follows the description of the greatness of Candrādityeśvara; the journey of the two [Candra and Āditya] to the forest of Badarī; by the command of Viṣṇu, their assumption of the form of luminaries in that great forest and the account of how they brought about the defeat of Śambara by means of that light; there, having seen the gods defeated by Śambara, Candra and Sūrya went and performed worship of Śiva, and the account of the arrival of Candra and Āditya at Śivagiri; and the account of the death of the camel in the great forest of Karabhasthalī, belonging to King Vīraketu, who had gone out on a hunt.

Then, by the command of someone, there is a description of Mahākāla attaining the state of Dailāsa; next, a description of the greatness of Karabheśvara’s limbs. Then follows a description of the greatness of the Daśabhadra Liṅga at Rājasthala, where King Puñjaya, having performed a sacrifice for his son, went to the Mahākāla forest, worshipped Śiva, and through His grace, [attained his goal]. Then, for the sake of victory, the gift of the kingdom was bestowed upon Karabheśvara.

The description of the means for bringing happiness and protection to the people from the fear of drought and other calamities; the description of the lineage of the lords of the royal lineages... Then follows the glorification of the majesty of Vaṭeśvara: therein, the departure of Maṇibhadra, known as Vaḍaṭa, with his wife to sport [in the forest]; there, the battle of Vaḍaṭa with the Rākṣasas who were guardians of the Kroḍavana forest; therein, the defeat of the Rākṣasas; and then, [the account] of one enraged by the actions of his own son.

The granting of a curse by the yakṣa Maṇibhadra to Vaḍala; Vaḍala’s journey to the Mahākālavana forest for the sake of removing that curse; a description of his attainment of liberation there; and a description of the necessity of visiting the Vaḍaleśvara shrine.

The subjects [of this work] include: a detailed description of Aruṇa, the son of Vinatā born from the egg, who, having gone to Mahākālavana at the instruction of Nārada, attained the greatness of Aruṇeśvara through the worship of Śiva; then, a description of the majesty of Puṣpadanta-īśvara, wherein a Brahmin named Śini, desiring to obtain a son, performed the propitiation of Lord Īśvara, and by His grace, a son named Puṣpadanta was born to him; and further, [the account of] Puṣpadanta in the Mahākālavana.

The installation of the Śiva-liṅga; the description of the greatness of the Puṣpadanta-liṅga at Avimukta. Then, the arrival at the sacred site of Avimukta at the word of King Citrasena’s daughter; the description of his attainment of liberation through the worship of the Śivaliṅga there; and the description of the greatness of the Avimukteśvara-liṅga. Next, the description of the greatness of the Hanumatkedāra-liṅga; therein, preceded by the description of the Hanumat-rākhī festival, the description of Hanumān’s attainment of boons through the worship of the directions.

(Vaśada) Now follows the description of the majesty of the *liṅga* of Viśveśvara, including how Kapila propitiated Śiva and obtained the boon of invincibility (*avadhyatva*), as well as how King Cilva propitiated Viṣṇu and made a request for a boon, saying, "Act in such a way that Kapila will say to me, 'I am afraid of you,'" and so forth; and how Viṣṇu, having said "So be it," granted the boon, and then Viṣṇu's own request to Kapila in order to make his own gift of the boon true.

In the context of the conversation between Unamejaya and Vāyana, during the time of the forest exile when the Pāṇḍavas had gone forth on their journey, there is the description of the regions of the Vindhya mountains; the description of the battle of Kṛṣṇa with Kapila, who disregarded his own words; the defeat of Kṛṣṇa therein; then, by the command of Śakra, King Bilva’s propitiation of Viśveśvara and the making of a verbal agreement through the mouth of Kapila, saying, "I am afraid of you"; and the description of the majesty of Vilveśvara.

The description of the attainment of the Dadhīra-tīrtha, preceded by the narration of the story of his own previous birth; the handing over of Dadhīra to Parīkṣit from afar; the cessation of Dadhīra’s suffering through the worship of Uttareśvara; the description of the majesty of the pilgrimage to Uttareśvara; and the concluding description of the majesty of the Caturaśīti-liṅga. Thus ends the second [chapter] on the majesty of the eighty-four liṅgas in the Āvantya-khaṇḍa. Va. The performance of penance; the granting of a boon to Vyāsa by that supreme Lord through the satisfaction of that penance; the composition of the Narmadā-stotra by Vyāsa; and the installation of a Liṅga of Śiva on the bank of the Narmadā by Vyāsa.

The description of the greatness of the confluence of the Eraṇḍī at Vyāsatīrtha, including the fruits of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites there; the grief caused by Anaṣūyā and her husband due to their childlessness; the arrival of the gods, beginning with Brahmā; the granting of a boon to Anaṣūyā by the gods for the attainment of sons; then the narration of the account of Anaṣūyā’s three sons named Durbasoda, Datta, and Soma; and subsequently, in connection with the description of the greatness of that holy place, the story of the sage named Govinda who was tormented by grief for his son.

The description of the narrative; therein, the description of his attaining a state of radiance while lying on that very ground; then, his wife’s departure for the purpose of bathing at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī; their liberation from suffering there through the giving of cows, land, gold, and other gifts; the description of Anasūyā’s asceticism upon hearing [the account] of Govinda; and the description of the majesty of the Eraṇḍī confluence. Oṃ. The arrival of Anasūyā at the Eraṇḍī confluence situated on the bank of the Narmadā to perform penance; and at the conclusion of her penance, the description of the greatness of the three [confluences].

The description of the majesty of Prabhāsa-tīrtha; the description of the majesty of Nāgeśvara-tīrtha; the description of the majesty of Mārkaṇḍeyeśa established by Mārkaṇḍeya; the description of the majesty of Saṃkarṣaṇa-tīrtha; and the description of the majesty of Manmadeśvara.

The battle between the gods and the demons; Indra’s journey to the banks of the Narmadā to perform penance after being overcome by the sin of Brahman-slaughter upon slaying Vṛtra; the arrival of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara there at the conclusion of his penance; the establishment of the three worlds by Indra according to their command; and a description of the greatness of Indratīrtha.
The description of the greatness of the Kahoḍītīrtha.

The journey of the Dānava named Kaṃlu to the banks of the Narmadā for the sake of penance; the granting of a boon to him by Karṇikāra, who was pleased by the power of that penance; the establishment of a Śivaliṅga by Kaṃlu; and the description of the majesty of the Kevalakṣetra-tīrtha, followed by the description of the majesty of the Suvarṇasikhā-tīrtha, the Karañja-tīrtha, and the Kāmarada-tīrtha.

The description of the greatness of Bhaṇḍārī Tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Rohiṇī Tīrtha preceded by the account of Rohiṇī’s performance of penance; the description of the greatness of Cakra Tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Dhautapāpa Tīrtha; in connection with Skanda Tīrtha, the narration of the story of Skanda’s birth; the installation of Skanda as the commander-in-chief (senāpati); the establishment of Śiva’s linga by Skanda; and the description of the greatness of Skanda Tīrtha.

The description of the greatness of Aśnira-satīrtha; the description of the greatness of Koṭitīrtha; the description of the greatness of Ayolani-sabhavatīrtha; the description of the greatness of Aṅgāraka-tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Pāṇḍu-tīrtha. [...]

The description of the greatness of Trilecana-tīrtha; the establishment of the image of Śiva by Bharata after he had performed penance with Soma; the description of the greatness of Somatīrtha and Candrahāsa-tīrtha; the description of the creation of the sixty [divisions] fashioned by Jahnu; the description of the establishment of the four castes; the terrifying sight of Yama mounted upon a buffalo created out of fear by a Brahmin who had heard the words "Kill! from one well-versed in good conduct; the granting of a boon to Indra through the praise of the Śatarudriya hymn; [and] the section concerning Yama.

The description of Mavavarṇana; the establishment of Kohanasvin; the description of the majesty of the Kohanasva-tīrtha; the description of the majesty of the Karmadeśvara-tīrtha; the description of the majesty of the Dhanmadeśvara-tīrtha; the explanation of the causes for the acquisition of the two names of the Sun, namely Āditya and Bhāskara; the description of the penance of Raviṅkata; the establishment of Śivari by Ravi; the description of the majesty of Ravitīrtha; and the description of the majesty of Ayoniprabhava-tīrtha.

(1) Description of the majesty of Annitīrtha; (2) Description of the majesty of Śarakuṭeśvaratīrtha; (3) Description of the majesty of Brahmatīrtha; (4) Description of the majesty of Devatīrtha; (5) In the narration of the origin of Nāgatīrtha, the account of the conflict between Vinatā and Kadrū and their subsequent union; (6) Description of the majesty of Naṇedavara Tīrtha; (7) Description of the majesty of Ādivārāha Tīrtha.

The description of the propitiation of Īśvara by the four Cakrapāṇis and the subsequent attainment of their desired boons; the installation of the Śivaliṅgas by the four world-protectors (Lokapālas); the narration of the majesty of the four Liṅgas beginning with Kavera; the description of the majesty of the Rāmeśvara Tīrtha; the description of the majesty of Siddheśvara; and the pronouncement of a curse upon Indra by Gautama for his illicit union with Aditi.

The liberation from the curse of Adilyā, who had been struck by Rāma with his foot; the removal of the sin of adultery committed by Ahalyā; a description of the greatness of the Ahalyeśvara Tīrtha; a description of the majesty of Karakakeṭeśvara;

Śakra performing penance for the sake of removing the curse given by Gautama and the installation of a Śiva-liṅga; a description of the greatness of Rakrekavara Tīrtha; a description of the greatness of Soma Tīrtha; and a description of the greatness of Laṃtāpiśvara Tīrtha.

...in the context of describing the majesty of Rukmiṇī-tīrtha: the narration of the account of Rukmiṇī’s marriage to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; therein, the description of the occasion for the battle between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the Magadhas and others; the description of the defeat of Rukmin brought about by Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the description of the ritual of the wedding of Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa; the description of the majesty of Rukmiṇī-tīrtha established by Rukmiṇī; and the description of the majesty of Yojanekṣaṇa-tīrtha.

(1) Description of the greatness of Dvādaśī; (2) Description of the greatness of Sītīrtha; (3) Detailed description of various rites such as bathing, giving gifts, recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), and the ancestral *śrāddha* and *ṛṣotsarga* performed at this Akṣayatīrtha; (4) Description of the greatness of the Sibdeśvara Tīrtha; (5) Description of the greatness of Maṅgalēśvaratīrtha; (6) Description of the greatness of Īśagavārāhatīrtha; (7) When Kāma was reduced to ashes by Śaṅkara, the gods offered a hymn of praise to obtain his restoration, and [the account of] the reconstitution of Anaṅga’s limbs.

The instrument; the performance of penance by Kāmadeva and the installation of Śiva; the description of the majesty of the Liṅga of Nāgeśvara; Chapter [number], page [number]; the subject matter: the description of the majesty of Ujjayinī-Vārāha-tīrtha; the description of the majesty of Bhārgaveśvara-tīrtha... [and so on].

Description of the majesty of Ādityeśvara Tīrtha; description of the majesty of Kalkaleśvara Tīrtha; the narrative of Cāṇakya, who was abandoned by two crows, during the account of the origin of Śuklatīrtha; Cāṇakya’s abandonment of crookedness (kauṭilya); description of the account of Cāṇakya’s attainment of perfection; description of the majesty of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at Śuklatīrtha; description of the majesty of Hakārasvāmin Tīrtha; description of the majesty of Saṅgameśvara Tīrtha; and description of the majesty of Anarakeda Tīrtha.

A description of the ripening of karma; a description of the stages of existence in the womb; a description of the greatness of the fruits of great gifts such as the gift of a cow and others; the greatness of offering lamps and other oblations to Yama on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina; a description of the greatness of the Anarakedvara Tīrtha; a description of the greatness of Mokṣatīrtha; a description of the greatness of Sapetīrtha; a description of the greatness of Gopeśvaratīrtha; a description of the greatness of Nāgatīrtha; and a description of the greatness of Sāvaireśvaratīrtha.

And [there is] the description of Caṇḍaka; the obtaining of boons by Rāvaṇa and others after performing penance from Śiva; the establishment of the Tera-kūra-da-varaṅga; the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Akr̥śvara-tīrtha; and, in the context of the story of Māṇḍavya’s impalement on a stake, the abduction of the daughter named Kāmapramodinī by King Devapanna—who had become a youth through the worship of Īśvara—by Śambara assuming the form of a hawk; and [the grief] of the princess named Kāmapramodinī caused by her abduction, as recounted by her friends.

The description of that oil-presser; O King, having heard what was reported by him, the king’s dispatching of his ministers and others to investigate the matter; the discovery of the royal lady’s ornaments at Māṇḍavya’s hermitage and the subsequent reporting of those events to the king; and then, by the king’s command, the description of Māṇḍavya’s impalement upon the stake.

Oṃ. The arrival of the sages at the sight of Māṇḍavya impaled on a stake; the description of the king’s curse and the subsequent livelihood of Aṣoṇā; then, the description by the great sage Māṇḍavya to the ṛṣis of the ripening of his karma; the departure of the sages to their own hermitage at the command of Māṇḍavya; and there, when Śāṇḍilya arrived with a sick man resting on his wife's shoulder, the husband’s staff happened to touch the foot of the Śūdra woman as she was unaware of it while walking along her path.

The conversation between Māṇḍavya, who was terrified because the staff of his trident shook due to the blow from another's foot, and the wife of Śāṇḍilya; their mutual cursing of one another; the return of the celestial sages (*devarṣi*) to Māṇḍavya’s hermitage; and their discourse.

The bringing of the patched garment (kanthā) by Devapanna-rāja; the description of the reasoning [behind] the curse of Māṇḍavya; the liberation from bondage of the Sun, who had been obstructed by the power of her own wifely fidelity (pativratā), by that Brahmin’s wife; the description of the restoration of life to Śāṇḍilya; the description of the greatness of bathing, giving, and other rites at Māṇḍavya-tīrtha; and the description of the greatness of Śaddheśvara-tīrtha.

— Description of the majesty of Gopīcandra Tīrtha; description of the majesty of Kapiḍeśvara Tīrtha, which was established by Kapila after he had performed austerities on the banks of the Narmadā for the sake of redeeming the sons of Sagara; description of the majesty of Kapiḍeśvara Tīrtha. Description of the majesty of Pigaḍeśvara Tīrtha.

Description of the majesty of Eraṇḍī Tīrtha. Description of the majesty of the excellent Kālāmṛta Tīrtha, including Garuḍa’s offering of praise to Cāmuṇḍā, the propitiation of Cāmuṇḍā by Garuḍa, and Garuḍa’s establishment of the Carāga [temple] at Kanakhala. Description of the majesty of the excellent Kālāmṛta Tīrtha. Va. (End of section).

[An account of] the interruption of the penance of Nara and Nārāyaṇa by an Apsaras and others.

Triśaṅku, desiring to ascend to heaven in his own physical body, made a request to Vasiṣṭha; [the narrative describes] how Triśaṅku, having performed austerities together with the peaceful Bhāryā for the sake of dispelling his severe diseases by means of the sun-god Bhānumarvīkāmu, caused the Gaṅgā to descend from the sky by uprooting the quarters, and how, at the command of Śiva, he established the deity named Vimaḍeśvara—explaining how Triraṅka attained the state of a Caṇḍāla—and the glorification of the Vimaḍeśvara Tīrtha through the narration of that episode. ...
When Vasiṣṭha stated that this was impossible, he harbored a stubborn resolve in his mind to question another teacher.

A description of the ritual for pilgrimage (*yātrā-vidhi*) to all the sacred sites (*tīrtha*) situated on the banks of the [river], in their proper sequence; specifically, regarding the sage Vasiṣṭha’s son Śirīka, who—disregarding the words of Vasiṣṭha—was intent on acting according to his own will at Durāmrada, followed by a description of his greatness; the bestowal of the curse, "Become an outcaste" (*caṇḍāla*); how, by that very means, he immediately attained the state of an outcaste and subsequently performed a pilgrimage to other sacred sites out of remorse, along with an account of the merit and power thereof. Na. Ā.

The departure of Triśaṅku, whose face was fierce, to the forest; the journey of Viśvāmitra with him; then, by Vidura, the enumeration of the number of holy fords (*tīrtha*), followed by a description of the sequence of the pilgrimage preceded by an account of the arrangement of all the holy fords. Having heard that account, Śatānanda made a vow, saying, "I shall lead you to heaven in this very body," and then the description of the fruit of giving the *Revākhaṇḍa* manuscript, preceded by the conclusion of the *Revākhaṇḍa*. ...
