And as they wandered together with that Caṇḍāla to various holy fords and shrines for the sake of dispelling his sin, this was the third section, the Revākhaṇḍa, within the Āvantyakhaṇḍa.

(—) The dialogue with Kaṇḍeya; the journey to Hāṭakeśvara at the word of Mārkaṇḍeya; the liberation of Triśaṅku from his state as a Caṇḍāla through the worship of the Hāṭakeśvara-liṅga; thereafter, the acceptance of the permission for them to perform the sacrifice that grants the attainment of heaven. ... Thus ends the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. 9.

Even though Brahmā had not granted permission for such an act to be performed, Viśvāmitra, through the power of his own asceticism, completed the twelve-year sacrifice—which had been interrupted by Indra—by means of a Brāhmaṇa; then, at the conclusion, he performed the ritual ablutions and other rites to bring the sacrifice to its completion.
Now, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, the sixth section, the Nāgara-khaṇḍa.

The departure for heaven by Vidurāmiśra after praising and receiving a boon from Śiva due to the absence of his own attainment of heaven; the commencement of the dialogue between Sūta and Nārada; there, having heard the praise of Śvetadvīpa, Vidurāmiśra composed the *Naraka-svarga* (Heaven of Naraka) to provide an answer to him and departed for heaven with his physical body.

In the context of Sūta’s description of the origin of the *Ṛgveda*, there is an account of Śiva, separated from his consort, going to the hermitage of the sages. Having seen the mutual dispute between Virabhadra and Brahmā, the gods approached Brahmā; thereafter, seeing the sky-clad [Śiva] in the heavens, they pronounced a curse upon him. Due to that curse, Śiva departed from that very place. Then, for the sake of maintaining the stability of the world, Brahmā and the others went into the presence of Virabhadra. [End of fragment] Virabhadra—ka—

The objects of the *Caraka* school: by virtue of the scriptural statement, because there is no other recourse, Triśaṅku’s departure to heaven; the voluntary return of Vidūratha’s son from his newly acquired kingdom; and the conclusion of the narrative of Triśaṅku.

Having heard of the splendor of Hāṭakeśvara, all people went there; even Vidurāmitra abandoned his own home and took up residence right there. Thinking that this Kṣatriya lineage was intent on liberation even without performing sacrifices and other rites, he established [the deity] at the foot of the Hāṭakeśvara mountain by the command of the Lord. Because of that, even the Nāgas traveled everywhere by means of its splendor. In the description of the majesty of Hāṭakeśvara, it is told how the daughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu, named Ramā, for the sake of obtaining a husband, [performed penance] directed toward Viṣṇu.

The performance of austerities; thereafter, the birth of the demon Vṛtra from the drops of Viṣṇu’s perspiration; the departure of Dadhīci before Indra and the other gods to obtain his bones for the purpose of creating the thunderbolt at Viṣṇu’s request for the sake of slaying Vṛtra; the defeat of Vṛtra by the thunderbolt fashioned from Dadhīci’s bones; Śakra’s journey to Hāṭakeśvara to expiate the sin of *brahmahatyā* (killing a Brahmin) arising therefrom; and, at the command of Śakra, Saṃvartanīru’s dispatch to the serpent-hole (*nāgabila*) by Indra, followed by Saṃvartanīru’s departure to the serpent-hole at Śakra’s command.

The return of Saṃvarta, who had been terrified by the curse of Chigoddhava, to the city of Śakra; then, at the command of Bṛhaspati, Śakra’s departure to the presence of Himākhya in order to dispatch his sons for the purpose of performing the *vikhapūṣi* rite; and seeing that his three sons—named Bhena, Kanakandivardhana, and Raktaśrava—refused to accept the command despite being ordered by Himākhya to carry out Śakra’s business, Śakra’s pronouncement of a curse upon them.

Out of fear of a curse, he went there for the purpose of making the mountain named Raktaśṛṅga foul-smelling with serpents; thereafter, Devendra established numerous holy bathing places (tīrthas) that produce happiness on that mountain named Raktaśṛṅga, followed by a description of Indra’s encouragement of the peak of Raktaśṛṅga.

(The description of the greatness of Śaṅkhatīrtha: Camatkāradarpa’s hunting; the killing of the deer through the wonder of the doe who was giving her breast to the arrow struck by him; the attainment of leprosy by Camatkāradarpa due to the curse given by the doe; the journey to Śaṅkhatīrtha for the sake of removing that suffering and the curse; the description of the removal of the leprosy of Camatkāradarpa through bathing at Śaṅkhatīrtha; and the description of the majesty of Śaṅkhatīrtha.)

The cessation of faults through the worship of Hāṭakeśvara; the return to one's own abode; the description of the majesty of Hāṭakeśvara; and the account of the origin of Śaṅkhatīrtha in the dialogue between King Camatkāra and the sage.

Having perceived that the mark of the conch was drawn by the dust raised by the bull of Śikhita’s hermitage, and thinking it to be an act of theft, Śikhita caused the hand of Śaṅkha to be cut off. Thereafter, Śaṅkha performed penance at Hāṭakeśvara; pleased by his asceticism, Śiva granted a boon to Śaṅkha. When he related how his hand had been restored through the power of his former penance, Śiva established a Liṅga there under his own name. Following a description of the origin of Śaṅkhatīrtha, the majesty of Śaṅkhatīrtha is described.

King Camatkāra, having caused a city to be built for the Brahmins, established the foundations of the city and gave instructions regarding his sons at the command of the Brahmins. Receiving the blessing of Brahmadatta, he entrusted his kingdom to his sons and went to the temple of Oṭakeśvara to perform penance. There, having propitiated Śiva, he established a linga named Acadeśvara by the grace of Śiva.

Regarding the majesty of Acaṅeśvara: in the city of Camatkārapura, a certain cowherd’s one cow from his herd went into the forest out of a desire for grass. While the cow was being searched for, the cowherd also went into the forest. Then, after some time, both attained the state of being a *paśu* (a beast). Thereafter, the description of the cowherd’s birth in the family of a lord of thieves (*dāṇādhipati*) is given, as well as the cow’s birth in the family of a virtuous-minded person. Then, having recollected the events of their previous births, [they...]

The attainment of liberation via the path of the Taimānika through the performance of the *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) at Camatkārapura; a description of the greatness of the *dakṣiṇā* at Camatkārapura; a unique description of the excellence of the greatness of the *dakṣiṇā* at Camatkārapura, preceded by a description of the power of Raktasṛṅga; a description of the fruits and supreme benefits of serving Raktasṛṅga while standing upon the crest of the Red Coral Mountain (*raktamarakataśikhara*); a description of the fourteen holy sites (*tīrtha*) situated there in Camatkārapura, beginning first with the greatness of Gayāśiras.

In the course of the description, Vidūratha went into the forest on a hunt; while pursuing a deer there, Vidūratha’s horse, exhausted from galloping through the woods, fell to the ground. Then, leaving the horse right where it was, Vidūratha proceeded on foot after the deer. (Note: The final phrase "ka ga śane na" appears to be a scribal corruption or a non-standard notation and has not been translated.)

Then, after crossing the Kakkara, Kaka, and Daka rivers, and traveling further along the path, there occurs the description of the three Piśācas, Māṃsāda and the others. Following the account of Māṃsāda and the rest, [the narrative describes] King Vidūratha’s arrival at the hermitage (āśramapada) and his conversation with the sages, followed by the performance of the evening rites and the offering of the Śrāddha to Māṃsāda and the others. Then follows the departure of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā for the Pivṛkapikā-tīrtha; and there, by means of performing the Śrāddha—

The departure of Vidūratha from the hermitage of the sage Khaṇḍika despite the presence of Rāma and others; the narration by Vidūratha in a dream of his own liberation at the well of the sacred site of Gayā and other holy places; the description of Khara’s treachery and deceit as he set his mind upon killing Rāma and Sītā; the description of the Jāṭhayaṅgī Tīrtha; and the account of Mārkaṇḍeya’s birth, followed by Mārkaṇḍeya’s discourse on the greatness of the twelve sacred sites (dvādaśatīrtha) for the sake of long life.

Having reached Hāṭakeśvara and performed austerities, there is a description of the installation of the Liṅga. Then follows the account of Vāḍha-maṇḍana-tīrtha: how Diti, having been cursed by Śakra, went to Vāḍha-maṇḍana-tīrtha; how her fault was removed by bathing in that tīrtha; and how she subsequently set out toward the southern direction to the abode of Rāma. Having entered his belly, she gave birth to her sons by means of a saw (śastreṇa), and because of that, she wept with a broken heart.

For the sake of removing that fault, Śakra performed a rite of knowledge (*jñānakaraṇa*) at the Maṇḍana-tīrtha; through this pilgrimage to the tīrtha, Śakra’s fault was eliminated. This is the description of the majesty of Maṇḍana-tīrtha. In the description of Mṛga-tīrtha: hunters arrived there while deer were resting in the shade of a certain tree. Upon seeing the hunters, the deer fled from that place. The hunters pursued the deer, who immediately reached a lake by way of a hidden path.

The transgression against the human state; the bathing in that lake by hunters under the pretext of deer-faced women due to the power of that lake; the description of the greatness of the *mṛgatīrtha* (deer-ford) which led even the Cāṇḍālas to attain [liberation]; the description of how all of them attained liberation; and at the time of the secret union with the river, Vāmana, having covered the worlds with two steps, [took] the third step...

In the section on the divisions of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), [it describes] how, when the skull of a certain Brāhmaṇa was split by the messengers of Yama who had arrived from the abode of Yama, there followed the emergence of the Gaṅgā from his matted hair; then the greatness of the Viṣṇupada-tīrtha, including its origin and history; and the description of the greatness of the Gaṅgā at Viṣṇupada, wherein the removal of the sin of liquor consumption through the bathing therein of a certain Brāhmaṇa who was offering prayers for the cessation of that intoxication is recounted. This is the description of the greatness of the Gaṅgā at Viṣṇupada.

The description of the journey to the realm of Yama together with those who are negligent; therein, the inquiry by Yama as to which sin leads one to which hell; the departure of Gokarṇa for Camatkārapura by the permission of Yama; the description of liberation through bathing at the holy ford (tīrtha) there; the enumeration of the four ages beginning with Gokarṇa; the demonstration of the nature and magnitude of the four ages; the definition of the four-fold duties (cāturyyakarma); and specifically, the description of the origin of the Caṇḍālas, including washermen and others.

Description of the majesty of Kaḍikāra. In the dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Indra, a description of taking refuge in all sacred fords (*tīrthas*). When [the son] was established, at the command of his father Sūta, the great sage Vatsa performed the *śukrākaraṇa* rite. Therein, the great sage Vatsa recounts the history of his own previous birth: Devarāta, desiring to bathe in the Sanerāmra, beheld a certain woman and discharged his semen into the water; from that semen, a fetus was conceived; at the end of ten months, a daughter was born to Bharagīta.

Devarāta gave his daughter in marriage to Vatsa; after a long time had passed, the death of a friend occurred due to the bite of a serpent, and Vatsa set out for the forest. Although the sages offered him various consolations, he persisted in his grief over the snake-bite. While he was lamenting there, one serpent assumed a human form and engaged in conversation with him. As that being in human form explained to Vatsa the cause of the previous curse, [Vatsa said: "In my former birth, by me..."

Bha-nana-ki-da—ka----- --- -- -- - - -- Jyāḥ-na-a-savyaḥ. From the *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*: [The description of] the attainment of dharma through association with Īśa and others; then, the resolve in the mind of Vatsa, the sage, to perform the worship of Maheśvara due to his remorse for having killed a cow; the description of Vatsa’s attainment of perfection (*siddhi*) through the worship of Siddheśvara; and the account of the origin of Siddheśvara, wherein, at the command of Bṛhaspati, he established a linga named Putraparāpatya and performed its worship.

Upon the completion of that [account], there is a description of the majesty of Siddheśvara... then, in the course of describing the majesty of Nāgahada, the arrival of the nine nāgas at the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara by the command of Brahmā; their installation of a *liṅga* there under their own names; the description of King Indrasena’s death from the bite of a serpent; thereafter, his son’s arrival at his father’s funeral pyre and his account of how his father attained the state of a preta; and the son’s journey to the Nāgatīrtha at his father’s command, where—

The description of the father’s liberation through the performance of the ancestral *śrāddha* rites and the worship of the *liṅga*; the description of the Nāgatīrtha and the Saptarṣitīrtha along with the method for worshipping the seven sages (*saptarṣi*); the description of the origin of the Saptarṣitīrtha, including how the seven sages, being hungry during a twelve-year drought, wandered everywhere; their arrival in the kingdom of King Ṛṣabha; and how they made an effort to eat the newborn boy there in order to sustain themselves, at which point the sage Ṛṣabha appeared.

Having arrived there, he engaged in debate with them; then, without even consuming the food of the *sūpakumāra*, they went to the city of Camaṭakārapura, where they performed austerities and established a *ṭhiga*.

In the description of Agastya’s hermitage, when the Vindhya mountain and the earth were mutually competing, the sun’s path was obstructed; consequently, the sun went to Agastya’s hermitage. At the word of the sun, Agastya turned the mountain face downwards and proceeded toward Hāṭakeśvara in the southern direction. Having gone there with his wife Lopāmudrā, he established a linga. Regarding the greatness of Agastya’s hermitage (in the description of the reason for Agastya’s drinking of the ocean): first, during the battle between the gods and the Daityas, [the distress of] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the others...

The description of the defeat of the Daityas by Śaṅkara with the trident, including the determination that the defeat of the gods would surely result from the destruction of Dharma, the persecution of Brahmins—who perform sacrifices, yoga, and recitation—by the Daityas due to that very destruction, and the command of the Goddess (Jalabhrāyā) for the purpose of slaying those Daityas who dwell within her.

The account of Agastya’s departure to the western ocean; the drinking of the ocean by Agastya for the sake of the gods’ mission; the slaying of the Daityas by the gods; the description of the greatness of Citravarapīṭha—the seat established by Agastya which was made into his own body by the gods and named Citravarapīṭha; the description of the origin of the temple known as Duḥśīla; the description of the greatness of Dhundhumāreśvara Liṅga; ... [and] the description of the greatness of Yayātīśvara Liṅga.

The establishment of the stone slab by Brahmā on the broad [ground]; then, by the command of Brahmā, the arrival of Sarasvatī at that place for the purpose of bathing; then, after performing austerities there, the establishment of the *liṅga* by the great seer Maṅkaṇaka; and the description of the greatness (*māhātmya*) of Citraśikhā-maṅkaṇaka-īśvara-liṅga. ...;

The Daitya Bāṣkala, having oppressed Indra and the other gods, performed penance at Hāṭakeśvara under the command of Viṣṇu. Then, upon the advice of Bṛhaspati, on the day of Aśanyāśayana-tithi, he engaged in battle with Bāṣkali by the command of the Lord, after the Lord had been pleased by their worship. Having defeated the Daitya Bāṣkala, the Lord sent Śakra back to his own abode, took up residence there himself, and established the Ṛgveda; this is the description of the origin of Jalaśāyin.
The narration of the account of the origin of Viśvāmitra’s pool; therein, in the description of the meeting between Viśvāmitra and Menakā, Viśvāmitra’s exposition of the duties of women to Menakā.

Having disregarded the rules of chastity (*pātivratya-dharma*) as described by Viśvāmitra, when Menakā was deceived by Viśvāmitra regarding her questions such as "Where have you come from? and "Where are you going?", Viśvāmitra uttered a curse of reproach against their union. When their union was thus rejected by Viśvāmitra, Menakā, tormented by great sorrow, and Viśvāmitra mutually bestowed upon each other a curse consisting of the attainment of old age. Thereafter, [the story continues] with the biting of their ears (*kuṇḍalādana*).

The curse of Śakti; Viśvāmitra’s establishment of a sacrificial post there; [the episode of] Viśvāmitra and Kaṇva; the slaughter of the hundred sons of Viśvāmitra; the arrival of Nārada; [and] the departure of the sage.

In this description of the majesty of the Sarasvatī-tīrtha: the arrival of Ambuvīci—born from the bite of Balabhadra and afflicted with muteness—at the Sarasvatī-tīrtha for the sake of curing his son’s dumbness; there, through ritual bathing and the worship of Gaṇeśa, the removal of the son’s muteness; Ambuvīci’s hymn of praise to Sarasvatī; and the description of the majesty of the Sarasvatī-tīrtha.

In the description of the greatness of Mahākālavana: King Radrāsena, together with his wife, travels to Hāṭakedvara; having worshipped the Lord there and given many gifts to the brahmins, the king recounts the story of his own previous birth to the assembly of brahmins. Thereupon, that king, born of the merchant caste, who had fasted due to the lack of food and was accompanied by his wife, goes to Mahākālavana; there, he performs the worship of the Lord with skillful rites. By that—

Birth in a royal family through the power of merit; the greatness of the Umā-Maheśvara Liṅga at the Mahākūṭa and other excellent tīrthas; the worship of Umā-Maheśvara by Hariścandra for the sake of obtaining a son; the granting of a boon that bestows a son by Umā-Maheśvara, who were satisfied by his penance; Hariścandra’s departure for his own palace after receiving that boon; and then the installation of a Liṅga for the propitiation of Umā-Maheśvara in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara. Umā—

The description of the greatness of Maheśvara’s *Ṛgamāda*; the description of the greatness of Kaṭaśreṣṭha; the arrival of Dūrvāsas at the house of Kaṭadāpa; and the offering of food and other provisions by the sage to Dūrvāsas—who had come to perform the breaking of his Cāturmāsya vow—preceded by the rites of hospitality. There, seeing meat well-prepared with salt and other seasonings in the vessel of food, [Dūrvāsas said]: "Become a tiger!"

Thus ends the section on the curse and its removal. Herein is described the attainment of liberation from the tiger by the bull through a vow, following the dialogue between Nandinī and Vyāsa. In this account, Nandinī makes a solemn oath in the presence of the tiger; at the tiger’s word, Nandinī returns to her own place and causes the bull to perform a vow. Then all the cattle go before the tiger with Nandinī, and by that act, her truthfulness is established. Subsequently, the bull, having attained the state of a tiger due to the curse, seeks liberation from it through repentance and poses questions to her.

Description of the greatness of the Tripuṣkara-tīrtha through the worship of the Liṅga installed by Nandin after he was struck by an arrow; [Nandin’s] liberation from the curse that had caused him to become a tiger and his restoration to his former kingship; thereafter, having performed the propitiation of Hara, the installation of a Liṅga under his own name and his departure to the world of Śiva; description of the greatness of the Kaṭaroda Liṅga; ... description of the greatness of the Rudrakoṭi [Liṅga].

In this section concerning the description of the unborn embryo, there is an account of King Mitrasaha’s transformation into a Rākṣasa due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha; how that king, following the nature of a Rākṣasa, even killed Brāhmaṇas and others; how, by means of that [act], he was freed from the sin of Brāhmaṇa-slaughter after being released from the curse at the command of Vasiṣṭha by undertaking a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā); how, having been liberated from the sin of Brāhmaṇa-slaughter through bathing in those sacred fords, he resumed his former kingdom; and how, after his reign, he departed to the world of Śiva at the end.

And [therein is] a description of the greatness of Śraṇama; and a description of the greatness of Muṇḍā, preceded by a narrative concerning Nala and his nails, as well as a description of the greatness of the Neibara established by him under his own name, which wards off undesirable defects such as disease. In the Sāvāditya-māhātmya, [it describes] how Gākhva, having obtained a boon through the grace of Āditya, attained sons due to his lack of offspring by worshipping Sāṃbāditya, followed by a description of the greatness of Sāṃbāditya. ...

Description of the narrative of the pilgrimage to Gaṅgeya; description of the establishment of the four *chigas* performed by Gāṅgeya; description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Hivagāma... [and] the establishment of a Liṅga named after himself by Vidura after he had performed austerities for the sake of obtaining a son; description of the majesty of Vidureśvara; description of the account of the divine vision experienced by Vidura; and the establishment of the deity named Māhittha by the son of Mitra and Varuṇa; description of the majesty of Narādivyeśvara.

In the *Śarbhiṣṭhātīrthamāhātmya*, there is a description of the origin of the Poison-Maiden (*viṣakanyā*), and an account of how the sage met his death because he did not abandon her; furthermore, having heard the public censure in his own world, the Poison-Maiden’s departure for the forest to perform penance, the terrible asceticism—including the practice of the five fires—of the sorrowful Poison-Maiden who remembered her previous birth while on the road, and the arrival of Pārvatī in the form of Indrāṇī after she had observed her penance; and how, having received no boon from Indrāṇī, she once again engaged in austerity.

While [the sacrifice] was being performed, the chapters concerning the future subjects, beginning with the praise of Pārvatī by the daughter of the mountain; the departure for Kailāsa by the daughter of the mountain, accompanied by her friends; and the description of the Śarmiṣṭhā-tīrtha, etc.

The description of the greatness of Somanāthavarāha; the worship of Riga by Khoma, who was joined with a curse from Daśaśāpa, through the deception of Romaka Mahāreva; the manifestation of Soma’s curse through his own nature; the establishment of Riga under his own name; the description of the greatness of Somanātha-varāha. The description of the greatness of the goddess Dugodā, who causes wonder to the inhabitants of Camatkārapura. [Section] Ka, Ka. The description of the greatness of Ānaikeśvara and Dareśvara, and the narration of their origins. Ga, .

In the context of the description of Rāmahrada, there is the account of the slaughter of Jamadagni and the departure of [Paraśurāma] with his army. There, having witnessed the power of the *kāmadhenu*, when that cow was requested by the thousand-armed [Arjuna Kārtavīrya], Jamadagni, becoming enraged because she was not given away, was killed by the Daitya [Arjuna].

Having heard of his father’s death, Paraśurāma performed the funeral rites for his father and made a vow to rid the earth of the Kṣatriyas; thereafter, upon learning of Arjuna’s intent, Rāma slew the thousand-armed one.

After the slaughter of the thousand kings, Paraśurāma went to Hāṭakeśvara and performed the ancestral *śrāddha* rites with the blood flowing from the bodies of those thousand kings. Having thus pacified his ancestors, he bestowed the entire earth upon the Brāhmaṇas. Then, for the sake of his own dwelling, Paraśurāma caused the ocean to recede. Furthermore, having forcibly slain the Kṣatriyas who had seized the earth from the Brāhmaṇas, he cleared the world of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times and gave it back to the Brāhmaṇas.

The establishment of the holy site named Rāmahradā, which was reached by Ādibodha through the recitation of the *Jrādyaṇa* mantra; the description of the special fruit obtained through the *śrāddha* for those killed by Rākṣasas; a general account of the killing of the demon Tāraka, including the narrative of the origin of Kārttikeya; and the description of the majesty of the spear (*śakti*) established by Kārttikeya (Skanda).

Then follows the description of the installation of the deity Hāṭakeśvara by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others; subsequently, the account of Duryodhana’s marriage to Bhānumatī in Dvāravatī; then the journey of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas together with Vidura to Hāṭakeśvara; and the narration of events such as the construction of palaces by Dhṛtarāṣṭra; and therein, at Hāṭakeśvara, the installation of one hundred and one Liṅgas by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others.

The establishment of the *liṅgas* by the Pāṇḍavas, such as Savyadroṇa, and by the Yādavas, each according to their own individual names; the description of the installation of the Kauravas, Pāṇḍavas, and Yādavas; the description of the majesty of the sacrificial ground (*yajñabhūmi*); and the description of the triad of Tīrthas—Muṇḍīra, Kāṅpriyamūla, and Itibhāskara—at which site the story is told of a certain leper who, at the word of a Brāhmaṇa, was cured of his leprosy by bathing in those three Tīrthas. [The text continues with] Muṇḍīrakāṅpriyamūla...

Description of the greatness of the sacred site; at the time of the marriage of Hara and Pārvatī, the emission of Brahmā’s seed upon seeing Pārvatī; the removal of that sin by Brahmā through the propitiation of R̥dr̥śiras; description of the greatness of Harāśrayavedikā and the greatness of R̥dr̥kapiśa; the description of the removal of the sin of a certain Brāhmaṇa woman who was unchaste through the worship of Rudrī; and the description of how the queen of King Vidūratha likewise attained liberation through the grace of Rudrī.

Description of the majesty of Śudraśīrṣa (Jāgeśvara); description of the majesty of Vāṅkhilyāśrama; narration of the account of the Vāṅkhiilyas’ display of anger toward Śakra; the majesty of Vāṅkhilyāśrama; in the description of the majesty of Suparṇa: the giving of the vessel of ambrosia by Kaśyapa to his wife for the sake of obtaining [the nectar], after it had been consecrated with Atharvanic and Maitra mantras by the Vāṅkhiilyas; and the birth of Aruṇa from Kaśyapa through the consumption of that vessel of ambrosia.

The departure of Garuḍa with the two Nāga maidens for the purpose of choosing a bridegroom for the Brāhmaṇa’s daughter Mitrā; their meeting with Nārada on the way; the journey of them all to Hāṭakeśvara together with Nārada for the sake of seeing Viṣṇu; having gone there, the obtaining of an audience with Viṣṇu by Nārada and Garuḍa; and after receiving the audience from Viṣṇu, Garuḍa’s making a formal request to Viṣṇu for the hand of the daughter of the King of Mountains (Himavat) as a bridegroom.

The battle; indeed, seeing the emergence from a single pit of deities such as Rajavakra and Ashvamukhi, Garuda’s consumption of the sacrificial oblation; the bringing of the Brahmin together with his daughter to Vishnu’s side; for the sake of preventing the Brahmin girl from sitting upon Vishnu’s lap, the establishment of a rule by those two [Vishnu and Garuda] regarding the objects to be avoided by them; and having seen that the happiness was attained, the telling of the story and the pronouncing of a curse upon that girl, saying, "Become horse-faced."

Then, by his own command, the establishment of the image of Hāṭakeśvara; the description of the greatness of Ambābaddhā; likewise, the granting of a curse by Vipra, saying, "Become crooked-faced"; then, at the command of Ambābaddhā, Viṣṇu’s making of a mark on the daughter of King Camatkāra for the purpose of severing the influence of those deities who were causing harm to the Brahmins; and, by the order of Viṣṇu, the sending of the Brahmin along with his son to his own home by the goddess Ambābaddhā.

The act of placing his own sandals; the removal of the suffering of people through the gift of sandals; when Garuḍa laughed at Śāṇḍilī, who was standing before Viṣṇu and was bound by a curse, the Lord entered within her; the description of the Gaṅgā-tīrtha where the sandals were worshipped; the reduction of Garuḍa to ashes by the mental bestowal of a curse upon him by Saṃkarṣaṇa while he was performing meditation; the birth of a girl from the second ray of light; and the restoration of the body through the worship of the sandals according to the word of Śaṃkara.
The attainment of all perfections by Śāṇḍilī; the vision of Garuḍa and Viṣṇu; then the narration of the words of Śāṇḍilī;

the description of the greatness of the sandals (pādukā-māhātmya); Garuḍa’s journey to Hāṭakeśvara, his bowing to Sadāśiva, Kālabhairava, Nīlarudra, and others, and his performance of the worship of Śiva; the description of the greatness of the Bahiṣtīrtha; the younger brother Śantanu’s undertaking of a vow after his elder brother had died; and the description of Garuḍa’s golden wings once again.

The reviving of Saṃjñī; the granting of boons by the gods to that devoted wife for her steadfastness; the cursing of Śākalya Gaṅga by Yājñavalkya—who was enraged by his violation of his own command—with a curse that he should fall from heaven; the bestowing of a curse upon Yama by Māṇḍavya, which caused him to enter a Śūdra womb; the description of the birth of Dīkṣāgara; the offering of knowledge to that sage and his subsequent performance of sun-worship to acquire that knowledge; and then, by the Sun...

The narration of the cause of Māṇḍavya’s arrival at the tip of the stake... the bestowing of the knowledge of the *khādhima* upon Yājñavalkya; [how] she, having become a goat, took refuge near Sūrya’s ear and performed penance for the sake of removing Māṇḍavya’s curse regarding the King of Dharma (*Dharmarāja*); and the description of the origin of Dharmarājeśvara.

The recitation of the Vedas by Yājñavalkya, who had gone forth from the Sūryavaṃśa; the description of his grief following the death of his five-year-old son, the Brahmin named Upādhyāya, born of the Kadaca family; the composition of the ten Upaniṣads on the meaning of the Vedas by Yājñavalkya; and then, out of anger, the Brahmin’s bestowing of a curse upon Yama at Hāṭakeśvara in his own name; and the arrival of the cursed Yama before Brahmā.

A description of the greatness of the Yājñavalkyāśrama-tīrtha; the departure of Yama for Hāṭakeśvara to avoid the curse resulting from the words of Brahmā; then, by Yama assuming the form of a twice-born and describing the greatness of the Ṭiga-tīrtha which bestows sweet food, the story of the king named Vasusena who attained heaven through the performance of many gifts, followed by a description of his subsequent state of hunger; when Vasusena, afflicted by that hunger, questioned Indra, Nārada arrived there at that very moment.

Having seen him, Nārada related the entire account to him and delivered his father’s command and message to Satyasena, the son of Vasusena, instructing him to perform the daily offering of food and other rites for his father’s *śrāddha* and so forth. Upon hearing his father’s message through Nārada, Satyasena offered food to his father. Due to a drought and the resulting lack of food, Satyasena performed the worship of Śiva. Pleased by that worship, Śiva granted him whatever food and other desired things he wished for. Then—

Satyasena, under the name Miṣānnadeśvara, arrived there at Jābāli’s command in order to create an obstacle to Jābāli’s asceticism; there, Rambhā, having agitated the mind of Jābāli, sported with him in his third birth.

(Jābāli’s seeing his own daughter born from Raṃbhā and raising her; when Kumāravatī, Jābāli’s daughter, had reached youth, her departure for another Gandharva, Citrasena; the Gandharva taking that daughter of Jābāli and going to Devamandira; then, while searching for his daughter, Jābāli finding his own daughter at Devamandira and the beating of the Gandharva by Śvāḍa, as well as [the punishment] for the Gandharva. Taking that daughter of Jābāli, the Gandharva went to Devamandira. Then, while searching for his daughter, Jābāli found his own daughter at Devamandira and, with Śvāḍa, beat that Gandharva and [inflicted punishment] upon the Gandharva.

The bestowal of the curse; the performance of penance by the Gandharva for the sake of the cessation of the curse and the removal of that curse; the establishment of a Liṅga; the performance of penance by a Jābālinī named Phaladhavatī for the purpose of destroying the curse; when a dialogue in the form of a counter-response arose with that maiden who had attained a divine state through that penance, the refutation of her father Jābāli by that maiden; [the account] in the Citrāṅgada of Jābālīśvara. (Aḥ Bha Ka Sa Da Va Pi Ya)

Who is not established in the directions? The narration of the greatness of Miṣṭānnadeveśvara; the description of the majesty of the triad of Gaṇapatis. [The subjects of the Bhavyā chapter: Having gone to the house of a Brāhmaṇa, the giving of [the fruit] to his son by Dharmarāja; the installation of a Śiva-liṅga by Dharmarāja; in the description of the majesty of Amarareśvara, the defeat of the gods caused by the Daityas and the performance of worship to Ādityeśvara; the description of the narrative of the majesty of Rajeśvara.

...—the description of the defeat of the Daityas in the battle between the gods and the Daityas through such divine grace; the description of the narrative of the son of Dharmarāja because it bestows immortality; the naming of Śiva as Amareśvara; the description of the majesty of the Amareśvara-liṅga; the description of the manifestation of Amareśvara; the description of the names of Āditya, Vasu, Rudra, and others; the *Māhātmya* (glory) of the Amareśvara-kuṇḍa; the description of the birth of Vyāsa; and the description of the dialogue between Vyāsa and Luṣa.

... due to the separation from the letter of Śukācārya, his mother, suffering with grief, worshipped Śiva for the sake of obtaining a second son by means of another pill (*vaṭikā*) named Pigarā; she established a shrine in her own name as Vaṭikā, and there follows a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Vaṭikeśvara. ... * * * ...

In the description of the birth of Keliśvaśra: the birth of the Asura Andhaka from Hiraṇyakaśipu; the description of his attainment of the kingdom; then, after performing penance for sixty thousand years, Andhaka’s acceptance of a boon from Brahmā; and by means of that boon granted by Brahmā, the intoxicated Andhaka, having conquered the gods including Indra and even Śambhu, engaged in battle with the Goddess—who had arisen from the sacrificial fire-pit fashioned by Śambhu—along with her retinue.

— The description of the defeat of his own Daitya army; when Śukra, having been entreated by Andhaka, performed the invocation of the fire through Vāthavaṇika mantras as if for Śambhu himself; the description of the birth of Kelīśvarī; then, Andhaka having obtained a boon from that Goddess, his composition of a hymn to Kelīśvarī; and the description of the destruction of the pride of Kelīśvarī... —.

And in the *Andhakaśivasaṃvāda*, it is described how Śiva brought about the defeat of Andhaka; and how, being highly pleased by the hymn of praise offered by Andhaka, the Blessed One granted him the name Śṛṅgiriṭi and admitted him into his own retinue of Rudras.

Then, following the words of Vasiṣṭha, Suratha—who had been deprived of his kingdom—went to Hāṭakeśvara and installed Bhairava; by worshipping him, he regained his kingdom. This is followed by a description of the majesty of Bhairavaktra. In the description of the majesty of Cakrapāṇi, Arjuna, with Yudhiṣṭhira’s permission, went into the forest for the sake of protecting the Brahmins and the cows. Thereafter, having liberated the cows and completed his pilgrimage, Arjuna (Pārtha) traveled to Hāṭakeśvara.

The installation of Cakrapāṇi; the description of the majesty of Cakrapāṇi; the description of the majesty of Rūpatīrtha; the description of the origin of Tilottamā; the departure of Tilottamā for Kāśī by the command of Brahmā; upon seeing Tilottamā performing circumambulation after bowing to Śiva, Śiva’s mind became agitated; observing this, Pārvatī pronounced a curse upon Tilottamā, saying, "Become ugly"; then, taking Tilottamā with her, Pārvatī went to Rūpatīrtha at Hāṭakeśvara.

The journey; by means of that, the granting of boons to Viṅottamā, who was previously established there, by Pārvatī; the description of the origin and majesty of Apsaraḥkuṇḍa, and the description of the majesty of Citrareśvarīṣṭha. || 1 ||

After the dispute with Maṇibhadra, Maṇibhadra subjected the Brāhmaṇa named Puṣpa to mockery; then the city-dwellers, having offered him consolation, invited that Brāhmaṇa for a meal. Thereupon, while still engaged in eating, Puṣpaka departed for Camatkārapura to propitiate the Sun-god, accompanied by his mantra.

Having performed the fire sacrifice (*doma*) with his own flesh according to the ritual manuals, including the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and other rites, he observed the Sun-god returning to his presence. The Sun-god granted Puṣpa the power to assume the form of Maṇibhadra and to transform his own appearance, as well as knowledge of various sciences. Puṣpa, the Brāhmaṇa, established the deity Puṣpāditya after his own name. A description of the majesty of Puṣpāditya follows: by the power of a pill given by the Sun-god, Puṣpa assumed a form equal to that of Maṇibhadra and went to the house of Maṇibhadra. Of him—

Having gone to the house of Satyamāṇibhadra, he gratified the eunuch standing at the door with money and other gifts, and having gratified his wife with garments, ornaments, and the like, he enjoyed union with her in happiness. Then, at the word of Chatrimamāṇibhadra, Satyamāṇibhadra was reviled by the eunuch standing at the door. A description of the dispute between Chatrimamāṇibhadra and Attrimamāṇibhadra in the royal palace follows; then, by the king’s command, [the matter concerned] Attrimamāṇibhadra’s wife.

When he was not accepted as his own son, the king’s command led to the description of the artificial Maṇibhadra’s death at the hands of the royal messenger Śākhāvaṭu. Then, having summoned his circle of trusted associates, that artificial Puṣparūpamaṇibhadra is described as giving food, clothing, and other gifts; there is a description of his wealth of flowers. By means of Māhikā, the Puṣpa-brāhmaṇa assumes a body of flowers as before and causes Māhikā to take her vows. Then, by that Puṣpa—

Having given wealth to his own sons, he went to the Hāṭakeśvara-tīrtha for the expiation of the sin committed; there, he performed the *puraścaraṇa* and other rites, and invited Brāhmaṇas. [In the description of the greatness of the Puṣpāditya temple: the origin of the serpent Puṣpāditya-māhikā is described; in the account of the *puraścaraṇa-saptamī-vrata*, the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Roditāśva is related, along with the description of the ritual procedure (*vidhi*). The specific differences in worship for each month are described, and how Puṣpāditya was worshipped by a certain Brāhmaṇa named Caṇḍarāma.

The description of the ritual procedure for the *Puraścaraṇa-saptamī* vow; the humiliation of Caṇḍaśarman by the people when Puṣpa’s sin was destroyed through the penance prescribed by Caṇḍaśarman after he had thoroughly examined the scriptures; thereafter, the performance of austerities by that Brāhmaṇa Caṇḍaśarman; while Caṇḍaśarman was circumambulating the image of Puṣpa and performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) with his own flesh, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Bhairavas, offered his own head; [the account] of Sūryadatta.

The account of Puṣpacaṇḍa and Śāmeṇa attaining a beautiful form preceded by the removal of their sins; the description of the origin and history of the Brahmanas and Nāgaras; then, the journey of Puṣpacaṇḍa and Śāmeṇa once again to the bank of the Sarasvatī; there, having performed worship preceded by the construction of a linga by Damana, Caṇḍaśāmeṇa established a linga under the name Nāgareśvara; Śākaṃbharyā, the wife of Caṇḍaśāmeṇa, also established the goddess Śākambharī; and by Caṇḍaśāmeṇa, the installation of Nāgarāditya on the bank of the Sarasvatī.

The description of the greatness of Nāgareśvara, Varanāgara, Āditya, Śākambharī, and Tapaḥpati; ... the narration of the origin of Viśvāmitra; the departure of Ṛcīka to request the hand of Gādhi’s daughter; thereafter, the king’s vow that he would give his daughter upon receiving a thousand dark-spotted cows; for the sake of obtaining those dark-spotted cows, Ṛcīka performed austerities on the banks of the Sarasvatī; and then, through the power of his mantras, Ṛcīka went into the presence of Gādhi with the dark-spotted cows.

Description of the Aśvatīrtha festival. Contents: [The topics include] the gift-giving; the description of the greatness of the worship of the Śaṅkumācara; the description of the removal of the curse of Oḍḍāṃbarī; the arrival of the local deities there along with the Lord (Īśvara); when the group of Mothers (Mātṛgaṇa) departed from her presence to return to their respective abodes, the description by Sāvitrī of the account of the granting of boons to the Mātṛgaṇa; ... the description of the previous birth-story of Oḍḍāṃbarī preceded by her attainment of liberation; ... |

Brahmā summoned all the city-dwellers and, having performed the sacrifice, recounted to them the entire course of the sacrificial rite, including the origin of the holy ford (tīrtha). Then, for the sake of the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha-snāna), Brahmā departed for the Eastern Puṣkara. He granted boons to Brahmā, Dharā, and the others; at that time, Brahmā also granted a boon to Yakṣman who had arrived there. This is the description of the origin of the Yakṣman-tīrtha.

A description of the emergence of ill omens, such as portents and the like, arising at the time when Sāvitrī was about to enter the sacrificial pavilion; the arrival there of the Apsarases, Dhṛtācī and others; and a description of their singing, instrumental music, laughter, and so forth.

Nārada recounts to Sāvitrī the account of Gāyatrī’s marriage and other events; having heard that narrative related by Nārada, Sāvitrī is overcome with grief. At the word of Gaurī, she disregards Nārada’s speech and proceeds to the sacrificial pavilion of Brahmā. Sāvitrī causes Brahmā to fall asleep and bestows a curse upon him. Sāvitrī then pronounces curses upon Indra, Agni, the Nāgaras, the Brāhmaṇas, the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and others. Thereafter, Sāvitrī departs from there, traveling on foot.

The journey after ascending a mountain; the description of the greatness and the excellence of Sāvitrī; when Sāvitrī had departed, Gāyatrī, remaining there, first brought about the removal of all the curses given by Sāvitrī and then granted boons. ... us ...

The description of Svada’s performance of the *gāyatrī* hymn; the narration of the equal lifespans of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśāna; the description of the movement of time from a *nimeṣa* up to the end of a *kalpa*; and the description of the greatness of the sandals of the Lord who went to the two holy sites of Umārikā for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman. In the description of the two holy sites of Umārikā, there is the narration of the mutual friendship between the daughter of the Brāhmaṇa named Nāga and the daughter of the King of Ānarta named Ratnāvatī.

"The union of us two shall last until our marriage"—this was the thought in their minds. [End of the description of the account of the princess and the Brahmin’s daughter. [Sanskrit verse fragment]. Chapters and Subjects: The return of the King of Daśārṇa, Avadharavarman, to his city from Anarta. At that time, a certain son of Viśvāvasu named Parāvasu—a Brahmin learned in the Vedas—having gone to the house of a courtesan, was overcome by sleep at night and, due to the affliction of lust, committed an act of ignorance. Thereafter, filled with remorse, he went to Śaṅkhatīrtha in the morning, performed rites such as shaving, and stayed at a distance from the house of an outcaste woman.

The phrase "with those fellow-students" refers to the five [actions]. By means of a joking remark to those hundred fellow-students—specifically through the seizing of Rājñāvatī’s breast and the tasting of her lip—there would be liberation from that sin; such is the statement regarding the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Then, by the command of the preceptor, Viśvāvasu related the entire account. Now, seeing Viśvāvasu who had set out to undergo the expiation consisting of the consumption of clarified butter as prescribed for a Brahmin who has tasted [forbidden] liquor in the *Dharmaśāstra*, his mother and father spoke harsh words to him. Thus ends the section.

Thinking that the drinking of wine might be remedied by the grasping of the breasts and the tasting of the lips of Ratnāvatī, the Brahmin students, out of delusion, prescribed a penance. Having heard this, they returned with all the villagers to the king and made a plea for the life of the Brahmin. When the king said, "Let my own daughter be granted as a favor for the sake of the Brahmin's penance," she, out of love for her son, agreed to grant that penance to the Brahmin.

When the command was given for the purpose of drinking from her own lower lip after having her own breast milked, and when that Brahmin acted accordingly toward one such as me, there occurred a continuous flow of milk from the Brahmin’s mouth and from Ratnāvatī’s two breasts. Then, having heard the description of the other [incident], [the king] saw the taking of the hand [in marriage] by the Lord of the Vidyādharas himself, the stubborn insistence of Ratnāvatī upon the marriage, and the stubborn insistence of her friend, the Brahmin woman, upon not marrying even though the marriage of Ratnāvatī was about to take place. Thereafter, those two [women] were brought together.

The journey of Ratnāvatī and Tapasvinī to Bharatayajñaśara at the command of Bharatayajña; their performance of penance at Jalāśaya by his order; thereafter, upon the grace of Īśvara being attained, the establishment of the two *liṅgas* by them; and the description of the greatness of the two holy sites (*tīrtha*) of Śadrī and Brāhmaṇī.

[The description of the greatness of various sacred sites, such as the three seats (*pīṭha*), the three forests (*araṇya*), the three cities (*purī*), the three groves (*vana*), the three villages (*grāma*), the three holy fords (*tīrtha*), the three supreme mountains (*parvata*), and the three great rivers (*mahānadī*), preceded by accounts of their origins; ... || 200 || ... the description of the events concerning the Nāgara *jñātinīs* established by Bhadrayajña.]
Chapters: subjects; Chapter 10: improper subjects.
[End of section]

In the dialogue between Viśvāmitra and Bharṭṛyajña, when Viśvāmitra was censured by Bharṭṛyajña regarding the wealth of the Nāgaras, Śrī Rāma, by touching the dust of the feet of Aditī—who was in the form of a crest—caused him to be released from the curse; then Bharṭṛyajña, having realized the nature of the Tīrtha, gave him the pedestal (pīṭhikā) and other gifts. At the word of Rāma, he went to Dhāṭakeśvara, where he was honored by Aditī, Ahalyā, and Gautama.

The recitation of the *Pāvamānī* and other hymns (*sūkta*) for those afflicted by diseases such as leprosy, the reading of Upaniṣads such as the *Chāndogya*, and the worship of Ādināgara; the description of the greatness of Gautameśvara and Ahivyeścaraśatānandeśvara and the performance of the *Bhrada-nirṇaya*; and, in the description of the greatness of Śaṅkhatīrtha, the account of how the Lord of Ānarta, having become afflicted with leprosy, was approached by Nārada, and the inquiry made by Nārada to the Lord of Ānarta regarding which of the three types of *tārkṣya* should be given.

In this [chapter], there is the answer given by Bhartṛyajña to the question of Nāgara-praṇāmanī regarding the distribution of wealth; the description of his conduct in previous births; the narration that because the word of the Nāgaras is truthful for the purpose of purifying sins such as those committed with the thumb, the three [types of] wealth should be given by those very Nāgaras; the mention of Bhartṛyajña; therein, the description of the origin of Śaṅkhatīrtha; the account of the installation of Śaṅkhāditya; the description of the definitive statement regarding Śaṅkha...

...the description of the battle between the Nāgas and the Vidyādharas situated on Mount Dardara. ... In the context of explaining the causes of the defects of the Nāga-bearing [mountain], Nārada spoke to the Siddhasena named Ānata. [In the dialogue between Ānava and Viśvāmitra] there is the description of the battle between Hiraṇyākṣa and Indra; therein, having witnessed his own defeat, [the account of] the production of the fourteen jewels beginning with the Kaustubha is given. Therein, at the time of consuming the nectar (*amṛta*), Rāhu, who was joined by a trickster, had an encounter with Viṣṇu.

Then, in the dialogue between Ikṣvāku and Viṣṇu, there is a description by the illustrious Viṣṇu, the subduer of enemies, of how liberation occurs for those slain in battle despite their sins, including the severing of their heads and so forth, as well as the emergence of a stream from the water-pot of Airāvata’s temple-hill.

The narration by Viṣṇu to Śakra of the *preta-śrāddha* performed by Diti, her departure [from the womb], and the naming of her as Nāgāḍhānata-vānnāgavahvī; the description of the greatness of the fruit of the *gayā-śrāddha* in the dialogue between Śakra and Viṣṇu concerning the one named Vāṇīvatsaraka; and the constant journey of Śakra, having ascended the celestial chariot bestowed by Śakra through the propitiation of Cāpa—therein, Oṃ.

Having placed his trust in the words of Viṣṇu, Śakra mounted Airāvata and went to Himavat; there, having devoured the Tāmbūla that was being chewed by Rākradanta, who resided in Camatkārapura, he returned to his own abode. Then, by that Vāṇīvatsaraka, who had been honored with offerings by the sages dwelling in his hermitage, Śakra brought Nāgavahinī from the world of Śakra to the earth for the sake of establishing her fame among those people. This is the origin of those two.

The performance of *śrāddha* and other rites by assuming the form of Gayākara; the arrival of Brahmadeva there; and the description of the greatness of consuming the *tālukha* at all places, except for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.

The description of the worship of the Viśvedevas, stating that it must be performed and not in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; the narration by Brahmā of the curse upon the Viśvedevas from Indra’s teeth and the liberation from that curse through bathing at Śaṅkhatīrtha under the lordship of Ānata; the establishment of the rules for Śaṅkha following the propitiation of Śacī and Hutāśana; the mention of the names of the deliverers (*uttāra*) such as Kūṣmāṇḍa and others; and the greatness of Bāṭamaṇḍanaka-tīrtha, including a detailed account of the origin of the holy site (*tīrthotpatti*). ... [and so forth].

The description of the greatness of the Viśvāmitrīya-tīrtha and the praise of Viśvāmitra; the description of the great festivals of the Sun, Dhanvantari, Pañcarātra, and the Moon; the giving of a gift to Indra by Gautama following an incident of sexual union with Ahilyā; the description of the greatness of the Vāpī; and the account of the king of Ayodhyā, Ratnākṣa, assuming the garb of a pilgrim for the sake of curing his leprosy.

Then, at the instruction of his brother Gautama, Vasiṣṭha went to Nāḍhāṭakeśvara and, by bathing on the seventh lunar day at the Bhāskara-tīrtha and worshipping the Sun-god, he attained the removal of his defect; furthermore, within five nights, he obtained the reward of worship upon the earth, and [the text contains] a description of the greatness of the great festival of Indra lasting five nights.

The establishment of the holy site (tīrtha) named Ratnāditya; a description of the majesty of the Ratnāditya-tīrtha. ... Having heard that her mother Ahalyā had been subjected to the punishment of having her hair cut off by her own father, she resolved to die; [the text then] describes the establishment of a temple of the Lord known as Daravāsa. Śatānanda caused great suffering to Sāmba, the son of Kṛṣṇa, who was traveling along the royal highway, for the sake of his purification; thereafter, Gautama [consoled] Śatānanda.
