—The description of the account of Indradyumna’s journey to his own body in the world of Brahmā; after Indradyumna had resided there for a long time, the Brahman sent him back toward the earthly realm so that his fame might be manifested on earth again after a long interval; having returned to the earthly realm with joy, Indradyumna questioned Mārkaṇḍeya, who was living a long life on earth, regarding his own fame. Indradyumna [desired] to fully recognize his own glory...

Having seen people who were unable to describe the events connected with Rocaka-pura, [Indradyumna] went to the vicinity of Nāḍījaṅgha at the word of the inhabitants of Kāmpilyapura, together with Mārkaṇḍeya. There, after Indradyumna and Mārkaṇḍeya had explained the reason for their arrival to the distressed Nāḍījaṅgha, Nāḍījaṅgha related his own history, beginning with how he had attained the state of a ghost due to a curse in a previous birth. [He spoke of this] at the time of the sun's transit into Capricorn on the bank of the river...

The description of the granting of a boon to Vaka by Divodāsa, who was pleased with his offering of clarified butter as a covering; thereafter, the departure of Indradyumna from Nairṛta to the presence of Uddālaka Āruṇi, who possessed a longer life even than himself due to his mastery of the channels (*nāḍī*) and the *jīva*, and who was named Prācīnayogya Mākaṇḍeya.

Then, after Baka told Indra that he was ignorant of Indradyumna’s whereabouts, Indradyumnaprabha explained the cause of his own long life. To Indradyumnaprabha, who remained indifferent due to his ignorance of Indradyumna’s news, Baka demonstrated the fault of not knowing the location of Indradyumna; thus, by means of Baka’s account, Indradyumnaprabha sent Pradīndradyumna along with Mākaṇḍeya, Nāḍījaṅgha, and Baka to the vicinity of a vulture named Gandhamādana, who resided on Mount Gandhamādana and possessed a long life. By him—

The vulture’s narration of the circumstances regarding his own long life and his lack of knowledge concerning Indradyumna; the discovery by the vulture—upon learning of Indradyumna’s lack of recognition—that the indifferent king was preparing to enter the fire; the vulture’s own journey to the presence of Kama, who dwells in Lake Mānasa and possesses a long life, for the sake of requesting Prākārakarṇa; and the bringing of Indradyumna, Mārkaṇḍeya, Nāḍījaṅgha, and Prākārakarṇa to that spot; and [the events] among those who had gathered there on the shore of the lake.

Having seen the power of Indra, Kūma entered into the midst of the waters; thus ends the chapter. In the course of the story of Durvāsas, there was the hearing of the entire account of Indrayumna by a certain Maṭhapati named Nivāsa, who was standing nearby and listening intently to the objects of the senses. Then, when the vulture questioned him regarding the cause of his appearance as a Jaṭāmbara, he related the whole previous history of Indrayumna. When Indrayumna’s stake-fight was won, flowers were showered upon Indrayumna by the gods.

The bringing about of rain; then, at that very moment, Devadatta brought a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and made a request to Indradyumna to go toward the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*); Indradyumna, expressing his lack of desire to go to the world of Brahmā, questioned Kūma regarding the cause of his own long life.

The account begins with Kūrma’s narration of his own previous life, followed by his performance of hospitality for Indradyumna and others. Then, having met with the great sage Chāgaleya, they learn the cause of Chāgaleya’s long life; subsequently, all seven of them establish liṅgas after their respective names. Next follows the description of the origin of the *saprana* (the seven), and within the description of the measure of lifespan, the calculation of time starting from a *nimeṣa* up to the four ages beginning with Kṛta, as well as [the description of] the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices.

The description of attaining the worlds of the gods, the world of Brahmā, and so forth through various karmas; the description of the conditions, laws, and other matters of the celestial realms throughout the four ages (yugas); specifically, the determination of the Kali age following that; the description of the measure of the lifespans of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others; the description of the measures of the lunar, solar, and civil months; the statement of the measure of the sidereal month; and the description of the measure of the yugas.

Do not hide the basket with any deceptive pretext for the sake of deceiving him; for when much time has passed and at a certain point, you will go with Nivāśuca to the river Muruṇā along with the sage. There, having placed your own cloak in the hand of a disciple and having gone a great distance to perform the evacuation of urine and excrement and so forth, you will return and seize that cloak from the hand of the disciple of Nivāśuca. By this means, [you shall deceive] the one named Nivāśuca.

The head of the monastery, having learned of this, was filled with grief. Thereupon, Duḥśīla, having obtained wealth through that assistance, engaged in trade; after taking a wife, he claimed the status of being her son, and for the sake of obtaining a son, went to Camatkārapura together with his wife. Having met Durvāsas there, he reported to Durvāsas his own deceitful actions and wicked deeds committed out of brotherly affection; then, at the word of Durvāsas, Duḥśīla performed acts such as the giving of alms for the sake of his future life.

The establishment of the *liṅga* by [the author] under his own name; the narration of the account regarding the cause for bestowing the designation "Duḥśīleśvara" upon that *liṅga*; and the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Duḥśīleśvara and Dubāsaseśvara.

Duḥśīla established a temple named Niveśvara under the pretext of erecting a cowshed for his own cattle; then Duḥśīla’s wife, named Śākaṃbharī, established a cowshed for vegetables. When Duḥśīla had passed away, Duḥśīla’s wife Śākaṃbharī caused that Duḥśīla to be burned along with him in the fire. [This is] the description of the establishment of Duḥśīleśvara and Niveśvara and the existence of Śākaṃbharī. Then Śiva assumed eleven forms simultaneously in order to devour everyone at once.

The sages offered hymns of praise upon seeing that elevenfold form; therein is the installation of the eleven Rudras, the description of the origin and majesty of the eleven Rudras, and the enumeration of the names of the eleven Rudras. Following the description of the greatness of giving in the presence of the eleven Moon-like ones (Candras), there is the description of the twelve Ādityas. In the context of the sacrifice performed by Badhya, during the occasion when Indra brought the daughter of Govakra as the wife of Brahmā, she was led forth by Govakra from the mouth of a goat.

After the marriage of Gāyatrī and Brahmā, Sāvitrī’s arrival; the birth of Yājñavalkya by the name of that same person in the house of Cārāyaṇa—the great-grandson of Nyuṇaśepa—due to the curse bestowed upon the Grandfather (Brahmā) by Sāvitrī; seeing his son Yājñavalkya’s wickedness in the form of an obsession with the wives of others, his expulsion from his own hermitage by the grandfather Cārāyaṇa; thereafter, attaining discipleship under Śākalya and residing in his house; and then...

Once, while Yājñavalkya was traveling to the royal palace in succession to his disciples to offer blessings for peace, the king treated him with contempt. Thereafter, the king, filled with remorse, sent a chariot on the following day to request that very Yājñavalkya come to the royal residence again. Although the king issued an order for Yājñavalkya to go to the royal palace, Yājñavalkya’s teacher forbade him from going to the king's house, and he refused to go there in defiance of that command of his guru.

Then, because his guru was enraged by Yājñavalkya and pressed him excessively, he vomited up the knowledge he had studied from him; he then reported that knowledge back to his guru. Subsequently, for the sake of obtaining the [remaining] knowledge, he performed the propitiation of Sūrya. Having received the knowledge from Sūrya and honored him, he set out alone on an expedition and, with great eagerness, arrived at the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara. At that time, the students, having pledged to recite the subjects of the *Sūryajñāna*, arrived there in a great rush of eleven thousand. Then, the chapters and topics [were taught], and the *Sūryajñāna* was proclaimed.

The arrival of Yājñavalkya to the presence of his teacher Śākalya in order to give the preceptor’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*); thereafter, having recounted the *Sūryapañca-vidyā* to Śākalya as the preceptor’s fee, Yājñavalkya’s departure with his disciple to the vicinity of the twelve Ādityas along with Śākalya; the description of the origin of the twelve Ādityas, preceded by a description of the majesty of the origin of the Sun-god (*Āditya*), followed by the narration of the account of Yājñavalkya; and therein, the proclamation of the supreme authority of the *Skānda-mahāpurāṇa* and the *Āgama*.

The description of the destruction of Gāgara-khaṇḍa; the description of the majesty of Nāgara-khaṇḍa; the narration of the hearing of Nāgara-khaṇḍa; the description of the authority of the Guru and the disciple; and the description of the authority of Vyāsa, the narrator of the Purāṇas.
Thus ends the sixth section, the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. 6.
Now, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, the seventh section, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa. 7.
Now, in the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, first is the majesty of the Prabhāsa constellation.

(1) The auspicious invocation; the description of the occasion for the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka; the description of those who are qualified and unqualified to hear the narrative; the posing of questions by Śaunaka and others to Sūta; the definition of a narrative (*kathā*), and the exposition of its merits and defects; the examination of the characteristics of Vedic and human-authored texts; the sequential enumeration of the names of the eighteen *Mahāpurāṇas*; the sequential enumeration of the names of the *Upapurāṇas*; and the description of the number of verses contained within the *Mahāpurāṇas*.

The description of the greatness and the procedure for the gift of the manuscripts of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas; the description of Mount Kaiṭabha; therein, the description of Śiva’s throne on the peak of the mountain preceded by a vision of Śiva’s assembly; then, the hymn of praise to Śiva by the Goddess; the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī; thereafter, the description by Śrī Śiva to Pārvatī of the Yoga of Vibhūti (the power of manifestation); then, the description of the greatness of that [Yoga]; therein, specifically, the description of the greatness of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra; and [finally], the desire to hear the description of the greatness of the sacred sites situated within the Prabhāsa-kṣetra.

Pārvatī’s inquiry regarding Śaṅkara; [the dialogue] between Pārvatī and Śaṅkara, the best of the Pāśupatas, concerning the measurement of the land at the boundary of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra and the extent of the Jālandhara-kṣetra.

A description of the sequence of the three types of pilgrimages to Prabhāsa-kṣetra; a description of the pilgrimages according to the three divisions known as Māheśvara, Vaiṣṇava, and Bāhya; therein, a description of the various deities as well; a description of the fruits of reciting mantras such as the *mūrtiyoga*; a description of how even great sinners residing in the sacred precinct of Prabhāsa-kṣetra attain liberation; and a description of the majesty of the *dauvārika* (gatekeeper) attendants who protect the sacred site of Prabhāsa-kṣetra.

A description of the great sages such as Marīci and others, of the gods, of the celestial rishis, and of the holy rivers such as the Gaṅgā residing in the sacred precinct of Prabhāsa; a brief description of the merit of offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) in the field of Prabhāsa; a description of the greatness of various kinds of gifts in the field of Prabhāsa; and a description of the assembly of divine hosts dwelling there.

[The text contains] a description of the greatness of Śivābhīṣvara; a description of the manifested forms of Someśa, such as Pañcavakra and others; a hymn to Someśa; a description of the true nature [of the deity] through its various manifestations as Śiva’s servant and so forth during the eight Parvas; a description of the greatness of Someda; and, in the description of the origin of Someda, when the seventh Brahmā was presiding, the emergence of the *liṅga* named Somanātha, as related by Pārvatī, and how it was established by Śaṅkara at that time for all people.

A description of the Brahmas and Prajāpatis in sequential order by name; likewise, in that same context, a description of Someśa under a different name; and Śaṅkara’s narration to Pārvatī—preceded by a description of his various incarnations—as he points out the names of Pārvatī as they occurred in each of those instances. Then, during the seventh Brahmā named Rātānanda, Candra propitiated Śiva and, having obtained a boon from Śiva, established the shrine of Someśvara after his own name.

An extensive description of the location and situation of Prabhāsasthala; therein, a description of the divine abodes such as Devikā, Yamunā, Vīkaṣatrapīṭha, Bhagṛha, Goyulāśvamedhaka, and others; followed by a description of the majesty of all the holy fords (tīrthas) situated around Somanātha; a narrative account of the manifestation of Somanātha; further, in the narration of the majesty of Someśa, a description of the origin of the eight supernatural powers (siddhis), prosperity, and the Garuḍa-mantras and other sciences attained through the grace of Someśa; and the power gained through the worship of this Someśa.

The description of Gaṇḍa, Suṇḍa, and the others in their respective order; the description of Semeśvara and Īśvara; the explanation of the reason why he himself wears a garland of Suṇḍas; the account of how Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others were made intoxicated by him during the Rati-kalpa; the statement by Śiva that the subjects [of his power] are born from him; and the making of his eternal residence in the meritorious field named Bhramāsa during the Koṭi-kalpa—having heard these words of Śiva, the Goddess was filled with wonder.

The performance of the hymn of praise to Śiva; then, by Śiva, pleased with that hymn, the granting of a boon to Pārvatī, saying, "I shall describe the majesty of the *liṅgas* situated in Prabhāsa-kṣetra"; Pārvatī’s posing of questions regarding the incarnations of Viṣṇu, such as the Matsya and others; then, by Śaṃkara, the description of the dwellings of Brahmā and the other gods at Prabhāsa, and the description of the abode of Hari.

A description of the abodes of the five deities within the five great elements; a sequential description of the sacred bathing places (tīrthas) such as Chāgaraṇḍa and others, including those belonging to the deity Viṣṇu situated in various regions; a description of the greatness of the many Liṅga-tīrthas located in the site of Prabhāsa; and a description of how the Prabhāsa-kṣetra is the most excellent among all sacred fields.

Then follows the description of the eight principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas) surrounding Jambūdvīpa; the description of the nine divisions (navakhaṇḍa) constituting the boundaries of the extent of Jambūdvīpa; therein, the excellent description of Bhāratavarṣa as a land of great merit; the description of the arrangement of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) and planets above Bhārata situated in its own form; the description of Śivāvāsa located at a distance of nine hundred yojanas from Bhārata in the direction known as Parāmāsika; and the description of the Bhramāsakṣatra and the Citvānas.

The description of the origin of Prabhāsa-kṣetra through the power of Īśvara’s supreme word; the statement of the reason for naming that place "Pramāta"; the description of the origin of that [place] from the burning of Brahmā by the splendor of the divine Sun while he was dwelling in the Manu [age]; the description of its origin from the conjunction of the Sun and the Earth; then the emergence of the celestial bodies, followed by the creation of humans and other beings; and finally, the production of the deities of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, as well as the medicinal herbs.

(An account of the birth of Marīci and the other patriarchs, as well as the Daityas such as Hiraṇyakaśipu and others; the birth of Prahlāda from Hiraṇyakaśipu; the birth of Virocana, who was sonless, from Prahlāda; and the account of the birth of the daughter named Śarmiṣṭhā from Viśvakarman’s wife; the departure of Saṃjñā to perform penance after she could no longer endure the brilliance of the Sun and stationed Chāyā in his presence; and when Sureṇu adorned herself with ornaments upon seeing the Sun, the Sun became enraged.)

The granting of a curse by Kharaṇa-nāga and Palya; then the departure of Sureṇu to his father; then, after explaining the reason for his own arrival, Sureṇu’s return to Sūrya at his father’s command; then the description of the origin of the Śrāddhadevas in the realms of Yama, Yamunā, and Śanaiścara; and finally, due to a certain other cause, Sūrya’s arrival at the house of Viśvakarman to curse his mother-in-law, whereupon Viśvakarman joyfully performed hospitality and other rites for Sūrya.

The instrument [was forged]; then Viśvakarman began to fashion a means to diminish his [the Sun's] brilliance. While it was being made, the Seven Sages offered hymns of praise to the Sun; Viśvakarman composed a hymn for the Sun; Hāhā, Hūhū, Nārada, Tumburu, and others began to sing; Menakā and other Apsarases began to sing in the form of hymns to the Sun; various musical instruments were played; and when Saṃjñā, having gone to perform penance, assumed the form of a mare, [the Sun took the form of] a stallion...

The description of the birth of Sūryāda from the crookedness of the Aśvins, and the description of the origin of Rājamabhaṭa and Rārika; the description of the birth of Yama; the journey of Yama—who had been seized by his mother and rendered lame—to the holy site of Prabhāsa; having propitiated Śiva there, he cast off his lameness through the grace of Śiva and established a shrine for Śiva there by Śiva’s command; the description of the greatness of Yameśvara; and [the account] of how, while wandering in Piśākadvīpa, the act of carving was performed upon him by Śiva as he stood on a lathe.

Immediately following the [section on] Truth (Satya-yuga), there is the descent of the Sun (Vibhāvasu) onto the earth by means of his golden form; his renown under the names Sūrya, Savitṛ, Bhāskara, and Arkastha during the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages; the description of the greatness of the Sun (Arka) in connection with the prohibition against eating leaves; the description of the greatness of the gift of a buffalo and other items at the Arka-kastha-tīrtha; and the narration of the origin of the place known as Prabhāsa-pavitra. ... Śīdha.

A description of the worship of Akaiṣṭhala preceded by the recitation of mantras, and the account of the greatness of Siddheśvara and Jaigīṣavyeśvara; the performance of penance by Jaigīṣavya at Prabhāsa, including the observance of fasts, kṛcchra, cāndrāyaṇa, and other austerities; the granting of a boon bestowing the knowledge of yoga by Sthāṇu, who was pleased by his long penance, to that Jaigīṣavya; and the installation of the two deities Jaigīṣavyeśvara and Siddheśvara by Jaigīṣavya.

The description of the greatness of the Jaigīṣavyeśvara-siddha; the description of the origin and greatness of Pāpanāśana; the chapters concerning how Prabhākara, having seen the triple world eclipsed by the splendor of the Rākṣasas stationed in Pātāla, performed meditation on the Lord; the falling of those Rākṣasas from the sky to the earth as they were gazed upon with eyes inflamed by anger; then the departure of those Rākṣasas to Pātāla; and finally, the installation of the Liṅga at the confluence of that [river] and the Khadgadhārā.

A description of the greatness of the fruit of giving *sakhanāna*; its establishment under the name *Śrīmukhadvāra*; a description of the origin of the host of Mātṛs such as Sunandā from the openings of Pātāla; and a statement on the procedure for worship and the majesty of Sunandā and the others.

Now follows the description of the ritual for the worship of Ākāśala; therein is the description of the Sun as consisting of the three Vedas (*trayīmaya*). First, regarding the cleaning of the teeth, there is the determination of the appropriate times—forenoon and afternoon—for the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), and the description of the method of cleaning the teeth. Then follows the description of how one becomes afflicted with leprosy and other diseases by touching the rays of the sun without first rinsing the mouth. Next is the description of the procedure for the acquisition of knowledge and other virtues while standing in the shadow of the *arka* tree. Following that is the recitation of the mantra of the Sun (*sūryamantra*) preceded by the description of its great power, and the description of the *japa* (muttered prayer). Finally, there is the description of the ritual of worship (*upasthāna*) with the hymn "ud u tyam," and the description of the Sun as the messenger of the gods (*agnidūta*).

The description of the ritual procedure for Āditya through the sixteen services beginning with *kaṣṇena*; the description of the worship of the deities of the *ṛṅga-pīṭha* and others on all sides; the description of the offering of various types of maṇḍalas and other gifts; the description of the majesty preceded by the hymn of praise to Akaiṣṭha; and, in the context of describing the account of the moon’s origin as an ornament upon Śiva’s head, the description of the account of Vārāhaka.

In that [section], there is a description of the origin of the moon when the ocean was being churned for the sake of producing the fourteen jewels; the holding of that moon by Śiva upon his head; the description of the sixteen digits (kalās) of the moon according to the sequence of the lunar days (tithis) because of its being held on the head—[the moon] thus being known as "Moon-adorned" (Śaśibhūṣaṇa); a description of the wheel of the parts of the body from the big toe up to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa); and a brief description of the life-stories of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśāna during the first *parārdha* of Brahmā’s lifespan. Then...

In the second [section], following the account of the birth and other details of Dakṣa and others, there is a description of the births of the seven sages (Saptarṣis) and others, as well as the accounts of the incarnations (avatāras) of Candra, Dattātreya, and so forth; a description of the various incarnations of Viṣṇu occurring simultaneously during the different ages (yugas); a description of the commencement of the Kṛtayuga and the reigns of the Cakravartins (universal emperors) such as Bharata and others; and a description of the incarnations of Vyāsa and others.

In the narration of the sequence of the incarnations of the Daityas: Hiraṇyakaśipu’s journey to the worlds of Indra and others to perform austerities; his attainment of the status of conqueror of the three worlds through those penances; then the account of the birth of Bali and so forth, followed by a description of Bali’s power; the description of Prahlāda’s birth and life story; the description of the birth of Kārtavīrya; the origin of Viśravas; and the account of the births of Kuvera, Rāvaṇa, and the others.

The narration of Śrī Rāma’s destruction of Rāvaṇa; the account of Śiñjāpāṭha’s birth; the description of the names of the nine Pūṣṭis; the description of the lineage of Puṣkara, Harṣa, Maga, and others; here, the mention of the wives of Atri, namely the Apsarases Dhṛtācyā, Anajajā, and Bhadrā, as well as the Bhāskarapallīs beginning with Bhadrā; the description of how Soma-rasa was produced by Pramāka in his wife Bhadrā; and then, while Atri was performing austerities after drinking that Soma-rasa, [it flowed] from his two eyes.

The description of the origin of the *soma* plant from the flow of the *prāita-soma-rasa*; how the various quarters took that *soma* and created coolness everywhere; the description of the origin of medicinal herbs; the account of the production of grains such as *kuṭattha*, *kaśyāmāka*, and others; the description of the origin of the constellations (*nakṣatras*) along with the *ṛtus* (seasons) and *vighātis*; the conclusion of the narrative regarding the granting of sovereignty over the constellations, herbs, and so forth, to the Moon; and how the Moon, having commenced the *Rājasūya* sacrifice, approached Brahmā seated upon the sacrificial ground.

Having installed Viṣṇu, Sanatkumāra, and others in their respective positions, and having commenced the sacrifice, he gratified the sacrificial sages at its conclusion with fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other offerings. Then follows the narration of the origin of the Ṛkṣas: by the command of Brahmā, Daśa begot sixty daughters; there, from Dharma and the others, [the lineage of] those daughters [proceeded].

The gift of Pṛśni; the giving of twenty-seven daughters to Soma; the enumeration of the names of the ten wives of Dharma; the description of Kaśyapa’s wives numbering twenty-seven, and the wives of Soma, Aṅgiras, and Āyu; the description of their lineages preceded by the mention of the names of the wives of Īśvara and Aśva; and the account of how Candra, neglecting Rohiṇī, caused discord with the other wives of Candra.

The narration of the entire account: thereafter, having heard from Dakṣa that Candra had developed an unequal affection for other maidens, Dakṣa related the story of how he had bestowed the disease of consumption upon Candra. Then, at the word of Dakṣa, Candra went to the vicinity of the Southern Ocean with the intent of performing worship to Śiva in order to be liberated from the affliction of the disease of consumption (yakṣmakuṣṭha).

Having gone to the Prabhāsakṣetra with Candra, [he] saw the mountain named Kṛtasmara; likewise, on that mountain, having taken up the discipline of various fasts and other practices from the sages such as Marīci, and having performed ablutions and circumambulations toward them, he then offered praise to Śiva, who had appeared through the grace of Śiva attained by means of divine worship. Having heard the description of the mountain’s excellence and its various features as told by Candra, Śiva, with a delighted heart, [bestowed his favor] upon Candra.

The granting of boons preceded by the establishment of the curse of Dakṣa; the description of the power of Śiva, gods, and brahmins; the discourse on the nature of the sinless; and the description of the qualities of brahmins.

"Oṃ! Having taken the command from Candra regarding the installation of the Liṅga for Viśvakarman, he then considered his own world and issued an order to Candra, who was in the presence of Hemagarbha, to bring the sacrificial materials to Prabhāsa for the performance of the sacrifice. At Candra’s word, Hemagarbha’s minister procured the sacrificial requisites and went to the region of Prabhāsa. Then Viśvakarman constructed the sacrificial hall, the wife’s quarters, and other structures; thereafter, Candra, together with Brahmā and the others, emerged from the sacrificial ground."

Having caused the gods and the Vasus and others to enter their respective positions and having established them in their proper places, when the sacrificial ritual has commenced, he should ensure the satisfaction of all by providing no deficiency in any material. Having appointed the *ṛtvij*s and others, and having made the moon together with Rohiṇī the *adhvaryu*, he should perform the selection of all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*s) together with Brahmā accompanied by Sāvitrī. Then, having assigned the office of *hotṛ* to Bṛhaspati, the office of *adhvaryu* to Vasiṣṭha, the office of *udgātṛ* to Marīci, and the office of *brahman* to Nārada, he should appoint the Sanatkumāras to the positions of the *sadasyas*.

Having directed all [the priests] to perform the worship, having given the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the commencement of the sacrifice was made; having completed the sacrifice with the *avaśratha* and other rites, the installation of the image of Someśvara was performed. On the following day, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, he worshipped Śaṅkara by means of the Rodinī mantra, making him manifest before his eyes and offering hymns of praise; then, being pleased, Śiva granted him the attainment of the supreme state of union with the divine.

The description of how Śiva granted a boon to the Moon; the narration of the sequence for the worship of Somanātheśvara; the description of the fruits of the pilgrimage to Somanātha; the description of the Moon’s liberation from his affliction; the enumeration of the flowers dear to Somanātheśvara; the departure of Candrabhāgā and the others to their respective abodes by the command of Vibhu (Śiva); and when Pārvatī questioned Śaṅkara regarding the reason for granting boons to wicked people, [the response] by Śaṅkara.

A description of devotees characterized by the qualities of goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), and darkness (tāmasa); an exposition on the non-difference between Hara and Īśvara; a description of the incarnations of the Blessed One as Narasiṃha and others; a description of the discourse on liberation through the attainment of similarity with the Divine (sārūpya) and other states; a description of the rules for the Somavāra-vrata, fasting, and other observances. [In the section] describing the majesty of the Somavāra-vrata: while Sudīlā’s husband was staying at Svayaṃprabha-nagara together with his wife, a Gandharva named Ghana produced a daughter named Gandharvasenā after a long time had passed. [This is] the account of Gandharvasenā.

The Contents of the Chapter titled "Ghana" regarding the Ritual for Taking the Hand (Marriage): First, the description of the ritual for the gift of Somanātha; a detailed account of the procedure for the pilgrimage to Somanātha; the determination of the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the fruit of the pilgrimage; an exposition on what should be avoided or not avoided by a person desiring to undertake a pilgrimage to a sacred site (*tīrthayātrā*), including instructions on what must be performed; the declaration of the merit (*puṇya*) resulting from the performance of great gifts (*mahādāna*); [and] the [description of] the sacred precinct of Prabhāsa.

The description of the fear arising from the attack of enemies; the statement regarding the rules for those who have been struck down; the description of the fruits of giving sixteen articles by Bhinnasena on the sixteen lunar days (*tithis*); the description of the fruit of dying in the sacred precinct of Prabhāsa; the statement concerning eligibility for going to the world of Śiva; the recitation of mantras during bathing at a holy ford (*tīrtha*); the procedure for the pilgrimage to the holy ford, including the making of offerings by Gandharva through his servant; and [the scene where] Rikhaṇḍika, the leader of the Gaṇas, was traveling through the path of the sky.

Having heard the words of the Gandharva maiden named Gandharvasenā, beginning with "No one at all possesses a form as beautiful as mine," Śikhaṇḍin, upon seeing the Gandharva maiden proud of her beauty, gave her a curse that brought leprosy. Having heard the plea of Śikhaṇḍin, Gandharvasenā accepted the curse. At the word of Śikhaṇḍin, she went to the hermitage of the sage Godāyana on Mount Himavat to dispel her leprosy.

The narration by the demon named Ghana to the sage Geraṅgasunu of his daughter along with the full account of events; the description of the means employed by Gokhagaṇa upon hearing that news to eliminate the demon; and the description of the demon named Ghana and the army of Gandhaveśa.

The journey to Someśvara at Gośṛṅga; there, having performed the worship of Śiva through vows such as the *khoma* fast, and in the introduction to the description of the greatness of Sannitīrtha, first performing the shaving of the head and other rites at Padyatīrtha, and again taking up the staff of Śiva (*śivadhras*), he obtained a boon from Śiva that included the complete eradication of leprosy. It is stated that by performing the bathing and other rites for Śiva, the fruit is twice that even of bathing at the Someśvara Tīrtha. [Regarding] women, [there is the mention of] the *kṣuraka*... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a Sanskrit narrative concerning a pilgrimage to the Someśvara shrine at Gośṛṅga, detailing the rituals and spiritual rewards associated with visiting specific holy sites along the way.)

The departure of the Gandharva army to their own homes; the description of the prohibition against shaving on Mondays; the description of women tearing out their hair with both thumbs and cutting it off; the description of the various procedures for shaving and other rites; and the description of the prohibition against touching the great ocean without having undergone a shave.

The Gandharva named Vana [approached] the sage Gośṛṅga for the sake of fully understanding the procedure for the Monday vow (somavāratrata). Then, after he had performed that vow and other rites, there is the account of how, by the grace of Śiva, his leprosy was eradicated. Subsequently, when that same vow was undertaken there by the Gandharva named Vana, the sage—fearing a breach of his own knowledge—considered the ocean to be a refuge and entered it with a loud cry.

The procedure for concealment; the ritual of libation (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth following the calculation of mantras; the observance of the Monday vow (*somavāravratam*); the description of the ritual following the attainment of the state of Soma by Dakṣa, who had become emaciated through fasting; therein, the description of the greatness of the fruit of giving gifts such as bulls; the preparation of materials for the worship of the Lord (*Īśvara*); the description of the ritual for the worship of Śiva accompanied by all mantras; and [the account of] the ninth Soma, who, by giving food including meat and other items to the Brāhmaṇas, [brought them satisfaction].

The description of the procedure for performing the *udyāpana* (concluding rite) and other rituals during the obstruction of the Monday [vow] caused by the fault of eating meat; the narration of how the Ocean gave a curse to the Brahmins, saying "May you become [outcastes like] Bhaurāṇikas," so that they might satisfy the gods, gurus, and others, when such [degradation] had occurred; the description of the giving of gifts at the end of the meal and so forth; then, having completed the Monday vow (*somavāravrata*) according to the method described by Gośṛṅga, the Ocean made a prayer to the Brahmins.

An account of the establishment of the holy site known as Vaḍavānala-tīrtha; the curing of leprosy for Gandharvasenā by the gracious Śiva; a description of the procedure for the performance of the Abhītīrtha pilgrimage; and, after performing the bath and other rites there, the offering of a vow as an ancillary to the bath.

To the north of Someśvara, the Gandharva named Ghanadāha, known as Gandharveśavara, performed the installation of the quarters; having worshipped Gaṇapati for a day at Gandharva, he proceeded to Someśvara, where he performed the worship of Someśvara with the sixteen-fold offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra), followed by a description of the majesty of the Lord (Īśvaramāhātmya). ...

— and likewise the description of the ritual injunctions, the description of the majesty of the worship of Someśvara; the installation of Gaṇeśa by Gandharvasenā, the daughter of the Gandharva Ghanavāha; the departure toward the hermitage when the war between the gods and the asuras broke out on account of Soma and the Daityas were defeated; then the description of the majesty of Seneśa-vigama; and the description of the offering of their respective weapons by all the gods to the great sage Ṛddhivin.

Viṣṇu’s command for the mare Vaḍavā to cease her pursuit of the ocean; then, having drunk the essence of the *allāṇas* established by the gods along with the water, Dadhīci departed for the northern direction with his wife named Subhadrā. Thereafter, while staying at that hermitage, Dadhīci put on a garment permeated by semen and went to the river where Subhadrā was bathing; there, in that river, he entered the womb of Bhadrā as she was performing her ablutions.

Due to the emission of semen, there was conception; then, having gone to the foot of an *aśvattha* tree, she cast off the fetus and uttered a curse: "May that wicked one by whom the conception of a fetus was caused in my womb—whether through knowledge or ignorance—die. Then, while she was performing the ritual of circumambulation there, the gods arrived. Knowing that Dadhīci had been reduced to ashes, the gods made preparations to seize his bones. For the purpose of fashioning the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and other weapons, Dadhīci [was requested].

The act of abandoning the body; then, the gods such as Indra taking the bones of Dadhīci and fashioning their respective vajras, staffs, nooses, and other implements; and then, Subhadrā, who was overwhelmed with grief due to the death of Dadhīci.

The gods brought about a reconciliation; Subhadrā, having heard that a son had been born from Dadhīci, was filled with joy; Subhadrā performed the *auṣvedika* rites and others for the child; there is a description of the birth of the four classes of beings—viviparous, oviparous, sweat-born, and soil-born; Subhadrā gave her son the name Pippalāda and performed the sacraments prescribed in the Vedas; thereafter, Pippalāda made a vow to kill the gods who had slain his father and went to the mountain named Himavat to perform worship.

The departure; for the sake of creating a daughter, Pippalāda churns his own thigh and produces a mare (*vaḍavā*) joined with a stallion (*vāḍava*); then the description of the birth of the *baḍavānala* (submarine fire) from that stallion and mare; at the word of Pippalāda, the *baḍavānala* goes to the sky to devour the gods; then the description of the account of the deception of the *baḍavānala* by Mahāviṣṇu, who was praised by the gods; and Sarasvatī, having been pacified by Brahmā, takes the *baḍavānala* and goes to the ocean.

The subduing of Vaṇra by Sarasvatī at the hoof of the mare; the glorification of Sarasvatī, the mare, and the ocean; the aquatic creature’s seeking refuge with Kṛṣṇa when the water of the ocean was about to be consumed by the mare’s snorting; Kṛṣṇa granting them a promise of safety; then, seeing the ocean filled with inexhaustible water, the performance of the worship of Viṣṇu by the gods; and the description of the greatness of the descent of Sarasvatī at the Bhṛbhāsa-kṣetra.
