Part 75

The departure of the Sarasvatī from the root of the Pippala tree toward the eastern direction; then her turning eastward as far as Siddheśvara; then her turning northward and subsequently westward; then a description of the various holy bathing places (*tīrthas*) situated along the banks of the Sarasvatī; a description of the five streams beginning with Hariṇī; and the account of the confluence of the Sarasvatī with the ocean.

In the description of the majesty of Prācīsarasvatī: after the destruction of the Kauravas, the Pāṇḍavas set out for Hastināpura with Kṛṣṇa. Then, at the time of Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Arjuna, and Sahadeva’s departure for Gajapura, Yudhiṣṭhira addressed the gatekeepers, saying, "Nara and Nārāyaṇa are to be excluded. When the ignorant gatekeepers, desiring to know about the Niṣadha kingdom, made inquiries regarding them, those [gatekeepers] [reported] their [identity]—[namely, that they were] Bhīṣma, Duryodhana, and other kinsmen.

The prohibition against being a vessel for faults by means of carrying [the burden]; then, having been thus exhorted, the ignorant one’s posing of questions to Śrī Kṛṣṇa regarding the means for the removal of sin and the methods of expiation; thereafter, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s description of the removal of sin through bathing at the Prācī-Sarasvatī Tīrtha; following that, his departure with Kṛṣṇa toward the Prācī-Sarasvatī; there, his effecting the removal of his own sins through observances such as fasting for three nights and bathing for three nights; and the power of the Prācī-Sarasvatī.

Having learned that Bhīma, Nakula, Sahadeva, and others had also arrived there, he dispelled their sins through the smelling of [the smoke] and other means, as if they were not born of human parents; then follows the description of the majesty of the Prācī-Sarasvatī. . . .

When Śiva was asked by Pārvatī, "Why was a bracelet thrown into the water at Sānakaṭha?", he related the story of Indumatī. In that account, the great seer Kaṇva arrived at the presence of King Bṛhadratha; having performed the rites of hospitality for Kaṇva, the two engaged in a conversation concerning dharma. Thereafter, Indumatī, desiring to know the cause of her own misfortune, offered herself to Kaṇva, who then [bestowed his grace] upon her, Indumatī.

The narration of the events of her previous birth; therein, the account of the life of Mahāśūdrakā in that previous birth; the falling of the bracelet from the hand of Mahāśūdrakā at the time of performing the ritual bath at the Someśvara Tīrtha; the narration of how, by the power of that bracelet’s fall at the holy site, she was born as a princess in another life; and upon hearing those words of Kaṇva, Indumatī turned her face away and remained silent, after which Kaṇva departed for his own abode.

Then, having gone with Nandumatī to the banks of the Sarasvatī in the region of Vahadratha for the purpose of casting the marriage bracelets, there is the description of how Vahadratha and Indumatī attained divinity through that act; the description of the greatness of casting the bracelets; and within the description of the greatness of the Lord Kapardin, the account of the Daityas being terrified and the gods offering hymns of praise to Pārvatī. Then, trusting the words of the Goddess, the gods went to the holy site of Someśvara and other places, performed their ablutions and other rites, and [worshipped] the Lord Kapardin.

Furthermore, through worship, the performance of sovereignty [is attained]; there is a description of the majesty of Kapardin-Vināyaka; in the description of the Prabhāsa pilgrimage, there is the journey to the Kedāreśvara Tīrtha north of the Kedāreśvara fire; then, the worship of the Vṛddhaliṅga situated near Bhīmeśvara; in the description of the majesty of Kedāreśvara, King Śaśavidu, together with his wife, undertakes a pilgrimage and goes to Kedāreśvara; there, upon seeing the groups of sages such as Rebhya, the king performs the vigil (jāgara) and other rites; then, by Rebhya and the others...

Śakbida, in order to know the events of his previous birth, abandoned Someśvara and set out for Kedāreśvara to discover the reason for his arrival there; subsequently, when the king recounted the history of his own previous life, he described his birth as Candra, a base official distinguished by his service to a Brahmin worshipper. Then, during a time of drought, he told how he, afflicted by hunger along with his wife, went to Prabhāsakṣetra. There—

Having bathed in all the sacred bathing places (*tīrthas*) and performed various rites of worship and so forth, he then went to Rāmasaras. Every day, he would gather the lotuses found in Rāmasaras, sell them, and sustain himself with that very income. Then, at one time, while staying with his wife in a certain part of the forest near Kāśī, he suddenly heard the sound of a cry. Realizing that a vigil was being held in a certain spot, he went there with his wife to sell lotus stalks (*kamaṭas*).

The journey; there, the sight of the deity Vṛddhikeśvara, who is also known by the name Kedāreśvara; there, the meeting with Anaṅgavatī while she was alone; when that Śūdra was asked by another man about the cause for his wakefulness, the description of the fruits of keeping a vigil on Śivarātri given to him; then, the description of how that Śūdra, together with his wife, by performing the vigil and fasting on Śivarātri, obtained birth in a royal family in another life; and the description of the greatness of Kedāreśvara (Rudreśvara).

The establishment of the *ṛṣi* [liṅga] named Śvetaketvīśvara by Śvetaketu at Prabhāsa after performing austerities; then, in the Dvāpara age, Bhīmasena, filled with devotion, performed a pilgrimage and, through the worship of the deity, bestowed the name Bhīmeśvara; the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Bhīmeśvara; the description of the majesty of the *ṛṣi* Śānaiścareśvara, wherein Dānaiśvara propitiated Śiva on Saturdays to attain the state of a *rahasya*; and the description of the majesty of Devamātābhairaveśvara at Caṇḍa.

Following the description of the ritual procedure for the worship of Caṇḍīśa, who was propitiated by the established host of Caṇḍas, there is a description of the majesty of Māda Ādityeśvara. [Then] follows the description of the majesty of Someśvara. [Next] is the narration of the account of the origin of Aṅgāraka from the falling of a tear upon the earth from the eye of Śiva, who desired to burn Tripura, as well as the description of the majesty of Aṅgāreśvara.

(Description of the greatness of Budheśvara established by Budha; description of the greatness of Bṛhaspatīśvara established by Guru; Śukra, having propitiated Rudra and obtained the *sajjīvanī* mantra through Rudra’s assistance, attained lordship and established a *liṅga* in his own name—description of the greatness of Śukreśvara; thereafter, Rāhu established a *liṅga* with the permission of Śiva; and the statement of the fruits resulting from the worship of Saurīśvara, such as the removal of the affliction caused by the planet Saturn.)

At one time, having heard from the mouth of Vasiṣṭha that "when Śani pierces Rohiṇī, there will be a two-year drought and a famine," Daśaratha mounted his chariot and went by way of Ākāśagiri to the presence of Raśanāveśvara to wage war against him. When Niśicara saw Daśaratha’s valor and observed the destruction of all his weapons prompted by his glance, he spoke out of fear, saying, "Choose a boon. Then—

The excellent propitiation of Śanaiścara by Daśaratha, who was wandering about distressed due to the affliction caused by Rāhu; then, the composition of a hymn to Śanaiścara by Daśaratha; the declaration by Śanaiścara that he would not cause further suffering through the recitation of his own hymn; and the description of the majesty of Śanaiśvareśvara. The description of the majesty of Rāhaveśvara, installed by Rāhu.

For the sake of attaining lordship over the planets, Ketu propitiated Śiva and, by his command, established Ketavīśvara to the north of Rāhu; the description of the majesty of Ketavīśvara. Thus ends the [section].

Ka. Ma: A description of the majesty of the five Siddhādi-liṅgas. First, a description of the majesty of Kapiñjaleśvara, who was established by King Kapila after he had performed austerities; [this is] the description of Soma through twenty-seven verses, including the propitiation of Somīśvara at Prabhāsa for the sake of Soma’s favor, and the installation of the liṅga named Varāroheśvara in the vicinity of Somīśvara, [namely] the Varāroheśvara-liṅga.

To Śaṅkara, Pārvatī said: "Since you lack a sixth face, how can the six-faced [Skanda] be given? O Lord, describe the majesty of the Goddess. Thus, by means of the three powers of Rudra, there is the protection of those beginning with Sadojāta and ending with Picu from fear and distress in the various directions; the description of the majesty of the Goddess Ajā; the description of the majesty of the Goddess Rudrīcasvarā; therefore, the description of the majesty of the Lord Ajādha; the description of the majesty of Lakṣmīśvara.

... 7. A description of the greatness of Bāḍaveśvara Liṅga: ... [The goddess Sarasvatī, assuming the form of a mare, arrived at Prabhāsa-kṣetra; having performed rites such as the acquisition of knowledge in the ocean, she established two Liṅgas. A description of the greatness of the Ṛṣyeśvara Liṅga. ... ;

The description of Pārvatī performing penance in the great forest of Krodhana out of anger toward Śiva; then, the granting of boons to Pārvatī by the gratified Śiva; the statement that the sight of that penance grove yields the fruit of the accomplishment of all goals; the installation of a *liṅga* there; the description of the majesty of Gaurī’s penance grove; and the description of the majesty of the Gaurīśvara *liṅga*. ... va.

[Description of the greatness of the mobile *liṅga* of Varuṇeśvara installed by Varuṇa; description of the greatness of Īśiśvara installed by the wife who was tormented by grief for her husband; ... description of the greatness of Jaḍhavāsa Gaṇapati.]

[And] the description of the greatness of Kumāreśvarī established by Śākalya at Ṣaṇmukha; [and] how, having propitiated Śiva through royal offerings, Śākalya installed a liṅga; and how that liṅga was given the names Īśvara, Gaurīśvara, Śākalyeśvara, and Śākalyeśvara during the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages; [and] the description of the greatness of Śākalyeśvara-liṅga.

The mention of names such as Kalakaleśvara, who exists differently across the four yugas, and Kamīśvara, Aṇueśvara, Nāradeśvara, Daśavareśvara, and Kalakaleśvara; the account of how, once during the junction between the Kali and Dvāpara ages, Nārada established the *liṅga* at Prabhāsa in Veṅkaṭa; and thereafter, having gone to Gāṃva, Nārada performed the great sacrifice named Pauṇḍarīka—these are the subjects of the chapters.

Chapter 10: Indivisible objects of perception; a description of the great temple of Ṭhakurī Rāmā near Karakaṭheśvara; a description of the majesty of the Uttakeśvara Liṅga established there by Viṣṇu after he had cast the Daitya Medhavāhana into his own belly with a kick from his foot, where it remained under the name Ādinārāyaṇa; and the account of its continued presence.

The description of the greatness of Ādinārāyaṇa; the account of a certain bird who, together with his wife, built a nest on a single tree; then the narration of the incident involving the food offered by the one named Saṃnidhi; there, Viṣṇu, along with his retinue, took up residence; thereafter, for the protection of the nest, the bird, accompanied by his wife, abandoned Mathurā and went to Prabhāsa; and then, at the time of their capture—Viṣṇu and the others.

On the shore of the ocean, by the power of performing a circumambulation of Vaiśvānareśvara even without effort, Kṛṣṇa brought Saṃnihitī there in a previous birth through mere meditation; the description of the fruit of merit obtained by bathing therein is given. Then follows the description of the succession of births of Agastya, and the description of the power of making gifts and other acts performed there by Agastya as he remembered his previous birth. Finally, there is the description of the majesty of Saṃnihitī.

(The description of the exhaustion of the fruits of their actions; the description of the majesty of Vaiśvānareśvara; during the period of living incognito, the establishment of directions by the Pāṇḍavas upon reaching Prabhāsa with five [names]; the description of the majesty of Chakulīśvara; the description of the majesty of the [sacred] sites; the description of the majesty of the Gautameśvara site; the enumeration of the names of the eleven Rudras; therein, first, the description of the majesty of Bhūteśvara Rudra.)

In the first section, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Daityasūdana," there is a description of the names beginning with Vāmana and ending with Daityasūdana; then follows the description of the greatness of Nīrasadra. Therein, during the hymn of Viṣṇu by Daityajita, there is an account of the various incarnations of Viṣṇu; thereafter, the description of the sacred sites (tīrthas) of Cakrapālīśvara Rudra by Viṣṇu.

[The account of] how, with the assistance of Dha, the gods slew the Daityas and established the Blessed One at the command of the slayer of Daityas; a description of the names of Vṛṣabheśvara occurring in the Bhṛtikalpa; a description of the greatness of the Liṅga named Vṛṣabheśvara installed by Vṛṣabha, including the narrative of the fruits of worship such as fasting and other rites performed during the month of Māgha.

A description of the origin of Cakratīrtha and the greatness of its gift; a detailed account of Ayaṃbakeśvara, including the mention of its names and designations in each Yuga; the performance of bathing, giving of gifts, and other rites at Ayaṃbakeśvara; the slaying of Mahiṣāsura—who had become intoxicated by the boon granted by Brahmā—after he died, and the subsequent unification of the gods to perform the funeral rites; the description of the Phalaka; and a description of the greatness of Ayaṃbakeśvara.

Nārada accepted that woman as his wife; Mahiṣāsura’s obedience to his command; Nārada’s speech; the description of the majesty of Aghoreśvara; having heard [this], Mahiṣāsura went with his army to the presence of that woman; the description of Mahiṣāsura by Mahākāleśvara; the description of its fame in that age by the name Citrāṅgadeśvara; and the Goddess, having observed the intention in Citrāṅgada... from her own body.

The slaying of Rātaśca and the manifestation of the Goddess; thereafter, the establishment of the fame of that Goddess by the Lord under the name Mahākāleśvara and the description of the majesty of the Mahākāleśvara Liṅga; the destruction of the demon Mahiṣāsura and the hymn of praise offered to that Goddess by the gods; and then, the description by the gods of the majesty of that Goddess as Bhaireveśvara.

In that very place, there is the description of the establishment [of the deity], the exposition of the ritual for the worship of the Goddess, the recitation of the sword-mantra (*khaḍgamantra*), and the glorification of the greatness of the threefold hymn to the goddess Dugodā. Therein is the description of the three types of *kūṭha*, the glorification of the greatness of the lineage of the lords of yoga (*yogīśvaravaṃśa*), and the glorification of the greatness of the temple of Kāmeśvara.

— Chapter 6: The sages, oppressed by the Daityas known as Meṣavāhana, perform a hymn of praise to Viṣṇu; having heard that hymn, [Viṣṇu] out of compassion describes the majesty of the Yogeśvara Liṅga; and for the sake of the auspicious Daṇḍapāṇi, the Earth, oppressed by the burden of the Daityas, goes to Prabhāsa.

Therein, after establishing the Earth-goddess in her proper place and propitiating Rudra, there is a description of obtaining Rudra’s grace; a description of the majesty of Prithvishvara (Chandreshvara); and within the description of the majesty of Kshirodadhisha, an account of how Paundraka, while residing in Varanasi, assumed the emblems of Vasudeva and engaged in battle with Vasudeva, wherein Vasudeva slew Paundraka.

The creation of a magical female spirit (*kṛtyā*) by Vāsudeva, the son of Pāṇḍu; the defeat of that *kṛtyā* by Vāsudeva in the form of Sudarśana; the flight of that vanquished *kṛtyā* to heaven for refuge; then, for the sake of protecting the *kṛtyā*, Śaṅkara’s striking of Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana—sent forth by Viṣṇu—with his own arrows; and seeing Sudarśana approaching after having accomplished its task and returned with the arrow of Śiva, the Blessed One [Viṣṇu] held the discus in his hand together with Śiva’s shaft.

Having undertaken the destruction of the *kṛtyā* created by Kālabhairava, [Kṛṣṇa] departed for Kāśī. There, at the request of the Gaṇas known as Daṇḍapāṇis who were stationed in that city for its protection, Kṛṣṇa remained under the name Cakradhara. A description of the majesty of Daṇḍapāṇi and Cakradhara follows, including the humiliation of Durvāsas. Then, out of anger, Durvāsas bestowed a curse upon Sāmba, saying, "Become a eunuch! Subsequently, Nārada arrived at Dvārakā to take away Kṛṣṇa’s discus.

Sāmba, arrogant because of his physical beauty, treated [the Gopīs] with contempt. Having resolved upon that enmity, at a certain time when Śrī Kṛṣṇa had begun playing in the water with His friends, Sāmba suddenly arrived there at the word of Nārada. Seeing Sāmba arrive at the door, the women became mentally distressed; Śrī Kṛṣṇa then gave them a curse, saying, "You shall fall into the hands of a thief," and He also bestowed a curse upon Sāmba that would bring him misfortune. Thereafter, by Sāmba... [previous]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the narrative continuity up to the point where the source text concludes.)

Having remembered the curse bestowed by the sage Durvāsas, Sāmba, being greatly distressed, went to the sacred field of Prabhāsa and performed the propitiation of the Sun-god (Āditya). There, he offered a hymn of praise to the Sun; at the conclusion of the hymn, the Sun, being pleased, granted the desired boons to Sāmba and brought about the removal of his leprosy. Then the name of that [place] was declared as Āditya. Right there, Sāmba installed the deity named Sāṃbādityeśvara. [This concludes] the description of the greatness of Sāṃbādityeśvara. In that place...

The description of the goddess Kaṇṭakañjashodhinī, who dwells near the Sāmbādityeśvara temple, by Sāmba—who was born of Kṛṣṇa and Jāmbavatī and was proud of his beauty—regarding the improper conduct [of the deity]. Topics: At the sacrifice of Dṛścya, Saṃkara arrived in the guise of a rogue, holding a skull-cup; he cast the skull-cup into the middle of the sacrificial pavilion. Seeing that skull-cup there, everyone assumed a state of joy. Then, through the praise of the great sages, he established a Liṅga in the Pramāsakṣetra under his own name.

The description of the installation of the *liṅga* by Prasyuṣeśvara; the description of the greatness of Anirasthāpiteśvara; the installation of a *liṅga* by the Vasu named Prabhāsa; the description of the greatness of Prabhāseśvara; the manifestation of his own form by Maheśvara; the installation of a *liṅga* there under the name Kapāṭeśvara; the description of the greatness of Kapāṭeśvara; and how it became renowned by the name Koṭīśvara after ten million Brahmins performed austerities at Kapāṭeśvara and installed a *liṅga*.

The instrument [of creation]; the description of the greatness of Koṭīśvaraṅga; within the description of the greatness of Brahmā, the description of the greatness of the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) in his forms as Bādarūpin and Dadhirūpin; thereafter, the calculation of the duration of Brahmā’s lifespan from day to night; the separate enumeration of the names of twenty-seven kalpas, fourteen Indras, and fourteen Manus; the description of the establishment of the Liṅga at Brahmeśvara after explaining the reason for Brahmā’s performance of penance and the installation of the Liṅga at Prabhāsa.

In the middle section of the pilgrimage, there is a description of the majesty of the Lord; a description of how Yama meted out punishment to the lords of the four quarters who reviled the Brahmins; a statement regarding the fruits of protecting the twice-born; a description of the various classes of Brahmins, such as the Prājāpatya and others; a description of the rules for the Cāndrāyaṇa and other vows within the duties of the four castes; a description of the praise of Brahmins; a description of the ritual for worship with the sixteen services accompanied by mantras; and a description of the Brahma-pilgrimage, [beginning with] Brahmā’s...

The description of the abode of residence; the praise of the greatness of Brahmā in his form as Bāra; the description of the majesty of each of the Īśvaras; the birth of a son named Prayūṣa—counted among the eight Vasus—from the maiden Viśvānī, one of the sixty daughters given by Dakṣa to Dharma; and, in the context of describing the procedure for the worship of Brahmā by that son named Prayūṣa, the description of the honor accorded to Nārāyaṇa through his excellence and his status as the one to be worshipped.

In the description of the Brahma-pūjā, there is a detailed account of various forms of devotion; then follows the exposition of the *pañcagavya* ritual. Next is the departure of Rāma—accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa—into the forest, along with the description of the *gāyatrī-nyāsa* and the *rameśvara-tīrtha*. Thereafter, having completed his journey, Rāma proceeds to Prabhāsa. There, at night, the sleeping Rāma beholds his father in a dream riding a chariot. Subsequently, Rāma reports the events of the dream to the Brahmins, and then, according to the words of the Brahmins, by Rāma...

The performance of a *śrāddha* ceremony by taking large, sweet fruits such as jujubes (*badara*); the establishment of the deity named Rāmeśvara; a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Rāmeśvara field; [the description of the majesty of Maṇeśvara established by Lakṣmaṇa]; [the description of the majesty of Jānakīdeva established by Sītā]; and in the description of the majesty of Vāmanasvāmī, the carrying away of Bali to the netherworld (*pātāla*) by Viṣṇu after requesting three strides of land.

In the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*, the description of the origin of the Viṣṇupadī Gaṅgā through the establishment of the second foot [of Viṣṇu]; the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Vāmanasvāmī; the majesty of the Viṣṇupadī Gaṅgā; the description of the majesty of Puṣkara resulting from the Viṣṇupadī Gaṅgā’s arrival at Puṣkara; the description of the majesty of Puṣkareśvara; and the description of the majesties of Śaṅkhodakakuṇḍeśvara and Gaurī, as well as the description of the majesty of Bhūtanātheśvara.

In the *Gopyādityavīryamāhātmya*, [it is told] how Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by his sons and the cowherd girls, went to Prabhāsa; how the Yādavas, having reached Mount Raivataka there, established pavilions marked with banners and discs everywhere; likewise, the gift of land filled with palanquins; then, having set aside plots of land measuring one cubit at intervals, the construction of temples and other structures throughout those spaces; and the mention of the names of the sixteen cowherd girls who became the consorts of Kṛṣṇa.

In that very place, the construction of sixteen thousand charming dwellings by the gopīs, the installation of the Sun-god there, the naming of him Gopyāditya, the return of all those men and all those women to Dvārakā, and a description of the great festival upon the granting of the boon to Gopyāditya.

The description of the majesty of the manifestation of the goddess Balātibala-Daityayanī; the narration of the birth of the Daityas Balātibala and Atibala; how those two Daityas, along with their armies, defeated the gods and established their sovereignty over the three worlds; the listing of the names of the sixty-four Yoginīs; the description of the majesty of the goddess Balātibala-Daityayanī; and the description of the majesty of Gopīśvara, who was installed by Gopī.

The son of Jamadagni, Rāma, established a *liṅga* at Prabhāsa after killing Mārica. Then, the Gandharva king Citrāṅgada, having propitiated the Lord, performed the installation of a *liṅga* there. Regarding the description of Citrāṅgada: while Rāvaṇa was traveling by means of the Puṣpaka aerial chariot on his world-conquest, he saw that the chariot had become stuck at Prabhāsa; [thereupon] Arundhatī, having performed penance for the sake of increasing her husband’s good fortune, [established a deity] there as Saubhāgyarūpā Tārā.

A description of the greatness of Śāṇḍilyeśvara established by Śāṇḍilya, who, after performing penance for the destruction of Tāraka, was aided by the daughter of Ṛtadhvaja (Umā) when Indra and the other gods had been defeated; and a description of the greatness of Kṣemaṅkareśvara.

Then follows the description of the majesty of Sāgarāditya; [therein] the performance of a hymn of praise by Kaṇva to remove his suffering. Having heard that hymn composed by him, the Goddess assumed a form of great splendor and, holding lotuses in many hands, engaged in battle with the two Daityas, Bala and Atibala. Therein, the Goddess brought about the destruction of the Daityas Bala and Atibala. Then follows the description of the majesty of the sixty-four Yoginīs. "What is this? Come here!"—thus [ends the section].

[The account of] the swift execution of his own command by the messenger, who, having arrived at the Prabhāsa-kṣetra with low-caste attendants, reported the greatness of the Prabhāsa-tīrtha to Rāvaṇa; then, the descent of Vibhāṇa at that Prabhāsa-kṣetra by that Rāvaṇa, the establishment of a shrine in his own name there at the word of Sarvanāgara, and the description of the greatness of the Rāvaṇeśvara [liṅga].

Then, having attained *siddhi*, the installation of the Goddess and the naming of her as Saubhāgyeśvarī; the description of the taking up of Saubhāgyeśvarī; the consecration of the linga; the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Paureśvara; the description of the majesty of Akṣamālādevī and Maraseneśvara; [and] the topics concerning Bhavvāyā. (Skanda Purāṇa)

The sale of Bhavānī by the four attendants, Pāṇḍupata and others; the propitiation of the God and the installation of the image of Pāṇḍupati by the son of Pāṇḍu; the description of the great beauty of the river Citrapathā; when Yama, having beheld the wonderful temple, offered his own two eyes, the description of the majesty of the boon-granting Pāṇḍupati. ...

The sister named Citrā remains in the form of a river for the sake of searching for her own brother; the description of the origin of the great Dhuveśvara on the Citrapathā river; Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, worships the Lord at Prabhāsa and performs a hymn of praise to Śiva; the installation of the Liṅga named Dhruveśvara; the description of the majesty of the Dhruveśvara Liṅga; and the description of the majesty of the Kapardicintāmaṇi.

Description of the various seats and holy sites (*pīṭasthāna*) in Prabhāsa within the majesty of the Vaiṣṇavī power named Siddhalakṣmī; therein, the description of the majesty of Citreśvara; the description of the majesty of the Siddhalakṣmī seat located in the sacred field (*kṣetra*) of Prabhāsa; the description of the majesty of Vicitreśvara; [the description of the majesty of] Mahākālī-pīṭha; ... the description of the majesty of Puṣkara-kuṇḍa.

The journey of Brahmā to Prabhāsa together with the gods while the sacrifice of Soma was being proclaimed; the description of the greatness of Gajakumbhodra for the purpose of establishing Somanātha; the invitation extended to Brahmā by Candra; and then, when the time for the installation of the Linga arrived, the curse of Pitāmaha.

The establishment of the quarters by Dharmarāja after performing austerities at Prabhāsa; the mental recollection of Puṣkara during the festival of Yameśvara on the banks of the Narmadā; the arrival of the Puṣkaras there due to that recollection; the naming of that holy site Puṣkarāvarta because of the formation of whirlpools right there; and the description of the greatness of the Puṣkarāvarta river and the Brahmakuṇḍa created by Brahmā. In the section on the greatness of Kuṇḍaleśvara, King Sudhanvan married Sunandā, the daughter of the King of Gāndhāra, and [the account of] Queen Sunandā—

A description of the greatness of Śītalā Gaurī, who brings an end to suffering. ... Having received joy from her, [the king] performed vows such as the fast of Śivarātri together with her; therein is a description of the greatness of the Lord Romaśeśvara installed by Māṭhama at that place. — In the description of the greatness [of the vow], a merchant named Dhana performed the fast of Śivarātri; a description of the greatness of her Śivarātri vow, which was fulfilled through the grace of the Lord of Kāñcī.

While the merchant Kuṇḍalī was engaged in searching for the wife of the merchant named Dhana, he performed austerities for a thousand years, subsisting month after month on a drop of water from the tip of a blade of kusha grass; one night, he cut off the ear of the merchant Dhana’s wife and made it into a cloth filter—protect that [act]!

Having established the guardians of the directions and described the majesty of Vṛṣabheśvara, [the narrative proceeds as follows]: having heard the account of Karṇatāla, Koṭāhaṅka performed the severing of the skull of Kṛṇḍalī. When his father had passed away, the son named Citra, belonging to the scribe (kāyastha) family of Sarpamitra, went to Prabhāsa and performed the propitiation of the Sun. Then Anīka and Sudarśana went there to see that skull; having gone to Prabhāsa, Anīka and Sudarśana praised the Sun in many ways.

The granting of his own desired boon; then, seeing Kuṇḍarīka immersed in a lake for the purpose of bathing, the showing of the Kuṇḍakūpa; the description of the majesty of the Kuṇḍakūpa; by the command of Yama, Citra’s being led to the world of Yama along with Sadeda by the servants of Yama; and there, the description of the majesty of Prāṇibhairava as told by Yama.

The establishment of Vittrarupeśvara at Caritrarekhaka; the description of the greatness of Naradeśvara installed by Brahmā at Pramāsa under the name Citreśvara; the installation of Siga; the description of the greatness of Citrāditya and Agnideva; and the description of the greatness of Sāvitrīśvara and Mairava installed by Sāvitrī. Indeed, so it is.

When the sacrifice was commenced by Brahmā, he realized that it could not be completed due to the absence of sacrificial materials; thus, at dawn, he performed worship with whatever materials were available. Then, by the command of Śiva, Sarasvatī brought forth a stream of water in the form of material wealth. Having bound a golden lotus-stalk produced from that Sarasvatī to a great amount of wealth, Brahmā brought the sacrifice to completion. There, he installed the Liṅga known by the name Hiraṇyeśvara, and the majesty of Hiraṇyeśvara is described.

Description of the greatness of Gāyatrīdevī established by Gāyatrī. Description of the greatness of Viṣṇu, who, having performed penance, established the Raṇeśvara shrine and the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Description of the greatness of Ranneśvara and Satyabhāmeśvara. Description of the greatness of Anaṅgadeva established by Anaṅga. Description of the greatness of Raṇakuṇḍa. Description of the greatness of the Bhaṭāraka of Śaivaṭakarāja. Description of the greatness of Aṣṭakuṇḍeśvara. ...

The description of the greatness of the Nāsavyeśvara Liṅga; ... the description of the greatness of the Aśvineśvara Liṅga; ... the description of the greatness of Sāvitrī, including the account of the origin of the Vedas and the creation by Śaṃkara in his chariot; then, the performance of preparations for the sacrificial rite by Bṛhaspati; then, Bṛhaspati’s arrival at the Puṣkara Tīrtha and the clearing of the sacrificial ground; and when the Adhvaryu priest extended an invitation to Sāvitrī for the sacrifice, although she was invited, Sāvitrī [remained]... [the rest of the sentence appears to be truncated].

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Vaṭasāvitrī vow: therein, King Aśvapati, having expressed his concern regarding the removal of his childlessness by declaring to him, "She must not go alone," caused Sāvitrī to be attached to the task of fetching water for his household; thereafter, that Adhvaryu priest informed Brahmā, "Sāvitrī has not come."

Then, overcome with anger, Brahmā issued an order for Rākā to bring another wife; subsequently, Rākā took a certain cowherd girl and brought her to Brahmā’s presence; thereafter, Brahmā married that cowherd girl and commenced the sacrifice.

Then, the arrival of Sāvitrī, who was being escorted by the divine ladies, at that sacrifice; there, seeing the sacrifice commenced by Jaḍyaṇa after he had married another woman, Sāvitrī, overcome with anger, uttered a rebuke against Brahmā. When Brahmā explained the reason for marrying another wife upon hearing Sāvitrī’s words, Sāvitrī nevertheless bestowed a curse upon Brahmā in the form of his becoming unworthy of worship. Then, Śakra, having appointed an Ābhīrī woman for the sake of Jaḍya’s marriage, [engaged] with the gods in battle against Śakra.

The pronouncement of a curse that brings about defeat; likewise, Sāvitrī’s granting of a curse to Viṣṇu for causing the separation from her husband; Sāvitrī’s granting of a similar curse to other gods as well; Viṣṇu’s offering of praise to Sāvitrī; Gāyatrī’s granting of boons to all to dispel the curse given by Sāvitrī; the description of the procedure for the recitation (*japa*) of Gāyatrī; Sāvitrī’s departure to Prabhāsa; and the description of the greatness of the Sāvitrī-mādhava situated at Prabhāsakhetra. ...

The performance of worship and propitiation of Sāvitrī; the granting of a boon by the pleased goddess; the birth of a daughter named Sāvitrī to King Aśvapati; the firm resolve of that daughter Sāvitrī to marry none other than Satyavān as her husband; the narration of the entire account of Satyavān to Aśvapati by Nārada; the description of the marriage between Sāvitrī and Satyavān; and then, at a certain time, [her departure] for the purpose of gathering sacrificial wood, kuśa grass, and other materials.

Satyavat’s departure for the forest with Sāvitrī; while he was splitting wood, a headache arose, and Satyavat, abandoning the logs, approached Sāvitrī and fell asleep on her lap. At that moment, Yama arrived; the description of the dialogue between Yama and Sāvitrī; Yama extracting the life-force (*jīva*) from Satyavat’s body and departing; Sāvitrī following Yama; and although Yama made many attempts to dissuade Sāvitrī from following him, she remained steadfast.

The granting of a boon to her was witnessed; by the grace of Yama, having restored her husband to life, she completed the Sāvitrī-vrata over three nights. Then, together with Satyavat, she returned to her own hermitage. This section describes the greatness of the Sāvitrī-vrata, its rules, worship, offerings, and so forth, as well as the concluding rites (*udyāpana*) for the Sāvitrī-vrata.

In the description of the greatness of the Bhūtamātṛkās during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, following the account of Pārvatī’s birth on Mount Śveta from the curse of Dakṣa, there is a description of the birth of one Nārī from the menstrual flow (rajas) of Pārvatī while the two were sporting for many thousands of divine years after their marriage. This includes a description of that Nārī’s own form, a description of the names of her other companions, and likewise a description of the birth of one Puruṣa from the seed of Śiva.

The command issued by Kāreṇu for the two sons of Śiva to go to Prabhāsa; the granting of a place upon their shoulders; a description of the festival of the goddess Pratipatpraśṛti; a description of the birth of fifty million Kapi-dās from the body of that Bhūtamātṛ; a description of the majesty of Bhūtamātṛkā; a description of the greatness of Śālkaṭaṅkaṭā; and a description of the majesty of Śaravasvateśvarī.

Māna-dṛśaratha, having performed austerities, established Bharateśvara; the establishment of Bharateśvara by Bharata, the son of Āgnīdhra, who divided the continents into nine parts and assigned them to his nine sons, including the installation of Bharateśvara at Prabhāsa on the ninth continent, Dvīpārikā; a description of the majesty of Bharateśvara;
and a description of the majesties of Kuśakeśvara, Garageśvara, Puṣkareśvara, and Maitrayeśvara.

The description of the greatness of Kuntīśvara established by Kuntī at the time of the arrival of the Pāṇḍavas, endowed with splendor, at Prabhāsa; the description of the greatness of Arkaṣṭhala; ... the description of the greatness of Siddheśvara. (End of section.)

Having heard that Kṛṣṇa had gone to the state of being cooked after bringing about the destruction of the Yādavas, Balabhadra performed a ritual immersion (*mamana*) at Prabhāsa. There, he established a *liṅga*. Then, assuming the form of a serpent (*nāga*), he went to Pātāla to bestow a title upon Balabhadra; consequently, that *liṅga* was given the name Nāgeśvara. [This is] the description of the greatness of the descent of the Nāgeśvara [liṅga].... ...

A description of the greatness of the five Prabhāsas; therein, Śiva’s journey to the Dāruka forest for the sake of alms; a description of how the women there were inflamed with passion upon seeing the form of Śiva as he wandered in the Dāruka forest; then, by their husbands who were filled with anger, a curse was cast upon Śiva; by that curse, his fall occurred right there; a description of the trembling of the earth caused by that fall; and the destruction of the entire host of demons following the great lamentation and prayers of the sages.

The departure of the frightened gods to the presence of Viṣṇu; then, at the word of Viṣṇu, the departure of the gods to Prabhāsa; the establishment of that Liṅga in that very place. Description of the greatness of the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa-māhātmya*; description of the greatness of Rudreśvara... description of the greatness of Karmamoṭī... description of the greatness of Mokṣasvāmī... description of the greatness of Ajīgartavada... description of the greatness of Vidavekavara... description of the greatness of Amareśvara.

The introduction to the narration of the majesty of Vṛddhabhṛbhāsa; the departure of the sages for Prabhāsa with the desire to behold the Lord; the sages’ expression of grief upon seeing the Lord covered by a banyan tree; the sages’ determination regarding the matter of the *ṛgveda*; the killing of the Sūta by Caṇḍabhadra, who could not tolerate his own humiliation; and then, after Caṇḍabhadra felt remorse and lamented in sorrow, the hearing of the advice given by a voice from the sky.

Having approached Prabhāsa for the purpose of perceiving its defects, he performed austerities and established a Liṅga in his own name; having performed penance at Rāma, he performed further austerities, during which the sages undergoing penance were overtaken by old age; thereupon, the gratified God described to them the greatness of the Lord of the Liṅgas (Liṅgeśvara).

...the granting of a vision; the departure of the sages to their respective abodes following the recitation of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures; the establishment of a Liṅga by Maṅki at Prabhāsa for the purpose of dispelling the pride of Kuñjara, prompted by the sages' advanced age and their desire to hear the majesty of Maṅkeśvara; the naming of the place "Vṛddhaprabhāsa" due to the disrespect shown toward the Ṛgveda during his penance; a description of the majesty of Vṛddhaprabhāsa; ... a description of the majesty of Maṅkeśvara; ...

The establishment of the Liṅga by Paraśurāma after performing penance; a description of the majesty of Jalaprabhāsa; and a description of the greatness of the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean.

The description of the greatness of the Jāmadagnīśvarī-gamā; the narration of the procedure for *śrāddha* rites; the description of the times for *śrāddha*; the description of the purification of the seven types of substances; the description of the greatness of the five holy sites (*prabhāsakṣetra*) on the day of *śrāddha*;

the explanation of terms such as *pāvana* and others; the description of the Brahmins eligible for *śrāddha*; and, within the description of the greatness of the *smara* performed during *śrāddha*, first the account of Dakṣa’s arrangement of his hundred sons and the description of the examination of Brahmins.

Then, when the sacrifice was commenced by Dakṣa, Pārvatī, having witnessed her own insult, performed the renunciation of her body; followed by a description of the excellence of the rule of silence (*mauna*) through the narration of the *śrāddha* ritual, and a description of those entitled to the *śrāddha*. Next, there is a determination of the months and other times for the *śrāddha*; then, the account of how Śiva, being enraged, created Vīrabhadra and sent him with his armies to destroy Dakṣa’s sacrifice, including a description of the destruction of that sacrifice by Vīrabhadra, a description of the company at the *śrāddha* rite, and a detailed description of the *śrāddha* ceremony itself.

The inquiry into that; the description of the greatness of the fruit of giving food such as *vakharā* and other offerings during a *śrāddha* ceremony held by the gods who were defeated by Vīrabhadra near Viṣṇu at the Ocean of Milk; the consideration of worthy and unworthy recipients (*pātra-apātra*) regarding the act of giving; the departure; then, the engagement in battle between Viṣṇu and Vīrabhadra; therein, the partial defeat of Vīrabhadra; the exposition of the duties of the stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*); the exposition of the practice of duty during times of adversity; [and the matters] on the day of the *śrāddha*.

Upon seeing Śiva arrive there while he was engaged in sexual intercourse and other acts, Viṣṇu and the other gods spoke of the fault of that act. Then Śiva performed the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. Thereafter, Śiva deliberated upon the matter, taught the rules for the Ekādaśī vow, and established the determination regarding the Ṣaṭpiṇḍa and other rites.

Then follows the journey to the vicinity of the one who was unassailable even by the tormentors of Tāraka; the arousal of desire in the mind of Śiva by the command of Brahmā; the description of the taking up of Mākaṇḍeyeśvara as a boon; the request made to Kāmadeva by the gods to perform [the task]; and the reduction to ashes of Kāma, who had been appointed to his own office, upon being seen by Śiva.

Description of the greatness of Puruṣṭyeśvara; thereafter, the consolation of Rati, who was distressed by separation from her husband, through a voice from the sky; therein, a description of the greatness of Aṅgapuṣkareśvara; the establishment of [the deity]; a description of the greatness of Kṛtasmara, also known as Kāmakuṇḍa; a description of the greatness of Kratīśvara; and a description of the greatness of Kārabha-raśmaśāna.

The description of the supreme majesty of Kaśyapa; [the account of] Balabhadra drinking liquor for the sake of a journey during the time when the Kaurava-Pāṇḍava war was raging; the description of the supreme majesty of Kośikeśvara; his departure for the forest; there, having seen many sages and a charioteer residing in the hermitage of Kaśyapa, and likewise disregarding his own mind, the description of the supreme majesty of Kamāreśvara. Śaiva Purāṇa, Chapter 695.

The subjects of the fifth chapter: the description of the majesty of Gautameśvara; the description of the majesty of Bhairaveśvara; the description of the majesty of Devarājeśvara; the description of the majesty of Gaṅgā; the description of the majesty of Mānavairedavara; the description of the majesty of Gaṇapati; the description of the majesty of Nīlakaṇṭheśvara situated near Mārkaṇḍeya; and the description of the majesty of Vṛṣabhadhvajeśvara-Ṛṣigaṇa.

The description of the majesty of Pāṇḍavakūpa; the description of the majesty of Ṛṇamocaneśvara; the description of the majesty of Pāṇḍaveśvara; the description of the majesty of Rukmavatīśvara... [and] how Bharata, having performed ten horse-sacrifices at Bhṛbhāsa, established the Ṛgveda; the manifestation of the Daśāśvamedha Tīrtha (which appeared there under the name Gātrotsarga because Baṅbhadra sacrificed his own limbs), and the description of the majesty of Gātrotsargatīrtha.

The description of the greatness of Hātakya; the description of the greatness of performing śrāddha and other rites at Gātrotsarga-tīrtha; therein, within the description of Pretatīrtha, the greatness of the triad beginning with Śaṣṭhameṣa.

Then follows Gautama’s journey to the Gātroccarī-tīrtha; there, on the way, Gautama beholds the Vaiṣṇava forest; a description of the greatness of the Liṅga Durbāseśvara established by Durbāsas; there, upon seeing five ghosts (pretas) at that spot, Gautama causes them fear; the dialogue between Gautama and the ghosts; and how the ghosts, assuming their true forms before Gautama, perform a dance like that of the Yādava heroes, while the Yādavas are terrified by those ghosts who have become enraged.

The narration of the history of all [the Yādavas]; the description by the *pretas* of their own past actions that caused their state as *pretas*; the granting of a boon to the *Andhakas* for their liberation from *preta*-hood and the destruction of the *Kukura* clan; then, the description of the slaughter of the Yādava family by means of *eraka* grass; thereafter, having heard the cause, Gautama, by his command, went to the *Pretatīrtha* at Prabhāsa and performed the *śrāddha* rites for them; and by that, for all those who had died, [the liberation was achieved] through the remaining Yādava named Bāja.

The narration of the hymns of those [sages] beginning with Yadu; the description of the greatness of Pretatīrtha; the performance of the rites, the arrival at Bhr̥bhāsa, and the installation of the lingas; the description of the greatness of Vrajeśvara; the description of the greatness of Indrarāśeśvara; ... [238] the description of the greatness of Anarakeśvara; the command issued by Yama to his messengers to bring the Brāhmaṇa Devakṣema, a resident of Mathurā, preceded by the hearing of the duties to be performed; and the description of the greatness of Nāgarāditya.

The instrument [of the narrative]: then, having seen that Devadāru tree brought there, Yama’s refusal to bring it back, saying "We do not wish to take this," followed by the description of the greatness of Śrī Balarāma, Subhadrā, and Kṛṣṇa; the Brahmin’s display of his own lack of desire to go to the earth; then, the description by him [Yama] of the greatness of Śeṣa; and when questioned by the Brahmin, Yama’s description of hell to that Brahmin, including the defects such as sins that lead to the attainment of hell.

The description of the slaughter of Caṇḍa, Yuṇḍa, and others; the description of the Kāmarī-Mahāṣṭamī festival; the description of the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*); the description of the meritorious means for the destruction of hell; the description of the greatness of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) of Anarakeśvara and other mantras; the description of the greatness of Vicitraśvara; the description of the greatness of Megheśvara; and the description of the greatness of Nadayeśvara.

The description of the greatness of Piṅgānadīmāhasya; the description of the greatness of Barabhadreśvara; the description of the greatness of Gukeśvara; and the description of the greatness of Caṇḍeśvara. . . . ( . )

While King Durbhisahaka was offering a gift of grain and wealth to the sages, those sages prohibited that wealth and grain, abandoned it, and departed from there to go on a pilgrimage. Having traveled some distance, they saw lotus stalks (*bisāni*) in a pond; having gathered them and placed them on the bank, they performed their daily rites. Then, perceiving that someone had stolen those lotus stalks, they [realized] it was by truth.

The construction of the Dāpatha; there, Śakra, having arrived in the form of a dog, seized the food offerings—this being known, Śakra granted them boons. There, a pool was established under the name Ṛṣitīrtha, followed by a description of the greatness of Ṛṣitīrtha. Furthermore, King Nanda, afflicted with leprosy, established [a deity] for the propitiation of Sūrya; this is the description of the majesty of Nandāditya.

When the father passed away, Trita—the son of Atreya Khajañaka, the king of Saurāṣṭra, who was well-versed in the three Vedas (Ekata, Dvita, and Trita)—was established in the kingdom by his three brothers. Trita, however, became envious; he conspired with Ekata and Dvita to cast Trita into a well. Thereupon, Trita invoked the gods through mantras and satisfied them by means of those very incantations. Consequently, Ekata and Dvita were struck dumb and driven out from that place.

A description of the origin of Tanitakūpa; a description of the greatness of merit gained by performing *śrāddha* and other rites for the sake of one’s ancestors; a description of the greatness of Caritadūṣatīrtha. [The greatness of] Uvāṅeścara; a description of the greatness of Siddheśvara; a description of the greatness of Nyumatī; a description of the greatness of Bārāhasvāmī; a description of the greatness of Chāyāṅga; a description of the greatness of Nandinīguptā; and a description of the greatness of Kanaṅanada.
The description of the majesty of Kumbhīśvara; the description of the majesty of Gaṅgāpathagadavara; the description of the majesty of Camasodbheda; and the description of the majesty of Vidurāśrama.

The great sage Maṅkaṇaka, having approached the eastern Sarasvatī, performed austerities. When he had attained perfection through those austerities, he began dancing out of wonder and amazement at the production of sugar-cane juice from his hand. Thinking that the entire universe had begun to dance because Maṅkaṇaka was dancing, Śaṅkara arrived there and questioned Maṅkaṇaka regarding the cause of his dancing. Having learned the reason for Maṅkaṇaka’s dancing from him, Śaṅkara sprinkled ashes upon him with his own hand; by that, Maṅkaṇaka...

The cessation of activity by the astonished being; thereafter, the installation of the *liṅga* according to the word of Śaṅkara; a description of the majesty of the Jvālī-Sarasvatī-maṅka-śvara [temple]. ... (The topics include: a description of the majesty of the three cities (*tripura*) and the three parts (*aṅgatraya*). ... a description of the majesty of Rāḍa-tīrtha; ... a description of the majesty of Sūryaprācī. In that [section], a description of the majesty of Trinetreśvara. ... a description of the majesty of Umāpati at Devikā. & ( ,,. )

A description of the greatness of Bhūdharayajñavarāha. . . [Therein is described] how a certain other person named Śaidākha, having abandoned his own dharma, sustained his family by the profession of a hunter; how once, when he was engaged in the slaughter of animals along with his retinue, he was instructed in the principles of conduct regarding that month of Vaiśākha by sages; how they imparted a mantra to him; and how, through the power of that mantra, he attained the name of Vālmīki, and by the word of that sage, performed the worship of the Devikā river.

Description of the praise of the Siddhis; description of the majesty of Kāma, O Goddess; description of the majesty of Mūlasthāna; description of the list of one hundred and eight names of Sūrya; and, within the majesty of Cyavanāditya, description of the fruit of reciting the one hundred and eight names of Sūrya. . . .

The description of the majesty of Cyavaneśvara; the making of Aśvinīkumāras beautiful by Sukanyā; the restoration of her husband’s handsome form and youth by Sukanyā through their mutual effort; the description of how, at the word of Aśvinīkumāras, Cyavana attained a beautiful form by bathing with them in a pool; and the description of the majesty of Cyavaneśvara.

The performance of a sacrifice by Cyavana Maharṣi for the purpose of securing the right to participate in sacrifices for his two sons, Ādānī and Kumāra, whom he had assisted; and therein, within that sacrifice, the narration of the account of the emergence of the great Asura named Madana, who was created by Cyavana through the release of the *vajra* that had been obstructing the sacrificial portion of the Nāsatyas and by means of the power of the *chatyoddhava* mantra.

The description of Śakra’s seeking forgiveness from Cyavana after seeing him struck by an arrow; the account of Cyavana’s ascension to heaven and his requesting forgiveness for Śakra’s transgression; the description of the boon received by Cyavana; the description of the greatness of Sukanyā and the Apsaras; the description of the greatness of Daśāśramapada; and the description of the greatness of Ajāpāleśvarī.

Description of the greatness of Bārāka situated to the east of Agastya’s hermitage; description of the greatness of Bhadrakāśī; description of the greatness of the Bhadrakārī river. Description of the origin of Kumāra-sthāna and the greatness of Kuberamāhātmya; description of the greatness of the river Ṛṣitoyā; description of the greatness of the Bākhāka situated to the north of Agastya; narration of the conclusion of the story concerning how Vātāpi, who had assumed the form of a ram through deceit, was devoured by Agastya; and [the account] of Aṅgārapāta, Aṅgāreśvara, Viśvabhīṣaṇa, and Carvaṅgeśa.

The description of the greatness of the three [deities] beginning with Bhidhāṅga; the account of the origin of Kubera’s city and the description of the greatness of Somanātha established by Kubera; the description of the greatness of Puṣyaśvara, preceded by [the account of] Joganyeśvara.

The description of the greatness of Candrodaka-tīrtha, followed by the description of the greatness of Indrarāśi; the offering of praise by all the sages; then, by the gratified Brahmā, the sending of Sarasvatī to the Devadāru forest; the performance of penance there by the sages; the description of the origin of Ṛṣitoyā; the description of the merit of taking [the water] from Ṛṣitoyā; the description of the three pools known as Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava, and Raudra; and the description of the merit of visiting the Gapabhraya-tīrtha. 8.

*Caṃbha-ka*: Nārada, having seen himself pursued by a crow, gave a curse to Sāmba; Sāmba, in turn, gave the curse "Become possessed of old age" to Nārada. Nārada, for the removal of his old age, performed worship of the Sun (Āditya) and installed a *liṅga* at that very place, Trabhāsa. A description of the majesty of Nāradāditya follows. There, at Trabhāsa, Sāmba performed penance to counteract his own curse and installed a *liṅga*, [known as] Sāṃvāditya.

The description of the majesty of Māhchhatmya; the description of the majesty of Aparanāśayana; the description of the origin and majesty of Mūlacaṇḍī; the description of the majesty of Caturmukhavināyaka; the description of the majesty of Kebadeśvara; the description of the majesty of Gopārasāmihari; the description of the majesty of Bakuṭasvāmin; the description of the majesty of Uttarāka; the description of the majesty of the confluence at Ṛṣitīrtha; the description of the majesty of Marudāyodevī; and the description of the majesty of Kṣemāditya.

Description of the majesty of Mahodaya. ... Description of the majesty of Saṃgameśvara. ... Description of the majesty of Unnata-Vināyaka. ... Description of the majesty of Taṅasvāmin. Description of the majesty of Kālamegha.

Ka: A description of the majesty of Rakimiṇī; Dha: A description of the majesty of Rigeśvarabhadra; Śa: The defeat of the gods by the Daitya named Vaṅga, who arose from Śaṃśṛraṅga; thereafter, the Daitya’s propitiation of Lord Viṣṇu and his presentation of his own suffering; then, the battle between Viṣṇu and that [Daitya]; when their battle had commenced, Hara (Śiva) created the Taptodaka-kuṇḍa for the sake of destroying the fatigue of Viṣṇu; and [the account of] bathing there in that Taptodaka-kuṇḍa.

The laughter of Viṣṇu when his throat was stepped upon by Śambara with his palm; the granting of a boon to him by Viṣṇu who was pleased; the establishment [of the deity] under the name Taṅgasvāmī according to his word; the description of the majesty of Talasvāmī; the description of the majesty of the Śaṅkhāvatārī-tīrtha... In the description of the majesty of Goṣpada-tīrtha, the account of the birth of Pṛthu from Vena, the son of Aṅga; and [the account of] the earth being consumed by Pṛthu...
The description of the milking of the earth in the form of a cow for the sake of producing offspring, and the causing of the birth of subjects by Pṛthu as if by a son.

810.1 | Recalling the sinful deeds of his father again and again, Pṛthu traveled to many holy places (*tīrtha-kṣetra*) in order to purify him. Thinking that his father’s sins might not have been washed away anywhere else, Pṛthu went to Goṣpada. By performing ablutions and other rites at the Goṣpada-tīrtha, he shook off all the sins of his father and attained liberation (*mokṣa*). This is the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Goṣpada-tīrtha.

... [The description of the greatness of the *Huṃkāra* well; the description of the destruction of Nārāyaṇagṛha; the dragging away of Āpastamba by the fishermen; then, the fishermen, terrified of the fish, offered a prayer to Āpastamba; regarding the payment of the price for Āpastamba, the description of the greatness of the gift of cows in the dialogue between Nābhāga and Ambarīṣa; in that same place, the description of the greatness of the *Gomā* [river]; the establishment of the deity named Jāyeśvara; and the description of the greatness of Jāyeśvarī and Caṇḍīśvara.]...

The description of the greatness of Ādrāpūravinrarāja; the description of the greatness of the Karāṅgaṇḍa-tīrtha of Candreśvara; the description of the greatness of the ritual for the Kapi-khāṣaṣṭhī-vow at Kapiradhārā and the greatness of Kapiṭeśvara; the description of the greatness of Jaradraveśvara; the description of the greatness of Naṭeśvara; the description of the greatness of Karkoṭakārka; the description of the greatness of Hāṭakeśvara; the description of the greatness of Nāradeśvarī; and the description of the greatness of Maṃtravibhūṣaṇā-Gaurī.

The description of the majesty of Dugakūṭagaṇapati; the description of the majesty of Kauravendravārī; the description of the majesty of Suparṇeśā; the description of the majesty of Mahātīrtha; the description of the majesty of Karamāṭa; and the description of the majesty of Gaparaśvara.

The description of the greatness of Vahusuvarṇeśvara; likewise, the performance of penance by Āpastamba in the waters of the auspicious Sarasvatī; there, the objects of sense with Bharata and others along with the fishermen; the description of the greatness of Paṇaśageśvara... the description of the greatness of Koṭīśvara; the description of the greatness of Nārāyaṇatīrtha; the description of the greatness of Śṛṅgāreśvara; the description of the greatness of Mākaṇḍereśvara.

The description of the greatness of Koṭidamaṇḍukeśvara; the description of the greatness of the eleven Rudras. ... [The description of] the greatness of Hiraṇyatuṇḍapuradharyardhakandeśvara; the description of the greatness of Saṃbateśvara; and the description of the greatness of various scattered sacred sites (*prakīrṇasthāna*).
Thus ends the first chapter, the most delightful "The Glory of Prabhāsa," within the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa.
Now begins the second [chapter] on the majesty of Bakhrāpatha (Giranāra) in the Abhāsa-khaṇḍa.

In the *Dāmodara-māhātmya*, there is the arrival of many sages at the place known as Rajas belonging to a certain king; therein, the sages describe to the king the greatness of all the sacred fords (*tīrthas*) and the holy field (*kṣetra*). Then follows the description of the origin of the name, the description of the greatness of Dāmodara, the etymological derivation of the word *bhava*, the description of the establishment of the deity, and the description of the greatness of Bhava.

In that forest, through a certain reading of the *Vanapāṭha*, it was told to King Bhoja that there existed a description of the greatness of the Gandharva mountain, a description of the ritual for the pilgrimage to Cakratīrtha, and a vision of the twelve forms of Viṣṇu. Upon hearing this, the greedy Bhoja gave much wealth to that forest-guardian (*vanapāṭha*). Then, having gone to that forest with that forest-guardian, Bhoja [sought] that deer-faced girl.

Having taken her, he went to his own home; then, when Ogha asked that Bāṣkali about the cause for her attaining the state of a human-eater and a curved-beaked crane, she related it. Ogha then made offerings to the Brahmins. Thereafter, in the dialogue between Sarasvatī and King Bhīma, there was a description of the events concerning her past life, including her account of her own origin; and in the course of that conversation with the lotus-faced king, she went into another forest accompanied by Udākhala and Karva.

Therein is the account of the consumption of the *vīryabindu* (virile seed) by that [king]; then, by Mṛgāvatī, the consumption of the *udālaka-vīryabindu*; then, Mṛgāvatī’s narration to Bhoja of her own birth from Udālaka through Mṛgānanā; the description of the greatness of many holy places (*tīrtha*) such as Dvāravatī and Karuṣaṣṭha; and, regarding Svarṇarekhā, the account of Mṛgānanā’s previous birth, including how she attained a divine face by requesting it from Magamukha, followed by the story of her marriage to King Bhoja—[all] concerning Svarṇarekhā.

Description of the majesty of the *rekhā* in the dialogue between Sarasvatī and Bhārgava; in the dispute between Brahmā and Sadravi, the description of the destruction of Rudra’s splendor by Viṣṇu at the word of Brahmā; in the account of the Daśayajña sacrifice described by Viṣṇu, the description of the destruction of that Daśayajña; the description of the birth and marriage of Pārvatī; then, on one occasion, when Śaṅkara had vanished, Viṣṇu and the other gods, together with Pārvatī mounted upon a lion, went forth to search for Śiva; then, at Prabhāsa—

The journey of those [sages] to see Śaṅkara; by the command of Viṣṇu and others, the establishment of Śaṅkara as Bhava in his own form in the sacred field (kṣetra) of Sthāneśvara; and the description of the origin and greatness of Bhava.

A description of the regions of the *Vasāṣatha* field by the sage Sārasvata; a description of the sequence of the pilgrimage to the *Vasāṣatha* field; a description of the greatness of days such as *Gajacchāyā* for the performance of *Śrāddha*; a description of the fruits of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at Bhīmiśvara, Skāndra, Maheśvara, Varāyaṇya, and other holy sites; a statement on the fruit of remembering sacred fords (*tīrtha*); a description of the rules for pilgrimage; and therein, a statement on the fruit of the worship of Hari and Hara.

The description of giving seats, gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and the soliciting of deities and Brahmins; the description of the smoke-path (*dhūmamārga*) and the nature of the *moghī* [spell]; the description of the greatness of the *śrāddha* offerings and other rites. ... (In Vāmanapura, Vasistha, distressed by the loss of his son, performed austerities on the banks of the Svarṇarekhā and established a shrine there. Then follows the description of the greatness of Somanātha installed by Vāmana. Subsequently, Bali, having driven away the gods, sought refuge in Viṣṇu. Thereupon, for the sake of the gods' purpose, Viṣṇu assumed the form of Vāmana.)

In the assembly of sixty, after making the *baṅginī* gesture by lifting the earth with three steps, he propitiated Somanātha and established the quarters. Then follows the description of the origin of Someśvara. Vāmana went to the Raivataka forest to take the gift from Dāmodara; having worshipped Carasi there and performed the rites of bathing, giving, and so forth, he subsequently went to the holy site of Vasnāpatha to see Dāmodara. Having kept a vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) there, he departed for Siddhi. [This concludes] the section on the vigil at Dāmodara.

Then follows the description of the greatness [of Śiva], the journey of Nārada into the dense forest for the sake of pilgrimage, and his encounter on the way with various ascetics and others; the narration of the dialogue between Śiva and Vāmana; therein, the description of the greatness of Śivarātri as told by Brahmā to Vāmana; the exposition of the ritual procedure for the Śivarātri vow; and [the account of] Nārada seeing the Lord and, knowing that the Lord would also manifest in the form of the Vāmana incarnation to humble Bali, [speaking] before the presence of Brahmā.

Regarding the departure: there, Nārada, having agitated the mind of Bali by declaring that the splendor (*lakṣmī*) of Indra was even greater than his own, caused him to remember the deception practiced by the gods at the time of the churning of the ocean; then, having approached his own brother [Virocana], Nārada spoke to Śakra in exactly the same way. Thus, having mutually incited them through such disputes and the like, Nārada instructed Bali in the principles of statecraft (*rājanīti*), dharma, and legal procedure (*vyavahāra*).

The granting of boons by Hara and Hara (Śiva and Viṣṇu) to Mount Kūrmada; the daily arrival of Viṣṇu to see the Lord stationed in the temple of Viṣṇumandira on Mount Kūrmada, located to the south of Śabataka-parvata; the installation of Hari and Hara by the cook in that very Mount Kūrmada; the granting of boons to Mount Kūrmada by Hara and Hara; then, during the fifth Manvantara named Raivata, the birth of Ṛtuparṇa from Ṛtavāk and Mṛḍadhī; and the dialogue between Ṛtavāk and Garbha regarding his own son born of Revatī.

The removal of the fault of speech by Kaṅka through the practice of asceticism; the casting down of Revatī’s husband from his position by means of a false vision; thereafter, the digging of the Kumuda lake; the giving of Revatī to King Durdama by means of a deceptive statement; the birth of a son known as Revata due to the excavation of the Revatī-pool; a description of the greatness of the Śivāruka tree worshipped by Vaiṣṇavas; and Nārada’s narration to Bali of the rules for Vaiṣṇava vows, vigils, and so forth, as well as the [consequences] of performing such Vaiṣṇava vows and vigils without [proper conduct].

Having performed the preliminary rites (*rādika*) with great reverence for the purpose of the sacrifice’s commencement, he summoned the Brahmins by the command of Śukra; this section describes the undertaking of the sacrifice, the description of the power of the *balisacrifice*, the explanation of the methods such as the *śrāṇā* offering, the description of the eightfold production of the primary elements (*prakṛti*), the exposition of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, and the description of the method of meditating upon Bhava. Then, while Vāmana remained in the presence of Bhava, Nārada arrived before him, and [the following is] by Nārada [spoken] to Vāmana...

The narration of the account of the subjugation of Bali; Vāmana’s rebuke of Nārada for his futile boasting and arrogant nature; Nārada’s description of Bali’s endurance until the end of the kalpa; Nārada’s recounting to Vāmana of the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa and others; and then, at the word of Nārada, Vāmana, having approached the region of Bali to restrain him, requested three paces of land—even though it was already occupied by a boar—and thereafter, through his own expansion, pervaded the entire cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

The sub-section concerning the greatness of the Vakhāpatha-kṣetra, being the second [section] in the Śrabhā-khaṇḍa, which includes: the subjugation of Bala; the dialogue between Indra and Bali; Viṣṇu’s dwelling within the body of Bali following his subjugation; and the description of the fruits of hearing the majesty of the Vakhāpatha-kṣetra.
The chapters are the paths.
Now, in the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, the third section is the Abuda-khaṇḍa.

The commencement of the description of the greatness of Arbuda; therein, first, the departure of Vasiṣṭha to Arbuda; having performed austerities there, his sacrificial cow, having gone to the forest to graze on grass and other fodder, fell into a chasm; because the cow did not return in the evening, Vasiṣṭha became anxious; then Vasiṣṭha, approaching the vicinity of the chasm and hearing the lowing of his own cow, meditated upon the Sarasvatī for her emergence; by that meditation...

Sarasvatī filled the pit with her own water and caused the cow to emerge; taking that cow, she went to Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage. Then, having gone to the Himavat mountain to fill that pit, Sarasvatī related the extent of the pit to Himavat and described the origin of the auspicious river flowing from the Himavat. Following this, the account begins concerning the opening of a fissure near Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage, and [the story] of Uttaṅka, a disciple of Gautama, who was to give his preceptor’s fee.

At the request of his brother, Ruru went to the house of Saudāsa to bring back the earrings of Saudāsa’s wife, Madyantī; there, he made a vow to offer himself to Saudāsa—who had arrived with a tiger-like face to devour him—in exchange for the two earrings. Subsequently, he received the earrings from the queen and was liberated from Saudāsa’s curse. Then, while the disciple of Gautama was returning with the earrings, he placed them on the way, whereupon Takṣaka [seized one].

The abduction [of Soma], then Takṣaka’s audacity and his journey to Pātāla for the purpose of bringing him back; at that very time, the creation of a chasm there, and the description of the life of Uttaṅka, the disciple of Gītamara; by the command of Vasiṣṭha and the word of Himavat, the filling of the sky with clouds brought about by the wind-god and the serpent-king.

The description of the greatness of Abudāva: there, on the mountain named Divadhena, Vasiṣṭha performed penance while residing at Kiivāvāsā; Vasiṣṭha offered a hymn of praise to Śiva; then, by the grace of Śiva, Vasiṣṭha established a Liṅga named Acaledavara; Śiva made his residence at Mandākinī; and the description of the greatness of Acaledavara. ...
