In the *Auṇḍācara*, within the description of the *Nāgatīrtha* at Mācchatmya, in the dialogue between Yayāti and his son, there is a description of the *Nāgatīrtha* on the Gautamī. Therein, because her heart was agitated by a desire for a son, she conceived through a mere thought (*kevalajñāna*) when she had set out to know [the truth]. Then, as she was desiring to embrace her deceased husband, she heard a voice from the sky, whereby her intent to die was turned back. This is followed by a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the *Nāgatīrtha*.

The description of the greatness of Vañcakhīṣṭha-āśrama; the description of the power of Acaṭeda-vara; the description of the greatness of Adrakarṇa-davariṇetra-māda; ... in the description of the greatness of Gar-kadāra, Vasiṣṭha’s narration to Ajāpāla regarding his previous births—that because he had attained the status of a Śūdra, he would obtain the position of kingship in this life through the worship of Kedāra-deva at Kedāra; the description of the greatness of Kedāra-deva. ...

A description of the duration and other characteristics of the various ages; a discernment of the qualities and defects of the four yugas; a description of how all goals are attained through the power of the [Kali] age. A description of the greatness of Keṭīśvara; the attainment of a beautiful form by the Apsarā named Capūrṇā through bathing at Rūpatīrtha; a description of the majesty of Rūpatīrtha. In the description of the greatness of Ṛṣikiśa, the royal sage Ambarīṣa performed penance and established an image of Hari; a description of the greatness of Dabhīkeḍa by the Siddha named Viśvāvasu.

The installation of a *liṅga* through the grace of Śiva after propitiating him; a description of the majesty of Siddheśvarī. Seeing the Daityas defeated by the gods, the preceptor of the Daityas, Śukrācārya, reflected on how to achieve victory for the Daityas; having propitiated the God and obtained a boon, he brought about the victory of the Daityas and installed a *liṅga* there named Śukreśvara; a description of the greatness of the Śukreśvara *liṅga*. [Section] *viṣayāḥ*: By a certain woman named Maṇikikā, through the means of knowledge, her—

The narration of the *Khaṇḍakhya* (the section on the name) by one named Maṇikarṇika, who was devoted to attaining his true nature; a description of the greatness of Lord Maṇikarṇika. By a certain Brahmin named Guṇa, who had become lame, Śiva was propitiated and a holy site (*tīrtha*) was established; a description of the greatness of Pagutīrtha. Having dispelled his lameness, [the story of] Citrāṅgada, who had committed extreme sins, entering his own name [into the holy water].

The abduction of Citrāṅgada by Vṛṣāṇa; thereafter, the casting of the sinner Citrāṅgada into hell by the messengers of Yama; the attainment of bliss by the living beings there through the casting of Citrāṅgada into hell; then, having seen this wonder and observed it with his eye of knowledge, Yama reflected in his mind that because Citrāṅgada had performed a bath in his sacred ford (tīrtha), he would attain prosperity right there and thus was not a partaker of the suffering of the hellish realm, and consequently, his liberation from that hell. Then, for him...

The departure of Vitrāṅgada to heaven in a celestial chariot surrounded by hosts of Apsarases; a description of the greatness of Yamatīrtha; a description of the greatness of Bārāhatīrtha; Dakṣa’s bestowal of the Yakṣma disease upon the Moon as punishment for his partiality toward his own daughters, followed by the Moon’s performance of penance and the subsequent cure of his Yakṣma disease through that austerity; and the installation of a Liṅga by the Moon under the name Candrabhāsa.

The description of the greatness of the Candra-prabhāsa Tīrtha. The description of the greatness of the Piṇḍodaka Tīrtha. After the Dānava named Karālī had performed propitiation of the Goddess, he attained heaven by the grace of the Goddess; having placed Mount Pāriyātra upon his body, the Goddess made her own abode on its peak. By the gods, Śrīmātā was established as the Goddess; the description of the greatness of Śrīmātā. Now, the greatness of the Śūti Tīrtha: therein, [the merit of] those who were cast into the midst of the river by a washerman...

Because the sages attained the state of being horned (*śṛṅgitva*) by bathing at that sacred ford (*tīrtha*), it was given the name Śuḍatīrtha; this is the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Śuḍatīrtha. After the goddess had slain the demon Niśumbha, she established her residence there, and thus she was installed by the gods under the name Kātyāyanī; this is the description of the majesty of Kātyāyanī. (Skanda Purāṇa, Part 69).
The sixth chapter on the naming ceremony: Then, for the sake of the child's welfare, the naming ceremony was performed by Śiva; thus, his name was Mahāvināyaka, and she became known as Mahāvināyakī.
Not a bird; the narration of the nearness, the description of the greatness of Mahāvināyaka... [the description of the greatness of Kanakhala-tīrtha] [13, ra].

Description of the majesty of Cakratīrtha. ... Description of the greatness of Pārtheda-vara. Chapter 6: Description of the majesty of Manuṣyatīrtha. ... [In which] Brahmā and Viṣṇu, desiring to test each other’s greatness, were fighting with mutual hostility; in their midst, the creation of a single toothless [being]; the description of the birth of Ṭiga-danta; thereafter, by means of a divine voice, causing them both to cease from their battle; and [the account of] Suprabha-pati, who was intent on [eating] flesh, [seeing] her nursing at his breast...

Then, with an arrow, [Kārttikeya] struck Kharapra; subsequently, the king was told by Mṛgī, "You shall become Rudravyātra," and thus the bestowal of the curse occurred. For that very reason, the king’s [eightfold] form, extending as far as the tip of the linga, was manifested by Śiva.

The giving of false testimony by a Brahmin out of fear, the punishment of the ungrateful Ketaka, then the offering of a mind to Viṣṇu, the departure of Vyāsa, the description of the majesty of Kṛṣṇatīrtha; having performed these, returning to his own place, he went to the cow, gave milk to the calf, and [told] the news concerning the calf that had gone to the forest.

Having restrained her own companions by feigning an insistence on not eating, and having been prevented from departing even though she was being urged by them, the Goddess—pleased by the propitiation performed by her while she was tormented by the demon Mahiṣāsura—carried out the slaying of Mahiṣāsura. Therein is also the description of the greatness of the Kañjavīkāśrama.

Having disregarded the tiger, he returned; seeing this, the cow was filled with wonder and related the account of his rescue. [The text continues: "O fierce one, this is our well-known tradition; this is the sacred ford of the monkey, which is to be honored. Bha... [fragmentary].

A description of the greatness of Aśnitīrtha; a description of the greatness of Śivarkṣi following the arrival [of the deity], including how Kāma was reduced to ashes by the Fire of Desire and Rati was made to weep; having heard of that sorrow caused by the destruction of Rati’s husband, Indrasena departed for a foreign land to destroy Indra and seize his wealth; thereafter, the account of how Indra was restored to life after being rendered bodiless by Kāma through a messenger sent by Indrasena; and the establishment of a Linga by Kāma together with Rati, while it was said that Kāmasena was dead.

Because he spoke to her for the sake of that fruit, Indrasena was freed from his bodily affliction; there follows the description of the greatness of the Sīhavyādhiśvara [liṅga], and the performance of the *mānasa* (mental) pilgrimage to the holy sites located at Prabhāsa, such as Somatīrtha and others; and Indrasena’s journey to those places.

Chapter 9: The description of the origin of Mārkaṇḍeya’s hermitage, preceded by the illustrative narrative of his birth and so forth, following the performance of bathing at the Raktānubandha Tīrtha due to the absence of the removal of sin; Chapter 10: The description of the greatness of Udālakedāra; Chapter 11: The description of the greatness of Māheśvara.

Nivī-Udvasena took the child born of the deception and performed the rites for a son; because of the absence of a son, Śikha and Rohiṇī, thinking "this is a boy," performed those rites along with a certain intoxicated elephant. Then Rukmiṇī performed the birth-ceremonies for the infant brought from Bhogavatī by Śrī Kṛṣṇa. [Thus ends the third sub-section of the Durvāsas-pramāru-khaṇḍa.]
Thinking, "Has Rukmiṇī taken hold of water without [using] her bowstring? and unable to endure that, he [spoke] to her, Rukmiṇī.

The gift of the body. Then, having descended from the chariot with Duvasas, he established himself upon the ground; thereafter, together with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [he described] the objects of Bhavyā. Now begins the fourth section on the Greatness of Dvārakā within the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa.

Oṃ! The description of the greatness of Vyāsatīrtha. When the Kali Yuga arrived, Sūta, being questioned by Nārada and others as to where Viṣṇu’s place of residence would be, described the greatness of the Gautamāśrama-tīrtha. [He then] described the manner of his stay there; having performed his various incarnations and other deeds, he described the greatness of the Nakasaṃtaraṇa-tīrtha, preceded by the story of King Indumati, who offered praise to the infinite Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

When he had returned to his own place, seeing that the state of the world was mostly one of corruption, he wondered, "Where can there be a stable condition for those like us? Thus began the description of the greatness of Parāśara Muni. Having reflected, he spoke these words to the sages; and having heard those words of the sage Udālaka, [the king], oppressed by the pangs of hunger...
The description of the power of Koṭitīrtha; the departure of the sages, who had applied the means for attaining liberation for themselves, to the presence of Brahmā; [and] Udārka and the other sages—

The description of the greatness of the Candrodbheda-tīrtha; ... the offering of praise by Brahmā; then the sages, having entered [the cave], explain the reason for their arrival; at that time, Brahmā describes the majesty of the peak of Īśāna; ... [Brahmā] gives the reply, "I do not know the abode of Viṣṇu"; hearing Brahmā’s answer, the description of the greatness of the Jādyapada [birth] resulting from the act of abandoning one's life;
then, as the sages set out, Brahmā goes with the sages into the presence of Prahlāda; by Prahlāda, all...
Description of the majesty of Tripuṣkara. ... The performance of hospitality for the Brāhmaṇas by Prahlāda; and the narration of the reason for their arrival by the sages through the mouth of Brahmā.
Description of the greatness of Rādhāhrada. ... How the sages, having gone to Rādhāhrada in the Kali age, made a request concerning the presence of the Blessed One; how [they did so].

The description of the greatness of the Lord of the House (*Gṛheśvara-māhātmya*); the description by Prahlāda of the commencement of the *Kali-yuga* in order to give a reply to the sages; therein, the description of the greatness of the inseparable pair, Uddhava and Kṛṣṇa; and upon the conclusion of that dialogue, the account of Duvasu’s journey toward the bank of the Gomatī as he set out, followed by the description of the greatness of the Umā-Maheśvara Tīrtha.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇa and Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) went there for the sake of seeing Duvasu; thereafter, [the account] of Duvasu [meeting] Kṛṣṇa.

The description of the great majesty and power of Satī; then, having related his welfare out of fear to Durvāsas, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s making him enter Dvārakā; Durvāsas’s arrival at his own hermitage and his narration of his own power; the description of the greatness of the Gandhamādana mountain; and likewise, despite Kṛṣṇa’s persistent insistence, [Durvāsas] employing Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī to pull the chariot.
Description of the majesty of Kaṭeśvara and Gaṅgeśvara... [and] the description of the commencement of Dvauṣasa’s journey to Dvārakā; meanwhile, seeing Rukmiṇī thirsty on the way...

Description of the hearing of the fruits of the majesty of the Abudakaṇḍa... [Śrī Kṛṣṇa], having pierced the earth with his foot, brought [the serpent] from Bhogavatī who was oppressed by the underworld—Skanda Purāṇa, (topics; chapter: topics following in sequence).

The consolation of Durvāsas by Rukmiṇī; then, the description of leading Durvāsas to his own home and offering him the water used for washing his feet (*pādodaka*) along with food; the description of the rules for bathing; the description of the *śrāddha* ceremony to be performed, preceded by the worship of Viṣṇu and the gods; the fulfillment of one's own body’s purpose through the pilgrimage to Prabhāsa; the description of the greatness of the confluence with the Gomatī; and the description of the greatness of the Lord’s own form situated on the bank of the Gomatī.

[The section] on the curse bestowed upon Rukmiṇī by Duḥsāda, the making of many images [of Kṛṣṇa], the arrival of Nārada at the house of Rukmī, and the description of the greatness of the Rukmiṇī-hrada;—Nārada, having instructed Rukmiṇī in many ways, [she, together with Rukmiṇī, went to] the abode of Rukmiṇī.

In the description of the greatness of the Chakratīrtha, it is told how King Dgeṇa, having performed sacrifices and other rites, went daily to the Bhāgīrathītīrtha there to bestow gifts upon the officiating priests; there, in the Rukmiṇīvana situated on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, the account of his easily performing the gift of eleven thousand cows along with their ornaments is described. Then, one day, having heard the account of the woman named Ravimaṇi who was being measured by one called Jemini, he thought to himself, "How can my own word become false?"

Regarding those who perform the gift of a cow (*godāna*): after she had emerged from the house of her father-in-law and gone to the cow-pen of the King of Beasts (*Sṛgarāja*), Durvāsas pronounced a curse upon Bhāgīrathī, the trees in Rukmiṇī’s grove, and other trees. Subsequently, Nṛga gave that very cow to another Brāhmaṇa. As he was departing taking that cow, Rukmiṇī made a firm resolve to die; and as Rukmiṇī was on the verge of death with a noose around her neck, the Brāhmaṇa [intervened] in the midst of the road.

Jaimini, having learned that the cow given by Devadatta—which had been his own and had escaped from his residence—was there, mounted Garuḍa and arrived at that place along with Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Then Durvāsas, seeing this, engaged in a dispute with Jaimini and the Brāhmaṇa; as the two were thus contending with one another, Jaimini was defeated by Nārada.

Having thus personally felt remorse, thinking "What have I done?", he approached Rukmiṇī. Then, he described the departure of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī to the palace of Raivataka; thereafter, he related how they both bestowed a curse upon the King, saying "Become a lizard," and how he pacified them by seeking forgiveness for that curse, thereby liberating Rukmiṇī from her sorrow. (....)

The lifting of King Nṛga, who had become a crane, by Kṛṣṇa with his own hand; the mutual granting of boons between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Dvīpāsa; the granting of a boon to King Nṛga for the benefit of the people on the banks of the Gomatī by those known as the sixteen [Vṛṣṇis]; King Nṛga’s departure to heaven by means of a celestial chariot through the grace of the Lord’s smile; the measurement of the earth; and therein, a description of the majesty of the Gomatī river’s banks—a brief summary of the Dvārakāmāhātmya.

Description of the greatness of the Nṛga-tīrtha, also known by the name Kṛkalāsa. ... Description of its greatness; therein, within the dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Indra, an incidental description of the greatness of Kalikāṭa. Therein, following the bathing, giving of gifts, and other rites at Cakratīrtha and various other holy sites, a description of the greatness of Viṣṇupada-tīrtha, which removes the afflictions of Kali, exhaustion, madness, barbarians, and other evils. Description of the greatness of Gobhracāra-tīrtha: after the slaying of Kaṃsa, Gopī [approaches] Śrī Kṛṣṇa in order for him to speak of his own welfare.

He shall relate: Bṛhaspati’s consolation of the gods, including Indra; the dispatching of Goṅkuṭa for the sake of obtaining knowledge regarding the procedure for the journey to Dvārakā; the reception of Uddhava upon his arrival, including the offering of hospitality such as a seat and other honors by Nanda and the others; and the inquiry by the Gopīs regarding the reason for Uddhava’s coming.

In this forest of suffering, terrible with darkness and agitated by the heat of the waters, they praise that Self-knowledge which regards the eight types of gems and gold as equal. Here, it should be understood that "regarding the eight types of gems and gold as equal" is a qualification of knowledge. Because the reality of the Self is of the nature of existence (*sat*), it is non-dual; and because the eight types of gems and gold are, in ultimate reality, of the singular nature of consciousness (*cit*), the eight types of gems and gold are equal to consciousness through their non-distinction from it. Thus, the meaning is: some praise that Self-knowledge in which the eight types of gems and gold are equal.

Regarding this, in another version: "Intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), and the elements (*bhūtāni*), as well as the eleven organs (*indriyāṇi*)—these thirteen, along with the three qualities (*guṇas*), are the thirteen great planets (*mahāgrahas*). Furthermore, the knowable (*vāddhanya*), the thinkable (*mantavya*), the principle of egoity (*ahaṃtā*), and sound (*śabda*) itself; likewise, touch (*sparśa*), taste (*rasa*), form (*rūpa*), smell (*gandha*), speech (*vacana*), grasping (*ādāna*), movement (*visarga*), evacuation (*utsarga*), and pleasure (*ānanda*)—these are the thirteen great planets."

This must be understood as follows: by including the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), the elements (*bhūta*), the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), and the organs of action (*karmendriya*), there are thirteen. It should be understood that the elements are intended here as a single unit through their commonality. Regarding the objects, there is no dispute that the description of the qualities of the elements is strictly according to the respective organs of knowledge. Now begins the commentary on the greatness of the month of Kārttika.

In this world, the venerable Śrī Vyāsa established upon the earth this nectar-like ocean, which elucidates the means for achieving all human goals and proclaims the greatness of the month of Kārttika. At the commencement of that work, in order to pacify all obstacles, he performs a salutation to his chosen deity, characterized by the words "Nārāyaṇam. Here, by the term "Nārāyaṇa," there is the inclusion of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī), the Lord who reclines upon the waters, and Kṛṣṇa; for it is said: "The word 'nāra' refers to the multitude of individual souls (jīvas), and 'ayana' is their place of origin."

Sutta Nipāta: 1097–1104. The Chapter on the Great Chapter (Mahāvagga). The Discourse on the Great Chapter (Mahā-Vagga Sutta). 1097. The Discourse on the Great Chapter. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Great Chapter. Listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”—“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “What, bhikkhus, is the Great Chapter? It is: ‘The world is led by the mind, drawn along by the mind, and has become subject to the mind. This, bhikkhus, is called the Great Chapter. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “The world is led by the mind, drawn along by the mind, and has become subject to the mind. When the mind is pure, beings are purified; when the mind is defiled, they are defiled. Mind precedes all phenomena; mind is their chief, they are all mind-wrought. If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness follows one even as a shadow that never departs. If one speaks or acts with an impure mind, suffering follows one even as a wheel follows the hoof of the ox. Therefore, one should guard the mind thoroughly; well-restrained and well-guarded, it brings happiness. One should abandon evil thoughts and cultivate wholesome ones; having removed all unwholesome states, one should dwell in peace. Just as a skilled turner, turning his wheel, does not let it stop until it has come to rest, so too should a wise person, mindful and alert, restrain the mind from wandering among sense objects. Just as a bee, having gathered nectar from flowers, flies away without harming their color or scent, so too should a sage wander through the village, taking only the essence, like a bee from flowers. Not by mere silence does one become a recluse, nor by living alone in the forest; one who is full of lust and hatred is not a recluse, though he may wear the saffron robes. But one who has laid down the rod toward all beings, whether weak or strong, who is restrained in body, speech, and mind—he is indeed a recluse. One who has abandoned sensual pleasures and left behind the household life, dwelling in solitude, meditating day and night, with a mind well-concentrated and free from the five hindrances, he is called a bhikkhu. One who has cut off the stream, crossed over the flood, freed from all bonds, without acquisitions, having destroyed craving and attained the end of suffering, he is called a bhikkhu. One who has seen the Dhamma here and now, who has reached the final goal, the supreme security from bondage, having laid down the burden and lived the holy life, he is called a bhikkhu. One who has no attachment anywhere in the world, whether in the seen, heard, or sensed, who is free from clinging and has transcended existence, he is called a bhikkhu. One who has no longing for the past or the future, and whose mind finds no delight in the present, who is detached from both ends and the middle, he is called a bhikkhu. BU 33.1–10: The Story of Śuka and the Crane 1. Once upon a time, there lived a king named Brahmadatta in the city of Vārāṇasī. He was a man of great power and possessed of all virtues. His son was a prince named Śuka, who was wise, virtuous, and beloved by his father. 2. One day, as the prince was wandering about the city, he saw a crane standing on the bank of the river. The crane was very beautiful, with a long neck and a large beak, and it seemed to be enjoying itself. 3. Seeing the crane, the prince thought to himself, "How wonderful is this bird! It stands so gracefully here, free from fear. Having reflected thus, he approached the crane and asked him, "O crane, why do you stand here alone, appearing so contented? 4. The crane replied, "O Prince, I am a crane living in this forest. I have no fear of anyone, for I am satisfied with whatever food comes my way. I live here happily, free from anxiety. 5. The prince said, "But, O crane, how can you be happy when you have no home, no family, and no wealth? You must surely suffer from many hardships. 6. The crane answered, "O Prince, happiness does not depend on external things such as home or wealth. True happiness arises from contentment and the absence of desire. I have no attachment to anything, and therefore I am always happy. 7. Hearing these words, the prince was greatly moved. He realized that worldly pleasures are fleeting and that true peace comes from detachment. He then spoke to the crane, "O crane, you have taught me a great lesson. I shall now seek the path of liberation. 8. With these words, the prince returned to his father and told him everything that had happened. The king was pleased with his son's wisdom and gave him permission to pursue his spiritual quest. 9. The prince then went to the forest and became a disciple of a great sage. Under his guidance, he practiced meditation and studied the scriptures. In time, he attained deep insight into the nature of reality. 10. Having realized the truth, the prince lived in peace and joy. He showed compassion to all beings and taught others the path of virtue. Thus, through the instruction of the crane, he found the ultimate happiness that transcends all worldly desires.
